course.title: From Polynomials to Étale Triple Covers
course.subtitle: A proof-based route to the announced three-dimensional Jacobian counterexample
course.description: A 66-week spiral course that begins with proof fundamentals and repeatedly revisits one factorization until the learner can reconstruct its algebraic, local, global, projective, and representation-theoretic meaning.

masteryDimensions.label: Proof reasoning
masteryDimensions.description: Logical structure, theorem use, and justified claims.

masteryDimensions.label: Procedural fluency
masteryDimensions.description: Reliable execution of calculations and standard methods.

masteryDimensions.label: Transfer
masteryDimensions.description: Choosing and adapting ideas in unfamiliar situations.

misconceptions.label: Typed map data omitted
misconceptions.description: Treats a formula as a complete map without checking its domain, codomain, or the types of a composition.

misconceptions.label: One-sided inverse treated as two-sided
misconceptions.description: Uses only one composition identity to claim that two maps are mutual inverses.

misconceptions.label: Local conclusion promoted to global
misconceptions.description: Uses a local inverse, étale, or differential statement as if it established global injectivity or a global inverse.

misconceptions.label: Theorem hypothesis not checked
misconceptions.description: Invokes a theorem without verifying one or more hypotheses in the mathematical case under study.

misconceptions.label: Generic case substituted for a boundary case
misconceptions.description: Uses an argument valid on a generic or reduced locus at a repeated-root, singular, or degenerate point without further justification.

misconceptions.label: Set-theoretic and scheme-theoretic fibers confused
misconceptions.description: Identifies the visible points of a fiber with its complete scheme structure or multiplicity data.

misconceptions.label: Incidence and normalized fibers confused
misconceptions.description: Transfers cardinality or multiplicity claims between the ordinary incidence construction and its normalized simple-root model.

misconceptions.label: Normalization equations reversed
misconceptions.description: Interchanges the resultant normalization with the selected-coefficient normalization in the target construction.

misconceptions.label: Cancellation or division not justified
misconceptions.description: Cancels a factor or divides by an expression without proving that the operation is valid on the stated locus.

misconceptions.label: Equivariance confused with invariance
misconceptions.description: Treats a map that commutes with a group action as though its values were fixed by that action.

misconceptions.label: Source and target data conflated
misconceptions.description: Identifies coordinates, tangent directions, or base-change data that live on different sides of a map.

misconceptions.label: Dimension count used as a smoothness proof
misconceptions.description: Infers smoothness or étaleness from matching dimensions without proving the required differential or local-ring statement.

concepts.title: Functions and maps
concepts.summary: A function includes a domain, codomain, and assignment; a formula alone does not specify all three.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A function $f:X\to Y$ assigns each $x\in X$ exactly one value $f(x)\in Y$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$, $f(z)=z^2$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The expression $1/x$ without a stated domain is not yet a complete function.

concepts.title: Mathematical proof
concepts.summary: A proof makes assumptions, conclusions, and every inferential dependency explicit.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A proof is a finite argument that derives a stated conclusion from stated assumptions using accepted definitions and results.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Let $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to X$. If $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$ and $f\circ g=\operatorname{id}_Y$, then $f$ and $g$ are mutual inverses.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Testing an identity at many numerical points is evidence, not a proof of a polynomial identity.

concepts.title: Polynomial and binary form
concepts.summary: Polynomial arithmetic is the elementary surface of the entire construction.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A binary form of degree $d$ is a homogeneous polynomial in two variables of total degree $d$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $cT^2+dTS+eS^2$ is a binary quadratic.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: $T^2+S$ is not homogeneous and hence is not a binary quadratic form.

concepts.title: Complex roots and multiplicity
concepts.summary: A cubic’s root multiplicities control both its discriminant and the fibers of the marked-root map.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The multiplicity of $\zeta$ as a root of $p$ is the largest $m$ for which $(t-\zeta)^m$ divides $p(t)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $(t-1)^2(t+2)$ has a double root at $1$ and a simple root at $-2$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: $p(\zeta)=0$ alone does not say that $\zeta$ is repeated.

concepts.title: Repeated-root criterion
concepts.summary: A root is repeated exactly when the polynomial and its derivative vanish there.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $\zeta$ is a repeated root of $p$ if and only if $p(\zeta)=p'(\zeta)=0$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $p(t)=(t-1)^2$, both $p(1)$ and $p'(1)$ vanish.

concepts.title: Injectivity and bijectivity
concepts.summary: Injectivity is a global statement about the equality of images.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $f:X\to Y$ is injective when $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ implies $x_1=x_2$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $x\mapsto x+1$ on $\mathbb R$ is injective.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: $z\mapsto z^3$ on $\mathbb C^\times$ is not globally injective.

concepts.title: Local versus global invertibility
concepts.summary: An invertible derivative yields a local inverse; it does not prove a globally one-to-one polynomial map.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Local injectivity holds on a neighborhood of each point; global injectivity compares every pair of points in the full domain.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $w\mapsto w^3$ on $\mathbb C^\times$ has nonzero derivative everywhere but has three points in a generic fiber.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A nonzero Jacobian determinant is not, by itself, a proof of a polynomial inverse.

concepts.title: Vector spaces and dimension
concepts.summary: Binary forms of each degree form finite-dimensional complex vector spaces.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A vector space is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector-space axioms.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\operatorname{Sym}^d(\mathbb C^2)$ has dimension $d+1$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The set of degree-exactly-two polynomials is not closed under addition.

concepts.title: Symmetric powers
concepts.summary: Symmetric powers provide the natural representation spaces of binary forms.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $\operatorname{Sym}^d(V)$ is the quotient of $V^{\otimes d}$ identifying permutations of tensor factors.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\operatorname{Sym}^3(\mathbb C^2)$ is four-dimensional and models binary cubics.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The full tensor cube has dimension eight, not four.

concepts.title: Jacobian and total derivative
concepts.summary: The Jacobian matrix represents the derivative in coordinates.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$, $DF_x$ is the linear map best approximating $F$ near $x$; its coordinate matrix is the Jacobian.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $F(x,y)=(x+y^2,y)$, $DF=\begin{pmatrix}1&2y\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A symbolic determinant calculation without a theorem statement does not establish global behavior.

concepts.title: Inverse function theorem
concepts.summary: An invertible derivative gives a unique local inverse near the point.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, and let $x\in U$. If $DF_x$ is invertible, then there are open neighborhoods $V\subseteq U$ of $x$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $F(x)$ such that $F|_V:V\to W$ is a $C^1$ bijection with a $C^1$ inverse.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Viewed as a real $C^1$ map under $\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$, $z\mapsto z^3$ has a local $C^1$ inverse near every nonzero $z$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The theorem does not produce one inverse on all of $\mathbb C^\times$.

concepts.title: Group actions and symmetries
concepts.summary: Actions reveal the scaling direction multiplication forgets.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A group action of $G$ on $X$ assigns compatible transformations $g\cdot x$ for $g\in G$ and $x\in X$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $(L,Q)\mapsto(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$ preserves $LQ$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: An arbitrary coefficient change that does not respect composition is not a group action.

concepts.title: Ideals and quotient rings
concepts.summary: Equality on the variety is equality modulo its defining ideal.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $A/I$ identifies two elements of $A$ when their difference belongs to the ideal $I$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Polynomial inverse formulas for $X$ can be checked in $\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,e]/(f_1,f_2)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Ambient polynomial equality is stronger than equality in the quotient ring.

concepts.title: Localization
concepts.summary: Localization studies the open set where a chosen function is invertible.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $A_f$ is obtained from $A$ by adjoining an inverse for $f$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $X_a$ is studied by inverting $a$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: An isomorphism after inverting $a$ does not describe the missing divisor $a=0$.

concepts.title: Projective roots
concepts.summary: Homogeneous coordinates keep the root at infinity visible.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A nonzero binary form determines a divisor of roots on $\mathbb P^1$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: When $a=0$, the linear form $aT+bS$ has its root at $[1:0]$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The affine expression $-b/a$ cannot describe the case $a=0$.

concepts.title: Resultant
concepts.summary: The resultant detects a shared projective root and restores the relative scaling direction lost by multiplication.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ for $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)\ne0$ exactly when $L$ and $Q$ are coprime as binary forms.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The product $LQ$ alone cannot distinguish $(L,Q)$ from $(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$.

concepts.title: Discriminant
concepts.summary: The discriminant vanishes exactly when a polynomial has a repeated root.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $\operatorname{Disc}(C)$ is, up to normalization, $\operatorname{Res}(C,C')$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A cubic with three distinct roots has nonzero discriminant.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A nonzero discriminant does not select one distinguished root.

concepts.title: Affine varieties
concepts.summary: Affine geometry translates polynomial equations into geometric objects.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: An affine algebraic set is the common zero locus of a family of polynomials.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $X=\{\rho=1,\ ad+bc=1\}\subset\mathbb A^5$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A Euclidean neighborhood is generally not Zariski open.

concepts.title: Coordinate rings
concepts.summary: Regular functions on an affine variety form its coordinate ring.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $\mathcal O(V(I))=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I(V(I))$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $X\cong\mathbb A^3$ follows from an explicit isomorphism of coordinate rings.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A rational expression with a denominator is not automatically a global regular function.

concepts.title: Tangent spaces and differentials
concepts.summary: The Zariski tangent space consists of first-order directions that annihilate every function in the vanishing ideal.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $T_pX=\{v\in k^n:df_p(v)=0\text{ for every }f\in I(X)\}\cong\operatorname{Hom}_k(\mathfrak m_p/\mathfrak m_p^2,k)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $X=V(y-x^2)$ at $(1,1)$, the tangent equation is $v-2u=0$, so $T_{(1,1)}X=k(1,2)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Differentiating the nonradical presentation $x^2=0$ gives the wrong kernel for the reduced set $V(x)$; use generators of $I(V(x^2))=(x)$.

concepts.title: Fibers and base change
concepts.summary: A fiber collects all points sharing one image; base change restricts a map while preserving étaleness.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The fiber of $f:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $f^{-1}(y)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A generic cubic has three preimages corresponding to its three simple marked roots.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Generic fiber cardinality need not equal every actual fiber cardinality.

concepts.title: Étale maps
concepts.summary: Étaleness is the algebraic form of local biholomorphic behavior and is stable under base change.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For this course, an étale map can be recognized locally by an invertible differential and the standard algebraic hypotheses.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $(L,Q)\mapsto(LQ,\operatorname{Res}(L,Q))$ is étale when the resultant is nonzero.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Étale does not mean globally injective or proper.

concepts.title: Properness and nonproperness
concepts.summary: Nonproperness allows sheets of a local inverse to escape through the boundary.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Over complex varieties, properness is the algebraic counterpart of compact-preimage behavior.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A nonproper local homeomorphism need not be a global covering map.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Finite fibers alone do not establish properness.

concepts.title: The projective line
concepts.summary: $\mathbb P^1$ completes the affine root chart by adding the point at infinity.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $\mathbb P^1$ is the set of one-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb C^2$, written $[T:S]$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The charts $S\ne0$ and $T\ne0$ cover $\mathbb P^1$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: $\mathbb C$ alone omits the root at infinity.

concepts.title: Marked-root incidence
concepts.summary: The global map forgets which simple projective root was chosen.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A point of $X$ is a normalized cubic together with a chosen simple projective root.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Three simple roots give three admissible marked-root preimages.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A triple root gives no admissible factorization with resultant one.

concepts.title: Covering maps
concepts.summary: Covering-space language distinguishes local sheet structure from global properness.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A covering map evenly covers a neighborhood of every base point by disjoint homeomorphic sheets.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $z\mapsto z^n$ is an $n$-sheeted covering of $\mathbb C^\times$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A local homeomorphism with escaping sheets need not be a covering map.

concepts.title: $SL_2$ and binary forms
concepts.summary: $SL_2$ acts by change of variables on binary forms and makes multiplication equivariant.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $SL_2$ acts on $\operatorname{Sym}^d(\mathbb C^2)$ through its action on the variables $S,T$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Polynomial multiplication is $SL_2$-equivariant.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A coordinate formula that changes under basis change without an equivariance law is not intrinsic.

concepts.title: Torus weights and gradings
concepts.summary: The residual scaling action predicts the useful affine coordinates and their degrees.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A torus weight records how a coordinate transforms under a one-parameter scaling action.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\deg a=1$, $\deg y=-1$, and $\deg z=-2$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Ordinary polynomial degree and torus weight are different gradings.

concepts.title: Normal jets
concepts.summary: Corrected first and second normal coefficients motivate the coordinates $y$ and $z$ along $a=0$.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $b-1=ay$ identifies $y$ as a first normal coefficient; $c-1+\frac32ay=a^2z$ identifies a corrected second coefficient.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $y=2bd-ae$ is polynomial on the full threefold.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The visible quotient $(b-1)/a$ alone does not prove global regularity at $a=0$.

concepts.title: The normalized factorization threefold
concepts.summary: The central space $X$ normalizes both the resultant and one cubic coefficient and is polynomially isomorphic to affine three-space.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The explicit $(a,y,z)$ formulas give mutually inverse polynomial maps $X\leftrightarrow\mathbb A^3$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Solving only on $a\ne0$ does not establish the global isomorphism.

concepts.title: The Keller map
concepts.summary: Composing the affine coordinates with the cubic coefficient map yields the explicit constant-Jacobian polynomial map.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: $G:\mathbb A^3\to\mathbb A^3$ is obtained by composing the affine chart of $X$ with $(a,b,c,d,e)\mapsto(ac,ae+bd,be)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: $\det DG=-1$ while the map is generically three-to-one.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A constant nonzero Jacobian does not itself provide a global polynomial inverse.

concepts.title: Composition and inverse functions
concepts.summary: Composition tracks how one function feeds into another; an inverse must undo the function in both directions.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For functions $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$, the composite is $(g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x))$. A function $h:Y\to X$ is an inverse of $f$ when $h\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$ and $f\circ h=\operatorname{id}_Y$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $f(x)=2x+3$ on $\mathbb R$, the function $h(y)=(y-3)/2$ satisfies both composition identities, so it is the inverse of $f$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Checking only $h\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$ does not prove that $h$ is a two-sided inverse; the other composition can still fail.

concepts.title: Polynomial arithmetic and identities
concepts.summary: Polynomial calculations become proofs when coefficients are collected carefully and every claimed identity is checked for all inputs.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A polynomial identity is an equality between polynomials, so corresponding coefficients are equal. It may be established by expansion, factorization, or a theorem that applies over the stated coefficient field.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Expanding $(aT+bS)(cT^2+dTS+eS^2)$ gives $acT^3+(ad+bc)T^2S+(ae+bd)TS^2+beS^3$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Agreement at a few numerical values is evidence for an identity, but it is not a proof that two polynomials are equal.

concepts.title: Complex roots and multiplicity
concepts.summary: Root multiplicity records how many times a linear factor occurs and predicts whether a derivative vanishes at the root.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A complex number $r$ has multiplicity $m$ as a root of $p$ when $(t-r)^m$ divides $p(t)$ but $(t-r)^{m+1}$ does not.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The polynomial $(t-1)^2(t+2)$ has a double root at $1$ and a simple root at $-2$; both $p(1)$ and $p'(1)$ vanish.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The equation $p(r)=0$ alone proves that $r$ is a root, not that its multiplicity is greater than one.

concepts.title: Sets, complements, and fibers
concepts.summary: Set notation makes logical conditions visible and lets equations be read as inverse images of values.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For $A,B\subseteq U$, union means “in $A$ or $B$,” intersection means “in both,” and $U\setminus A$ means “in $U$ but not in $A$.” The fiber of $f:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $f^{-1}(y)=\{x\in X:f(x)=y\}$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: If $F:\mathbb C^5\to\mathbb C^2$ is $F=(f_1,f_2)$, then $V(f_1,f_2)=F^{-1}(0,0)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The notation $f^{-1}(y)$ for a fiber does not assume that $f$ has an inverse function.

concepts.title: Quantifiers and logical negation
concepts.summary: Precise quantifiers distinguish local claims from global ones and make a proposed negation checkable.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The negation of “for every $x$ there exists $y$ such that $P(x,y)$” is “there exists $x$ such that for every $y$, $P(x,y)$ is false.” Each quantifier changes and the final claim is negated.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The negation of injectivity is: there exist distinct $x,x'$ in the domain with $f(x)=f(x')$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Replacing “for every” by “there exists” without also negating the inner statement does not produce the logical negation.

concepts.title: Direct proof, contrapositive, and contradiction
concepts.summary: The proof method should match the logical form of the claim and should expose, rather than hide, the decisive implication.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A direct proof derives the conclusion from the hypotheses. A contrapositive proves “not $Q$ implies not $P$” instead of “$P$ implies $Q$.” A contradiction assumes the hypotheses and the negation of the conclusion and derives an impossibility.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: To prove that $ab$ odd implies $a$ and $b$ odd, prove the contrapositive: if either factor is even, then $ab$ is even.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Writing “this is obvious by contradiction” without stating the negated conclusion or the contradiction is not a complete proof.

concepts.title: Induction, equivalence, and counterexamples
concepts.summary: Induction proves a statement along the natural numbers, equivalence needs both implications, and one valid counterexample refutes a universal claim.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Induction requires a verified base case and a step proving $P(n)\Rightarrow P(n+1)$. An equivalence $P\Leftrightarrow Q$ requires proofs of both $P\Rightarrow Q$ and $Q\Rightarrow P$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The binomial formula follows by checking $n=0$ and deriving the case $n+1$ from the case $n$ with Pascal's identity.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Several successful examples do not prove a universal statement, while an induction step without a base case proves nothing about where the chain begins.

concepts.title: Bijections and two-sided inverses
concepts.summary: A concrete isomorphism is established by writing maps both ways and checking both compositions.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A function is bijective when it is injective and surjective. Functions $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to X$ are mutual inverses precisely when $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$ and $f\circ g=\operatorname{id}_Y$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: If polynomial maps $\Phi:\mathbb A^3\to X$ and $\Psi:X\to\mathbb A^3$ satisfy both identities, they give a polynomial isomorphism.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A left inverse proves injectivity and a right inverse proves surjectivity; either identity by itself is insufficient for bijectivity.

concepts.title: Linear systems and affine solution sets
concepts.summary: Row reduction reveals whether a system is inconsistent, uniquely solvable, or an affine translate of a kernel.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A linear system $Ax=b$ has solution set $x_0+\ker A$ whenever one particular solution $x_0$ exists. Its direction space is the kernel of the coefficient map.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The system $x+2y-z=3$, $2x+4y-2z=6$ has solution set $(3,0,0)+s(-2,1,0)+t(1,0,1)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The solution set of an inhomogeneous system need not be a vector subspace because it may not contain the zero vector.

concepts.title: Subspaces, bases, and dimension
concepts.summary: A basis gives unique coordinates and turns dimension into a count of independent directions.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A subspace is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. A basis is a linearly independent spanning family, and the dimension is the number of vectors in any basis.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The monomials $T^d,T^{d-1}S,\ldots,S^d$ form a basis of the binary forms of degree $d$, so the space has dimension $d+1$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A spanning list with redundant vectors is not a basis because its coordinates are not unique.

concepts.title: Linear maps and matrix representations
concepts.summary: A matrix records a linear map only after bases have been chosen, so basis changes alter coordinates but not the underlying map.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For a linear map $u:V\to W$ and ordered bases of $V$ and $W$, the matrix of $u$ has as its columns the coordinates of the images of the basis vectors of $V$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Multiplication by a fixed linear form sends the basis $(T^2,TS,S^2)$ of quadratics to three cubics whose coefficient columns form a $4\times3$ matrix.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The same abstract linear map can have different matrices in different bases; a matrix without its source and target bases is incomplete data.

concepts.title: Kernel, image, quotients, and exactness
concepts.summary: Kernel and image describe the directions a linear map loses and retains; quotient spaces and exact sequences record the same structure in forms that can be transported into later algebra.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For $u:V\to W$, $\ker u=\{v:u(v)=0\}$ and $\operatorname{im}u=\{u(v):v\in V\}$. If $V$ is finite-dimensional, then $\dim V=\dim\ker u+\operatorname{rank}u$. For a subspace $U\subseteq V$, the quotient $V/U$ identifies vectors whose difference lies in $U$. The corestricted map $V\to\operatorname{im}u$ induces an isomorphism $V/\ker u\cong\operatorname{im}u$. A sequence is exact at a space when the image of the incoming map equals the kernel of the outgoing map.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: If $u:\mathbb R^5\to\mathbb R^4$ is surjective, then $\ker u$ is one-dimensional, $\mathbb R^5/\ker u\cong\mathbb R^4$, and $0\to\ker u\to\mathbb R^5\to\mathbb R^4\to0$ is short exact.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The equation $B\circ A=0$ proves only $\operatorname{im}A\subseteq\ker B$, not exactness; and source and target dimensions alone do not determine exact kernel dimension unless the rank is known.

concepts.title: Determinants and oriented volume
concepts.summary: The determinant detects invertibility and measures how a linear map scales oriented volume.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The determinant is the unique alternating multilinear function of the columns that equals $1$ on the identity matrix. A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Multilinearity gives $\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)$, so a product is invertible precisely when both square factors are invertible.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A nonzero entry or a nonzero trace does not imply that the whole matrix is invertible.

concepts.title: Dual spaces and bilinear forms
concepts.summary: Linear functionals extract scalar information from vectors, while bilinear forms compare two vector inputs linearly in each slot.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The dual space $V^*$ consists of linear maps $\ell:V\to k$. A bilinear form is a map $B:V\times V\to k$ that is linear in each variable separately.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: On binary cubics, the rule that extracts the coefficient of $T^2S$ is a linear functional; its level set $\ell^{-1}(1)$ is an affine hyperplane.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A quadratic function such as $v\mapsto v^2$ is not a linear functional, even though it returns a scalar.

concepts.title: Tensor and symmetric powers
concepts.summary: Symmetric powers encode homogeneous polynomials and make multiplication between degrees into a natural bilinear map.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The symmetric power $\operatorname{Sym}^d(V)$ is obtained from $V^{\otimes d}$ by identifying tensors that differ only by a permutation of factors.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For a two-dimensional $V$, $\operatorname{Sym}^1(V^*)$, $\operatorname{Sym}^2(V^*)$, and $\operatorname{Sym}^3(V^*)$ model binary linear, quadratic, and cubic forms.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The full tensor power $V^{\otimes d}$ contains nonsymmetric tensors and is generally larger than $\operatorname{Sym}^d(V)$.

concepts.title: Total derivatives and the chain rule
concepts.summary: The total derivative is the best linear approximation, and the chain rule composes those linear approximations in the correct order.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For $F:k^n\to k^m$, the derivative $DF_x$ is the linear map satisfying $F(x+h)=F(x)+DF_x(h)+o(\lVert h\rVert)$. If $G\circ F$ is defined, then $D(G\circ F)_x=DG_{F(x)}\circ DF_x$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For multiplication $M(L,Q)=LQ$, differentiation gives $dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Differentiating each output coordinate separately without assembling the resulting linear map can obscure its domain, codomain, and kernel.

concepts.title: Local inversion
concepts.summary: An invertible derivative gives a unique inverse near one point but does not settle the behavior of the map on its whole domain.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The inverse function theorem says that if $DF_x$ is invertible, then $F$ restricts to an isomorphism between suitable neighborhoods of $x$ and $F(x)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The map $z\mapsto z^3$ is locally invertible at every $z\ne0$ because its derivative is $3z^2\ne0$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Local invertibility at every point does not imply global injectivity; cube roots of unity give different inputs with the same cube.

concepts.title: Implicit equations and simple-root branches
concepts.summary: A nonvanishing derivative in the solved-for variable lets an implicit equation select one local branch.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For an equation $F(s,t)=0$, if $F(s_0,t_0)=0$ and $\partial F/\partial t(s_0,t_0)\ne0$, the implicit function theorem gives a unique local function $t=t(s)$ through that point.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $F(s,t)=t^2-s$, a nonzero root $t_0$ lies on a unique local square-root branch because $2t_0\ne0$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: At $(s,t)=(0,0)$, the two square-root branches meet and the derivative in $t$ vanishes, so the uniqueness conclusion is unavailable.

concepts.title: Groups and symmetry actions
concepts.summary: A group action packages compatible symmetries and makes stabilizers and invariant quantities precise.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: An action of a group $G$ on a set $X$ satisfies $e\cdot x=x$ and $(gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$. The stabilizer of $x$ is $\{g:g\cdot x=x\}$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The action $\lambda\cdot(x,y)=(\lambda x,\lambda^{-1}y)$ of $\mathbb C^\times$ preserves the product $xy$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A family of transformations that is not closed under composition or does not contain the identity is not a group action.

concepts.title: Homomorphisms, orbits, stabilizers, and quotients
concepts.summary: A quotient should encode whole orbits without silently discarding exceptional ones.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The orbit of $x$ is $G\cdot x$, and its stabilizer records the group elements that fix it. An orbit-space quotient identifies points in the same orbit, while an algebraic quotient is usually described by invariant functions.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: On $x\ne0$, every orbit of $\lambda\cdot(x,y)=(\lambda x,\lambda^{-1}y)$ meets the slice $x=1$ exactly once.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: That slice misses every orbit with $x=0$, so it cannot represent the quotient of the entire plane.

concepts.title: Rings, fields, and homomorphisms
concepts.summary: Algebraic maps preserve operations, and their kernels record exactly what becomes zero.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A ring homomorphism preserves addition, multiplication, and the multiplicative identity. Its kernel is an ideal. A field is a commutative ring in which every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Evaluation at $a$, $k[x]\to k$, sends $p$ to $p(a)$ and has kernel $(x-a)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A rational expression with a vanishing denominator does not define a function on the whole field, even if cancellation produces a polynomial elsewhere.

concepts.title: Ideals and quotient rings
concepts.summary: A quotient ring turns selected polynomial relations into literal equalities of residue classes.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For an ideal $I\subseteq A$, the quotient $A/I$ identifies $f$ and $g$ exactly when $f-g\in I$. Multiplication is well defined because $I$ absorbs multiplication by elements of $A$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: In $k[x,y]/(xy-1)$, the classes of $xy$ and $1$ are equal, so the class of $x$ is invertible with inverse the class of $y$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Equality in a quotient ring need not be equality of the original polynomials in the ambient polynomial ring.

concepts.title: Divisibility, greatest common divisors, and Bézout
concepts.summary: Coprimality is useful because a Bézout identity lets divisibility pass through a product.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Elements $a,b$ are coprime when their greatest common divisor is a unit; in a principal ideal domain this is equivalent to the existence of $u,v$ with $ua+vb=1$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: If $\gcd(L,Q)=1$ and $L\mid \dot LQ$, multiply a Bézout identity $AL+BQ=1$ by $\dot L$ to conclude $L\mid\dot L$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: From $L\mid \dot LQ$ alone one cannot cancel $Q$ unless the required coprimality or non-zero-divisor hypothesis is established.

concepts.title: Modules and graded rings
concepts.summary: Modules generalize vector spaces to ring coefficients, while a grading tracks how algebraic pieces transform or combine.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: An $A$-module has addition and scalar multiplication by a ring $A$. A graded ring $R=\bigoplus_n R_n$ satisfies $R_mR_n\subseteq R_{m+n}$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Assigning weights $\deg a=1$, $\deg d=-1$, and $\deg e=-2$ makes the monomial $a^2e$ have total weight zero.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Weight is not ordinary polynomial degree; negative weights are allowed and two monomials of equal ordinary degree can have different weights.

concepts.title: Localization and principal open sets
concepts.summary: Localization permits division by one chosen function and describes the part of a variety where that function does not vanish.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For a ring $A$ and $f\in A$, the localization $A_f$ contains fractions $a/f^n$. Geometrically, it is the coordinate ring of the principal open set $D(f)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: On the open set $a\ne0$, the equations of $X$ can be solved for $d$ and $e$ using powers of $a$ in the denominator.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A formula in $A_a$ need not extend across the divisor $a=0$; extension requires a separate global argument.

concepts.title: Homogeneous coordinates and projective roots
concepts.summary: Projective coordinates retain roots at infinity that disappear in an affine ratio.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The projective line consists of nonzero pairs $[T:S]$ up to common scaling. A binary form vanishes at a projective point when its homogeneous evaluation there is zero.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The linear form $aT+bS$ has root $[-b:a]$; when $a=0$ and $b\ne0$, that root is $[1:0]$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The affine expression $-b/a$ is undefined at $a=0$ and therefore cannot describe every projective root.

concepts.title: Resultants
concepts.summary: The resultant detects whether two homogeneous forms share a projective root without solving for that root.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The resultant is a polynomial in the coefficients that vanishes exactly when the two forms have a common projective zero. For a binary linear form and quadratic it has bidegree $(2,1)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$, $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+b^2c$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A nonzero resultant proves that the factors share no projective root; it does not say that either factor has no root of its own.

concepts.title: Discriminants and repeated roots
concepts.summary: The discriminant detects when a polynomial loses distinct roots.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For a polynomial with roots $r_i$, the discriminant is, up to the conventional leading-coefficient factor, the product of $(r_i-r_j)^2$ over pairs. It vanishes exactly when a root is repeated.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $p(t)=t^3+ut+v$, the discriminant is $-4u^3-27v^2$; it vanishes for $(t-1)^2(t+2)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A small nonzero discriminant may indicate nearby roots, but only a zero discriminant proves an actual repeated root.

concepts.title: Equivariance and semi-invariants
concepts.summary: Equivariance says that a map respects an action, while a semi-invariant may scale by a predictable character.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A map $F:X\to Y$ is equivariant when $F(g\cdot x)=g\cdot F(x)$. A function $r$ is a semi-invariant of character $\chi$ when $r(g\cdot x)=\chi(g)r(x)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The resultant obeys $\operatorname{Res}(\lambda L,\mu Q)=\lambda^2\mu\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: An expression that changes under the action with no consistent character is neither invariant nor a semi-invariant.

concepts.title: The normalized factorization space
concepts.summary: Two normalization equations remove the relative scaling ambiguity from a linear–quadratic factorization.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The normalized space is $X=\{(a,b,c,d,e):a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}$. The first equation fixes the resultant and the second fixes a chosen cubic coefficient.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: On $a=0$, the equations force $b=c=1$, leaving the free coordinates $d,e$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Imposing only the resultant equation leaves a one-parameter relative scaling and does not produce the same three-dimensional space.

concepts.title: Affine algebraic sets and the Zariski topology
concepts.summary: Polynomial zero sets are the closed sets of affine algebraic geometry, and their inclusion order reverses ideal inclusion.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For $S\subseteq k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, the algebraic set $V(S)$ consists of the common zeros of every polynomial in $S$. These sets are the closed sets of the Zariski topology.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The identity $V(fg)=V(f)\cup V(g)$ follows because a product vanishes over a field exactly when one factor vanishes.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A finite union of algebraic sets is algebraic, but an arbitrary union of Zariski-closed sets need not be closed.

concepts.title: The algebra–geometry dictionary
concepts.summary: Passing between ideals and zero sets reverses arrows and translates geometric questions into ring questions.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A polynomial map $f:X\to Y$ induces a pullback homomorphism $f^*:k[Y]\to k[X]$ by $h\mapsto h\circ f$. This reversal is the contravariant algebra–geometry dictionary.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: An inclusion $I\subseteq J$ gives the reversed inclusion $V(J)\subseteq V(I)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Treating coordinate-ring maps as if they pointed in the same direction as geometric maps reverses compositions incorrectly.

concepts.title: Regular morphisms and rational maps
concepts.summary: Regular maps are defined everywhere by allowable functions; rational maps are only defined on a dense open set until an extension is proved.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A morphism of affine varieties is given by coordinate functions that are regular at every point. A rational map is an equivalence class of morphisms defined on dense open subsets.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The quotient $(b-1)/a$ defines a regular function on $a\ne0$; the identity $b-1=a(2bd-ae)$ proves that it extends globally as $2bd-ae$ on $X$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A denominator that happens not to vanish on one chart does not by itself prove global regularity.

concepts.title: Zariski tangent spaces and the Jacobian criterion
concepts.summary: Linearizing generators of the vanishing ideal gives the tangent space; a full-rank local complete-intersection presentation then detects smoothness.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: If $X\subseteq\mathbb A^n$ has vanishing ideal $I(X)=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$, then $T_xX$ is the kernel of the Jacobian matrix $(\partial f_i/\partial x_j)(x)$. For a reduced local complete intersection, full row rank gives the expected tangent dimension and proves smoothness near $x$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For a reduced variety locally cut out by two ideal generators in $\mathbb A^5$, Jacobian rank two gives a three-dimensional tangent space.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Writing $X=V(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$ does not by itself make $\ker J(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$ the Zariski tangent space: $V(x^2)=V(x)$, but $d(x^2)_0=0$ while $I(V(x^2))=(x)$ gives $T_0X=0$.

concepts.title: Dimension and complete intersections
concepts.summary: Dimension counts independent local parameters, while a complete intersection has exactly the codimension predicted by its defining equations.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The Krull dimension of an affine variety is the dimension of its coordinate ring. A variety cut out by $r$ equations in a smooth $n$-dimensional ambient space is a complete intersection when its codimension is $r$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The quotient $k[x,y,z]/(x-y^2,z-y^3)\cong k[y]$ has dimension one, so the twisted cubic chart has codimension two in affine three-space.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Counting displayed equations does not prove codimension when the equations are dependent or define embedded components.

concepts.title: Fiber products and universal properties
concepts.summary: A fiber product records pairs with the same image and is characterized by a universal mapping property.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For maps $X\to S$ and $Y\to S$, the fiber product $X\times_S Y$ consists of compatible pairs and comes with projections whose composites to $S$ agree.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $t=u^2$ and $t=v^3$, the fiber product is $V(u^2-v^3)\subseteq\mathbb A^2_{u,v}$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The ordinary Cartesian product $X\times Y$ does not enforce equality of the two images in the base $S$.

concepts.title: Finite and quasi-finite morphisms
concepts.summary: Finiteness is an algebraic integrality condition; quasi-finiteness only controls fiber dimension and is weaker.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: An affine morphism is finite when the target coordinate ring makes the source coordinate ring a finite module. A morphism is quasi-finite when its fibers are finite near every point.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: If a source coordinate $y$ satisfies a monic polynomial over the target ring, it is integral and can help prove that the morphism is finite.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Having finitely many points in a generic fiber does not by itself prove that the map is finite over every target point.

concepts.title: Unramified and étale morphisms
concepts.summary: An étale morphism is the algebraic analogue of a local isomorphism: it is smooth of relative dimension zero.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A morphism is étale when it is flat and unramified; for a map between smooth varieties of equal dimension, an invertible differential gives the local étale condition.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $t\mapsto t^2$ away from $t=0$, the derivative $2t$ is invertible, so the map is étale there.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A finite fiber does not imply étaleness; ramification can merge local sheets even when the fiber has few points.

concepts.title: Gröbner bases and elimination
concepts.summary: A Gröbner basis gives a terminating reduction process and can eliminate variables to reveal equations in selected coordinates.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A Gröbner basis is a generating set whose leading terms generate the initial ideal. With an elimination order, the basis elements using only the retained variables generate the elimination ideal.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For the basis $\{x-y^2,z-y^3\}$ with $x>z>y$, every residue class reduces to a polynomial in $y$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: An arbitrary generating set need not support unique normal forms or expose the elimination ideal.

concepts.title: The coefficient–resultant étale map
concepts.summary: Adding the normalized resultant removes the one-dimensional scaling kernel of multiplication and yields an equal-dimensional local map.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The map that records selected cubic coefficients together with $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)$ has differential combining the multiplication derivative with the derivative of the resultant.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The vector $(L,-Q)$ lies in the kernel of multiplication, but the bidegree $(2,1)$ makes the resultant derivative nonzero in that direction.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Checking only the multiplication differential leaves the scaling direction in the kernel and cannot prove étaleness.

concepts.title: Projective-line charts
concepts.summary: Two affine charts cover the projective line and their reciprocal transition keeps the point at infinity visible.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The standard charts $U_S=\{S\ne0\}$ and $U_T=\{T\ne0\}$ have coordinates $t=T/S$ and $s=S/T$, related by $s=1/t$ where both are defined.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The point $[1:0]$ is absent from the $t$-chart but appears as $s=0$ in the other chart.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: One affine chart is not the whole projective line, so an argument using only $T/S$ must separately handle $S=0$.

concepts.title: Symmetric powers of the projective line
concepts.summary: An unordered degree-$d$ divisor on the projective line corresponds to a binary form up to scale.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The symmetric power $\operatorname{Sym}^d(\mathbb P^1)$ parametrizes unordered $d$-tuples of points with multiplicity and is naturally isomorphic to $\mathbb P^d$ through binary forms.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A cubic with roots $p_1,p_2,p_3$ determines the divisor $p_1+p_2+p_3$, including repeated points when roots repeat.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: An ordered triple contains extra labeling data and is not the same object as a point of the symmetric power.

concepts.title: Incidence varieties and marked roots
concepts.summary: Marking one root creates a cover whose fiber records the distinct root choices.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The incidence variety $I=\{(C,p):C(p)=0\}$ maps to the space of cubics by forgetting $p$. Its fiber over $C$ is the set of distinct projective roots of $C$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A cubic with three distinct roots has three points in the incidence fiber; a double root and a simple root give two points.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Root multiplicity is not the same as the number of points in the fiber because the incidence pair records a root location only once.

concepts.title: Ramification and the resultant locus
concepts.summary: The marked-root cover ramifies exactly when the chosen linear factor meets its complementary factor.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: If $C=LQ$ and $L$ vanishes at the marked root $p$, then $p$ is repeated in $C$ exactly when $Q(p)=0$, equivalently when $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=0$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A double root makes the marked-root projection fail to have three separate local sheets at that cubic.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The discriminant or resultant locus is not merely a numerical accident; it is the geometric branch locus where roots collide.

concepts.title: The twisted cubic and osculating geometry
concepts.summary: Derivatives of the Veronese parametrization produce its tangent and higher-contact spaces.
concepts.definitionMarkdown:
The twisted cubic is the image of $
u:\mathbb P^1	o\mathbb P^3$, $[S:T]\mapsto[S^3:S^2T:ST^2:T^3]$. Its tangent line is spanned locally by $
u(t)$ and $
u'(t)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: On the chart $\nu(t)=[1:t:t^2:t^3]$, the tangent direction is $(0,1,2t,3t^2)$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The secant line through two distinct curve points is generally not the tangent line, although it approaches one as the points merge.

concepts.title: Hyperplane contact and root divisors
concepts.summary: The order of hyperplane contact with the twisted cubic matches the multiplicity pattern of the associated binary cubic.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Restricting a projective hyperplane equation to the parametrized twisted cubic gives a degree-three polynomial; its zero divisor records the contact points and their multiplicities.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A divisor $2p+q$ represents double contact at $p$ and simple contact at $q$, while $3p$ represents osculating contact.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Three points listed without multiplicity do not distinguish a tangent section from a transverse section.

concepts.title: Compactness and proper maps
concepts.summary: Properness prevents inverse images of compact sets from escaping to infinity and is the global condition needed to control covering sheets.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A continuous map is proper when the inverse image of every compact set is compact. In complex algebraic geometry, finite morphisms are proper after analytification.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A proper local homeomorphism with finite fibers is a covering map whose sheets cannot disappear along a convergent path in the target.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Local invertibility alone does not imply properness; a sequence in the source may escape while its image remains bounded.

concepts.title: Covering maps and power maps
concepts.summary: A covering map is locally a disjoint union of homeomorphic sheets, but it can be globally many-to-one.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A map $p:E\to B$ is a covering when every point of $B$ has a neighborhood whose inverse image is a disjoint union of open sets mapped homeomorphically onto it.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For every integer $n\ge1$, $z\mapsto z^n$ on $\mathbb C^\times$ is an $n$-sheeted covering and every nonzero value has $n$ distinct preimages.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A covering is locally injective on each sheet, not necessarily injective on the whole source.

concepts.title: Nonproperness and escaping sheets
concepts.summary: A nonproper étale map can lose a sheet at infinity, which is the mechanism that evades finite-cover rigidity.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A sequence $x_m$ is an escaping sheet over a convergent target sequence when $x_m$ leaves every compact subset of the source while $F(x_m)$ converges.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: If an étale map were also finite, its analytification would be proper, so such an escaping sequence could not occur.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Showing that a map is not injective does not by itself locate the failure of properness or exhibit an escaping sheet.

concepts.title: The normalized triple cover
concepts.summary: A cubic with three distinct roots has three normalized linear–quadratic factorizations, one for each marked root.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Choose a linear factor $L_i$ for each distinct root and put $Q_i=C/L_i$. Relative scaling can be chosen to impose the resultant normalization, producing one point of $X$ for each root.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A square-free cubic $C$ yields exactly three normalized pairs $(L_i,Q_i)$ above its coefficient data.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Counting scalar multiples of the same factorization as different points ignores the normalization that removes relative scaling.

concepts.title: Representations and equivariant maps
concepts.summary: A representation turns each group element into a compatible linear transformation and lets natural constructions be compared without choosing coordinates.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A representation of $G$ on $V$ is a homomorphism $G\to GL(V)$. A map between representations is equivariant when it commutes with every group action.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Multiplication $\operatorname{Sym}^1(V^*)\times\operatorname{Sym}^2(V^*)\to\operatorname{Sym}^3(V^*)$ is equivariant under change of variables.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A coordinate formula that works in one basis but has no transformation law has not been shown to define an equivariant map.

concepts.title: The $SL_2$ action on binary forms
concepts.summary: Changing variables by a determinant-one matrix acts on binary forms while preserving their intrinsic projective root geometry.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: For $g\in SL_2$, the induced action on a binary form is obtained by substituting the transformed variables. Degree-$d$ forms carry the representation $\operatorname{Sym}^d((\mathbb C^2)^*)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $g=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda,\lambda^{-1})$, the monomial $T^{d-i}S^i$ has weight $d-2i$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Scaling all coefficients arbitrarily is not an $SL_2$ change of variables and need not preserve the relevant invariants.

concepts.title: Torus weights and graded coordinate rings
concepts.summary: The residual one-parameter action assigns weights that predict homogeneous relations and useful coordinates.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: If $\mathbb G_m$ acts on a coordinate $x$ by $\lambda\cdot x=\lambda^w x$, then $x$ has weight $w$. Products add weights, giving a graded coordinate ring.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: With weights $1,0,0,-1,-2$ on $a,b,c,d,e$, each term of $a^2e-abd+cb^2$ has weight zero.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Ordinary degree and torus weight answer different questions; a quadratic monomial need not have weight two.

concepts.title: The tangent kernel and resultant correction
concepts.summary: Differentiating the scaling symmetry isolates the kernel of multiplication, and the resultant supplies the missing transverse coordinate.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The curve $(e^sL,e^{-s}Q)$ keeps $LQ$ fixed, so its derivative $(L,-Q)$ lies in $\ker dM$. The normalized resultant changes in this direction by its bidegree character.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Because the resultant has bidegree $(2,1)$, it scales by $e^s$ along this curve and has derivative $1$ at $s=0$ on the normalized locus.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A dimension count may predict a kernel direction, but the differentiated action identifies it and the resultant calculation proves it is removed.

concepts.title: The boundary stratum $a=0$
concepts.summary: The chart boundary is a genuine affine plane with explicit coordinates, not an exceptional set to be discarded.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Inside $X$, setting $a=0$ reduces the equations to $cb^2=1$ and $bc=1$, which force $b=c=1$ while $d,e$ remain free.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The maps $(d,e)\mapsto(0,1,1,d,e)$ and projection back to $(d,e)$ give inverse polynomial maps with $\mathbb A^2$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Solving only on $a\ne0$ misses this entire divisor and cannot establish a global description of $X$.

concepts.title: First and second normal jets
concepts.summary: Successive coefficients transverse to the boundary provide coordinates that remain meaningful when the visible quotient denominator vanishes.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The identities $b-1=ay$ and $c-1+\tfrac32ay=a^2z$ define corrected first and second normal coefficients along $a=0$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The first identity is realized globally by $y=2bd-ae$, a polynomial in the ambient coefficients.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Writing $y=(b-1)/a$ only on $a\ne0$ does not prove that $y$ extends regularly to the boundary.

concepts.title: Global polynomial representatives
concepts.summary: A quotient-ring identity can replace a chartwise fraction by one polynomial valid on the whole variety.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A regular function on an affine variety $X$ is represented by an element of its coordinate ring. To extend a fraction, prove that it equals a polynomial residue class modulo the defining ideal.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: In the coordinate ring of $X$, $b-1=a(2bd-ae)$, so $(b-1)/a$ agrees on $a\ne0$ with the global polynomial $2bd-ae$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Cancelling $a$ in the ambient polynomial ring would be invalid on $a=0$ and would not prove a global extension.

concepts.title: An explicit affine-space isomorphism
concepts.summary: A global coordinate chart requires polynomial formulas in both directions and verification of both compositions.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: An isomorphism $X\simeq\mathbb A^3$ consists of polynomial maps $\Phi:\mathbb A^3\to X$ and $\Psi:X\to\mathbb A^3$ whose two compositions are identity maps.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Coordinates $(a,y,z)$ together with the supplied polynomial formulas for $b,c,d,e$ give a candidate $\Phi$, while $y=2bd-ae$ is part of $\Psi$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A birational formula valid on $a\ne0$ is not yet an affine isomorphism because it may fail on the boundary divisor.

concepts.title: Classifying claims and evidence
concepts.summary: Before proving a statement, identify whether it is algebraic, local, global, or topological so the evidence matches the claim.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: An algebraic identity is checked in a ring, a local claim on neighborhoods, a global claim over all points, and a topological claim with properties such as compactness or properness.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A nonzero Jacobian establishes a local property; a separate fiber calculation is needed for global injectivity.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Using a local theorem as evidence for a global conclusion is a category error, even when every local calculation is correct.

concepts.title: The five-dimensional coefficient–resultant map
concepts.summary: The augmented factorization map records four cubic coefficients and one resultant so its source and target have equal dimension.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: From a linear form and a quadratic form, record the four coefficients of their product together with $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)$. This defines a polynomial map from affine five-space to affine five-space.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Its differential combines $dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$ with the derivative of the resultant.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The four coefficient functions alone define a map to affine four-space and necessarily retain at least one infinitesimal kernel direction.

concepts.title: A smooth threefold by base change
concepts.summary: The normalized factorization space is a fiber of an étale five-dimensional map, so smoothness descends through base change.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Étale morphisms are stable under base change. Pulling an étale map back along a smooth subspace gives an étale source over that subspace and preserves the expected dimension.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Fixing the normalized resultant and one coefficient cuts the five-dimensional target to a three-dimensional affine subspace; its inverse image is $X$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Counting two equations inside affine five-space does not prove smoothness unless their differentials have the required independence.

concepts.title: Polynomial inverse verification
concepts.summary: The inverse formulas must be checked in the coordinate ring, where the defining relations justify every simplification.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: To prove polynomial maps are inverse on $X$, substitute one formula into the other and reduce each coordinate difference modulo the defining ideal of $X$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: For $y=2bd-ae$, substitution into the forward chart and reduction by the two equations returns the original coordinate $y$.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Numerical checks or verification only on the dense chart $a\ne0$ do not prove the polynomial identities on all of $X$.

concepts.title: The explicit Keller map $G$
concepts.summary: Transporting the coefficient map through the affine chart produces a concrete polynomial self-map of affine three-space.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: Let $\Phi:\mathbb A^3\to X$ be the polynomial chart and let $H:X\to\mathbb A^3$ record the selected cubic coefficients. The Keller map is $G=H\circ\Phi$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: The derivative satisfies $DG=D H_{\Phi(a,y,z)}\,D\Phi_{(a,y,z)}$; the established local isomorphisms make its determinant the stated nonzero constant.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Calling a map a Keller map requires an explicit polynomial formula and constant nonzero Jacobian, not merely a factorization through smooth spaces.

concepts.title: Linear equivalence and the determinant chain
concepts.summary: Linear coordinate changes conjugate the constructed map to the original coefficient map and scale Jacobians by constant determinants.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: If $F_{\mathrm{orig}}=B\circ G\circ A$ for invertible linear maps $A,B$, then $DF_{\mathrm{orig}}=B\,DG\,A$ and $\det DF_{\mathrm{orig}}=\det(B)\det(DG)\det(A)$.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: Writing the actual matrices $A$ and $B$ proves that the two maps have the same fiber structure and relates their constant Jacobians.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: Saying that two maps are equivalent without displaying the coordinate changes leaves both the claim and the determinant factor unsupported.

concepts.title: Fiber cardinality and noninjectivity
concepts.summary: A single generic fiber with several explicit points disproves global injectivity even when the derivative is invertible everywhere.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: The fiber of $F:X\to Y$ over $y$ is $F^{-1}(y)$. If it contains two distinct points, then $F$ is not injective; a generic fiber count describes this on a dense target set.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A square-free binary cubic has three distinct marked roots, hence three distinct normalized factorizations and three corresponding preimages.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: The nonzero Jacobian proves that these preimages are locally separate; it does not collapse them into one global point.

concepts.title: Proof synthesis and mathematical exposition
concepts.summary: A finished proof portfolio makes every hypothesis, definition, implication, and claim boundary independently checkable.
concepts.definitionMarkdown: A complete exposition states the target, fixes notation, cites each theorem with its hypotheses, proves intermediate claims before use, and distinguishes local, global, algebraic, and topological conclusions.
concepts.exampleMarkdown: A final proof of $X\simeq\mathbb A^3$ displays both polynomial maps, checks both compositions, and then explains how the normalized product map becomes the stated affine map.
concepts.nonExampleMarkdown: A chain of correct formulas is not a readable proof when the objects, logical transitions, or scope of the conclusion remain unstated.
