lessons.title: Function data, formulas, and algebraic domains
lessons.summary: Distinguish a function from its formula and graph, determine exact domains and images in elementary cases, and simplify rational expressions without changing the function's domain.
objectives: Distinguish a function from its formula and graph, determine exact domains and images in elementary cases, and simplify rational expressions without changing the function's domain.

content.markdown:
## Why the formula is not the whole function

The course will compare maps by composing them, restricting them, and asking whether they have inverses. Those questions are ill-posed until the domain and codomain are fixed. The formula $1/x$, for example, can define a function on $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ or on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$; these are different functions even though the written formula is the same.

Today is also an algebra diagnostic. A cancellation or exponent rule is valid only under its stated hypotheses, and a simplified expression does not silently restore an excluded input.

## What this lesson assumes

No earlier Course R concept is required. You may use arithmetic with real numbers, linear and quadratic equations, the ordinary laws of exponents, and the convention that division by zero is undefined.

If a rational-expression step is slow, record the exact point of difficulty. The purpose of a diagnostic is to locate a repair, not to hide it.

## Function data and composition

A function $f:X\to Y$ consists of a domain $X$, a codomain $Y$, and a rule that assigns one value $f(x)\in Y$ to each $x\in X$. Its image is the subset $f(X)=\{f(x):x\in X\}\subseteq Y$. The graph is the set $\{(x,f(x)):x\in X\}\subseteq X\times Y$. A formula can help specify the rule, but it does not by itself state the domain or codomain.

If $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$, then $g\circ f:X\to Z$ is defined by $(g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x))$. The type condition matters: every output of $f$ must be an allowed input of $g$.

A map $h:Y\to X$ is a two-sided inverse of $f$ when $h\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$ and $f\circ h=\operatorname{id}_Y$. Both identities include their domains.

content.title: Separate a rule from a function
content.introMarkdown: Determine what data the two functions share, what data differ, and compute the image of each function.

data.markdown:
First check whether your answer separately named domain, codomain, rule, graph, and image.

A later statement such as “this map is onto” can change truth value when only the codomain changes.

Rewrite the two function signatures before revising the surjectivity sentence.

content.markdown:
## Rational-expression diagnostic: record exclusions first

For $R(x)=P(x)/Q(x)$, begin with the domain condition $Q(x)\ne0$. Factoring and cancelling can give a simpler expression on that domain. Cancellation does not define the original expression at a point where $Q$ vanished.

For a nested fraction, record every denominator from the inside outward. In $1/(1+1/x)$, the inner denominator requires $x\ne0$ and the outer denominator requires $1+1/x\ne0$, hence $x\ne-1$.

The next checkpoint contains the first ten of the syllabus's twenty rational expressions. Treat it as a diagnostic set: for each item, write the original domain before simplifying, show the factorization or common denominator that licenses the step, and keep every original exclusion in the final line.

content.title: Simplify rational expressions 1–10
content.introMarkdown: For every item, state the maximal real domain of the original expression, give the simplified formula on that domain, and identify the factor or denominator that controls each exclusion.

data.markdown:
In your numbered set, locate the earliest item whose original nonzero condition is missing or was checked only after cancellation.

A correct simplified formula on the wrong domain describes a different function.

Restore the domain calculation before keeping any later algebraic step.

content.markdown:
## Verify an inverse in both directions

Consider $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $f(x)=2x+3$, and $h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $h(y)=(y-3)/2$. The composites are well-typed because both maps have domain and codomain $\mathbb R$.

Direct calculation gives $h(f(x))=x$ for every $x\in\mathbb R$ and $f(h(y))=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$. The two identities prove that $h$ is a two-sided inverse. One identity alone would give only a one-sided inverse.

content.title: Type-check two inverse identities
content.introMarkdown: Compute both $h\circ f$ and $f\circ h$, including their domains, and decide whether $h$ is a two-sided inverse of $f$.

data.markdown:
Check first whether each composition was written in a type-correct order.

An algebraically plausible expression is not a composition unless the intermediate value belongs to the next domain.

Write the source and target of each composite, then recompute the identity that is still missing.

content.markdown:
## Boundary: a graph can hide a missing point

The functions $p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $p(x)=x+1$, and $q:\mathbb R\setminus\{1\}\to\mathbb R$, $q(x)=(x^2-1)/(x-1)$ agree at every input in the domain of $q$. They are not equal as functions because their domains differ.

A graph drawn at ordinary scale may make the missing point hard to see. The declared domain remains authoritative.

content.title: Diagnose a hidden hole
content.introMarkdown: Determine whether the two functions are equal, whether their formulas agree on the common domain, and how their graphs differ as sets of ordered pairs.

data.markdown:
If your image lost the value $6$, check whether another input still maps to $6$.

Removing one point from a domain removes an image value only when that point was its last preimage.

Solve $x^2+x=6$ before revising the image.

content.markdown:
## Complete model: invert a rational map without losing its types

Let $r:\mathbb R\setminus\{-1\}\to\mathbb R\setminus\{1\}$ be $r(x)=(x-1)/(x+1)$.

Find a candidate inverse, prove that its domain is exactly $\mathbb R\setminus\{1\}$, and verify both composition identities.

### Strategy

Set $y=(x-1)/(x+1)$ and solve for $x$. Then use the resulting formula to determine where the inverse denominator vanishes. Finally compute the two composites separately.

### Hypotheses

The source variable satisfies $x\ne-1$. The proposed target excludes $y=1$. No cancellation may use a denominator before its nonzero condition has been checked.

### Intermediate claims

From $y(x+1)=x-1$, obtain $x(y-1)=-(1+y)$. Since $y\ne1$,

$$x=\frac{1+y}{1-y}.$$

Define $s:\mathbb R\setminus\{1\}\to\mathbb R\setminus\{-1\}$ by $s(y)=(1+y)/(1-y)$. The value $s(y)$ cannot equal $-1$, because $(1+y)/(1-y)=-1$ would imply $1=-1$.

### Justification

For $x\ne-1$,

$$s(r(x))=\frac{1+(x-1)/(x+1)}{1-(x-1)/(x+1)}=x.$$

For $y\ne1$,

$$r(s(y))=\frac{(1+y)/(1-y)-1}{(1+y)/(1-y)+1}=y.$$

Each simplification is valid on the declared domain.

### Conclusion

The function $s$ is the two-sided inverse of $r$. The excluded values $-1$ and $1$ are part of the proof, not bookkeeping added afterward.

content.title: Invert a new rational function
content.introMarkdown: Derive a function $h:\mathbb R\setminus\{2\}\to\mathbb R\setminus\{4\}$ and prove that it is the two-sided inverse of $f$.

data.markdown:
Inspect the first line where you divided by $y-2$ or by $x-4$ without tying it to the declared domain.

The inverse formula and the composition identities are valid only for the typed functions in the question.

Correct the exceptional-value argument first, then recompute only the affected composition.

content.markdown:
## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-01, source lines 559 to 572.

**Resource version:** Khan Academy Precalculus, Course R registry snapshot 2026-07-28.

**Exact locator:** Units on composite functions, inverse functions, domain, range, and function notation in Khan Academy Precalculus course index.

**Reading purpose:** Review only the function data or inverse-function subtopic exposed by today's diagnostic; the complete assessed problems are stated in this lesson.

## Next: composition as an argument, not a substitution trick

Day 2 will use typed compositions to prove consequences of one-sided inverses. It will also return to the nested rational equation and solve it by reversing a composite in the correct order.
A complete function includes its domain and codomain. Algebra may simplify its rule on the original domain, while a two-sided inverse must satisfy two type-correct composition identities.

activities.title: Separate a rule from a function
activities.promptMarkdown:
Consider the rule $x\mapsto x^2$ first as $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and then as $g:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$.

Determine what data the two functions share, what data differ, and compute the image of each function.

Explain why the formula and graph coordinates are the same while the codomains differ. State whether each function is surjective onto its declared codomain.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
Both functions have domain $\mathbb R$ and use the rule $x\mapsto x^2$. Their graphs have the same ordered pairs $(x,x^2)$. Their images are both $[0,\infty)$.

The codomain of $f$ is $\mathbb R$, so $f$ is not surjective: no negative real number is a square. The codomain of $g$ is $[0,\infty)$, which equals its image, so $g$ is surjective. The formula therefore does not determine surjectivity without the codomain.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The response identifies the shared rule and graph, distinguishes the codomains, and gives the image $[0,\infty)$ for both maps.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: The surjectivity claims are justified by comparing each image with its declared codomain.

activities.title: Simplify rational expressions 1–10
activities.promptMarkdown:
Simplify these ten rational expressions over $\mathbb R$ without a calculator:
1. $\dfrac{x^2-1}{x-1}$.
2. $\dfrac{x^2-4}{x+2}$.
3. $\dfrac{x^2+5x+6}{x+2}$.
4. $\dfrac{x^2-9}{x^2-3x}$.
5. $\dfrac{x^2-2x}{x^2-4x+4}$.
6. $\dfrac{1}{1+1/x}$.
7. $\dfrac{1}{1-1/x}$.
8. $\dfrac{1/x+1/y}{1/(xy)}$.
9. $\dfrac{x^{-1}-y^{-1}}{x-y}$.
10. $\dfrac{(x+1)/x}{(x+1)/(x-1)}$.

For every item, state the maximal real domain of the original expression, give the simplified formula on that domain, and identify the factor or denominator that controls each exclusion.

Number the ten solutions. Do not merge the domain statements into one general disclaimer: each expression needs its own domain and decisive algebraic step.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
1. $(x^2-1)/(x-1)=x+1$ for $x\ne1$; the cancelled factor is $x-1$.

2. $(x^2-4)/(x+2)=x-2$ for $x\ne-2$; factor $x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)$.

3. $(x^2+5x+6)/(x+2)=x+3$ for $x\ne-2$; factor the numerator as $(x+2)(x+3)$.

4. $(x^2-9)/(x^2-3x)=(x+3)/x$ for $x\ne0,3$; cancel $x-3$ only after factoring the denominator as $x(x-3)$.

5. $(x^2-2x)/(x^2-4x+4)=x/(x-2)$ for $x\ne2$; the denominator is $(x-2)^2$.

6. $1/(1+1/x)=x/(x+1)$ for $x\ne0,-1$; the inner reciprocal excludes $0$ and the outer denominator excludes $-1$.

7. $1/(1-1/x)=x/(x-1)$ for $x\ne0,1$.

8. $(1/x+1/y)/(1/(xy))=x+y$ for $x\ne0$ and $y\ne0$.

9. $(x^{-1}-y^{-1})/(x-y)=-1/(xy)$ for $x\ne0$, $y\ne0$, and $x\ne y$.

10. $((x+1)/x)/((x+1)/(x-1))=(x-1)/x$ for $x\ne-1,0,1$; besides the written denominators, the divisor $(x+1)/(x-1)$ must be nonzero.

Every equality is an equality on the original domain. A simplified formula does not restore a cancelled or previously undefined input.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: All ten simplified formulas are correct and each original maximal domain is stated.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: Every cancellation, negative power, nested denominator, and division by a rational expression is tied to its specific nonzero condition.

activities.title: Type-check two inverse identities
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be $f(x)=5x-7$ and let $h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be $h(y)=(y+7)/5$.

Compute both $h\circ f$ and $f\circ h$, including their domains, and decide whether $h$ is a two-sided inverse of $f$.

Write the two composite calculations on separate lines. Finish by matching each result to the correct identity map.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
Both composites are maps from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R$. For every $x\in\mathbb R$,

$$h(f(x))=\frac{(5x-7)+7}{5}=x,$$

so $h\circ f=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R}$. For every $y\in\mathbb R$,

$$f(h(y))=5\frac{y+7}{5}-7=y,$$

so $f\circ h=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R}$. Both identities hold, hence $h$ is a two-sided inverse of $f$.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: Both compositions are computed correctly and identified with the identity on the correct copy of $\mathbb R$.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: The conclusion that $h$ is a two-sided inverse explicitly depends on both identities.

activities.title: Diagnose a hidden hole
activities.promptMarkdown:
Compare $u:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $u(x)=x^2+x$, with $v:\mathbb R\setminus\{2\}\to\mathbb R$, $v(x)=x(x+1)$.

Determine whether the two functions are equal, whether their formulas agree on the common domain, and how their graphs differ as sets of ordered pairs.

Give one ordered pair that belongs to the graph of $u$ but not to the graph of $v$. Then state the image of $v$ as precisely as you can.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
The formulas $x^2+x$ and $x(x+1)$ agree for every real $x$, so they agree on the common domain $\mathbb R\setminus\{2\}$. The functions are not equal because their domains differ.

The pair $(2,6)$ belongs to the graph of $u$ and is missing from the graph of $v$. Since the value $6$ also occurs at $x=-3$, removing $x=2$ does not remove $6$ from the image. The quadratic $x^2+x$ has minimum $-1/4$, so the image of $v$ remains $[-1/4,\infty)$.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The response distinguishes formula agreement from function equality, identifies the missing graph point $(2,6)$, and gives the image $[-1/4,\infty)$.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: The image claim accounts for the second preimage $-3$ of the value $6$ rather than assuming that a missing input always removes an output.

activities.title: Invert a new rational function
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $f:\mathbb R\setminus\{4\}\to\mathbb R\setminus\{2\}$ be $f(x)=(2x+3)/(x-4)$.

Derive a function $h:\mathbb R\setminus\{2\}\to\mathbb R\setminus\{4\}$ and prove that it is the two-sided inverse of $f$.

Solve $y=f(x)$ for $x$, justify both excluded values, and calculate $h\circ f$ and $f\circ h$ on their exact domains.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The proposed inverse is $h(y)=(4y+3)/(y-2)$, both exceptional values are justified, and both composite identities are correct.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: Every division is licensed by a stated nonzero condition, and the conclusion names the exact domains and codomains.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
Solve $y=(2x+3)/(x-4)$:

$$y(x-4)=2x+3,\qquad x(y-2)=4y+3.$$

Because $y\ne2$, define

$$h(y)=\frac{4y+3}{y-2}.$$

This value cannot equal $4$, since $(4y+3)/(y-2)=4$ would imply $3=-8$. Thus $h$ maps $\mathbb R\setminus\{2\}$ into $\mathbb R\setminus\{4\}$.

For $x\ne4$, direct substitution and collection over the nonzero denominator $x-4$ give $h(f(x))=x$. For $y\ne2$, substitution into $f$ gives $f(h(y))=y$. Therefore $h$ is the two-sided inverse of $f$ with the stated source and target.

lessons.title: Composition, one-sided inverses, and proof
lessons.summary: Use typed composition to prove the injective and surjective consequences of one-sided inverses, then reverse a composite to solve a nested rational equation on its exact domain.
objectives: Use typed composition to prove the injective and surjective consequences of one-sided inverses, then reverse a composite to solve a nested rational equation on its exact domain.

content.markdown:
## Composition exposes structure

Substitution can compute a composite, but typed composition also carries logical information. If a map can be undone on the left, two inputs with the same image must have been equal. If it can be undone on the right, every target value has a preimage.

These claims are small enough to prove completely. They are the right place to begin treating algebraic strings as arguments whose assumptions, intermediate equalities, and conclusions must all be explicit.

## Retrieve the function data

For $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$, the composite $g\circ f:X\to Z$ is defined by $(g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x))$. Before composing, check that the codomain of the inner map matches the domain of the outer map.

A left inverse of $f$ is a map $g:Y\to X$ with $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$. A right inverse is a map $h:Y\to X$ with $f\circ h=\operatorname{id}_Y$.

## What makes a calculation a proof

A proof derives a stated conclusion from stated hypotheses through justified steps. For a map theorem, begin by naming the functions and their types. Expand the definition of the property to be proved. Then mark the exact step where each inverse identity is used.

To prove that $f$ is injective, start with arbitrary $x_1,x_2\in X$ satisfying $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ and derive $x_1=x_2$. To prove that $f$ is surjective, start with an arbitrary $y\in Y$ and construct $x\in X$ such that $f(x)=y$.

content.title: State the proof obligations
content.introMarkdown: State the exact hypotheses and the arbitrary-element proof obligation needed to prove that $f$ is injective.

data.markdown:
Check first whether your assumed equality is $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ rather than the desired conclusion $x_1=x_2$.

A proof of injectivity must show that equality of outputs forces equality of inputs.

Rewrite the implication with its universal pair of inputs before reading the model.

content.markdown:
## Complete proof model: a left inverse forces injectivity

Let $f:X\to Y$ have a left inverse $g:Y\to X$, so $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$.

Prove from the definitions that $f$ is injective.

### Strategy

Expand injectivity. Begin with equal outputs, apply the same function $g$ to both sides, and then use the left-inverse identity.

### Hypotheses

The maps have types $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to X$. The identity $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$ holds at every point of $X$.

### Intermediate claims

Take arbitrary $x_1,x_2\in X$ and assume $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$. Applying $g$ gives $g(f(x_1))=g(f(x_2))$.

### Justification

Because $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$, the last equality becomes $x_1=x_2$. Applying $g$ was legal because both values $f(x_i)$ lie in $Y$, the domain of $g$.

### Conclusion

Every pair of inputs with equal images is equal. Therefore $f$ is injective.

content.title: Reconstruct the decisive equality
content.introMarkdown: Write the shortest complete equality chain from $x_1$ to $x_2$ and annotate the use of the left-inverse identity.

data.markdown:
Find the first equality that does not follow either from $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ or from $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$.

The proof is only as strong as the first unsupported equality in its chain.

Label the source of each equality, then delete any unused hypothesis.

content.markdown:
## A right inverse forces surjectivity

Suppose $h:Y\to X$ satisfies $f\circ h=\operatorname{id}_Y$. Given any $y\in Y$, the element $h(y)\in X$ is a candidate preimage. The identity gives $f(h(y))=y$.

This proof has a different shape from the injectivity proof. It constructs an input for an arbitrary target rather than comparing two inputs.

content.title: Prove the right-inverse consequence
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $f$ is surjective by constructing a preimage of an arbitrary $y\in Y$.

data.markdown:
Check whether the chosen preimage was written as $h(y)$ and shown to lie in $X$.

Surjectivity is an existence claim for every target value, so the proof must construct an input in the correct domain.

Start the revision with an arbitrary $y\in Y$ and keep only steps that construct and verify its preimage.

content.markdown:
## Boundary: one side does not supply the other

Let $i:\{0\}\to\{0,1\}$ be the inclusion and let $r:\{0,1\}\to\{0\}$ be the only possible map. Then $r\circ i=\operatorname{id}_{\{0\}}$, while $i\circ r$ sends both elements to $0$ and is not $\operatorname{id}_{\{0,1\}}$.

The map $i$ has a left inverse and is injective, but it is not surjective. The map $r$ has a right inverse and is surjective, but it is not injective.

content.title: Build both one-sided counterexamples
content.introMarkdown: State both function tables, compute both possible composites, and identify which inverse identity holds.

data.markdown:
Check the direction of each composite before assigning the labels left inverse and right inverse.

Changing the order of composition changes both the domain and the theorem it supports.

Write the source and target above each composite, then recompute the function table that failed.

content.markdown:
## Complete calculation model: reverse a nested composite

Solve $1/(2+1/x)=1/3$ over $\mathbb R$.

Express the equation as a composite, reverse the component maps, and verify the solution on the exact domain.

### Strategy

Use the reciprocal $r(t)=1/t$ and translation $q(t)=2+t$. The expression is $(r\circ q\circ r)(x)$. Determine the domain before applying inverses in reverse order.

### Hypotheses

The inner reciprocal requires $x\ne0$. The outer reciprocal requires $2+1/x\ne0$, equivalently $x\ne-1/2$.

### Intermediate claims

The equation is $(r\circ q\circ r)(x)=1/3$. Since $r^{-1}=r$ and $q^{-1}(u)=u-2$, reverse the maps:

$$(q\circ r)(x)=3,\qquad r(x)=1,\qquad x=1.$$

### Justification

Each inverse is applied to both sides while its input lies in the correct domain. The candidate $1$ is not excluded.

### Conclusion

Substitution gives $1/(2+1)=1/3$, so the solution set is $\{1\}$. The domain check prevents extraneous use of a reciprocal.

content.title: Set up the target composite
content.introMarkdown: Determine the exact domain of $r\circ s\circ r$, rewrite the equation as a composite, and apply only the inverse of the outer $r$.

data.markdown:
Check the outermost operation first: its inverse must be applied before the translation or the inner reciprocal is undone.

Inverse maps reverse the order of a composite, so one misplaced step changes the equation.

Write the composite with parentheses and cross out only the outer $r$ before continuing.

content.markdown:
## Boundary: numerical agreement is not a proof

A calculation at finitely many inputs can reveal an error, but agreement at those inputs does not establish an identity on an infinite domain. Given tested inputs $a_1,\ldots,a_n$, the nonzero polynomial $P(x)=\prod_{j=1}^n(x-a_j)$ vanishes at every tested point.

Exact algebra can prove an identity when it reduces the difference to the zero expression under stated hypotheses.

content.title: Separate evidence from proof
content.introMarkdown: Decide what this agreement proves and construct a nonzero polynomial that also vanishes at all five inputs.

data.markdown:
If your counterexample is the zero polynomial, replace it with a product having exactly the tested values as roots.

The counterexample must be nonzero to distinguish numerical agreement from polynomial identity.

Multiply one linear factor for each tested input and verify one factor vanishes at each point.

content.markdown:
## Complete the target without copying the model

Return to $1/(1+1/x)=2$. Keep the corrected domain and first reversed step. Apply the remaining inverses in reverse order, then test the candidate in the original nested expression.

Your written solution should make the logical order visible: domain, typed composite, reverse operations, candidate, membership in the domain, and substitution.

content.introMarkdown: Give a complete domain-aware solution, applying the inverse maps in reverse order and verifying the final value in the original equation.

data.markdown:
Compare your first incorrect or missing step with the ordered list: domain, outer inverse, translation inverse, inner inverse, verification.

A correct final number does not show that every transformation preserved the original equation.

Repair the earliest broken transition and recompute forward from that point.

## Next: classify maps and control one-sided inverses

Day 3 will define injectivity and surjectivity together, construct the three requested kinds of examples, and use the composition proof method to prove uniqueness of a two-sided inverse.

A left inverse proves injectivity, a right inverse proves surjectivity, and neither one-sided identity alone proves a two-sided inverse. Reversing a composite is valid only after its component maps and exact domain are fixed.

activities.title: State the proof obligations
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to X$ satisfy $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$.

State the exact hypotheses and the arbitrary-element proof obligation needed to prove that $f$ is injective.

Do not prove the result yet. Write the typed maps, the inverse identity, the assumed equality, and the equality that must be derived.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
The typed data are $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to X$. The hypothesis is $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$.

For arbitrary $x_1,x_2\in X$, assume $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$. The proof obligation is to derive $x_1=x_2$. Establishing that implication for every such pair proves that $f$ is injective.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The response states both map types, the identity $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$, and the injectivity implication for arbitrary $x_1,x_2\in X$.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: The conclusion is not assumed, and no right-inverse identity is added.

activities.title: Reconstruct the decisive equality
activities.promptMarkdown:
Assume $f:X\to Y$, $g:Y\to X$, $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$, and $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ for $x_1,x_2\in X$.

Write the shortest complete equality chain from $x_1$ to $x_2$ and annotate the use of the left-inverse identity.

Explain why every composition in the chain is well-typed. End by naming the property of $f$ that has been proved.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The equality chain begins at $x_1$, ends at $x_2$, and uses the left-inverse identity at the correct two positions.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: The response checks the types and concludes injectivity rather than surjectivity or bijectivity.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
$$x_1=(g\circ f)(x_1)=g(f(x_1))=g(f(x_2))=(g\circ f)(x_2)=x_2.$$

The first and last equalities use $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$. The middle equality applies $g$ to the assumed equality $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$. It is well-typed because $f(x_i)\in Y$, the domain of $g$. Thus $f$ is injective.

activities.title: Prove the right-inverse consequence
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $f:X\to Y$ and $h:Y\to X$ satisfy $f\circ h=\operatorname{id}_Y$.

Prove that $f$ is surjective by constructing a preimage of an arbitrary $y\in Y$.

Name the candidate preimage, verify that it belongs to $X$, and use the right-inverse identity exactly once.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: For arbitrary $y\in Y$, the response chooses $h(y)\in X$ and proves $f(h(y))=y$.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: The final sentence invokes the definition of surjectivity and does not claim injectivity.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
Take an arbitrary $y\in Y$. Since $h:Y\to X$, the element $x=h(y)$ belongs to $X$. The right-inverse identity gives

$$f(x)=f(h(y))=(f\circ h)(y)=\operatorname{id}_Y(y)=y.$$

Thus every $y\in Y$ has a preimage in $X$, so $f$ is surjective.

activities.title: Build both one-sided counterexamples
activities.promptMarkdown:
Use the sets $A=\{0\}$ and $B=\{0,1\}$ to construct an injective nonsurjective map and a surjective noninjective map linked by one-sided inverse identities.

State both function tables, compute both possible composites, and identify which inverse identity holds.

Explain why neither one-sided identity proves that the two maps are mutual inverses.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
Define $i:A\to B$ by $i(0)=0$ and $r:B\to A$ by $r(0)=r(1)=0$. The map $i$ is injective and misses $1$, so it is not surjective. The map $r$ is surjective and satisfies $r(0)=r(1)$ with $0\ne1$, so it is not injective.

The composite $r\circ i:A\to A$ fixes $0$, hence equals $\operatorname{id}_A$. The composite $i\circ r:B\to B$ sends both $0$ and $1$ to $0$, hence is not $\operatorname{id}_B$. Only the left-inverse identity holds for $i$; mutual inverses require both identities.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The two maps have correct types and tables, their injective or surjective status is correct, and both composites are computed.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: The response names the one identity that holds and explains why the missing identity prevents a two-sided inverse.

activities.title: Set up the target composite
activities.promptMarkdown:
For $1/(1+1/x)=2$ over $\mathbb R$, let $r(t)=1/t$ and $s(t)=1+t$ with their natural typed domains.

Determine the exact domain of $r\circ s\circ r$, rewrite the equation as a composite, and apply only the inverse of the outer $r$.

Stop after the first reversed step. State which restrictions come from the inner and outer reciprocals.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
The inner reciprocal requires $x\ne0$. The outer reciprocal requires $1+1/x\ne0$, so $x\ne-1$. Hence the composite has domain $D=\mathbb R\setminus\{0,-1\}$.

The equation is $(r\circ s\circ r)(x)=2$. Applying only $r^{-1}=r$ gives

$$(s\circ r)(x)=r(2)=\frac12.$$

No later inverse has yet been applied.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The domain is $\mathbb R\setminus\{0,-1\}$, the composite is ordered correctly, and the first reversed equation is $(s\circ r)(x)=1/2$.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: The response stops at the requested point and assigns each exclusion to the denominator that creates it.

activities.title: Separate evidence from proof
activities.promptMarkdown:
Two polynomial expressions agree at the five inputs $-2,-1,0,1,2$.

Decide what this agreement proves and construct a nonzero polynomial that also vanishes at all five inputs.

Use the constructed polynomial to explain why five numerical checks cannot prove equality of arbitrary polynomial expressions.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
The agreement is evidence that the expressions may be equal, but it does not prove an identity. The nonzero polynomial

$$P(x)=(x+2)(x+1)x(x-1)(x-2)$$

vanishes at all five tested inputs. Thus the zero polynomial and $P$ agree on the five tests but are not the same polynomial. A proof needs exact symbolic reasoning or an applicable theorem with a degree bound and enough roots.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The response gives a correct nonzero polynomial vanishing at all five listed inputs and states that the tests provide evidence only.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: The conclusion is limited to arbitrary polynomial identities and does not invoke an unstated degree bound.

activities.title: Solve the nested equation completely
activities.promptMarkdown:
Solve $1/(1+1/x)=2$ over $\mathbb R$ by treating the left side as $r\circ s\circ r$.

Give a complete domain-aware solution, applying the inverse maps in reverse order and verifying the final value in the original equation.

State the inverse of each component map, show every reversed step, and give the solution set.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
Let $r:\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ be $r(t)=1/t$ and $s:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be $s(t)=1+t$. Then $r^{-1}=r$ and $s^{-1}(u)=u-1$.

The composite has domain $D=\mathbb R\setminus\{0,-1\}$. From $(r\circ s\circ r)(x)=2$, reverse the maps:

$$(s\circ r)(x)=\frac12,$$

$$r(x)=-\frac12,$$

$$x=-2.$$

The value $-2$ belongs to $D$, and $1/(1+1/(-2))=2$. Therefore the solution set is $\{-2\}$.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The response obtains the exact domain, reverses $r\circ s\circ r$ in the correct order, finds $x=-2$, and verifies it.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: Every inverse application is justified by its type and the final statement gives the exact solution set rather than only a candidate.

lessons.title: Injective, surjective, bijective, and inverse
lessons.summary: Classify maps as injective, surjective, or bijective; construct one-sided inverse counterexamples; and write a complete proof that a two-sided inverse is unique.
objectives: Classify maps as injective, surjective, or bijective; construct one-sided inverse counterexamples; and write a complete proof that a two-sided inverse is unique.

content.markdown:
## Three different questions about a map

Injectivity asks whether two inputs can share an output. Surjectivity asks whether every declared target value is reached. Bijectivity requires both. The distinctions are global: they involve every relevant input or every target value.

An inverse packages both properties. The proof that a two-sided inverse is unique will show how two composition identities interact, rather than treating “undoing” as an informal picture.

## Reactivate typed functions

A statement about injectivity or surjectivity refers to a function $f:X\to Y$, not to an untyped formula. The image is $f(X)\subseteq Y$. The map is surjective exactly when $f(X)=Y$.

From Day 2, retain the two one-sided results: a left inverse implies injectivity, and a right inverse implies surjectivity.

## Definitions and diagnostic examples

A function $f:X\to Y$ is injective if $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ implies $x_1=x_2$ for all $x_1,x_2\in X$. It is surjective if for every $y\in Y$ there exists $x\in X$ with $f(x)=y$. It is bijective if it is both injective and surjective.

The shift $s:\mathbb N_0\to\mathbb N_0$, $s(n)=n+1$, is injective and misses $0$. The absolute-value map $a:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb N_0$, $a(n)=|n|$, is surjective and satisfies $a(1)=a(-1)$. The affine map $x\mapsto2x+3$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R$ is bijective.

A two-sided inverse exists exactly for a bijection. This week proves the consequences directly; later weeks will place them inside a broader theory of maps.

content.title: Classify three typed maps
content.introMarkdown: For each map, decide whether it is injective and whether it is surjective onto its declared codomain.

data.markdown:
Check whether a missing value was tested against the declared codomain rather than against the real numbers by habit.

Surjectivity can change when the formula stays fixed and only the codomain changes.

Rewrite each function signature beside its image before revising the classification.

content.markdown:
## One-sided inverses need not be unique

Let $i:\{0\}\to\{0,1,2\}$ be the inclusion $i(0)=0$. A left inverse $r:\{0,1,2\}\to\{0\}$ is forced here because the codomain has one point. To see genuine nonuniqueness, enlarge the source instead.

Let $j:\{0,1\}\to\{0,1,2\}$ be the inclusion. Any left inverse $r:\{0,1,2\}\to\{0,1\}$ must satisfy $r(0)=0$ and $r(1)=1$, but $r(2)$ may be either $0$ or $1$. The freedom lies outside the image of $j$.

A two-sided inverse has no such freedom because the other composition controls every point of the larger set.

content.title: Locate the freedom outside the image
content.introMarkdown: Construct two distinct maps $r_1,r_2:\{a,b,c,d\}\to\{a,b\}$ satisfying $r_i\circ j=\operatorname{id}_{\{a,b\}}$.

data.markdown:
Check whether both proposed maps fix $a$ and $b$ after composition with the inclusion.

A map is a left inverse only when it undoes the inclusion on every point of the smaller source.

Fix the values on the image first; vary only the values at $c$ and $d$.

content.markdown:
## Complete proof model: uniqueness from two-sided identities

Let $a$ be a nonzero real number and suppose $b,c\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $ab=ba=1$ and $ac=ca=1$.

Prove that the two proposed reciprocals $b$ and $c$ are equal.

### Strategy

Start with one candidate, insert an identity involving the other candidate, reassociate, and then use the remaining identity.

### Hypotheses

The multiplication is associative. The displayed equations state that both $b$ and $c$ undo multiplication by $a$ on both sides.

### Intermediate claims

Insert $ac=1$ after $b$: $b=b\cdot1=b(ac)$. Associativity gives $b(ac)=(ba)c$.

### Justification

Since $ba=1$, the last expression is $(ba)c=1\cdot c=c$.

### Conclusion

Therefore $b=c$. The proof uses one identity from each proposed reciprocal and associativity to connect them.

content.title: Plan the inverse-uniqueness proof
content.introMarkdown: Prepare a proof plan for $g=h$ that lists the four composition identities, the identity map to insert, and the role of associativity.

data.markdown:
Check whether the identity inserted beside $g$ is $\operatorname{id}_Y=f\circ h$, whose source and target allow the composition.

Using $h\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$ in that position would produce a type mismatch.

Write the source and target above $g$, $f$, and $h$, then choose the identity map on the intermediate set.

content.markdown:
## Build the central chain one justified equality at a time

The proof begins with $h=h\circ\operatorname{id}_Y$. To introduce the other inverse $k$, replace $\operatorname{id}_Y$ by $f\circ k$. Associativity then exposes $h\circ f$, which can be replaced by $\operatorname{id}_X$.

Every equality has one job: insert an identity, use an inverse hypothesis, reassociate, or close the target.

content.title: Justify the middle equality
content.introMarkdown: Complete and justify the chain $h=h\circ\operatorname{id}_Y=h\circ(f\circ k)=\cdots=k$.

data.markdown:
Find the first adjacent pair of maps whose source and target do not match, or the first equality with no named law.

The decisive proof step is a typed associativity argument, not a rearrangement of symbols.

Restore the types, then annotate the chain from left to right before rewriting it as prose.

content.markdown:
## Why both sides appear in the proof

The uniqueness chain uses $f\circ k=\operatorname{id}_Y$ to insert $f\circ k$ and uses $h\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$ to remove $h\circ f$. A left-inverse identity for each candidate would not supply the first replacement.

The inclusion example showed the resulting freedom: two left inverses can agree on the image and differ elsewhere. The final proof must therefore name the side used at each step.

content.title: Prove two-sided inverse uniqueness
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $g=h$, with every function type, inverse identity, and use of associativity explicit.

data.markdown:
Inspect the first equality whose source and target are not both $Y\to X$, or whose inverse identity has the wrong order.

A proof of uniqueness depends on a type-correct chain that reaches the second candidate without assuming the conclusion.

Repair the first invalid equality, then relabel the exact left- or right-inverse hypothesis used at every later replacement.

## Next: local behavior, global collisions, and exact computation

Day 4 will preview the difference between local and global injectivity without using Jacobians. It will also use symbolic composition to separate exact algebraic proof from finite numerical evidence.

Injectivity compares inputs with equal outputs, surjectivity constructs an input for every target, and bijectivity combines both. Two-sided inverse uniqueness follows from a typed equality chain that uses one identity on each side.

activities.title: Classify three typed maps
activities.promptMarkdown:
Classify $s:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$, $s(n)=n+2$; $q:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb N_0$, $q(n)=n^2$; and $c:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $c(x)=x^2$.

For each map, decide whether it is injective and whether it is surjective onto its declared codomain.

Give either a definition-based proof or one explicit collision or omitted target value for every negative classification.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
The shift $s$ is injective because $n_1+2=n_2+2$ implies $n_1=n_2$. It is surjective because $m=s(m-2)$ for every $m\in\mathbb Z$. Hence $s$ is bijective.

The square map $q$ is not injective because $q(1)=q(-1)$. It is not surjective onto $\mathbb N_0$ because, for example, $2$ is not an integer square.

The real square map $c$ is not injective because $c(1)=c(-1)$. It is not surjective onto $\mathbb R$ because no negative real lies in its image.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: All six injective or surjective classifications are correct.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: Each negative claim has a valid collision or missing target, and each positive claim is proved from arbitrary elements.

activities.title: Locate the freedom outside the image
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $j:\{a,b\}\to\{a,b,c,d\}$ be the inclusion.

Construct two distinct maps $r_1,r_2:\{a,b,c,d\}\to\{a,b\}$ satisfying $r_i\circ j=\operatorname{id}_{\{a,b\}}$.

Give both function tables, verify the left-inverse identity, and explain exactly which values remain unconstrained.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
Both maps must satisfy $r_i(a)=a$ and $r_i(b)=b$. For example, define $r_1(c)=r_1(d)=a$ and define $r_2(c)=r_2(d)=b$. Then each composite $r_i\circ j$ fixes $a$ and $b$, so both equal the identity on $\{a,b\}$.

The maps are distinct because, for example, $r_1(c)=a\ne b=r_2(c)$. The left-inverse identity constrains values only on the image $\{a,b\}$ of $j$; the values at $c,d$ are free. Thus a left inverse need not be unique.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: Two distinct complete function tables are supplied and both satisfy $r_i\circ j=\operatorname{id}_{\{a,b\}}$.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: The response identifies the complement of the image as the source of nonuniqueness and does not claim a two-sided inverse.

activities.title: Plan the inverse-uniqueness proof
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $f:X\to Y$ and suppose $g,h:Y\to X$ are both two-sided inverses of $f$.

Prepare a proof plan for $g=h$ that lists the four composition identities, the identity map to insert, and the role of associativity.

Do not write the full equality chain. State which candidate the chain starts from and which candidate it must reach.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
The hypotheses are $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$, $f\circ g=\operatorname{id}_Y$, $h\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$, and $f\circ h=\operatorname{id}_Y$.

Start from $g:Y\to X$. Insert $\operatorname{id}_Y=f\circ h$ on its input side, reassociate $g\circ(f\circ h)$ as $(g\circ f)\circ h$, and replace $g\circ f$ by $\operatorname{id}_X$. The chain then reaches $h$. Associativity of composition licenses the middle regrouping.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The plan states all typed maps, the two inverse identities actually used, the identity inserted, and the target equality $g=h$.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: Associativity is named at the regrouping step, and the answer stops before expanding the full proof.

activities.title: Justify the middle equality
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $f:X\to Y$ and let $h,k:Y\to X$ be two-sided inverses of $f$.

Complete and justify the chain $h=h\circ\operatorname{id}_Y=h\circ(f\circ k)=\cdots=k$.

Label the equality that uses associativity and the equality that uses $h\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
$$h=h\circ\operatorname{id}_Y=h\circ(f\circ k)=(h\circ f)\circ k=\operatorname{id}_X\circ k=k.$$

The second equality uses $f\circ k=\operatorname{id}_Y$. The third uses associativity of composition. The fourth uses $h\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$. The final equality is the identity law on maps $Y\to X$.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The completed chain is type-correct and ends at $k$.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: Associativity and each inverse identity are attached to the exact equality where they are used.

activities.title: Prove two-sided inverse uniqueness
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $f:X\to Y$. Suppose $g,h:Y\to X$ are both two-sided inverses of $f$.

Prove that $g=h$, with every function type, inverse identity, and use of associativity explicit.

After the proof, identify one equality that uses the right-inverse side and one that uses the left-inverse side. Explain why the earlier one-sided counterexample prevents either side from being dropped without another hypothesis.

rubric.label: Typed hypotheses
rubric.description: The functions $f,g,h$ and the four composition identities are stated with the correct domains and codomains.

rubric.label: Equality chain
rubric.description: A valid chain proves $g=h$ and uses associativity at the correct step.

rubric.label: Use of both sides
rubric.description: The proof identifies the right-inverse and left-inverse identities used and explains why a one-sided assumption alone is insufficient.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
Since $g$ and $h$ are two-sided inverses,

$$g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X,\quad f\circ g=\operatorname{id}_Y,\quad h\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X,\quad f\circ h=\operatorname{id}_Y.$$

Then, as maps $Y\to X$,

$$g=g\circ\operatorname{id}_Y=g\circ(f\circ h)=(g\circ f)\circ h=\operatorname{id}_X\circ h=h.$$

The equality $g\circ\operatorname{id}_Y=g\circ(f\circ h)$ uses the right-inverse identity $f\circ h=\operatorname{id}_Y$. The equality $(g\circ f)\circ h=\operatorname{id}_X\circ h$ uses the left-inverse identity $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$. The middle regrouping uses associativity.

A left inverse alone need not be unique because it can vary away from the image of $f$, as the finite-set inclusion example shows. Thus the two-sided hypotheses supply exactly the two replacements used above.

lessons.title: Local versus global behavior and symbolic evidence
lessons.summary: Use the definition of injectivity to distinguish neighborhood restrictions from global collisions, and use exact symbolic composition to establish polynomial identities without confusing finite tests with proof.
objectives: Use the definition of injectivity to distinguish neighborhood restrictions from global collisions, and use exact symbolic composition to establish polynomial identities without confusing finite tests with proof.

content.markdown:
## A map can behave well nearby and fail globally

A global collision compares points anywhere in the domain. A local injectivity statement restricts attention to a neighborhood of one point. These are different quantifier patterns.

The course will later prove local invertibility using derivatives and Jacobians. Today gives only a concrete preview based on intervals where a familiar function is monotone. No Jacobian or local-inverse theorem is assumed or assessed.

## Retrieve injectivity through function restrictions

A restriction $f|_U:U\to Y$ uses the same rule as $f$ on a smaller domain $U\subseteq X$. The restricted function may be injective even when $f:X\to Y$ is not.

A collision is a pair $x_1\ne x_2$ with $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$. To prove injectivity on an interval, take two arbitrary points in that interval and show equal outputs force equal inputs.

## Preview: local injectivity without calculus

For this preview, say that $f:X\to Y$ is locally injective at $x_0\in X$ when there is an open interval $I$ containing $x_0$ such that the restriction to $I\cap X$ is injective. This interval formulation is enough for the examples below. The general topological and analytic definitions arrive later.

On a positive interval, the squaring function is strictly increasing. On a negative interval, it is strictly decreasing. Thus a domain made from one negative interval and one positive interval can give local injectivity at every point while retaining global collisions between $x$ and $-x$.

This block introduces the local-versus-global distinction only as vocabulary and motivation. The graded evidence below remains attached to functions, proof, and injectivity, whose definitions are already available.

content.title: Exhibit the global failure
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $f$ is not globally injective by giving a collision inside $X$.

data.markdown:
Check whether both proposed inputs lie strictly inside the two open intervals.

A collision outside the declared domain says nothing about injectivity of the restricted map.

Choose a positive point between $1$ and $2$ and its negative.

content.markdown:
## Complete model: local interval, global collision

Let $X=(-2,-1)\cup(1,2)$ and $f(x)=x^2$ on $X$.

Prove directly that the restriction is injective on a suitable interval around every $x_0\in X$, while the full function is not injective.

### Strategy

Separate the positive and negative components. Use an interval contained in the component of $x_0$, and factor equality of squares.

### Hypotheses

The point $x_0$ is nonzero and lies in exactly one component of $X$. A sufficiently small open interval around it stays entirely positive or entirely negative.

### Intermediate claims

Choose $\varepsilon>0$ so that $I=(x_0-\varepsilon,x_0+\varepsilon)$ stays in the same component of $X$. If $u,v\in I$ and $u^2=v^2$, then $(u-v)(u+v)=0$.

The numbers $u,v$ have the same strict sign, so $u+v\ne0$. Hence $u-v=0$ and $u=v$.

### Justification

The interval exists because each component is open. The factorization of $u^2-v^2$ proves injectivity on $I$. Globally, $f(3/2)=f(-3/2)$ gives a collision.

### Conclusion

The restriction is injective near every point of $X$, while $f$ is not injective on all of $X$. This is a concrete preview of the local/global distinction.

content.title: Construct a neighborhood proof
content.introMarkdown: At the point $x_0=-3$, give an explicit open interval $I$ and prove that $q|_{I\cap Y}$ is injective.

data.markdown:
Verify first that the whole interval stays in the negative component of the domain.

content.markdown:
## Complete calculation model: symbolic composition

Let $p(x)=x^2+1$ and $q(x)=2x-3$ as polynomial functions $\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$.

Compute both compositions by hand and state what an exact symbolic expansion verifies.

### Strategy

Substitute the complete inner formula before expanding. Compute the two hand expansions first, then ask SymPy to expand the same substitutions and subtract the hand results.

### Hypotheses

Both maps have domain and codomain $\mathbb R$, so both compositions are defined for every real input. SymPy must use an exact symbol, not floating-point sample values.

### Intermediate claims

$$p(q(x))=(2x-3)^2+1=4x^2-12x+10,$$

$$q(p(x))=2(x^2+1)-3=2x^2-1.$$

Run the following exact script:

```python
from sympy import symbols, expand

x = symbols("x")
p = x**2 + 1
q = 2*x - 3
p_after_q = expand(p.subs(x, q))
q_after_p = expand(q.subs(x, p))
check_pq = expand(p_after_q - (4*x**2 - 12*x + 10))
check_qp = expand(q_after_p - (2*x**2 - 1))
(p_after_q, q_after_p, check_pq, check_qp)
```

Expected output: `(4*x**2 - 12*x + 10, 2*x**2 - 1, 0, 0)`.

### Justification

The two final zeros are exact zero polynomials, not rounded numerical agreements. They certify that the SymPy expressions equal the hand expansions coefficient by coefficient.

If SymPy is unavailable, use the honest manual fallback: write both substitutions, expand by distributivity, collect like powers of $x$, and subtract the claimed polynomial. Report that exact hand check as the evidence and do not claim that code was executed.

### Conclusion

The two compositions are different polynomial functions. Exact symbolic or exact manual zero differences verify the displayed formulas for all real inputs; a finite list of matching evaluations would provide evidence only.

content.markdown:
## What exact symbolic equality proves

If exact expansion reduces the difference between two polynomial expressions to the zero polynomial, then the expressions are identical. This is an algebraic proof because the permitted operations preserve equality and every coefficient of the difference is zero.

Numerical evaluation has a different role. It can refute a proposed identity with one mismatch. It cannot prove an unrestricted identity from finitely many matches.

Day 5 combines the algebra diagnostic, typed composition, injective and surjective distinctions, and the two-sided-inverse proof. The final question requires a clean general argument rather than a symbolic check.
A restriction can be injective near each point while the full map has distant collisions. Exact symbolic equality can prove a polynomial identity, while finite numerical agreement remains evidence.

activities.title: Exhibit the global failure
activities.promptMarkdown:

Prove that $f$ is not globally injective by giving a collision inside $X$.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The points $3/2$ and $-3/2$ are distinct and both belong to $X$. Their images satisfy $f(3/2)=9/4=f(-3/2)$. Therefore $f$ is not injective on its full domain.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
Take $I=(-7/2,-5/2)$, which contains $-3$ and lies inside $(-4,-2)$. If $u,v\in I$ and $q(u)=q(v)$, then $u^2=v^2$, so $(u-v)(u+v)=0$.

Both $u$ and $v$ are negative, hence $u+v<0$ and cannot vanish. Therefore $u-v=0$, so $u=v$. Thus $q|_I$ is injective.

activities.title: Verify two polynomial compositions
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $f(x)=x^2-1$ and $g(x)=x+1$ as polynomial functions $\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$.

Compute and expand $f\circ g$ and $g\circ f$ by hand and in exact symbolic form, then state the boundary of the conclusion.

Show the substitutions and expansions. If you run SymPy, include the exact `symbols`, `subs`, `expand`, and zero-difference commands with their outputs. If no SymPy runtime is available, label the exact hand expansion as the fallback and do not claim code execution. Name one stronger claim not established by either calculation.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
$$f(g(x))=(x+1)^2-1=x^2+2x,$$

$$g(f(x))=(x^2-1)+1=x^2.$$

One exact SymPy check is:

```python
from sympy import symbols, expand
x = symbols("x")
f = x**2 - 1
g = x + 1
fg = expand(f.subs(x, g))
gf = expand(g.subs(x, f))
(expand(fg - (x**2 + 2*x)), expand(gf - x**2))
```

The expected output is `(0, 0)`. If SymPy is unavailable, expanding the two substitutions by hand and obtaining the same zero differences is the valid exact fallback; it must be reported as a hand check.

Either exact route proves the two composition formulas for every real input.

The calculation does not prove, for example, that either map or either composite is globally invertible. Such a conclusion requires a separate injectivity and surjectivity argument.

lessons.summary: Synthesize function data, rational-expression domain control, injective and surjective classifications, and a fully justified proof that a two-sided inverse is unique.

content.markdown:
## The week's pieces now have to work together

A correct inverse proof begins before the equality chain. The functions must be typed, every rational formula must retain its exclusions, and the two composition identities must be distinguished.

This is same-week synthesis. It is not a spaced-review event: no earlier scheduled interval is due in Week 1. The questions move from reconstruction to a final proof with no supplied chain.

## Reactivate the typed definition

For $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$, the composite $g\circ f$ maps $X$ to $Z$. A candidate inverse $h:Y\to X$ is two-sided when $h\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$ and $f\circ h=\operatorname{id}_Y$.

When a formula contains a denominator or a negative exponent, state the nonzero condition before simplifying.

## A compact Week 1 map

Function data answer: what are the source, target, assignment, graph, and image? Algebraic domain control answers: where is the written rule defined, and which cancellations are legal? Injectivity and surjectivity answer: does the map identify inputs, and does it reach every target? A proof records how the hypotheses force the conclusion.

The exponent law $x^m/x^n=x^{m-n}$ requires $x\ne0$ when negative powers or division occur. A cancellation such as $(t^2-1)/(t-1)=t+1$ requires $t\ne1$. These conditions remain part of the function after simplification.

## Rational-expression diagnostic: exponent rules under pressure

For a negative exponent, $x^{-n}=1/x^n$ requires $x\ne0$. In a quotient, record every written denominator and also require the entire divisor to be nonzero. Apply exponent laws only after these conditions are visible.

The next checkpoint contains expressions 11–20 of the syllabus diagnostic. Together with Day 1, they form twenty distinct rational simplifications. Work without a calculator and keep the original domain beside every simplified formula.

content.markdown:
## Complete models: linear and quadratic equations

For the linear equation $5(2t+1)-3=4t+20$, expand and collect like terms: $10t+2=4t+20$, so $6t=18$ and $t=3$. Substitution gives $5(7)-3=32=12+20$.

For the quadratic equation $2z^2+3z-2=0$, factor as $(2z-1)(z+2)=0$. The zero-product property gives $z=1/2$ or $z=-2$, and substitution verifies both roots.

The boundary matters: dividing a linear equation by its variable coefficient is legal only when that coefficient is nonzero, and factoring a quadratic is useful only when the factorization is verified. When simple integer factoring fails, the quadratic formula remains available.

content.markdown:
## Complete model: verify a non-affine inverse

Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be $f(x)=x^3+2$ and let $h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be $h(y)=\sqrt[3]{y-2}$.

Verify both composition identities and conclude that $f$ is bijective with inverse $h$.

### Strategy

Compute the two compositions on separate variables. Use that the real cube and real cube-root functions undo each other on all of $\mathbb R$.

### Hypotheses

The real cube root is defined for every real number. Thus both maps have domain and codomain $\mathbb R$, and both composites are well-typed.

### Intermediate claims

For $x\in\mathbb R$,

$$h(f(x))=\sqrt[3]{(x^3+2)-2}=x.$$

For $y\in\mathbb R$,

$$f(h(y))=(\sqrt[3]{y-2})^3+2=y.$$

### Justification

The first equality uses $\sqrt[3]{x^3}=x$ for real $x$. The second uses $(\sqrt[3]{u})^3=u$ for real $u$.

### Conclusion

Both identity maps are obtained, so $h$ is the two-sided inverse of $f$. Hence $f$ is bijective.

## Final synthesis

Write the general inverse-uniqueness proof without copying the chain from Day 3. Then connect it to the week's diagnostic: explain why a function must be typed, why a formula may retain excluded inputs after simplification, and why one-sided inverse evidence is insufficient.

The final answer should read as one coherent argument with a short preliminary distinction, the proof, and one boundary example.

## Next week: polynomial arithmetic

Week 2 treats polynomial addition, multiplication, long division, the factor and remainder theorems, root multiplicity, and degree. The domain discipline and proof structure from this week will control every cancellation and divisibility claim.

Week 1 is complete when you can manipulate the algebra without losing its domain, classify a typed map, distinguish one-sided from two-sided inverse evidence, and prove inverse uniqueness from first principles.

activities.title: Reconstruct composition and inverse
activities.promptMarkdown:
Without consulting the earlier pages, consider typed functions $f:X\to Y$ and $h:Y\to X$.

State the definition of a two-sided inverse and identify the source and target of each composite.

Give one error that would invalidate an inverse check, and explain which identity would remain unproved.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
The function $h$ is a two-sided inverse of $f$ when

$$h\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X\quad\text{and}\quad f\circ h=\operatorname{id}_Y.$$

The composite $h\circ f$ maps $X$ to $X$, while $f\circ h$ maps $Y$ to $Y$. Checking only $h\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$ leaves the second identity unproved, so it establishes only that $h$ is a left inverse of $f$.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: Both inverse identities and the source and target of each composite are correct.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: The invalidating error identifies a genuinely missing or mistyped identity and states the resulting logical limit.

activities.title: Simplify rational expressions 11–20
activities.promptMarkdown:
Simplify these ten rational expressions over $\mathbb R$ without a calculator:
11. $\dfrac{x^{-2}-1}{x^{-1}-1}$.
12. $\dfrac{x^{-3}-x^{-1}}{x^{-2}}$.
13. $\dfrac{a^2b^{-1}}{a^{-1}b^2}$.
14. $\dfrac{x^3-8}{x-2}$.
15. $\dfrac{x^4-1}{x^2-1}$.
16. $\dfrac{x^2+2x+1}{x^2-1}$.
17. $\dfrac{1/x-1/(x+1)}{1/(x(x+1))}$.
18. $\dfrac{x/y}{y/x}$.
19. $\dfrac{1-x^{-2}}{1-x^{-1}}$.
20. $\dfrac{(u^{-2}v^3)^2}{(u^{-1}v)^3}$.

For every item, state the original maximal real domain, simplify completely, and name the exponent law, factorization, or nonzero-divisor condition that licenses the decisive step.

Number the answers 11–20. A formula without its original domain does not count as a completed simplification.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
11. $(x^{-2}-1)/(x^{-1}-1)=(x+1)/x$ for $x\ne0,1$.

12. $(x^{-3}-x^{-1})/x^{-2}=(1-x^2)/x$ for $x\ne0$.

13. $(a^2b^{-1})/(a^{-1}b^2)=a^3/b^3$ for $a\ne0$ and $b\ne0$.

14. $(x^3-8)/(x-2)=x^2+2x+4$ for $x\ne2$.

15. $(x^4-1)/(x^2-1)=x^2+1$ for $x\ne-1,1$.

16. $(x^2+2x+1)/(x^2-1)=(x+1)/(x-1)$ for $x\ne-1,1$.

17. $(1/x-1/(x+1))/(1/(x(x+1)))=1$ for $x\ne0,-1$.

18. $(x/y)/(y/x)=x^2/y^2$ for $x\ne0$ and $y\ne0$; the divisor $y/x$ must itself be nonzero.

19. $(1-x^{-2})/(1-x^{-1})=(x+1)/x$ for $x\ne0,1$.

20. $(u^{-2}v^3)^2/(u^{-1}v)^3=v^3/u$ for $u\ne0$ and $v\ne0$.

The domains come from the original expressions, including every negative power and every rational expression used as a divisor.

rubric.description: All ten formulas are simplified correctly, including the negative-exponent and compound-fraction cases.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: Each answer retains every exclusion from the original expression and identifies the law or factorization used.

activities.title: Solve one linear and one quadratic equation
activities.promptMarkdown:
Solve the linear equation $3(2x-1)-5=4x+7$ and the quadratic equation $(y-3)(y+2)=4$ over $\mathbb R$.

Give the complete solution set of each equation and verify every proposed solution in the original equation.

Show the expansion and collection step for the linear equation. For the quadratic, reduce to standard form and use the quadratic formula or a verified factorization.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
For the linear equation, $3(2x-1)-5=4x+7$ becomes $6x-8=4x+7$, so $2x=15$ and $x=15/2$. Substitution gives $3(15-1)-5=37$ and $30+7=37$.

For the quadratic equation, $(y-3)(y+2)=4$ becomes $y^2-y-6=4$, hence $y^2-y-10=0$. The discriminant is $1+40=41$, so

$$y=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{41}}{2}.$$

Each value satisfies $y^2-y-10=0$, which is equivalent to the original equation. Thus the solution sets are $\{15/2\}$ and $\{(1-\sqrt{41})/2,(1+\sqrt{41})/2\}$.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The linear solution is $15/2$ and the quadratic solutions are $(1\pm\sqrt{41})/2$.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: The expansion, standard-form reduction, solution method, and substitutions are explicit and logically reversible.

activities.title: Extract the general proof architecture
activities.promptMarkdown:
Suppose $g,h:Y\to X$ are both two-sided inverses of the same map $f:X\to Y$.

Identify the two specific inverse identities needed to transform $g=g\circ\operatorname{id}_Y$ into $h$.

Write the two replacements in order and state where associativity is used. Do not write the final polished proof.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
First replace $\operatorname{id}_Y$ by $f\circ h$, using the right-inverse identity for $h$. This gives $g\circ(f\circ h)$.

Use associativity to rewrite it as $(g\circ f)\circ h$. Then replace $g\circ f$ by $\operatorname{id}_X$, using the left-inverse identity for $g$. The expression becomes $\operatorname{id}_X\circ h=h$.

rubric.label: Mathematical content
rubric.description: The response selects $f\circ h=\operatorname{id}_Y$ first and $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$ second.

rubric.label: Justification and scope
rubric.description: Associativity is placed between the two substitutions, and the response stops at proof architecture rather than presenting an unsupported shortcut.

activities.title: Complete the Week 1 synthesis
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $f:X\to Y$ and suppose $g,h:Y\to X$ are both two-sided inverses of $f$.

Prove $g=h$ from the four typed inverse identities, then relate the proof to the distinction between a function, its formula, its graph, and its image.

Your answer must contain: (1) a complete equality-chain proof; (2) the exact use of one left- and one right-inverse identity; (3) a one-sided-inverse counterexample; and (4) a rational-expression example where simplification does not restore an excluded input.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
A function consists of its domain, codomain, and assignment. Its graph is the set of input-output pairs, and its image is the subset of the codomain actually reached. A formula alone does not determine all of these data.

Because $g$ and $h$ are two-sided inverses,

$$g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X,\quad f\circ g=\operatorname{id}_Y,\quad h\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X,\quad f\circ h=\operatorname{id}_Y.$$

Using equality and associativity of typed maps $Y\to X$,

$$g=g\circ\operatorname{id}_Y=g\circ(f\circ h)=(g\circ f)\circ h=\operatorname{id}_X\circ h=h.$$

The first substitution uses the right-inverse identity $f\circ h=\operatorname{id}_Y$; the second uses the left-inverse identity $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X$.

One side cannot simply be dropped. For the inclusion $j:\{a,b\}\hookrightarrow\{a,b,c\}$, distinct left inverses can agree on $a,b$ and choose different values at $c$.

Likewise, $(x^2-1)/(x-1)=x+1$ only for $x\ne1$. The simplified formula has a value at $1$, but the original rational function does not. The domain remains part of the function.

rubric.label: Function data
rubric.description: The answer accurately distinguishes function, formula, graph, image, and the retained domain of a simplified rational expression.

rubric.label: Inverse uniqueness proof
rubric.description: A type-correct equality chain proves $g=h$ and justifies associativity and both inverse substitutions.

rubric.label: Boundary example
rubric.description: A correct one-sided-inverse example explains why two-sided hypotheses matter.

lessons.title: Polynomial identities and coefficient collection
lessons.summary: Treat a polynomial as finite coefficient data, prove identities by coefficient collection, and pass between a binary cubic and a linear-times-quadratic factorization.
objectives: Treat a polynomial as finite coefficient data, prove identities by coefficient collection, and pass between a binary cubic and a linear-times-quadratic factorization.

content.markdown:
## Coefficients carry the construction

The later course will record a binary cubic by four coefficients. Today establishes why multiplying a binary linear form by a binary quadratic produces exactly those four coefficients and why a numerical spot-check cannot replace an identity.

## Reactivate typed functions and Week 1 algebra

A polynomial $p:K\to K$ is a function only after the coefficient field $K$ and domain are declared. Recall also that algebraic equality must preserve every stated domain condition. We work over a field $K$, usually $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$.

## Polynomials, degree, and binary forms

A polynomial over $K$ is a finite sum $p(t)=\sum_{j=0}^d a_jt^j$ with coefficients $a_j\in K$. If $a_d\ne0$, its degree is $d$. The zero polynomial has no degree in this convention.

Two polynomials are equal exactly when the coefficient of every power agrees. A binary form of degree $d$ is a homogeneous polynomial in $T,S$: every monomial has total degree $d$. Thus $cT^2+dTS+eS^2$ is a binary quadratic, while $T^2+S$ is not homogeneous.

content.title: Collect a numerical coefficient tuple
content.introMarkdown: Give the coefficients of $T^3,T^2S,TS^2,S^3$ in that order.

data.markdown:
Check the first mixed coefficient whose two contributions were not both written.

A missing contribution changes the coefficient map used throughout the course.

Rebuild the two distributed rows, then collect like exponent pairs.

content.markdown:
## Complete model: the four coefficients

Expand $(aT+bS)(cT^2+dTS+eS^2)$ over a commutative field $K$.

Collect the coefficients of $T^3,T^2S,TS^2,S^3$ without omitting either contribution to a mixed term.

### Strategy

Distribute the $aT$ and $bS$ terms separately, then group monomials with the same exponent pair.

### Hypotheses

The coefficients lie in a commutative field, so distribution and reordering of scalar products are valid.

### Intermediate claims

$aT(cT^2+dTS+eS^2)=acT^3+adT^2S+aeTS^2$.

$bS(cT^2+dTS+eS^2)=bcT^2S+bdTS^2+beS^3$.

### Justification

The $T^2S$ coefficient receives $ad$ and $bc$; the $TS^2$ coefficient receives $ae$ and $bd$. These are the only terms with those exponent pairs.

### Conclusion

$$(aT+bS)(cT^2+dTS+eS^2)=acT^3+(ad+bc)T^2S+(ae+bd)TS^2+beS^3.$$

## Complete model: verify a chosen factorization

Multiply $(T+2S)(3T^2-TS+4S^2)$.

Produce and verify the complete coefficient tuple of the resulting binary cubic.

### Strategy

Use $(ac,ad+bc,ae+bd,be)$ with $(a,b,c,d,e)=(1,2,3,-1,4)$.

### Hypotheses

All coefficients lie in $\mathbb Z\subset K$; no division or nonzero assumption is needed.

### Intermediate claims

$ac=3$, $ad+bc=-1+6=5$, $ae+bd=4-2=2$, and $be=8$.

### Justification

The four computations correspond in order to $T^3,T^2S,TS^2,S^3$.

### Conclusion

$$(T+2S)(3T^2-TS+4S^2)=3T^3+5T^2S+2TS^2+8S^3.$$

lessons.title: Long division, remainders, and factors
lessons.summary: Execute polynomial long division over a field, prove the remainder theorem, and use evaluation to decide divisibility by a linear factor.
objectives: Execute polynomial long division over a field, prove the remainder theorem, and use evaluation to decide divisibility by a linear factor.

content.markdown:
## Division turns a root into a factor

Evaluation says whether $p(\alpha)$ vanishes. Long division explains why that numerical fact is equivalent to the structural statement that $t-\alpha$ divides $p$.

## Reactivate the exact dependencies

Day 1 established polynomial equality by coefficient comparison. Week 1 established typed functions, so evaluation is taken in a declared field. A quotient-remainder equality is a polynomial identity over that field. The leading coefficient of the divisor must be invertible; over a field this is automatic for every nonzero divisor.

## The division algorithm

For $p,g\in K[t]$ with $g\ne0$, there are unique $q,r\in K[t]$ such that $p=gq+r$ and either $r=0$ or $\deg r<\deg g$.

At each step, divide the leading term of the current dividend by the leading term of $g$, subtract the resulting multiple of $g$, and continue until the degree drops below $\deg g$.

content.title: Make the first division step
content.introMarkdown: Give the first quotient term and the new partial dividend after subtraction.

data.markdown:
Check whether the divisor’s leading term was used to cancel the dividend’s leading term.

Every later subtraction depends on the first quotient term.

Restore the zero quadratic coefficient and realign the subtraction.

content.markdown:
## Complete model: long division by a linear polynomial

Divide $t^3+2t^2-5t-6$ by $t+3$.

Display every quotient term and subtraction, then verify the quotient-remainder identity.

### Strategy

Cancel the current leading term successively with $t^2$, then $-t$, then $-2$.

### Hypotheses

The divisor $t+3$ is nonzero and monic in $K[t]$.

### Intermediate claims

Subtract $t^2(t+3)=t^3+3t^2$ to obtain $-t^2-5t-6$.

Subtract $-t(t+3)=-t^2-3t$ to obtain $-2t-6$.

Subtract $-2(t+3)=-2t-6$ to obtain $0$.

### Justification

Each subtraction cancels the current leading term, and the final remainder has degree below one.

### Conclusion

$t^3+2t^2-5t-6=(t+3)(t^2-t-2)$, with remainder $0$.

content.title: Complete a divisible cubic
content.introMarkdown: Find the quotient and remainder, then verify the product.

data.markdown:
Find the first subtraction whose signs do not match the multiple being removed.

A sign error can create a false nonzero remainder.

Multiply the divisor by each quotient term on a separate line before subtracting.

content.markdown:
## Remainder and factor theorems

Divide $p(t)$ by $t-\alpha$. The remainder is a constant $r$, so $p(t)=(t-\alpha)q(t)+r$. Evaluating at $t=\alpha$ gives $p(\alpha)=r$.

Therefore $p(\alpha)=0$ exactly when the remainder is zero, which is exactly when $t-\alpha$ divides $p(t)$. This is the factor theorem.

content.title: Use evaluation as a remainder
content.introMarkdown: Determine the remainder without long division and decide whether $t+1$ is a factor.

data.markdown:
Check whether you evaluated at $-1$ rather than $1$.

The divisor $t+1$ corresponds to the root candidate $-1$.

Rewrite the divisor as $t-(-1)$ and repeat the single evaluation.

content.markdown:
## Complete model: from evaluation to factor

For $p(t)=t^3-7t+6$, use the root $1$ to obtain a factorization.

Check the evaluation, divide by $t-1$, and verify the resulting identity.

### Strategy

First compute $p(1)$. Then use long division, retaining the missing $0t^2$ coefficient.

### Hypotheses

$p\in K[t]$ and $t-1$ is a nonzero linear divisor.

### Intermediate claims

$p(1)=1-7+6=0$, and division gives quotient $t^2+t-6$ with remainder $0$.

### Justification

The factor theorem licenses divisibility; multiplication verifies $(t-1)(t^2+t-6)=t^3-7t+6$.

### Conclusion

$p(t)=(t-1)(t^2+t-6)=(t-1)(t-2)(t+3)$.

content.title: Turn a root into a verified factor
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $t-2$ divides $p$ and compute the cubic quotient.

data.markdown:
Locate the first missing coefficient in the cubic quotient.

The factor theorem proves existence, but the quotient still requires exact division.

Multiply your quotient by $t-2$ and correct the earliest mismatching coefficient.

content.markdown:
## Write the algorithm before calling a computer

A reliable implementation stores coefficients in descending degree, inserts zeros for missing powers, and repeats the leading-term cancellation until the remainder is shorter than the divisor. A computer-algebra quotient is a later verification, not the first explanation.

content.title: Execute and specify the division algorithm
content.introMarkdown: Compute quotient and remainder manually, then give pseudocode precise enough to reproduce the calculation.

data.markdown:
Check the degree of the remainder and the reconstruction identity.

An algorithm has not finished if the remainder is still divisible in degree.

Repeat leading-term cancellation until the remainder degree is below two, then verify.

content.markdown:
## Boundary: the coefficient ring matters

The field hypothesis makes leading coefficients invertible. Long division in an arbitrary coefficient ring can fail in this form. Also, $p(\alpha)=0$ proves only that $\alpha$ is a root; it does not yet determine the root’s multiplicity.

lessons.title: Why degree bounds the number of roots
lessons.summary: Prove by sequential factorization that a nonzero degree-$d$ polynomial over a field has at most $d$ distinct roots, transfer the bound to identity testing, and use the elementary factor definition of root multiplicity.
objectives: Prove by sequential factorization that a nonzero degree-$d$ polynomial over a field has at most $d$ distinct roots, transfer the bound to identity testing, and use the elementary factor definition of root multiplicity.

content.markdown:
## A finite coefficient list cannot hide infinitely many roots

The root-count theorem converts local facts $p(r_i)=0$ into a global restriction from degree. It is the first proof this week in which each repeated use of the factor theorem must be justified.

## Reactivate the factor theorem and proof structure

Day 2 established the factor theorem and exact quotient identity: $p(\alpha)=0$ implies $p=(t-\alpha)q$. Week 1 established typed domains and explicit proof hypotheses. Work over a field $K$ and assume $p\ne0$.

## Sequential factorization at distinct roots

Suppose $r_1,\ldots,r_m$ are distinct roots. The factor theorem gives $p=(t-r_1)q_1$. At $r_2$, the equation $0=(r_2-r_1)q_1(r_2)$ and $r_2-r_1\ne0$ imply $q_1(r_2)=0$. Thus $q_1=(t-r_2)q_2$.

Repeating this argument gives $p=(t-r_1)\cdots(t-r_m)q_m$. Because $p\ne0$, also $q_m\ne0$, so $\deg p=m+\deg q_m\ge m$.

content.introMarkdown: Explain which wording is mathematically sound and why the zero polynomial must be excluded.

Rewrite the theorem with all hypotheses before analyzing the proof.

content.markdown:
## Complete proof model: a cubic cannot have four distinct roots

Assume a nonzero cubic $p\in K[t]$ has four distinct roots $r_1,r_2,r_3,r_4$.

Derive a contradiction by applying the factor theorem sequentially.

### Strategy

Factor at one root, then prove each remaining root descends to the quotient before factoring again.

### Hypotheses

$K$ is a field, $p\ne0$, $\deg p=3$, and the four roots are pairwise distinct.

### Intermediate claims

$p=(t-r_1)q_1$.

Since $0=p(r_2)=(r_2-r_1)q_1(r_2)$ and $r_2-r_1\ne0$, $q_1(r_2)=0$.

Continuing at $r_3,r_4$ gives $p=(t-r_1)(t-r_2)(t-r_3)(t-r_4)q_4$.

### Justification

The field has no zero divisors, so each nonzero difference may be cancelled. The product of four linear factors has degree four, and $q_4\ne0$ because $p\ne0$.

### Conclusion

The right side has degree at least four, contradicting $\deg p=3$. Therefore a nonzero cubic has at most three distinct roots.

content.markdown:
## Generalize without skipping the descent step

For $m$ distinct roots, the proof needs $m-1$ descent arguments of the form $0=(r_j-r_i)q(r_j)$. Merely writing “factor all the roots” conceals the reason that a root of $p$ remains a root of the current quotient.
