**Reading purpose:** Use the complete appendix sequence to consolidate the week’s construction and check every source, target, and quotient relation.
Week 16 will differentiate polynomial maps; the multiplication map studied here becomes a concrete source of Jacobian computations.
Week 15 is complete when you can reconstruct the symmetric-power quotient, derive its binary-form basis, build the graded product, and prove that linear changes of variables act compatibly.

activities.title: Retrieve counterexample and repair
activities.promptMarkdown:
Claim: for all homogeneous binary forms $F$ and $G$, the sum $F+G$ is homogeneous.

Disprove the claim and state a correct replacement with the missing hypothesis.

Use nonzero forms of different degrees, then prove the corrected statement.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The counterexample and repaired statement are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The missing same-degree hypothesis is identified and used in a proof.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Take $F=T$ and $G=S^2$. Both are homogeneous, but $F+G=T+S^2$ has terms of degrees one and two, so it is not homogeneous. A correct statement is: if $F$ and $G$ are homogeneous of the same degree $d$, then $F+G$ is either zero or homogeneous of degree $d$. Every surviving monomial in the sum still has degree $d$.

activities.title: Retrieve rank-nullity on a symmetric square
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A:k^2\to k^2$ satisfy $A(T)=T$ and $A(S)=0$. Consider $\operatorname{Sym}^2(A)$.

Compute its kernel and image in the basis $(T^2,TS,S^2)$ and verify rank-nullity.

Name bases for both subspaces.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The kernel, image, rank, nullity, and dimension check are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The theorem is verified from explicit basis images.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The induced map sends $T^2\mapsto T^2$, $TS\mapsto0$, and $S^2\mapsto0$. Its image is $\langle T^2\rangle$, so its rank is one. Its kernel is $\langle TS,S^2\rangle$, so its nullity is two. Since the domain has dimension three, $1+2=3$ verifies rank-nullity.

activities.title: Retrieve a dual pullback
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A:W\to V$ be $A(t,s)=(t+s,t-s)$ in domain coordinates $(t,s)$. Let $(T,S)$ be the target coordinate functionals.

Compute $A^\vee(T)$ and $A^\vee(S)$ from the definition.

Evaluate each composite on a general $(t,s)$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both pulled-back coordinate functionals are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The computation begins from precomposition and keeps the direction of the map explicit.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: By definition $A^\vee(\ell)=\ell\circ A$. Hence $(A^\vee T)(t,s)=T(t+s,t-s)=t+s$, so $A^\vee(T)=t+s$ as a functional on $W$. Similarly $(A^\vee S)(t,s)=t-s$, so $A^\vee(S)=t-s$.

activities.title: Prove multiplication commutes with pullback
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A:W\to V$, $F\in\operatorname{Sym}^1(V^\vee)$, and $G\in\operatorname{Sym}^2(V^\vee)$.

Prove $(FG)\circ A=(F\circ A)(G\circ A)$ and express it as compatibility of symmetric-power maps with $\mu_{1,2}$.

Evaluate both sides at an arbitrary $w\in W$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The pointwise identity and typed symmetric-power identity are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Equality is proved by evaluation and then translated into the graded-map language.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For every $w\in W$, $((FG)\circ A)(w)=(FG)(A(w))=F(A(w))G(A(w))=((F\circ A)(G\circ A))(w)$. Therefore the forms are equal. Equivalently, $\operatorname{Sym}^3(A^\vee)(\mu_{1,2}(F,G))=\mu_{1,2}(\operatorname{Sym}^1(A^\vee)F,\operatorname{Sym}^2(A^\vee)G)$.

activities.title: Transfer the two-route verification
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $L=2T-S$, $Q=T^2+TS$, and $B^\vee(T)=T+S$, $B^\vee(S)=S$.

Compute the transformed cubic directly and factorwise, then show the two results coincide.

Display both routes separately before comparing.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: First $LQ=2T^3+T^2S-TS^2$. Direct substitution gives $2(T+S)^3+(T+S)^2S-(T+S)S^2=2T^3+7T^2S+7TS^2+2S^3$. Factorwise, $B^\vee(L)=2(T+S)-S=2T+S$ and $B^\vee(Q)=(T+S)^2+(T+S)S=T^2+3TS+2S^2$. Their product is again $2T^3+7T^2S+7TS^2+2S^3$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both transformed cubics agree and are correctly computed.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The two independent routes verify the compatibility identity in a concrete case.

activities.title: Audit a compressed argument
activities.promptMarkdown:
A proposed solution says: “$V^{\otimes d}=\operatorname{Sym}^dV$, every polynomial of degree at most $d$ lies in that space, and $A$ sends a form forward by $F\mapsto F\circ A^{-1}$.”

Correct each assertion with the smallest precise replacement.

Do not replace the paragraph with a vague warning; state three corrected claims.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: First, $\operatorname{Sym}^dV$ is a quotient of $V^{\otimes d}$, generally of smaller dimension. Second, under a dual-basis identification it corresponds to homogeneous forms of exactly degree $d$, not all forms of degree at most $d$. Third, a map $A:W\to V$ pulls a form on $V$ back to $W$ by $F\mapsto F\circ A$; the formula with $A^{-1}$ describes a different convention and requires invertibility.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All three conflations are corrected precisely.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Each repair names the relevant construction, degree, or map direction and its hypotheses.

activities.title: Synthesize the Week 15 construction
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $V$ be two-dimensional with dual basis $(T,S)$, and let $A:W\to V$ be linear.

Prove the binary-form realization of $\operatorname{Sym}^d(V^\vee)$, verify dimensions $2,3,4$ for $d=1,2,3$, construct $\mu_{1,2}$ on the monomial bases, and prove that pullback by $A$ commutes with this multiplication.

Include one explicit boundary statement distinguishing the quotient from the full tensor power.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Every required construction, dimension, product, and compatibility claim is correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof connects the stages in order and preserves the tensor-quotient and pullback boundaries.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The symmetric power is the quotient of $(V^\vee)^{\otimes d}$ by permutation relations. With dual basis $(T,S)$, each tensor-word class reduces to exactly one monomial $T^{d-i}S^i$ for $0\le i\le d$, and every element has a unique linear-combination expression in these monomial classes. An element such as $T^d+S^d$ is therefore not generally one monomial. Polynomial coefficient uniqueness proves that the monomial classes are independent, so they form a basis and identify the space with homogeneous degree-$d$ binary forms. For $d=1,2,3$ the bases have respectively $2,3,4$ elements. Multiplication $\mu_{1,2}(L,Q)=LQ$ is bilinear, and its basis products are $T(T^2)=T^3$, $T(TS)=S(T^2)=T^2S$, $T(S^2)=S(TS)=TS^2$, and $S(S^2)=S^3$. For $w\in W$, $((LQ)\circ A)(w)=L(Aw)Q(Aw)=((L\circ A)(Q\circ A))(w)$, proving compatibility with the induced pullbacks. The full tensor power is generally larger: when $d=3$, it has dimension eight, while the symmetric quotient has dimension four.

lessons.title: The derivative is a linear approximation
lessons.summary: Derive the Jacobian columns from the definition of differentiability and distinguish the total derivative from partial and directional derivatives.
objectives: Derive the Jacobian columns from the definition of differentiability and distinguish the total derivative from partial and directional derivatives.

content.markdown:
## Why begin with an error term?

In one variable, a derivative is more than a collection of slopes: it is the linear map that predicts the whole first-order change. The same idea survives in several variables, but the linear map is now represented by a matrix.

Starting from that approximation prevents a common mistake. A table of existing partial derivatives is not, by itself, a proof that a function is differentiable.

## Reactivate maps, norms, and matrices

A linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ has a matrix once bases are fixed. The Euclidean norm measures the size of the input increment $h$, and matrix multiplication computes $Ah$.

Week 11 separated a linear map from its matrix. Week 13 related a square matrix to its determinant. Week 15 supplied polynomial maps that we will differentiate later.

## Differentiability at a point

Let $F:U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ and let $a$ be an interior point of $U$. We say that $F$ is differentiable at $a$ when there is a linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ such that

$$F(a+h)=F(a)+Ah+r(h),\qquad \frac{\|r(h)\|}{\|h\|}\longrightarrow0\quad(h\to0).$$

The quotient says that the error is small compared with every first-order displacement. The linear map is unique and is denoted $DF_a$.

content.title: Read a remainder estimate
content.introMarkdown: Prove from the displayed inequality that $A$ satisfies the differentiability remainder condition.

data.markdown:
Compare the remainder with $\|h\|$, not with the constant $1$.

Differentiability controls the error relative to the size of the displacement.

Write the quotient inequality for nonzero $h$ and take its limit.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Let $F:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ be $F(x,y)=(x^2+xy,\,y^2)$ and fix $a=(a_1,a_2)$.

Derive $DF_a$ directly by expanding $F(a+h)$ and prove that the remainder is $o(\|h\|)$.

### Strategy

Expand both coordinates, collect every term linear in $h=(u,v)$ into one map, and bound the remaining quadratic terms.

### Hypotheses

Use $|u|,|v|\le\|h\|$ and the triangle inequality.

### Intermediate claims

Expansion gives the linear part $((2a_1+a_2)u+a_1v,\,2a_2v)$ and remainder $(u^2+uv,\,v^2)$.

### Justification

The remainder norm is at most a fixed multiple of $\|h\|^2$, because each of $|u|^2$, $|uv|$, and $|v|^2$ is bounded by $\|h\|^2$.

### Conclusion

$DF_a(u,v)=((2a_1+a_2)u+a_1v,2a_2v)$, represented in standard coordinates by $\begin{pmatrix}2a_1+a_2&a_1\\0&2a_2\end{pmatrix}$.

content.title: Derive a derivative without quoting partials
content.introMarkdown: Display the linear map, the remainder, and a bound proving that the remainder divided by $\|(u,v)\|$ tends to zero.

data.markdown:
Separate terms linear in $(u,v)$ from terms containing two increments.

Only the linear part can be the derivative; the rest must satisfy the small-error condition.

Expand both components, box the linear terms, and bound the remaining pair by a constant times $\|(u,v)\|^2$.

content.markdown:
## Partial derivatives are columns of the derivative

Assume $F$ is differentiable at $a$. Put $h=te_j$, where $e_j$ is the $j$th coordinate vector. Dividing

$$F(a+te_j)-F(a)=tDF_a(e_j)+r(te_j)$$

by $t$ and taking $t\to0$ gives $\partial_jF(a)=DF_a(e_j)$. Thus the $j$th Jacobian column is forced by the total derivative; it is not an independent definition of differentiability.

content.title: Recover every Jacobian column
content.introMarkdown: Prove carefully that the coordinate partial derivative $\partial_jF(a)$ exists and equals $Ae_j$.

data.markdown:
Replace $t$ by $|t|$ inside the norm comparison.

The derivative limit approaches from both signs, so the norm estimate must be sign-safe.

Set $h=te_j$, divide the vector equation, then estimate the norm of the remainder quotient.

content.markdown:
## Existing directional derivatives need not assemble into a derivative

For a differentiable map, every directional derivative satisfies $D_vF(a)=DF_a(v)$ and therefore depends linearly on $v$. The converse fails: all directional derivatives can exist while no single linear map gives a uniform first-order approximation.

The function $f(x,y)=x^3/(x^2+y^2)$ away from the origin, with $f(0,0)=0$, is a standard warning. Its directional derivatives exist, but their dependence on the direction is not linear.

content.title: Detect nonlinearity in the direction
content.introMarkdown: Compute $D_{(p,q)}f(0,0)$ and use its dependence on $(p,q)$ to prove that $f$ is not differentiable at the origin.

data.markdown:
Test the direction map on $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, and their sum.

One derivative must assign directional rates through a single linear map.

Compute the three values and compare the value at the sum with the sum of the values.

content.markdown:
## A complete derivative argument

For a polynomial map, expansion provides a reliable proof pattern: identify the constant value, collect the homogeneous degree-one increment, and prove that all terms of increment degree at least two form an $o(\|h\|)$ remainder.

content.title: Prove differentiability from first principles
content.introMarkdown: At an arbitrary $(a,b)$, derive $DH_{(a,b)}$ from the differentiability definition and give its $3\times2$ Jacobian matrix.

data.markdown:
Locate the first increment term whose degree was classified incorrectly.

A single misplaced quadratic term changes either the proposed derivative or the required error estimate.

Re-expand one coordinate at a time, group by total degree in $(u,v)$, and bound the degree-two-or-higher group.

content.markdown:
## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-16, source lines 713 to 722.

**Resource version:** MIT OpenCourseWare 18.024, Chapter C notes, Spring 2011.

**Exact locator:** Chapter C, pp. 1–2: differentiability as a linear approximation, uniqueness of the derivative, and the Jacobian matrix in MIT OpenCourseWare 18.024, Multivariable Calculus with Theory, Chapter C notes, Spring 2011.

**Reading purpose:** Read the definition beside the expansion proofs and compare the derivative map with its Jacobian matrix.
Day 2 turns the definition into efficient computations for triangular maps while retaining the distinction between local derivative data and global behavior.
Day 1 is complete when you can extract a linear approximation, bound its remainder, derive its Jacobian columns, and explain why directional derivatives alone are insufficient.

activities.title: Read a remainder estimate
activities.promptMarkdown:
Suppose $F(a+h)=F(a)+Ah+r(h)$ and $\|r(h)\|\le 3\|h\|^2$ whenever $\|h\|<1$.

Prove from the displayed inequality that $A$ satisfies the differentiability remainder condition.

Divide by $\|h\|$ for $h\ne0$ and state the limit explicitly.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $0<\|h\|<1$, $0\le\|r(h)\|/\|h\|\le3\|h\|$. The right-hand side tends to $0$ as $h\to0$, so the squeeze theorem gives $\|r(h)\|/\|h\|\to0$. Thus the error is $o(\|h\|)$ and $A$ is the derivative.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The little-o condition follows correctly from the quadratic bound.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response divides by the input scale and completes the limiting argument.

activities.title: Derive a derivative without quoting partials
activities.promptMarkdown:
For $G(x,y)=(x^2-y,\,xy)$, derive $DG_{(a,b)}$ from the remainder definition.

Display the linear map, the remainder, and a bound proving that the remainder divided by $\|(u,v)\|$ tends to zero.

Use the worked expansion as an architecture, but compute this new target completely.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The derivative, remainder, bound, and coordinate matrix are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The argument is derived from the definition instead of assuming differentiability from formal partials.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $G(a+u,b+v)-G(a,b)=(2au-v,\,bu+av)+(u^2,uv)$. Hence $DG_{(a,b)}(u,v)=(2au-v,bu+av)$. Since $\|(u^2,uv)\|\le\sqrt2\|(u,v)\|^2$, its quotient by $\|(u,v)\|$ tends to zero. The Jacobian matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}2a&-1\\b&a\end{pmatrix}$.

activities.title: Recover every Jacobian column
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ be differentiable at $a$ with derivative $A$.

Prove carefully that the coordinate partial derivative $\partial_jF(a)$ exists and equals $Ae_j$.

Track the sign of $t$ when dividing the norm estimate.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The coordinate derivative is correctly identified with the corresponding derivative column.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof uses the remainder estimate on a coordinate line and handles absolute values correctly.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Write $F(a+te_j)-F(a)=tAe_j+r(te_j)$. For $t\ne0$, division by $t$ gives $[F(a+te_j)-F(a)]/t=Ae_j+r(te_j)/t$. Moreover $\|r(te_j)/t\|=\|r(te_j)\|/\|te_j\|\to0$, because $\|e_j\|=1$. Therefore the difference quotient converges to $Ae_j$.

activities.title: Detect nonlinearity in the direction
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $f(0,0)=0$ and $f(x,y)=x^3/(x^2+y^2)$ otherwise.

Compute $D_{(p,q)}f(0,0)$ and use its dependence on $(p,q)$ to prove that $f$ is not differentiable at the origin.

A total derivative would have to be a linear functional of the direction.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The directional derivative formula and the explicit failure of linearity are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The answer invokes a necessary consequence of total differentiability rather than merely asserting discontinuity.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $(p,q)\ne(0,0)$, $f(tp,tq)/t=p^3/(p^2+q^2)$, so $D_{(p,q)}f(0,0)=p^3/(p^2+q^2)$. This direction map is not additive: it takes $(1,0)$ to $1$, $(0,1)$ to $0$, but $(1,1)$ to $1/2$. If $f$ were differentiable, these values would equal one linear map applied to the directions, which is impossible.

activities.title: Prove differentiability from first principles
activities.promptMarkdown:
Define $H:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^3$ by $H(x,y)=(x^2y,\,x-y^2,\,xy)$.

At an arbitrary $(a,b)$, derive $DH_{(a,b)}$ from the differentiability definition and give its $3\times2$ Jacobian matrix.

Your proof must show a norm bound for the complete remainder, not only list partial derivatives.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All three linear components, the remainder, its bound, and the matrix are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The conclusion follows from the definition and preserves the distinction between the linear map and its coordinate matrix.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $h=(u,v)$, the linear increment is $(2ab\,u+a^2v,\,u-2bv,\,bu+av)$. The remainder is $(bu^2+2auv+u^2v,\,-v^2,\,uv)$. For $\|h\|\le1$, its norm is at most $C_{a,b}\|h\|^2$ for a constant depending only on $(a,b)$, so the remainder quotient tends to zero. Hence $DH_{(a,b)}(u,v)$ is the displayed linear increment and its matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}2ab&a^2\\1&-2b\\b&a\end{pmatrix}$.

lessons.title: Triangular maps and structured Jacobians
lessons.summary: Compute Jacobians of triangular maps, derive their determinant, and state exactly what the pointwise calculation does and does not prove.
objectives: Compute Jacobians of triangular maps, derive their determinant, and state exactly what the pointwise calculation does and does not prove.

content.markdown:
## Why triangular form matters

A triangular polynomial map makes dependence visible: the first output uses the first input, the second may use the first two, and so on. Its Jacobian inherits zeros above the diagonal, so its determinant is the product of diagonal derivatives.

The structure accelerates calculation, but it does not license an automatic global inverse claim.

## Reactivate the derivative and triangular determinants

Day 1 defined $DF_a$ as a linear approximation and identified its coordinate columns with partial derivatives. Week 13 proved that the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries.

## The dependency pattern

A lower triangular map has the form $F_i(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=F_i(x_1,\ldots,x_i)$. Therefore $\partial F_i/\partial x_j=0$ whenever $j>i$, and $JF$ is lower triangular.

Its determinant is $\prod_i \partial F_i/\partial x_i$. This conclusion comes from matrix structure after differentiability is known.

content.title: Read zeros from variable dependence
content.introMarkdown: Compute $JF(x,y,z)$ and decide whether the map is lower triangular in the stated variable order.

data.markdown:
Check the derivative of the second output with respect to $z$.

One nonzero entry above the diagonal destroys lower triangularity.

Write the full dependency table and then compare row and column indices.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$T(x,y,z)=(x,\,y+x^2,\,z+xy)$.

Compute the Jacobian, determinant, and inverse by back-substitution.

### Strategy

Differentiate row by row, use triangularity for the determinant, then recover inputs in the same order as the outputs reveal them.

### Hypotheses

The standard coordinates are fixed, and polynomial maps are differentiable.

### Intermediate claims

$JT=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\2x&1&0\\y&x&1\end{pmatrix}$, so $\det JT=1$. From $(X,Y,Z)=T(x,y,z)$, first $x=X$, then $y=Y-X^2$, then $z=Z-X(Y-X^2)$.

### Justification

A triangular determinant is the diagonal product. Each back-substitution uses only values already recovered.

### Conclusion

This particular unitriangular polynomial map has an explicit global polynomial inverse; that conclusion comes from the construction, not from the determinant alone.

content.title: Compute and invert a new triangular map
content.introMarkdown: Compute $JS$, its determinant, and the explicit inverse map.

data.markdown:
Recover $x$ before substituting into the equation for $y$.

Triangular inversion is an ordered argument; later coordinates depend on earlier ones.

Rename the outputs $(X,Y,Z)$ and solve the three equations from top to bottom.

content.markdown:
## A parameterized triangular family

For $F(x,y)=(f(x),g(x,y))$,

$$JF(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}f'(x)&0\\ \partial_xg(x,y)&\partial_yg(x,y)\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det JF=f'(x)\partial_yg(x,y).$$

The formula isolates two possible local degeneracies. It does not say that nonzero diagonal derivatives make $F$ globally one-to-one.

content.title: Analyze a triangular family
content.introMarkdown: Compute the Jacobian determinant and describe exactly where it vanishes.

data.markdown:
Decide whether $e^x+3y^2$ can ever be zero.

A product equation should not create a nonexistent branch of the zero set.

Prove the second factor is positive, then solve $3x^2-c=0$ by cases on $c$.

content.markdown:
## Nonzero Jacobian is local information

For a continuously differentiable square map, an invertible derivative at one point gives a local inverse near that point by the inverse function theorem, introduced next week.

It does not by itself give a global inverse. Even in one variable, a map on a disconnected domain can have nonzero derivative everywhere and still take the same value on different components.

content.title: Refute a premature global conclusion
content.introMarkdown: Show that $f'(x)$ never vanishes on $U$ but $f$ is not injective.

data.markdown:
Choose one positive input and its negative inside the two components.

A global injectivity claim is disproved by one collision, even when all derivatives are nonzero.

Verify domain membership, compute both images, and state why the derivative test does not exclude the collision.

content.markdown:
## Structured computation with a proof boundary

A polished triangular-map solution has four parts: the dependency pattern, the full Jacobian, its determinant, and a separately justified conclusion about the original map. The determinant can support a local claim; global claims require additional reasoning such as explicit back-substitution.

content.title: Complete a triangular-map analysis
content.introMarkdown: Compute $JF$, its determinant, and prove by explicit recursion that $F$ has a global polynomial inverse.

data.markdown:
Find the first recovered coordinate that still contains an unrecovered input.

A recursive inverse formula must depend only on output data and already recovered coordinates.

Solve the four output equations in order and then substitute the earlier formulas into each later one.

content.markdown:
## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-16, source lines 713 to 722.

**Resource version:** MIT OpenCourseWare 18.02SC, Fall 2010.

**Exact locator:** Unit 2, Part A, Sessions 26–27: partial derivatives and local linear approximation in MIT OpenCourseWare 18.02SC Multivariable Calculus, Fall 2010.

**Reading purpose:** Use the sessions to reinforce row-by-row differentiation, then apply the stronger remainder interpretation established on Day 1.
Day 3 proves how derivatives compose. The triangular examples will become concrete checks of the matrix order in the chain rule.
Day 2 is complete when you can exploit triangular structure without confusing an invertible derivative with a global inverse.

activities.title: Read zeros from variable dependence
activities.promptMarkdown:
$F(x,y,z)=(x^2,\,y+xz,\,z+y^2+x)$.

Compute $JF(x,y,z)$ and decide whether the map is lower triangular in the stated variable order.

Inspect each output's actual dependencies before naming the matrix shape.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $JF=\begin{pmatrix}2x&0&0\\z&1&x\\1&2y&1\end{pmatrix}$. The entry $\partial F_2/\partial z=x$ lies above the diagonal, so the map is not lower triangular in the order $(x,y,z)$, despite several zeros.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Every entry and the matrix-shape conclusion are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response tests the defining zero pattern rather than judging by appearance.

activities.title: Compute and invert a new triangular map
activities.promptMarkdown:
$S(x,y,z)=(2x,\,3y+x^2,\,-z+xy)$.

Compute $JS$, its determinant, and the explicit inverse map.

Solve successively for $x$, then $y$, then $z$.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $JS=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&0\\2x&3&0\\y&x&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\det JS=2\cdot3\cdot(-1)=-6$. If $(X,Y,Z)=S(x,y,z)$, then $x=X/2$, $y=(Y-X^2/4)/3$, and $z=xy-Z=X(Y-X^2/4)/6-Z$. These formulas define the inverse on all of $\mathbb R^3$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The matrix, determinant, and all inverse coordinates are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The global conclusion is justified by two-sided back-substitution.

activities.title: Analyze a triangular family
activities.promptMarkdown:
$F_c(x,y)=(x^3-cx,\,e^x y+y^3)$, where $c\in\mathbb R$.

Compute the Jacobian determinant and describe exactly where it vanishes.

Solve the product equation by treating each factor separately.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The determinant and its parameter-dependent zero set are complete.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The positivity of the second factor is used to eliminate spurious cases.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $JF_c=\begin{pmatrix}3x^2-c&0\\e^xy&e^x+3y^2\end{pmatrix}$, so $\det JF_c=(3x^2-c)(e^x+3y^2)$. The second factor is always positive. Hence the determinant vanishes exactly when $3x^2=c$: at no real point if $c<0$, at $x=0$ if $c=0$, and on the two vertical lines $x=\pm\sqrt{c/3}$ if $c>0$.

activities.title: Refute a premature global conclusion
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $U=(-2,-1)\cup(1,2)$ and define $f:U\to\mathbb R$ by $f(x)=x^2$.

Show that $f'(x)$ never vanishes on $U$ but $f$ is not injective.

Give an explicit pair of distinct points with the same image.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The derivative condition and the explicit collision are both correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response states the precise logical gap between local derivative data and a global map property.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $f'(x)=2x$, which is nonzero because $0\notin U$. Nevertheless $3/2$ and $-3/2$ both belong to $U$ and have image $9/4$. Thus pointwise invertibility of the derivative does not imply global injectivity.

activities.title: Complete a triangular-map analysis
activities.promptMarkdown:
$F(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=(x_1,\,x_2+x_1^2,\,2x_3+x_1x_2,\,-x_4+x_2x_3)$.

Compute $JF$, its determinant, and prove by explicit recursion that $F$ has a global polynomial inverse.

Use named output coordinates and write every recovery formula.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The full matrix, determinant, recursive formulas, and inverse conclusion are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The global inverse is established by construction rather than inferred from a constant determinant.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $JF=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&0\\2x_1&1&0&0\\x_2&x_1&2&0\\0&x_3&x_2&-1\end{pmatrix}$, so $\det JF=-2$. For output $(X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4)$, recover $x_1=X_1$, $x_2=X_2-X_1^2$, $x_3=(X_3-x_1x_2)/2$, and $x_4=x_2x_3-X_4$. Each expression is polynomial in the outputs, and substitution into the defining equations proves both composite identities.

lessons.title: Proving the matrix chain rule
lessons.summary: Prove the multivariable chain rule from remainder estimates and use source and target dimensions to determine the matrix order.
objectives: Prove the multivariable chain rule from remainder estimates and use source and target dimensions to determine the matrix order.

content.markdown:
## Why the order must be proved

For $F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ and $G:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p$, the derivative of $G\circ F$ must send an $n$-dimensional increment to a $p$-dimensional one. This already predicts the order $DG_{F(a)}DF_a$.

The proof must also show that the composed error remains negligible after the inner map distorts the increment.

## Reactivate linear approximation

Write $F(a+h)=F(a)+Ah+r(h)$ and $G(b+k)=G(b)+Bk+s(k)$ with $b=F(a)$. The little-o statements are $\|r(h)\|/\|h\|\to0$ and $\|s(k)\|/\|k\|\to0$.

## Substitute the inner approximation

Set $k=F(a+h)-F(a)=Ah+r(h)$. Then

$$G(F(a+h))=G(F(a))+B(Ah+r(h))+s(Ah+r(h)).$$

The candidate derivative is $BA$. The remaining terms are $Br(h)$ and $s(Ah+r(h))$; both must be divided by $\|h\|$ and controlled.

content.title: Identify the composed remainder
content.introMarkdown: Substitute exactly and separate the linear term in $h$ from the complete remainder.

data.markdown:
Check what vector is substituted for the outer increment $k$.

The outer error estimate applies to $F(a+h)-F(a)$, not directly to $h$.

Name $k=Ah+r(h)$ first, then expand and place every non-linear term in one bracket.

content.markdown:
## The bounded-ratio bridge

Since $r(h)=o(\|h\|)$, the ratio $\|r(h)\|/\|h\|$ is bounded near zero. Therefore

$$\frac{\|Ah+r(h)\|}{\|h\|}\le \|A\|+\frac{\|r(h)\|}{\|h\|}$$

is bounded. This bridge lets us convert $s(k)=o(\|k\|)$ into $s(k)=o(\|h\|)$ for the special increment $k=Ah+r(h)$.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is differentiable at $a$, and $G:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p$ is differentiable at $F(a)$.

Prove that $G\circ F$ is differentiable at $a$ with derivative $DG_{F(a)}\circ DF_a$.

### Strategy

Expand both maps, isolate the candidate composition, and split the outer remainder quotient into a product of two controlled ratios.

### Hypotheses

Let $A=DF_a$, $B=DG_{F(a)}$, $r(h)=o(\|h\|)$, and $s(k)=o(\|k\|)$.

### Intermediate claims

The remainder is $R(h)=Br(h)+s(Ah+r(h))$. The first term satisfies $\|Br(h)\|/\|h\|\le\|B\|\|r(h)\|/\|h\|\to0$. For $k(h)=Ah+r(h)$, $k(h)\to0$ and $\|k(h)\|/\|h\|$ is bounded.

### Justification

When $k(h)\ne0$, $\|s(k(h))\|/\|h\|=[\|s(k(h))\|/\|k(h)\|][\|k(h)\|/\|h\|]$, whose first factor tends to zero and second is bounded. At $k(h)=0$, the numerator is zero.

### Conclusion

$R(h)=o(\|h\|)$, so $D(G\circ F)_a=B\circ A$. In standard bases, $J(G\circ F)(a)=JG(F(a))JF(a)$.

## Matrix order is fixed by types

If $JF(a)$ is $m\times n$ and $JG(F(a))$ is $p\times m$, only $JG(F(a))JF(a)$ has the required size $p\times n$. Reversing the order may be undefined; when both matrices are square, it may be defined but still wrong.

lessons.title: Determinant chain rule and differential viewpoint
lessons.summary: Derive the determinant chain rule for square maps, interpret derivatives as maps between coordinate tangent copies, and preserve the boundary with later algebraic tangent-space theory.

content.markdown:
## From composition to volume scaling

For maps between equal-dimensional Euclidean spaces, the determinant of the derivative records infinitesimal signed volume scaling. The chain rule composes the linear maps; determinant multiplicativity then multiplies the scaling factors.

This interpretation is powerful, but it remains pointwise. It does not turn a local determinant identity into a global theorem.

## Reactivate two theorems

Day 3 proved $D(G\circ F)_a=DG_{F(a)}DF_a$. Week 13 proved $\det(BA)=\det(B)\det(A)$ for square matrices of the same size.

## The determinant chain rule

Let $F,G:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be differentiable at the required points. Taking determinants in the matrix chain rule gives

$$\det J(G\circ F)(a)=\det JG(F(a))\,\det JF(a).$$

No new calculus proof is hidden here: the result is precisely the chain rule followed by determinant multiplicativity.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$F(r,\theta)=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ and $G(x,y)=(x+y,x-y)$.

Compute the determinant of $G\circ F$ by the chain rule and verify it directly.

### Strategy

Find both Jacobian determinants, evaluate the outer one at $F(r,\theta)$, multiply, then differentiate the explicit composition.

### Hypotheses

Both maps are differentiable on $\mathbb R^2$.

### Intermediate claims

$\det JF(r,\theta)=r$ and $\det JG(x,y)=-2$. Hence the rule predicts $\det J(G\circ F)(r,\theta)=-2r$.

### Justification

$G\circ F=(r(\cos\theta+\sin\theta),r(\cos\theta-\sin\theta))$, whose direct Jacobian determinant simplifies to $-2r$.

### Conclusion

The factors are evaluated at their proper points and the direct calculation confirms the product.

content.markdown:
## Differential notation as typed linear algebra

At a point $a\in\mathbb R^n$, we may write the derivative as $dF_a:T_a\mathbb R^n\to T_{F(a)}\mathbb R^m$. For Euclidean spaces, these tangent spaces are canonical copies of $\mathbb R^n$ and $\mathbb R^m$ that remember their base points.

Then the chain rule is $d(G\circ F)_a=dG_{F(a)}\circ dF_a$. This is a coordinate-free restatement of the theorem, not a new calculation.

content.markdown:
## Preview boundary: not yet the Zariski tangent space

Today $T_a\mathbb R^n$ means the ordinary tangent copy used in multivariable calculus. Later, an affine algebraic set will be defined by polynomial equations, and its Zariski tangent space will be cut out by their differentials.

We are only previewing that destination. We have not yet defined affine varieties, coordinate rings, or proved that the kernel of a Jacobian gives the correct algebraic tangent space.

content.markdown:
## Why multiplication is the right synthesis

Week 15 made polynomial multiplication a bilinear map. Bilinearity makes its first-order change visible by expansion: two linear terms appear, followed by one product of increments.

That last product is quadratic in the joint increment, so it is exactly the remainder that the total-derivative definition knows how to control.

## Three scheduled retrievals

The synthesis needs a typed proof boundary from Week 8, determinant multiplicativity from Week 13, and the symmetric-power multiplication map from Week 15. Each review below retrieves the exact earlier object before it is used in the new derivative argument.

For this real multivariable-calculus chapter, set $V_d=\mathbb R[T,S]_d$. Thus the dimensions $2,3,4$ and the displayed $4\times5$ matrix are real dimensions and a real matrix. The same coefficient formula also extends complex-linearly, but that is not the scalar setting used in today's derivative proof.

## Deliberate review: function data after eight weeks

A derivative belongs to a declared map. Before differentiating multiplication, identify its source product space and target space; otherwise even the size of the derivative is undetermined.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Let $B:E\times F\to G$ be a continuous bilinear map between finite-dimensional normed vector spaces.

Derive the total derivative of $B$ at $(x,y)$ directly from the remainder definition.

### Strategy

Expand $B(x+h,y+k)$ using bilinearity, collect the two terms linear in the joint increment, and bound the final mixed term.

### Hypotheses

Finite-dimensional continuity gives $\|B(h,k)\|\le C\|h\|\|k\|$ for some $C$.

### Intermediate claims

$B(x+h,y+k)-B(x,y)=B(h,y)+B(x,k)+B(h,k)$. The candidate derivative is $(h,k)\mapsto B(h,y)+B(x,k)$.

### Justification

With the product norm $\|(h,k)\|=(\|h\|^2+\|k\|^2)^{1/2}$, $\|B(h,k)\|\le C\|h\|\|k\|\le(C/2)\|(h,k)\|^2$, so the remainder quotient tends to zero.

### Conclusion

$DB_{(x,y)}(h,k)=B(h,y)+B(x,k)$. Both summands are needed because both inputs vary.

content.markdown:
## The derivative of polynomial multiplication

Apply the bilinear rule to $M(L,Q)=LQ$. At $(L,Q)$ and increment $(\dot L,\dot Q)$,

$$DM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot L\,Q+L\,\dot Q,$$

because $(L+\dot L)(Q+\dot Q)-LQ$ has the additional remainder $\dot L\dot Q$, quadratic in the joint coefficient increment.

content.markdown:
## Kernel behavior at degenerate factors

The formula changes character at $(L,Q)=(0,0)$: the derivative is the zero map although $M$ itself is not constant. At a point with one zero factor, only variation in the other factor contributes at first order.

This is not a contradiction. Derivatives describe first-order behavior at one base point; the omitted product of increments is second order.

content.markdown:
## Week synthesis

The week's ideas now form one chain: differentiability is a uniform linear approximation; its coordinate matrix is the Jacobian; composition multiplies derivative maps in typed order; determinants multiply only for square derivative matrices; and bilinear multiplication differentiates by retaining its two first-order terms.

Therefore each derivative $DM_{(L,Q)}$ is a linear map from a five-dimensional space to a four-dimensional space and has a $4\times5$ matrix after bases are chosen.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The typed map and all source and target dimensions are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The derivative matrix size follows from the declared map rather than from memorized coefficients.

activities.title: Decide whether a derivative determinant exists
activities.promptMarkdown:
$DM_{(L,Q)}:V_1\times V_2\to V_3$ has matrix size $4\times5$.

Explain why $\det DM_{(L,Q)}$ is not defined and state one square matrix naturally associated with this derivative.

Do not assign determinant zero merely because the map has a kernel.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The derivative matrix has four rows and five columns, so it is not square and has no determinant. A natural square associated matrix is $DM_{(L,Q)}DM_{(L,Q)}^{\mathsf T}$, which is $4\times4$, although its determinant answers a different question about rank and volume in the target.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The determinant is correctly rejected and the associated square matrix has the correct size.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The answer distinguishes undefined determinant from a zero determinant and limits the interpretation of the replacement.

activities.title: Reconstruct the coefficient map
activities.promptMarkdown:
$L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.

Expand $LQ$ and write $M(a,b,c,d,e)$ in the cubic monomial basis $(T^3,T^2S,TS^2,S^3)$.

Collect each total degree-three monomial once.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $LQ=acT^3+(ad+bc)T^2S+(ae+bd)TS^2+beS^3$. Hence $M(a,b,c,d,e)=(ac,ad+bc,ae+bd,be)$ in the stated basis.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All four cubic coefficients are correct and in the declared order.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The result is reconstructed from multiplication rather than recalled as an unexplained tuple.

activities.title: Transfer the product rule to matrices
activities.promptMarkdown:
$B:\operatorname{Mat}_{m\times n}\times\operatorname{Mat}_{n\times p}\to\operatorname{Mat}_{m\times p}$ is $B(A,C)=AC$.

Derive $DB_{(A,C)}(H,K)$ and identify the remainder using a submultiplicative matrix norm.

Expand $(A+H)(C+K)$ completely.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both linear terms and the quadratic matrix remainder are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof transfers the bilinear expansion and supplies a norm estimate.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $(A+H)(C+K)-AC=HC+AK+HK$. Thus $DB_{(A,C)}(H,K)=HC+AK$ and the remainder is $HK$. A submultiplicative norm gives $\|HK\|\le\|H\|\|K\|\le\tfrac12(\|H\|^2+\|K\|^2)$, which is quadratic in the joint increment.

activities.title: Compute the multiplication Jacobian
activities.promptMarkdown:
$M(a,b,c,d,e)=(ac,ad+bc,ae+bd,be)$.

Compute $JM(a,b,c,d,e)$ and verify that its action on $(\dot a,\dot b,\dot c,\dot d,\dot e)$ matches $\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.

Order columns by $(a,b,c,d,e)$ and rows by $(T^3,T^2S,TS^2,S^3)$.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $JM=\begin{pmatrix}c&0&a&0&0\\d&c&b&a&0\\e&d&0&b&a\\0&e&0&0&b\end{pmatrix}$. Multiplication by the increment vector gives coefficients $(c\dot a+a\dot c,\,d\dot a+c\dot b+b\dot c+a\dot d,\,e\dot a+d\dot b+b\dot d+a\dot e,\,e\dot b+b\dot e)$, exactly those of $\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Every Jacobian entry and coefficient comparison is correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The coordinate computation is reconciled with the basis-free bilinear derivative.

activities.title: Analyze three base points
activities.promptMarkdown:
Use $DM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.

Describe the derivative at $(0,0)$, at $(L,0)$ with $L\ne0$, and at $(0,Q)$ with $Q\ne0$; give each kernel.

Use that the polynomial ring over a field has no zero divisors.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All three derivative maps and kernels are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The kernel conclusions use the integral-domain property exactly where needed.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: At $(0,0)$ the derivative is zero, so its kernel is all $V_1\times V_2$. At $(L,0)$ it is $(\dot L,\dot Q)\mapsto L\dot Q$; since $L\ne0$, multiplication by $L$ is injective, so the kernel is $V_1\times\{0\}$. At $(0,Q)$ it is $(\dot L,\dot Q)\mapsto\dot LQ$, whose kernel is $\{0\}\times V_2$ because $Q\ne0$.

activities.title: Prove the multiplication derivative and its scope
activities.promptMarkdown:
$M:\mathbb R[T,S]_1\times\mathbb R[T,S]_2\to\mathbb R[T,S]_3$ sends $(L,Q)$ to $LQ$.

Prove the derivative formula from the total-derivative definition, derive its $4\times5$ matrix, verify one directional derivative, and explain why neither a determinant nor global invertibility follows.

Use the product norm and make the quadratic remainder estimate explicit.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The derivative proof, remainder bound, matrix, directional check, and scope limits are all correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The solution integrates the week's definitions and theorems without applying square-matrix conclusions to a rectangular map.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Expansion gives $M(L+\dot L,Q+\dot Q)-M(L,Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q+\dot L\dot Q$. The first two terms define a linear map in $(\dot L,\dot Q)$. In finite-dimensional coefficient norms, $\|\dot L\dot Q\|\le C\|\dot L\|\|\dot Q\|\le(C/2)\|(\dot L,\dot Q)\|^2$, so the quotient by the joint increment norm tends to zero. Hence $DM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$. In the ordered coefficient bases its matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}c&0&a&0&0\\d&c&b&a&0\\e&d&0&b&a\\0&e&0&0&b\end{pmatrix}$. Along direction $(R,S)$ the directional derivative is $RQ+LS$, as the total derivative predicts. The matrix is rectangular, so it has no determinant; moreover dimension and factorization collisions prevent any conclusion that $M$ is globally invertible.

lessons.title: What the inverse function theorem actually says
lessons.summary: State the inverse function theorem with every hypothesis, derive the derivative of the local inverse, and distinguish its neighborhood conclusion from a global inverse claim.
objectives: State the inverse function theorem with every hypothesis, derive the derivative of the local inverse, and distinguish its neighborhood conclusion from a global inverse claim.

content.markdown:
## A theorem with a deliberately local conclusion

An invertible derivative says that a map has an invertible first-order model at one point. The inverse function theorem upgrades that approximation to a genuine inverse only after restricting both source and target to suitable neighborhoods.

The neighborhoods are part of the conclusion. Removing them changes the theorem into a false global statement.

## Reactivate the derivative and matrix inverse

Week 16 proved that a derivative is a linear map and that derivatives compose. Week 13 established the determinant test for an invertible square matrix. Recall also that injectivity is a property of a declared map on its whole domain, not of its formula near one point.

## Precise inverse function theorem

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuously differentiable, and let $a\in U$. If $Df_a$ is invertible, then there are open neighborhoods $V\subseteq U$ of $a$ and $W$ of $f(a)$ such that

$$f|_V:V\longrightarrow W$$

is bijective. Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is continuously differentiable. The theorem asserts existence of some suitable $V$ and $W$; it does not say that $f$ is injective on all of $U$ or surjective onto all of $\mathbb R^n$.

content.title: Separate hypotheses from conclusions
content.introMarkdown: Rewrite the statement with the missing domain, regularity, neighborhoods, restriction, and inverse codomain.

data.markdown:
Find the first missing typed set or regularity hypothesis.

Without open neighborhoods and a restricted map, the theorem statement is false.

Write the source open set, the $C^1$ hypothesis, the point, and then name $V$, $W$, $f|_V$, and $g$.

content.markdown:
## Derivative of the local inverse

On $V$, the identity $g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_V$ holds. Differentiating at $a$ and using the chain rule gives

$$Dg_{f(a)}Df_a=I,$$

so $Dg_{f(a)}=(Df_a)^{-1}$. The formula follows after the local inverse exists; the formula alone does not construct that inverse.

content.title: Derive the inverse derivative with types
content.introMarkdown: Prove the formula for $Dg_{f(a)}$ and state the source and target of each derivative.

data.markdown:
Check whether the outer derivative is evaluated at $f(a)$.

The inverse begins at the image point, so its derivative must be evaluated there.

Write the tangent-space arrows, differentiate $g\circ f$, and solve the resulting matrix equation.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$F(x,y)=(x+y,\,y+x^2)$ at $a=(0,0)$.

Verify the theorem, construct the branch of the inverse near the origin, and identify why another algebraic branch does not belong to the same local inverse.

### Strategy

Compute $DF_0$, apply the theorem, then solve the output equations and choose the branch passing through the base point.

### Hypotheses

$F$ is polynomial and therefore $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^2$. Its derivative at the origin is $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, with determinant one.

### Intermediate claims

For output $(u,v)$, $y=u-x$ and $x$ satisfies $x^2-x+(u-v)=0$. The root near $x=0$ is $x=(1-\sqrt{1-4(u-v)})/2$, and then $y=u-x$.

### Justification

At $(u,v)=(0,0)$ the minus branch gives $x=0$, whereas the plus branch gives $x=1$. Restricting to a sufficiently small neighborhood keeps the square root defined and isolates the branch through the chosen point.

### Conclusion

The theorem supplies neighborhoods on which the minus branch is the unique $C^1$ inverse. It makes no claim that the quadratic equation has only one solution globally.

content.title: Apply the theorem to a related map
content.introMarkdown: Verify every inverse-function hypothesis, state the complete local conclusion, and compute the derivative of the local inverse at $H(0,0)$.

data.markdown:
Check the base image or one entry of the derivative before taking its inverse.

Every later conclusion depends on applying the theorem at the correct source and target points.

Compute $H(0,0)$, then $DH_{(0,0)}$, then its determinant and inverse, and only then state $V$ and $W$.

content.markdown:
## Invertible everywhere still need not mean globally injective

Consider $P(x,y)=(e^x\cos y,e^x\sin y)$. Its Jacobian determinant is $e^{2x}>0$ at every point, so the theorem gives a local inverse around every point.

But $P(x,y+2\pi)=P(x,y)$. The map wraps the plane around the punctured plane infinitely many times, so it has no global inverse on $\mathbb R^2$.

content.title: Locate the local and global evidence
content.introMarkdown: Compute the determinant, state the local theorem conclusion, and give an explicit global collision.

data.markdown:
Check whether your collision changes the angle by a full period.

A global counterexample must use two distinct domain points with exactly the same image.

Compute the determinant first, invoke the theorem locally, then compare $y$ with $y+2\pi$.

content.markdown:
## The application checklist

A complete inverse-function argument names an open source, verifies $C^1$ regularity, evaluates a square derivative at the chosen point, proves it invertible, and states restricted neighborhoods. Only then may it differentiate the inverse.

content.title: Write a complete local-inverse proof
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $F$ has a $C^1$ local inverse near $a$, compute that inverse's derivative at $F(a)$, and state why your proof does not give a global inverse on $\mathbb R^2$.

data.markdown:
Find the first theorem hypothesis or neighborhood omitted from your proof.

A determinant computation alone is not the full inverse-function argument.

Rebuild the proof in order: regularity, base image, derivative, invertibility, neighborhoods, inverse derivative, collision.

content.markdown:
## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-17, source lines 723 to 732.

**Resource version:** Michael Spivak, Calculus on Manifolds, 1965 edition.

**Exact locator:** Chapter 2, Theorem 2-11, p. 35: complete real inverse function theorem statement, neighborhood restriction, and derivative of the inverse in Michael Spivak, Calculus on Manifolds, W. A. Benjamin, 1965 edition.

**Reading purpose:** Compare every hypothesis and neighborhood in the theorem statement with the application checklist used on this page.
Day 2 applies the theorem to the complex cube map, where local invertibility coexists with an exact three-point global fiber.
Day 1 is complete when you can state the theorem without enlarging its conclusion and derive the local inverse derivative from the chain rule.

activities.title: Separate hypotheses from conclusions
activities.promptMarkdown:
A draft states: “If $\det Df_a\ne0$, then $f$ has a differentiable inverse.”

Rewrite the statement with the missing domain, regularity, neighborhoods, restriction, and inverse codomain.

Your corrected theorem must make the word “local” visible through typed sets.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, and $a\in U$ with $Df_a$ invertible. Then there are open neighborhoods $V\subseteq U$ of $a$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $f(a)$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$. No global injectivity or surjectivity is asserted.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Every theorem hypothesis and the restricted inverse conclusion are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response prevents a local theorem from being read as a global claim.

activities.title: Derive the inverse derivative with types
activities.promptMarkdown:
$f|_V:V\to W$ and $g:W\to V$ are the local inverse maps supplied by the theorem.

Prove the formula for $Dg_{f(a)}$ and state the source and target of each derivative.

Differentiate the correct composite at the correct point.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The composition, evaluation points, identity map, and inverse formula are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof derives the formula from the chain rule after establishing typed local inverse maps.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $Df_a:T_a\mathbb R^n\to T_{f(a)}\mathbb R^n$ and $Dg_{f(a)}:T_{f(a)}\mathbb R^n\to T_a\mathbb R^n$. Since $g\circ f$ is the identity on $V$, the chain rule gives $Dg_{f(a)}Df_a=I_{T_a\mathbb R^n}$. Because $Df_a$ is invertible, right multiplication by its inverse yields $Dg_{f(a)}=(Df_a)^{-1}$.

activities.title: Apply the theorem to a related map
activities.promptMarkdown:
$H(x,y)=(x-y,\,e^y+x)$ at $(0,0)$.

Verify every inverse-function hypothesis, state the complete local conclusion, and compute the derivative of the local inverse at $H(0,0)$.

Do not attempt to invent global neighborhoods.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The base image, derivative, determinant, local conclusion, and inverse derivative are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response verifies hypotheses before invoking the theorem and keeps the conclusion neighborhood-sized.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $H$ is $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^2$, $H(0,0)=(0,1)$, and $DH_{(0,0)}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $2$. Hence there are neighborhoods $V$ of $(0,0)$ and $W$ of $(0,1)$ such that $H|_V:V\to W$ is a $C^1$ bijection. The local inverse derivative is $(DH_{(0,0)})^{-1}=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}$.

activities.title: Locate the local and global evidence
activities.promptMarkdown:
$P(x,y)=(e^x\cos y,e^x\sin y)$.

Compute the determinant, state the local theorem conclusion, and give an explicit global collision.

Keep the three claims in separate sentences.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The determinant, local conclusion, and collision are all correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response assigns each piece of evidence to the claim it actually proves.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $DP=\begin{pmatrix}e^x\cos y&-e^x\sin y\\e^x\sin y&e^x\cos y\end{pmatrix}$, so $\det DP=e^{2x}>0$. At each point, the inverse function theorem supplies neighborhoods on which $P$ is a $C^1$ bijection. Globally, $(x,y)$ and $(x,y+2\pi)$ are distinct but have the same image, so $P$ is not injective on $\mathbb R^2$.

activities.title: Write a complete local-inverse proof
activities.promptMarkdown:
$F(x,y)=(x\cos y,\,x\sin y)$ at $a=(2,0)$.

Prove that $F$ has a $C^1$ local inverse near $a$, compute that inverse's derivative at $F(a)$, and state why your proof does not give a global inverse on $\mathbb R^2$.

Include a concrete global collision after the local proof.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All hypotheses, matrices, neighborhoods, inverse derivative, and the global collision are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof keeps theorem-based local evidence separate from the global counterexample.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $F$ is $C^1$ and $F(2,0)=(2,0)$. Its derivative is $DF_{(x,y)}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos y&-x\sin y\\\sin y&x\cos y\end{pmatrix}$, so $DF_{(2,0)}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ is invertible. Therefore neighborhoods $V$ of $(2,0)$ and $W$ of $(2,0)$ exist such that $F|_V:V\to W$ has a $C^1$ inverse $g$. Moreover $Dg_{(2,0)}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1/2\end{pmatrix}$. Globally $F(2,0)=F(2,2\pi)$, so the unrestricted map is not injective.

lessons.title: The cube map: locally invertible, globally three-to-one
lessons.summary: Analyze the cube map on the punctured complex plane through its real Jacobian, local inverse neighborhoods, and exact global fibers.
objectives: Analyze the cube map on the punctured complex plane through its real Jacobian, local inverse neighborhoods, and exact global fibers.

content.markdown:
## One map, two different scales

The map $z\mapsto z^3$ is the smallest model for the course's later three-sheeted constructions. Near any nonzero input, one cube-root branch can be selected. Across the whole punctured plane, three inputs differ by cube roots of unity and share one output.

## Reactivate complex multiplication as a real map

Write $z=x+iy$ and identify $\mathbb C$ with $\mathbb R^2$. Then a complex polynomial becomes a real polynomial map, so Day 1's real inverse function theorem applies after we compute its $2\times2$ Jacobian.

## Real Jacobian of the complex cube

For $f(z)=z^3$,

$$f(x,y)=(x^3-3xy^2,\,3x^2y-y^3).$$

Its real Jacobian is $\begin{pmatrix}3x^2-3y^2&-6xy\\6xy&3x^2-3y^2\end{pmatrix}$, whose determinant is $9(x^2+y^2)^2=9|z|^4$. It is invertible exactly when $z\ne0$.

content.title: Derive the cube-map determinant
content.introMarkdown: Compute the full real Jacobian, simplify its determinant, and identify its singular set.

data.markdown:
Check the sign in the off-diagonal derivative of the real part.

One sign error changes the determinant from a positive square to an incorrect locus.

Differentiate each component row-wise, compute $ad-bc$, and complete the square in $x^2$ and $y^2$.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Study $f(z)=z^3$ at the base point $z_0=1$.

Prove the existence of one local cube-root branch through $1$ and compute its derivative.

### Strategy

Apply the real inverse function theorem at $(1,0)$ and translate the inverse derivative back into complex multiplication.

### Hypotheses

The cube map is polynomial, hence $C^1$, and its real derivative determinant at $1$ is $9$.

### Intermediate claims

There are neighborhoods $V$ of $1$ and $W$ of $1$ such that $z\mapsto z^3$ restricts to a $C^1$ bijection $V\to W$.

### Justification

The complex derivative is multiplication by $3z_0^2=3$, so the derivative of the selected local inverse branch at $1$ is multiplication by $1/3$.

### Conclusion

Exactly one cube root lying in $V$ is selected for each $w\in W$. The other two global cube roots lie outside the chosen source neighborhood.

content.title: Move the local branch to another base point
content.introMarkdown: Prove that a local inverse branch through $i$ exists near $-i$ and compute its complex derivative at $-i$.

data.markdown:
Evaluate $3z_0^2$ before inverting it.

Different preimages of the same value support different local branches.

Compute $i^3$, verify nonzero determinant, state $V$ and $W$, then invert multiplication by $-3$.

content.markdown:
## Global fibers and cube roots of unity

Let $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$. Then $1,\omega,\omega^2$ are distinct and each has cube $1$. More generally, if $z^3=w\ne0$, then the complete fiber is

$$\{z,\omega z,\omega^2z\}.$$

Indeed, any second root $u$ satisfies $(u/z)^3=1$. This is a global algebraic statement, not a contradiction to local injectivity.

content.title: Classify a nonzero fiber
content.introMarkdown: List the three roots and prove there are no others.

data.markdown:
After listing roots, justify why a fourth root cannot occur.

A global fiber classification needs both existence and completeness.

Divide an arbitrary root by $-2$ and solve the resulting cube-root-of-unity equation.

content.markdown:
## The origin is a genuine branch point

At $z=0$, the derivative of $z^3$ is the zero map, so the inverse function theorem does not apply. More strongly, no inverse branch through $0$ can be differentiable with finite derivative: along positive reals it would behave like $w^{1/3}$.

content.title: Explain the failure at zero
content.introMarkdown: Show that such a $g$ cannot be differentiable at zero with a finite real derivative.

data.markdown:
Use the magnitude of a cube root rather than choosing an arbitrary argument branch.

The magnitude obstruction applies to every possible local selection.

Set $w=t>0$, use $|g(t)|=t^{1/3}$, divide by $t$, and take the limit.

content.markdown:
## Complete two-scale analysis

The final argument must use different evidence at different scales: derivative invertibility for a neighborhood result, roots of unity for the global fiber, and a singular derivative plus growth estimate at the excluded origin.

content.title: Analyze the cube map locally and globally
content.introMarkdown: Prove local invertibility at every domain point, classify every global fiber, and explain precisely what changes if zero is added to source and target.

data.markdown:
Find the first claim supported by evidence from the wrong scale.

A local derivative theorem cannot classify a global fiber, and a global collision does not negate local invertibility.

Write three separate paragraphs: nonzero local theorem, nonzero global fiber, and the origin boundary.

content.markdown:
## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-17, source lines 723 to 732.

**Resource version:** Michael Spivak, Calculus on Manifolds, 1965 edition.

**Exact locator:** Chapter 2, Theorem 2-11 and proof, pp. 35–40: local one-to-one restriction and continuously differentiable inverse in Michael Spivak, Calculus on Manifolds, W. A. Benjamin, 1965 edition.

**Reading purpose:** Use the theorem statement to check exactly which parts of the cube-map analysis come from calculus and which require the roots-of-unity argument.
Day 3 turns local inversion into the implicit function theorem, which solves selected variables as functions of the remaining ones near a regular solution.
Day 2 is complete when you can prove local cube-root branches, classify the three-point global fibers, and isolate the singular origin.

activities.title: Derive the cube-map determinant
activities.promptMarkdown:
$f(x,y)=(x^3-3xy^2,3x^2y-y^3)$.

Compute the full real Jacobian, simplify its determinant, and identify its singular set.

Factor out the common $3$ only after differentiating both components.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $Df=\begin{pmatrix}3x^2-3y^2&-6xy\\6xy&3x^2-3y^2\end{pmatrix}$. Its determinant is $9(x^2-y^2)^2+36x^2y^2=9(x^2+y^2)^2$. It vanishes only at $(0,0)$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The matrix, determinant identity, and singular set are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The computation connects complex nonvanishing with real derivative invertibility.

activities.title: Move the local branch to another base point
activities.promptMarkdown:
Apply the cube map at $z_0=i$, where $f(i)=-i$.

Prove that a local inverse branch through $i$ exists near $-i$ and compute its complex derivative at $-i$.

Use the inverse of multiplication by $3i^2$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The base image, determinant, neighborhoods, and inverse derivative are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The selected branch is tied to the chosen preimage rather than to an unspecified global cube root.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Since $i\ne0$, the real Jacobian determinant is $9|i|^4=9$, so the inverse function theorem supplies neighborhoods $V$ of $i$ and $W$ of $-i$ on which the cube map is a $C^1$ bijection. Its derivative at $i$ is multiplication by $3i^2=-3$, so the local inverse derivative at $-i$ is multiplication by $-1/3$.

activities.title: Classify a nonzero fiber
activities.promptMarkdown:
Find every $z\in\mathbb C^\times$ satisfying $z^3=-8$.

List the three roots and prove there are no others.

Start with one root and multiply by the three cube roots of unity.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All three roots are correct and completeness is proved.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The quotient argument classifies the whole fiber instead of displaying only examples.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: One root is $-2$. The three roots are $-2$, $-2\omega$, and $-2\omega^2$, and they are distinct. If $u^3=-8$, then $(u/(-2))^3=1$, so $u/(-2)$ is one of $1,\omega,\omega^2$. Hence the list is complete.

activities.title: Explain the failure at zero
activities.promptMarkdown:
Suppose a local inverse $g$ through $0$ satisfied $g(w)^3=w$ and $g(0)=0$.

Show that such a $g$ cannot be differentiable at zero with a finite real derivative.

Restrict to $w=t>0$ and examine $|g(t)|/t$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The difference quotient and its divergence are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response goes beyond failure of a theorem hypothesis and proves a concrete obstruction.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For positive real $t$ in the target neighborhood, any cube root has magnitude $t^{1/3}$. Thus $|g(t)-g(0)|/|t-0|=t^{1/3}/t=t^{-2/3}\to\infty$. A differentiable map at zero would have bounded difference quotients near zero, so no differentiable inverse branch through the origin exists.

activities.title: Analyze the cube map locally and globally
activities.promptMarkdown:
$f:\mathbb C^\times\to\mathbb C^\times$ is $f(z)=z^3$.

Prove local invertibility at every domain point, classify every global fiber, and explain precisely what changes if zero is added to source and target.

Use the real Jacobian for the theorem and roots of unity for the fiber.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The pointwise determinant, local conclusion, complete fibers, and origin obstruction are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof assigns the inverse theorem, algebraic classification, and difference quotient to their proper claims.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Under $\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$, $\det Df_z=9|z|^4$, which is positive for every $z\in\mathbb C^\times$. The real inverse function theorem therefore gives a $C^1$ local inverse near each nonzero point. If $z^3=w\ne0$, then all preimages are $z,\omega z,\omega^2z$, and any preimage has this form because its quotient by $z$ is a cube root of unity. Thus the map is globally three-to-one, not globally injective. If zero is included, the derivative at zero is singular and any cube-root selection through zero has difference quotients of magnitude $t^{-2/3}$ along positive reals, so no differentiable local inverse exists there.

lessons.title: Solving equations locally with the implicit function theorem
lessons.summary: State and derive the implicit function theorem for a selected variable block, solve two equations locally, and distinguish a local graph from a global solution formula.
objectives: State and derive the implicit function theorem for a selected variable block, solve two equations locally, and distinguish a local graph from a global solution formula.

content.markdown:
## Equations can define functions without displaying them

A system $F(x,y)=0$ may not provide a formula for $y$. If the derivative with respect to the variables $y$ is invertible at one known solution, the implicit function theorem proves that nearby solutions form the graph of a unique function $y=g(x)$.

## Reactivate block matrices and the inverse theorem

Partition the variables as $x\in\mathbb R^n$ and $y\in\mathbb R^m$. Week 16 supplies the blocks $D_xF$ and $D_yF$; Day 1 supplies local inversion for a square map.

## Precise implicit function theorem

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+m}$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$, let $(a,b)\in U$, and suppose $F(a,b)=0$. If the square block $D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m$ is invertible, then there are open neighborhoods $A\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $a$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ of $b$, with $A\times B\subseteq U$, and a unique $C^1$ map $g:A\to B$ such that

$$F(x,y)=0\text{ for }(x,y)\in A\times B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=g(x).$$

The equivalence is local inside $A\times B$. It does not classify solutions elsewhere.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Assume the hypotheses of the implicit function theorem for $F(x,y)$.

Derive the local solution graph from the inverse function theorem using an augmented map.

### Strategy

Define $\Phi(x,y)=(x,F(x,y))$, prove its derivative is invertible, invert it locally, and read the zero-level slice.

### Hypotheses

$D\Phi(a,b)=\begin{pmatrix}I_n&0\\D_xF(a,b)&D_yF(a,b)\end{pmatrix}$ is block lower triangular.

### Intermediate claims

Its determinant is $\det D_yF(a,b)\ne0$, so $\Phi$ has a local inverse. Because the first component of $\Phi$ is $x$, that inverse has the form $\Phi^{-1}(x,z)=(x,h(x,z))$.

### Justification

Set $g(x)=h(x,0)$. Then $\Phi(x,g(x))=(x,0)$, hence $F(x,g(x))=0$. Conversely, local injectivity of $\Phi$ forces every nearby solution of $F(x,y)=0$ to have $y=g(x)$.

### Conclusion

The implicit theorem is a structured inverse theorem. Differentiating $F(x,g(x))=0$ gives $Dg(a)=-D_yF(a,b)^{-1}D_xF(a,b)$.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$F(x,y,u,v)=(x+y+u^2-1,\,x-y+v-1)$ at $(1,0,0,0)$.

Solve $(x,y)$ locally as functions of $(u,v)$ and verify the derivative formula.

### Strategy

Use the $(x,y)$ block for the theorem, then solve the linear equations explicitly as a check.

### Hypotheses

$F(1,0,0,0)=0$ and $D_{(x,y)}F=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $-2$.

### Intermediate claims

The equations give $x=(2-u^2-v)/2$ and $y=(v-u^2)/2$.

### Justification

These formulas are $C^1$ and pass through $(x,y)=(1,0)$ at $(u,v)=(0,0)$. Their derivative at zero agrees with $-D_{(x,y)}F^{-1}D_{(u,v)}F$.

### Conclusion

The solution set near the base point is a graph over the two free coordinates $(u,v)$.

content.markdown:
## A singular chosen block does not end every analysis

For $F(x,y)=y^2-x$ at $(0,0)$, $\partial F/\partial y=0$, so the theorem does not solve $y$ as a $C^1$ function of $x$ there. But $\partial F/\partial x=-1$, so the same equation solves $x=y^2$ as a function of $y$.

Failure of one selected block means that one theorem application is unavailable. It does not say the solution set has no local description.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $D\Phi(a,b)=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\D_xF&D_yF\end{pmatrix}$ has nonzero determinant because $D_yF(a,b)$ is invertible. The inverse function theorem gives a local inverse $(x,z)\mapsto(x,h(x,z))$. Set $g(x)=h(x,0)$. Then $F(x,g(x))=0$. If a nearby $(x,y)$ also satisfies $F(x,y)=0$, then $\Phi(x,y)=(x,0)=\Phi(x,g(x))$, and local injectivity gives $y=g(x)$. lessons.title: Why the central solution set has three local coordinates
lessons.summary: Apply the implicit function theorem to the two defining equations of X, solve two coordinates near the regular point, and justify the resulting three-complex-coordinate count without importing later holomorphic-manifold theory.
objectives: Apply the implicit function theorem to the two defining equations of X, solve two coordinates near the regular point, and justify the resulting three-complex-coordinate count without importing later holomorphic-manifold theory.

content.markdown:
## The course's central equations enter the analysis

Let $X\subseteq\mathbb C^5$ be cut out by

$$f_1=a^2e-abd+cb^2-1=0,\qquad f_2=ad+bc-1=0.$$

Two independent complex equations should leave three complex coordinates free. Today makes that count local and exact at one regular point.

## Scalar-setting boundary

We identify $\mathbb C^5$ with $\mathbb R^{10}$ and the two complex equations with four real equations. An invertible complex $2\times2$ coordinate block becomes an invertible real $4\times4$ block. The real implicit theorem then gives six real free coordinates, grouped naturally as three complex coordinates. Holomorphic dependence is not claimed until Week 18.

## Verify the regular point and gradients

Take $p=(0,1,1,0,0)$. Both equations vanish there. Their complex coordinate gradients are

$$\nabla f_1=(2ae-bd,\,-ad+2cb,\,b^2,\,-ab,\,a^2),$$

$$\nabla f_2=(d,c,b,a,0).$$

At $p$ these become $(0,2,1,0,0)$ and $(0,1,1,0,0)$, which are linearly independent.

content.markdown:
## Choose the variables that the equations solve

Use $(a,d,e)$ as free coordinates and $(b,c)$ as solved coordinates. The selected complex derivative block is

$$D_{(b,c)}(f_1,f_2)(p)=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},$$

with determinant one. Its realification is invertible, so the real implicit function theorem solves $(b,c)$ uniquely near $(1,1)$ as a $C^1$ function of $(a,d,e)$ near $(0,0,0)$.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$G_1=b+c+a-2$ and $G_2=b-c+d$ at $(a,b,c,d,e)=(0,1,1,0,0)$.

Construct the local solution graph over $(a,d,e)$ and reconcile complex and real dimensions.

### Strategy

Check the selected $(b,c)$ block, solve the linear system explicitly, and view the same formulas on real and imaginary parts.

### Hypotheses

$D_{(b,c)}G=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $-2$.

### Intermediate claims

The equations give $b=1-(a+d)/2$ and $c=1-(a-d)/2$, while $e$ remains free.

### Justification

The formulas are complex-linear in the three free complex coordinates. Their realification is a graph from $\mathbb R^6$ to $\mathbb R^4$.

### Conclusion

The zero set has three free complex coordinate slots and real dimension six near the point. In this linear model, holomorphic dependence is explicit; the nonlinear central example currently uses only the real $C^1$ conclusion.

content.markdown:
## Local dimension is not a global coordinate system

The implicit theorem supplies one graph near $p$. Another point may require solving a different pair of coordinates, and a single global formula for $(b,c)$ need not exist.

Nor does independent gradient data prove that $X$ is globally isomorphic to affine three-space. That much stronger statement belongs to the later algebraic and geometric parts of the course.

A global isomorphism requires an explicit globally defined inverse or another global theorem.

activities.promptMarkdown:
$X=\{f_1=f_2=0\}\subseteq\mathbb C^5$ with $f_1=a^2e-abd+cb^2-1$, $f_2=ad+bc-1$, at $p=(0,1,1,0,0)$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Both equations vanish at $p$. Their gradients are $(0,2,1,0,0)$ and $(0,1,1,0,0)$, and the $(b,c)$ minor is $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant one. Realifying the two complex equations gives four real equations, while this complex block becomes an invertible real $4\times4$ block. The real implicit function theorem therefore gives a unique local $C^1$ graph $(b,c)=g(a,d,e)$ near $p$. Its domain has three complex coordinate slots, hence six real coordinates, so the solution set is locally six-real-dimensional at $p$. This does not yet prove that $g$ is holomorphic, that the same coordinates work at every point, or that $X$ is globally isomorphic to $\mathbb C^3$.

## Four earlier objects now meet one theorem

Local-versus-global logic, translated solution sets, pullbacks, and the matrix chain rule each control a different step in local inversion. The scheduled reviews retrieve those objects before the final proof asks you to coordinate them.

## Retrieval rules

Each review repeats one exact earlier object after 16, 8, 3, or 1 weeks. The surrounding problem is new: the retrieved object must now serve a local inverse or implicit-function argument.

## Deliberate review: Week 1 after sixteen weeks

A map can be injective on a neighborhood of each point without being injective on its whole domain. The distinction is now supported by derivatives rather than interval inspection.

## Complete worked model

$F:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^2$ is $F(x,y,z)=(x+y+z,\,x-y+z^2)$ at the origin.

Solve $(x,y)$ locally in terms of $z$, compute the solution derivative, and state the exact scope.

### Strategy

Verify the point, invert the $(x,y)$ block, invoke the implicit theorem, and compare with the explicit formulas.

### Hypotheses

$D_{(x,y)}F(0)=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $-2$.

### Intermediate claims

Solving gives $x=-(z+z^2)/2$ and $y=(-z+z^2)/2$.

### Justification

The formulas define the unique nearby graph through the origin and have derivative $(-1/2,-1/2)$ at zero, agreeing with the block formula.

### Conclusion

content.markdown:
## The regularity upgrade

Week 17 produced local inverses that were only known to be real $C^1$. A holomorphic map carries extra structure: its real derivative is complex-linear. When that derivative is invertible, the local inverse preserves the same complex structure.

The conclusion is still local. Holomorphic regularity strengthens the inverse inside the chosen neighborhoods; it does not enlarge those neighborhoods to the whole domain.

## Reactivate the real theorem

Identify $\mathbb C^n$ with $\mathbb R^{2n}$. Week 17 says that an invertible real derivative gives a $C^1$ inverse between neighborhoods. We now track the additional fact that the derivatives are complex-linear.

## Holomorphic maps and their derivatives

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be open. A map $F:U\to\mathbb C^m$ is holomorphic when it is complex differentiable in a neighborhood of every point. Equivalently for the maps used here, $F$ is real $C^1$ and every real derivative $DF_z:\mathbb R^{2n}\to\mathbb R^{2m}$ is complex-linear.

In one variable, writing $F=u+iv$, complex linearity is exactly the Cauchy-Riemann system $u_x=v_y$ and $u_y=-v_x$.

content.markdown:
## Complex inverse function theorem

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $a\in U$. If the complex-linear map $DF_a$ is invertible, then there are open neighborhoods $V\subseteq U$ of $a$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ of $F(a)$ such that

$$F|_V:V\longrightarrow W$$

is bijective and its inverse $G:W\to V$ is holomorphic. Moreover, $DG_{F(a)}=(DF_a)^{-1}$.

## Complete worked model

Explain why the real inverse supplied for a holomorphic $F$ is holomorphic.

Derive the complex theorem from the real theorem and complex-linearity of derivatives.

### Strategy

Realify $F$, apply Week 17, then inspect the derivative of the inverse at every point of the target neighborhood.

### Hypotheses

An invertible complex-linear map is invertible as a real map, and its real inverse is again complex-linear.

### Intermediate claims

The real theorem gives a $C^1$ inverse $G$. At $w=F(z)$, the chain rule gives $DG_w=(DF_z)^{-1}$.

### Justification

Because $DF_z$ is complex-linear and invertible on a smaller neighborhood, $DG_w$ is complex-linear. A real $C^1$ map with complex-linear derivative at every point is holomorphic.

### Conclusion

The inverse is holomorphic on $W$. The argument upgrades regularity but preserves the same local neighborhoods.
