Confusing the ideal with all polynomials vanishing on its zero set is a major algebraic-geometry error.

End after proving $P-Q\in I$ implies agreement; label the converse as later material.

content.markdown:
## Preview the coordinate-ring language

When an affine set $X$ is described by polynomial equations, its coordinate ring records polynomial functions on $X$. The eventual intrinsic definition uses the full vanishing ideal $I(X)$.

For this week, $R/(f_1,f_2)$ is the displayed quotient in which we verify formulas. The precise affine-variety and coordinate-ring dictionary is taught in Week 32, so neither concept is assessed for mastery today.

## Independent reduction with scope control

A complete quotient calculation contains the ambient ring, the ideal, a certificate for the difference, the class equality, and any pointwise consequence. It does not invent the converse.

**Reading purpose:** Compare the general polynomial-quotient examples with the lesson's exact two-relation computations.
Day 5 retrieves earlier proof tools and integrates them with the quotient universal property and the two defining relations.
Day 4 is complete when you can certify a quotient identity and state exactly what it does and does not prove about formulas on $X$.

activities.title: Reduce a direct relation
activities.promptMarkdown:
Work in $A=R/(f_1,f_2)$.

Prove $[2ad+2bc-3]=[-1]$.

Subtract the proposed representatives and express the difference as a multiple of $f_2$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The reduction is an exact multiple of the defining generator.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The conclusion is explicitly scoped to the quotient ring.

activities.title: Derive the key class identity
activities.promptMarkdown:
In $A$, consider $a^2e-abd+cb^2-1+a(ad+bc-1)$.

Prove that its class is zero.

Identify an explicit combination of $f_1$ and $f_2$ and expand it once.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The two-generator certificate expands to the exact difference.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof uses only permitted ideal combinations.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The displayed polynomial is exactly $f_1+af_2$. Both summands lie in $I$, so their sum lies in $I$ and its class is zero in $A$. Expanding gives $a^2e-abd+cb^2-1+a^2d+abc-a$, which verifies the certificate.

activities.title: Pass from ideal membership to pointwise agreement
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $I=(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\subseteq k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and suppose $P-Q=\sum h_i g_i$.

Prove that $P$ and $Q$ agree at every point of $V(I)$.

Evaluate the displayed certificate at an arbitrary point of $V(I)$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The evaluation proof establishes the correct one-way implication.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The conclusion is limited to what ideal membership proves.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Take $x\in V(I)$. Then $g_i(x)=0$ for every generator, so $(P-Q)(x)=\sum h_i(x)g_i(x)=0$. Therefore $P(x)=Q(x)$. This proves only the implication from ideal membership to pointwise agreement.

activities.title: Check a relation and its geometric consequence
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $X=V(f_1,f_2)\subseteq\mathbb C^5$.

Prove that $a^2e-abd+cb^2$ and $1$ agree on $X$.

Give the quotient certificate and then evaluate it on $X$ without asserting the converse.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The quotient and pointwise conclusions are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The answer states the exact direction of implication.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Their difference is $a^2e-abd+cb^2-1=f_1\in I$, so their classes are equal in $A=R/I$. If $x\in X=V(f_1,f_2)$, then $f_1(x)=0$, hence $(a^2e-abd+cb^2)(x)=1$. No converse from pointwise agreement to membership in $(f_1,f_2)$ is used.

activities.title: Prove and interpret the defining quotient identity
activities.promptMarkdown:
Use $A=\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,e]/(f_1,f_2)$ with the syllabus definitions of $f_1$ and $f_2$.

Prove $[b-1]=[a(2bd-ae)]$ and conclude that the two formulas agree on $X=V(f_1,f_2)$.

Supply an exact ideal certificate, distinguish all three equality scopes, and state why the converse is unavailable.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The exact relation and one-way geometric implication are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Ambient, quotient, and pointwise equality are kept distinct.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: In the ambient ring, $(b-1)-a(2bd-ae)=f_1-bf_2$, so the difference lies in $I=(f_1,f_2)$. Therefore $[b-1]=[a(2bd-ae)]$ in $A$. Evaluating the certificate at any point of $X$ makes both $f_1$ and $f_2$ vanish, so the two formulas agree pointwise on $X$. They are not equal as ambient polynomials. Pointwise agreement alone would not imply membership in the displayed ideal without an additional radical or Nullstellensatz result.

lessons.title: Retrieve, diagnose, and synthesize quotient reasoning
lessons.summary: Retrieve earlier proof tools and combine them into a complete quotient-ring argument with correct geometric scope.
objectives: Retrieve earlier proof tools and combine them into a complete quotient-ring argument with correct geometric scope.

content.markdown:
## Make the construction retrievable

The week ends by recovering four earlier tools at increasing independence, then using them to diagnose a false converse, factor a homomorphism, and reduce an expression in the defining quotient.

## Keep the proof layers separate

An ideal certificate proves quotient equality. Evaluation then proves pointwise agreement on the zero set. A universal factorization needs a kernel-containment hypothesis. None of these steps substitutes for another.

## Deliberate review: factor theorem as a certificate

Retrieve the Week 6 factor-theorem discipline. Today the factorization will serve as a certificate that a difference belongs to a principal ideal.

content.title: Recover a principal-ideal certificate
content.introMarkdown: Prove $p\in(x-2)$ in $\mathbb C[x]$.

data.markdown:
Check the quotient polynomial by expansion.

A false factorization invalidates every quotient equality built from it.

Multiply the proposed factors and compare every coefficient.

## Deliberate review: kernel controls a factorization

Retrieve the linear principle that a map constant on cosets of a kernel descends to a quotient. State the typed map rather than relying on analogy alone.

content.title: Descend a linear functional

data.markdown:

The same proof architecture governs quotient-ring factorization.

Start with equal cosets, subtract representatives, and apply the kernel condition.

## Deliberate review: invariance and descent

Retrieve the distinction between a function being constant on equivalence classes and a classification of all such functions.

data.markdown:

Descent requires constancy on every equivalence class.

Compare the two possible orbit representatives before defining the descended function.

## Deliberate review: kernel ideal

Retrieve the Week 21 kernel proof on a new evaluation map. The result identifies the exact quotient that removes the relation.

data.markdown:
Find the first missing inclusion or unstated surjectivity argument.

A quotient isomorphism needs the exact kernel and image.

Prove the kernel biconditional, then name the constant preimages.

## Diagnose the false converse

Ideal membership always gives pointwise vanishing on the zero set. The reverse implication may fail for a nonradical ideal.

content.title: Refute pointwise membership
content.introMarkdown: Show that $x$ vanishes on $V(I)$ but $x\notin I$.

data.markdown:
Check whether the response established both halves of the counterexample.

This boundary prevents an invalid converse in every later coordinate-ring argument.

Compute $V(I)$ first, then separately prove $x\notin I$.

content.markdown:
## Factor a concrete polynomial map

The universal property becomes useful when a map respects a relation. Verify the relation lies in the kernel before writing the quotient map.

content.title: Factor evaluation through a quadratic quotient
content.introMarkdown: Construct the unique $\bar\varphi:\mathbb C[x]/(x^2-1)\to\mathbb C$ with $\bar\varphi\circ\pi=\varphi$.

data.markdown:
Locate the first skipped hypothesis or quotient-map obligation.

A quotient factorization is invalid unless the defining relation is killed.

Check the generator at $1$, then follow the four-part universal-property proof.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Let $S=\mathbb C[u,v]$, $J=(uv)$, and let $\psi:S\to\mathbb C[t]$ satisfy $\psi(u)=t$ and $\psi(v)=0$.

Factor $\psi$ through $S/J$ and prove $[u^2v+v]=[v]$ in that quotient.

### Strategy

First show that the generator $uv$ is killed, then apply the universal property and give a separate ideal certificate for the class identity.

### Hypotheses

$\psi(uv)=t\cdot0=0$, so every multiple of $uv$ lies in $\ker\psi$.

### Intermediate claims

The forced map is $\bar\psi([P])=\psi(P)$. It is well defined because $J\subseteq\ker\psi$. Also $(u^2v+v)-v=u(uv)\in J$.

### Justification

The universal-property proof supplies the ring laws and uniqueness. The displayed multiple of the generator supplies the independent quotient reduction.

### Conclusion

The map factors uniquely through $S/J$, and the two stated classes are equal although the ambient polynomials differ.

## Assemble the week's proof architecture

The capstone combines construction, the universal property, and the exact two-relation computation. Keep every ring and equality scope visible.

data.markdown:
Find the earliest missing universal-property obligation, sign error, or unsupported converse.

This capstone is the durable quotient-ring proof model used by later geometry weeks.

Use labelled parts for factorization, reduction, and pointwise scope; verify the certificate by expansion.

activities.title: Recover a principal-ideal certificate
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $p(x)=x^3-4x^2+x+6$.

Prove $p\in(x-2)$ in $\mathbb C[x]$.

Evaluate at $2$, invoke the factor theorem, and exhibit the quotient polynomial.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The evaluation and factorization are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Divisibility is translated into principal-ideal membership.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $p(2)=8-16+2+6=0$, so the factor theorem gives $x-2\mid p$. Division yields $p=(x-2)(x^2-2x-3)$. Hence $p\in(x-2)$ with an explicit certificate.

activities.title: Descend a linear functional
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $T:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be $T(x,y)=x+y$ and let $K=\ker T$.

Define the induced map $\bar T:\mathbb R^2/K\to\mathbb R$ and prove it is well defined.

Use equality of cosets to compare the outputs.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The quotient map and representative proof are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Coset equality is translated through the kernel equation.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Define $\bar T((x,y)+K)=x+y$. If $(x,y)+K=(x',y')+K$, then $(x-x',y-y')\in K$, so $(x-x')+(y-y')=0$. Thus $x+y=x'+y'$, proving well-definedness.

activities.title: Descend an even polynomial
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $\{\pm1\}$ act on $\mathbb R$ by sign and let $h(x)=x^4+2x^2$.

Prove $h$ is constant on each orbit and define the induced function on the set of orbits.

Check invariance directly, then state the induced value.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The invariance calculation and descended function are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The answer proves representative independence directly.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $h(-x)=(-x)^4+2(-x)^2=x^4+2x^2=h(x)$, so $h$ has the same value on the orbit $\{x,-x\}$. Define $\bar h(\{x,-x\})=h(x)$. The invariance calculation proves this is well defined.

activities.title: Recover an evaluation kernel
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $\operatorname{ev}_{-1}:\mathbb C[x]\to\mathbb C$ be evaluation at $-1$.

Prove $\ker(\operatorname{ev}_{-1})=(x+1)$ and identify the quotient.

Use the factor theorem and the first isomorphism theorem.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The kernel and quotient are correctly identified.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Both directions of the kernel equality and surjectivity are supplied.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: A polynomial lies in the kernel exactly when $p(-1)=0$, which by the factor theorem is equivalent to divisibility by $x+1$. Hence the kernel is $(x+1)$. Evaluation is surjective because constants are in its image, so $\mathbb C[x]/(x+1)\cong\mathbb C$.

activities.title: Refute pointwise membership
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $I=(x^2)\subseteq\mathbb C[x]$.

Show that $x$ vanishes on $V(I)$ but $x\notin I$.

Compute the zero set and use degree or divisibility for nonmembership.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The counterexample proves the converse fails.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Zero-set computation and ideal nonmembership are both explicit.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $V(x^2)=\{0\}$, and $x(0)=0$, so $x$ vanishes on $V(I)$. If $x\in(x^2)$, then $x=x^2q$ for some polynomial $q$, which is impossible by degree (and also by divisibility). Thus $x\notin(x^2)$. Pointwise vanishing does not imply membership in this displayed ideal.

activities.title: Factor evaluation through a quadratic quotient
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $\varphi:\mathbb C[x]\to\mathbb C$ be evaluation at $1$ and let $I=(x^2-1)$.

Construct the unique $\bar\varphi:\mathbb C[x]/(x^2-1)\to\mathbb C$ with $\bar\varphi\circ\pi=\varphi$.

Check $I\subseteq\ker\varphi$, define the map, and prove well-definedness and uniqueness.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The kernel containment and complete factorization proof are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Well-definedness and uniqueness use different steps.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Since $(x^2-1)(1)=0$, every multiple of $x^2-1$ lies in $\ker\varphi$, so $I\subseteq\ker\varphi$. Define $\bar\varphi([p])=p(1)$. If $[p]=[q]$, then $p-q\in I$, hence $(p-q)(1)=0$, so the map is well defined. It preserves the ring operations because evaluation does. Any factorization must send $[p]=\pi(p)$ to $\varphi(p)=p(1)$, so it is unique.

activities.title: Synthesize ideals, quotients, and the defining relations
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $R=\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,e]$, $I=(f_1,f_2)$ with the syllabus definitions, $A=R/I$, and $X=V(I)$.

Prove the universal property of $R/I$, derive $[a^2de]=[d(1+b-2b^2c)]$, and state the exact pointwise consequence on $X$.

Write three labelled parts and include the boundary on the missing converse.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The universal theorem, exact reduction, and pointwise implication are all correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Every claim is matched to its necessary hypothesis and equality scope.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Universal property: if $\varphi:R\to B$ satisfies $I\subseteq\ker\varphi$, define $\bar\varphi([P])=\varphi(P)$. Equality of classes makes $P-Q\in I$, so the kernel containment proves well-definedness; the ring laws descend from $\varphi$, and surjectivity of the quotient map proves uniqueness. Reduction: $a^2de-d(1+b-2b^2c)=df_1+bdf_2\in I$, so $[a^2de]=[d(1+b-2b^2c)]$ in $A$. Pointwise consequence: evaluating this certificate at any point of $X$ proves the two formulas agree there. They are not equal as ambient polynomials, and pointwise agreement alone does not prove membership in $(f_1,f_2)$ without an additional radical or Nullstellensatz theorem.

lessons.title: Division with remainder and the Euclidean algorithm
lessons.summary: Use and justify polynomial division over a field, then compute a monic greatest common divisor by the Euclidean algorithm.
objectives: Use and justify polynomial division over a field, then compute a monic greatest common divisor by the Euclidean algorithm.

content.markdown:
## Replace factor guessing by a terminating method

Divisibility questions become manageable when one variable is distinguished and the coefficient ring is a field. Division with remainder reduces the degree at every step; repeating that reduction finds a greatest common divisor and records enough information to reconstruct a proof.

The hypotheses matter. Today the ambient ring is $k[t]$ with $k$ a field. Several-variable factorization and the failure of blanket Bézout claims are handled later in the week.

## Reactivate the week's algebraic inputs

Earlier polynomial and proof work established degree, leading coefficients, multiplication, divisibility, and the factor theorem. Week 21 supplied domains and legal cancellation. Week 22 supplied generated ideals, which will encode Bézout identities on Day 2. Week 15 supplied binary-form spaces, and Week 16 supplied the derivative of their multiplication map; those last two inputs will be used on Day 4.

## Division with remainder

For $f,g\in k[t]$ with $g\ne0$, there are unique $q,r\in k[t]$ such that $f=qg+r$ and either $r=0$ or $\deg r<\deg g$.

Existence removes the leading term of the current remainder. If $r_0=f$ and $\deg r_0\ge\deg g$, subtract $(\operatorname{lc}(r_0)/\operatorname{lc}(g))t^{\deg r_0-\deg g}g$. The degree strictly falls, so the process terminates.

content.title: Remove one leading term
content.introMarkdown: Carry out the first two leading-term cancellations and state the resulting remainder.

data.markdown:
Find the first quotient term or subtraction sign that is wrong.

Every later Euclidean step depends on reliable degree reduction.

Match leading terms before subtracting and recompute the new polynomial coefficient by coefficient.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Divide $t^4+2t^3-t+1$ by $t^2+1$ in $\mathbb Q[t]$.

Find $q,r$ and prove that no second pair satisfying the degree bound exists.

### Strategy

Continue the leading-term cancellation, then subtract two hypothetical decompositions.

### Hypotheses

The divisor is nonzero and its leading coefficient is invertible in the field $\mathbb Q$.

### Intermediate claims

The remaining division step subtracts $-1\cdot(t^2+1)$, leaving $-3t+2$. Thus $q=t^2+2t-1$ and $r=-3t+2$. If $f=qg+r=q'g+r'$, then $(q-q')g=r'-r$.

### Justification

If $q-q'\ne0$, the left side has degree at least $\deg g$, while the right side has degree below $\deg g$. This is impossible. Hence $q=q'$ and then $r=r'$.

### Conclusion

$t^4+2t^3-t+1=(t^2+2t-1)(t^2+1)+(-3t+2)$, and the quotient and remainder are unique.

content.title: Locate the hypothesis in uniqueness
content.introMarkdown: Explain why the comparison is valid over a field and identify what can fail over a ring with zero divisors.

data.markdown:
Check whether the answer names a domain property or only repeats the conclusion.

A theorem remains trustworthy only when its proof dependencies are visible.

Write the degree equality and identify the nonzero-product fact that supports it.

content.markdown:
## The Euclidean algorithm

Apply division repeatedly: $r_{i-1}=q_i r_i+r_{i+1}$ with strictly decreasing nonzero remainder degrees. The last nonzero remainder divides the preceding remainder; substituting upward shows it divides every earlier remainder and therefore the original pair.

Conversely, any common divisor of the original pair divides every remainder. The last nonzero remainder is therefore a greatest common divisor, determined up to a nonzero scalar. We choose the monic representative.

content.title: Run a short Euclidean chain
content.introMarkdown: Compute the monic gcd and justify it from the remainder chain.

data.markdown:
Find the first incorrect division equation or unjustified gcd claim.

A gcd is a divisibility statement, not just the final line of an algorithm.

Verify the division identity and state explicitly why the last nonzero remainder divides both inputs.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Let $f=t^4-1$ and $g=t^3-1$ in $\mathbb Q[t]$.

Compute their monic greatest common divisor.

### Strategy

Divide the larger degree by the smaller, then divide again until the remainder vanishes.

### Hypotheses

$\mathbb Q[t]$ is Euclidean with size function degree.

### Intermediate claims

$f=tg+(t-1)$. Also $g=(t^2+t+1)(t-1)$. Hence the last nonzero remainder is $t-1$.

### Justification

Every common divisor of $f$ and $g$ divides $f-tg=t-1$. Conversely, $t-1$ divides both polynomials by the factor theorem.

### Conclusion

$\gcd(t^4-1,t^3-1)=t-1$ in monic normalization.

content.title: Prove the two divisibility directions
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $f$ and $g$ have exactly the same common divisors as $g$ and $r$.

data.markdown:
Locate the first missing direction or missing divisibility witness.

This invariant is the proof behind every Euclidean gcd computation.

Write separate forward and reverse implications, expanding each divisibility claim as an equation.

content.markdown:
## Independent division and gcd

A complete solution separates computation from certification: first record the remainder chain, then state why the last nonzero remainder has both gcd divisibility properties.

Normalize only at the end. Multiplying a gcd by a nonzero scalar does not change which polynomials it divides, but the monic convention makes the answer unique.

content.title: Compute and certify a polynomial gcd
content.introMarkdown: Use division with remainder to find the monic gcd, and prove the result from the remainder equations.

data.markdown:
Find the earliest arithmetic error or missing half of the gcd proof.

Later Bézout and factorization arguments use the certified gcd, not an unchecked computation.

Verify each division identity, then state separately why the candidate divides both inputs and why every common divisor divides it.

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-23, source lines 781 to 788.

**Resource version:** MIT OpenCourseWare RES.18-012, Spring 2022.

**Exact locator:** Lecture 12 §12.2, Definition 12.5, Proposition 12.6, and Example 12.8, pp. 59–60: Euclidean domains and polynomial division over a field in MIT 18.702 Algebra II Student Notes, Spring 2022.

**Reading purpose:** Connect the explicit polynomial algorithm to the general Euclidean-domain proof.
Tomorrow, the same remainder equations will be read backward to express the gcd as a linear combination.
Day 1 is complete when a gcd calculation ends with a proof of both divisibility directions, not merely a final remainder.

activities.title: Remove one leading term
activities.promptMarkdown:
Work in $\mathbb Q[t]$ with $f=t^4+2t^3-t+1$ and $g=t^2+1$.

Carry out the first two leading-term cancellations and state the resulting remainder.

Display each multiple of $g$ that you subtract.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: First subtract $t^2g=t^4+t^2$, leaving $2t^3-t^2-t+1$. Next subtract $2tg=2t^3+2t$, leaving $-t^2-3t+1$. One more step would be needed because this remainder still has degree two.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both leading terms are cancelled correctly.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response explains why each quotient term is chosen.

activities.title: Locate the hypothesis in uniqueness
activities.promptMarkdown:
In the uniqueness proof, the key comparison is $\deg((q-q')g)\ge\deg g$ when $q-q'\ne0$.

Explain why the comparison is valid over a field and identify what can fail over a ring with zero divisors.

Name the exact product-degree fact, not merely “division works.”
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Over a field, $k[t]$ is an integral domain, so nonzero products are nonzero and degrees add: $\deg((q-q')g)=\deg(q-q')+\deg g\ge\deg g$. With zero divisors, leading coefficients can multiply to zero, so a nonzero product may lose degree or even become zero; that degree contradiction is then unavailable.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The product-degree hypothesis and its failure are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response points to the exact line of the uniqueness proof.

activities.title: Run a short Euclidean chain
activities.promptMarkdown:
In $\mathbb Q[t]$, take $f=t^3-t$ and $g=t^2-1$.

Compute the monic gcd and justify it from the remainder chain.

Write the division equation and then check the divisor in both polynomials.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $t^3-t=t(t^2-1)+0$, so the last nonzero remainder is $t^2-1$. It is already monic and divides both $f=t(t^2-1)$ and $g=t^2-1$. Thus $\gcd(f,g)=t^2-1$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The remainder chain and monic gcd are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The last nonzero remainder is checked against both inputs.

activities.title: Prove the two divisibility directions
activities.promptMarkdown:
Suppose one Euclidean step gives $f=qg+r$ in $k[t]$.

Prove that $f$ and $g$ have exactly the same common divisors as $g$ and $r$.

Prove both implications using only the definition of divisibility.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both implications follow directly from divisibility.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof writes explicit witnesses rather than relying on an algorithm slogan.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $d\mid f$ and $d\mid g$, write $f=da$ and $g=db$. Then $r=f-qg=d(a-qb)$, so $d\mid r$. Thus $d$ divides both $g$ and $r$. Conversely, if $d\mid g$ and $d\mid r$, write $g=db$ and $r=dc$. Then $f=qg+r=d(qb+c)$, so $d\mid f$. Hence the common-divisor sets coincide.

activities.title: Compute and certify a polynomial gcd
activities.promptMarkdown:
Work in $\mathbb Q[t]$ with $f=t^4+t^3-t-1$ and $g=t^3-t$.

Use division with remainder to find the monic gcd, and prove the result from the remainder equations.

Show the full chain and both parts of the gcd certificate.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The complete chain and monic gcd are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The answer certifies both universal divisibility conditions.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: First $f=tg+(t^3+t^2-t-1)$, and subtracting once more gives $f=(t+1)g+(t^2-1)$. Next $g=t(t^2-1)+0$. Thus the last nonzero remainder is $t^2-1$. It divides $g=t(t^2-1)$ and $f=(t+1)g+(t^2-1)$, hence divides both inputs. If $d$ divides both $f$ and $g$, then it divides $f-(t+1)g=t^2-1$. Therefore every common divisor divides the monic polynomial $t^2-1$, so $\gcd(f,g)=t^2-1$.

lessons.title: Bézout identities in one variable
lessons.summary: Derive a polynomial Bézout identity from the Euclidean algorithm and prove the coprime case without extending it falsely to several variables.
objectives: Derive a polynomial Bézout identity from the Euclidean algorithm and prove the coprime case without extending it falsely to several variables.

content.markdown:
## Read the remainder chain backward

The Euclidean algorithm does more than identify a gcd. Every remainder is built from the two preceding polynomials, so the last nonzero remainder is a polynomial linear combination of the original pair.

When the monic gcd is $1$, the resulting equation $Af+Bg=1$ is a Bézout certificate. It proves coprimality in $k[t]$ and turns many divisibility claims into one-line arguments.

## Reactivate polynomial identities

An equality in $k[t]$ is coefficientwise. Week 2 taught expansion and collection of like powers; Day 1 supplied the remainder chain. Week 22 defined the generated ideal $(f,g)$ as all combinations $Af+Bg$. Today every certificate is checked by expansion, not accepted because an algorithm allegedly produced it.

## Back-substitution begins at the last remainder

Suppose the final nonzero remainder is $d$. The preceding division equation writes $d$ as a combination of the two remainders before it. Substitute the earlier remainder equations one at a time until only the original $f$ and $g$ remain.

Normalize consistently. If the last remainder is a nonzero constant $c$, divide the whole identity by $c$ to obtain a certificate for the monic gcd $1$.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Let $f=t^3-2t+2$ and $g=t^2-1$ in $\mathbb Q[t]$.

Compute the gcd and produce an explicit Bézout identity.

### Strategy

Run the Euclidean algorithm, solve the final equation for its constant remainder, then substitute the first remainder.

### Hypotheses

$\mathbb Q[t]$ is a Euclidean domain.

### Intermediate claims

$f=tg+r$ with $r=-t+2$. Next, $g=(-t-2)r+3$. Therefore $3=g+(t+2)r=g+(t+2)(f-tg)$.

### Justification

Expanding gives $3=(t+2)f+(1-t^2-2t)g$. The final nonzero remainder is the unit $3$, so the monic gcd is $1$.

### Conclusion

$1=\frac{t+2}{3}f+\frac{1-t^2-2t}{3}g$, a complete coprimality certificate.

content.markdown:
## Why the gcd is always a linear combination

Each remainder belongs to the ideal $(f,g)$ because it is formed by subtraction and multiplication from earlier remainders. Hence the last nonzero remainder $d$ lies in $(f,g)$ and has the form $Af+Bg$.

Conversely, $d$ divides both $f$ and $g$, so it divides every combination $Af+Bg$. Therefore $(f,g)=(d)$. In particular, $\gcd(f,g)=1$ exactly when $(f,g)=k[t]$, equivalently when a Bézout identity exists.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Let $a,b,c\in k[t]$ satisfy $\gcd(a,b)=1$ and $a\mid bc$.

Prove that $a\mid c$.

### Strategy

Multiply a Bézout identity for $a,b$ by $c$ and use the two given divisibilities.

### Hypotheses

There are $u,v\in k[t]$ with $ua+vb=1$, and there is $h\in k[t]$ with $bc=ah$.

### Intermediate claims

$c=uac+vbc=a(uc+vh)$.

### Justification

Both terms on the right are multiples of $a$: the first visibly, the second because $bc=ah$.

### Conclusion

$a\mid c$.

## Independent extended Euclidean proof

A polished Bézout solution contains three layers: the remainder chain, the backward substitution, and a final expansion or coefficient check. Skipping the middle layer hides where the coefficients came from.

The conclusion belongs to $k[t]$. In $k[T,S]$, two polynomials can share no nonunit factor without generating the unit ideal; that boundary is central to Day 3.

lessons.title: Unique factorization and Gauss's lemma
lessons.summary: Distinguish irreducible from prime elements, use Gauss's lemma to pass unique factorization to polynomial rings, and separate gcd from Bézout in several variables.
objectives: Distinguish irreducible from prime elements, use Gauss's lemma to pass unique factorization to polynomial rings, and separate gcd from Bézout in several variables.

content.markdown:
## Keep the true multivariable theorem

Polynomial division by degree makes $k[t]$ especially strong, but the later course works in rings such as $\mathbb C[T,S]$. There, division by an arbitrary polynomial and the equivalence “gcd one means Bézout identity” both fail.

What survives is unique factorization. That structure is enough for the divisibility theorem needed tomorrow, and it avoids smuggling a one-variable argument into two variables.

## Reactivate factors and units

Week 21 classified units and domains; Day 2 proved Bézout only in $k[t]$. A factorization is unique only up to reordering and multiplication of irreducible factors by units. Every gcd statement below is likewise understood up to a unit unless a normalization is specified.

## Irreducible and prime are different definitions

In a domain $A$, a nonzero nonunit $p$ is irreducible when $p=ab$ forces $a$ or $b$ to be a unit. It is prime when $p\mid ab$ forces $p\mid a$ or $p\mid b$.

Prime implies irreducible in every domain. In a unique factorization domain, the converse also holds: if an irreducible $p$ divides $ab$, uniqueness forces an associate of $p$ to occur among the irreducible factors of $a$ or $b$.

content.title: Separate the two definitions
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $p$ is irreducible.

content.markdown:
## Gcd one need not mean Bézout in two variables

The elements $T,S\in k[T,S]$ have no common nonunit factor, so their gcd is $1$. Yet there are no $A,B\in k[T,S]$ with $AT+BS=1$.

The gcd claim can be checked before invoking the later UFD theorem. The linear polynomial $T$ is irreducible by total degree. A divisor of $T$ is therefore a unit or an associate of $T$, and $T$ does not divide $S$ because setting $T=0$ in $S=TH$ would give the false polynomial identity $S=0$.

Indeed, evaluating a proposed identity at $(T,S)=(0,0)$ gives $0=1$. Thus $(T,S)$ is a proper ideal even though the two generators have gcd $1$. This is the precise place where the Day 2 equivalence stops.

This boundary prevents an invalid proof of tomorrow's true divisibility theorem.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Let $A$ be a unique factorization domain. A polynomial in $A[x]$ is primitive when no irreducible element of $A$ divides all its coefficients.

Prove that the product of two primitive polynomials is primitive.

### Strategy

Assume an irreducible $p$ divides every coefficient of the product and reduce the two factors modulo $(p)$.

### Hypotheses

In a unique factorization domain, an irreducible $p$ is prime, so $A/(p)$ is a domain. Primitive polynomials remain nonzero after reduction modulo $p$.

### Intermediate claims

If $f$ and $g$ are primitive, their reductions $\bar f,\bar g\in(A/(p))[x]$ are nonzero. Since a polynomial ring over a domain is a domain, $\bar f\bar g\ne0$.

### Justification

If $p$ divided every coefficient of $fg$, its reduction would be the zero polynomial, contradicting $\bar f\bar g\ne0$.

### Conclusion

No irreducible element divides all coefficients of $fg$, so $fg$ is primitive.

content.introMarkdown: Derive a contradiction after reducing coefficients modulo $p$.

data.markdown:
Locate the first missing link between primitivity, nonzero reduction, and nonzero product.

Gauss's lemma is the engine that carries unique factorization into new polynomial variables.

Write the three implications explicitly: primitive gives nonzero reductions; domain gives nonzero product; divisibility gives zero reduction.

content.markdown:
## Polynomial rings in several variables are unique factorization domains

Gauss's lemma yields the theorem: if $A$ is a unique factorization domain, then $A[x]$ is a unique factorization domain. Factor the content in $A$, factor the primitive part over the fraction field, and use Gauss's lemma to return the factors to $A[x]$.

Starting with the field $k$, apply the theorem repeatedly: $k[T]$ is a unique factorization domain, then $k[T][S]=k[T,S]$ is one, and similarly for any finite number of variables.

content.markdown:
## Euclid's lemma in a unique factorization domain

In a unique factorization domain, $\gcd(a,b)=1$ means that the irreducible factorizations of $a$ and $b$ share no factor. If $a\mid bc$, every irreducible factor of $a$, with its full multiplicity, must occur in the factorization of $bc$.

None can come from $b$, so all must come from $c$. Hence $a\mid c$. This proof is valid in several variables and uses no Bézout identity.

activities.promptMarkdown:

Prove that $p$ is irreducible.

Start with $p=ab$, apply primality to that product, and use cancellation.

rubric.label: Mathematical result

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Because $p=ab$, we have $p\mid ab$. Since $p$ is prime, $p\mid a$ or $p\mid b$. Suppose $p\mid a$, so $a=pc$. Then $p=ab=pcb$. Since $A$ is a domain and $p\ne0$, cancellation gives $1=cb$, so $b$ is a unit. The other case similarly makes $a$ a unit. Thus every factorization of $p$ is trivial, and $p$ is irreducible.

activities.title: Disprove a multivariable Bézout claim
activities.promptMarkdown:

Show that their gcd is $1$ but no polynomial combination $AT+BS^2$ equals $1$.

Give a factor argument for the gcd and an evaluation argument for the failed identity.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The linear polynomial $T$ is irreducible by total degree. Any divisor of $T$ is therefore a unit or an associate of $T$. But $T$ does not divide $S^2$: if $S^2=TH$, setting $T=0$ would give the false polynomial identity $S^2=0$. Hence every common divisor of $T$ and $S^2$ is a unit, so their gcd is $1$. If $AT+BS^2=1$, evaluating at $(0,0)$ makes the left side zero and the right side one, a contradiction. Therefore gcd one does not imply a Bézout identity in $\mathbb C[T,S]$.

activities.title: Reconstruct the decisive Gauss step
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $f,g\in\mathbb Z[x]$ be primitive and suppose a prime integer $p$ divides every coefficient of $fg$.

Derive a contradiction after reducing coefficients modulo $p$.

Explain why both reduced factors are nonzero and why their product cannot vanish.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The reduction argument proves the primitive-product claim.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Every use of primitivity and the domain property is named.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Because $f$ is primitive, not every coefficient of $f$ is divisible by $p$, so its reduction $\bar f\in\mathbb F_p[x]$ is nonzero. The same holds for $\bar g$. The field $\mathbb F_p$ is a domain, hence $\mathbb F_p[x]$ is a domain, so $\bar f\bar g\ne0$. But if $p$ divided every coefficient of $fg$, then the reduction of $fg$ would be zero. Since reduction respects multiplication, this says $\bar f\bar g=0$, a contradiction.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: A field is a unique factorization domain. Gauss's theorem therefore makes $k[T]$ a unique factorization domain. Applying the same theorem again with coefficient ring $k[T]$ makes $k[T][S]$ a unique factorization domain. The canonical identification $k[T][S]=k[T,S]$ gives the claim.

activities.title: Prove the UFD divisibility theorem
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A$ be a unique factorization domain and let $a,b,c\in A$ satisfy $\gcd(a,b)=1$ and $a\mid bc$.

Prove that $a\mid c$ by irreducible multiplicities.

Treat the zero and unit cases briefly, then compare the exponent of every irreducible factor of $a$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The multiplicity proof establishes the full divisibility statement.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response handles boundary cases and never invokes a false Bézout identity.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $a$ is zero, then $0\mid bc$ implies $bc=0$; because $A$ is a domain and $\gcd(0,b)=1$, $b$ is a unit, so $c=0$ and $0\mid c$. If $a$ is a unit, the result is immediate. Otherwise write $a=u\prod p_i^{\alpha_i}$. Coprimality says each $p_i$ has exponent zero in $b$. Since $a\mid bc$, the exponent of $p_i$ in $bc$ is at least $\alpha_i$. Additivity of factor exponents then forces the exponent of $p_i$ in $c$ to be at least $\alpha_i$. Thus the full product $\prod p_i^{\alpha_i}$ divides $c$, and the unit $u$ is irrelevant; hence $a\mid c$.

content.markdown:
## Turn a factorization theorem into an exact kernel

Week 16 computed the derivative of multiplication but deliberately stopped before identifying its generic kernel. Unique factorization now supplies the missing step.

The calculation is algebraic: we work with fixed-degree binary forms and the linear map $(\dot L,\dot Q)\mapsto\dot LQ+L\dot Q$. Later affine geometry will interpret such kernels as tangent spaces. Today that language is only a preview and is not assessed.

## Reactivate the derivative formula

Let $V_1$ be the linear binary forms, $V_2$ the quadratic binary forms, and $V_3$ the cubic binary forms. For $M:V_1\times V_2\to V_3$, $M(L,Q)=LQ$, Week 16 proved

$$DM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q.$$

Day 3 proved that $\mathbb C[T,S]$ is a unique factorization domain. Both facts are used below.

## A nonzero linear form is prime

A nonzero linear form $L=aT+bS$ is irreducible: a factorization $L=FG$ has total degrees adding to one, so one factor has degree zero and is a nonzero scalar, hence a unit.

Because $\mathbb C[T,S]$ is a unique factorization domain, irreducible elements are prime. Therefore $L\mid AB$ implies $L\mid A$ or $L\mid B$.

content.markdown:
## The syllabus divisibility lemma

Let $L,Q,\dot L\in\mathbb C[T,S]$ satisfy $\gcd(L,Q)=1$ and $L\mid\dot LQ$. The Day 3 UFD theorem immediately gives $L\mid\dot L$.

For the binary-form application, $L$ and $\dot L$ are both linear. If $L\ne0$ and $\dot L=Lh$, total degree forces $h$ to be a scalar, so $\dot L=\lambda L$.

content.markdown:
## Why coprimality cannot be removed

If $L$ and $Q$ share a factor, a factor of $L$ may already be supplied by $Q$ rather than by $\dot L$. The product divisibility then gives no cancellation.

For example, with $L=T$, $Q=TS$, and $\dot L=S$, the polynomial $L$ divides $\dot LQ=TS^2$, but $T$ does not divide $S$.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Consider multiplication $N:V_1\times V_1\to V_2$ at $(A,B)=(T,S)$.

Compute the kernel of $DN_{(T,S)}(\dot A,\dot B)=\dot A S+T\dot B$.

### Strategy

Write both perturbations in the basis $(T,S)$ and equate the three quadratic coefficients.

### Hypotheses

$\dot A=\alpha T+\beta S$ and $\dot B=\gamma T+\delta S$.

### Intermediate claims

$\dot AS+T\dot B=\gamma T^2+(\alpha+\delta)TS+\beta S^2$. It vanishes exactly when $\gamma=0$, $\beta=0$, and $\delta=-\alpha$.

### Justification

The monomials $T^2,TS,S^2$ are linearly independent. Hence $(\dot A,\dot B)=\alpha(T,-S)$.

### Conclusion

$\ker DN_{(T,S)}=\mathbb C(T,-S)$.

Exhibiting a vector does not determine a kernel; spanning requires the converse argument.

content.markdown:
## The exact binary-form kernel

Let $L=aT+bS$ be nonzero and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$, with $\gcd(L,Q)=1$. If $(\dot L,\dot Q)$ lies in the derivative kernel, then $\dot LQ=-L\dot Q$, so $L\mid\dot LQ$.

The divisibility lemma gives $\dot L=\lambda L$. Substitution yields $L(\lambda Q+\dot Q)=0$; the domain property gives $\dot Q=-\lambda Q$. Conversely, every pair $\lambda(L,-Q)$ visibly maps to zero.

Later, after affine varieties and Zariski tangent spaces are defined, this derivative kernel will receive a geometric interpretation. No geometric mastery claim is made today.

Use irreducible multiplicities or Euclid's lemma in the UFD; do not invoke a Bézout identity in two variables.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The syllabus implication follows from the valid UFD theorem.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof matches each symbol to the general theorem and rejects the invalid route.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Day 3 proved that $\mathbb C[T,S]$ is a unique factorization domain and that in any UFD, $\gcd(a,b)=1$ together with $a\mid bc$ implies $a\mid c$. Apply that theorem with $a=L$, $b=Q$, and $c=\dot L$. The hypotheses are exactly $\gcd(L,Q)=1$ and $L\mid Q\dot L$, so $L\mid\dot L$. No multivariable Bézout identity is used.

activities.title: Build a failed-cancellation witness
activities.promptMarkdown:
Use $L=T$, $Q=TS$, and $\dot L=S$ in $\mathbb C[T,S]$.

Verify $L\mid\dot LQ$, disprove $L\mid\dot L$, and identify the failed hypothesis.

Give explicit divisibility witnesses and compute the gcd up to a unit.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $\dot LQ=S(TS)=T S^2=L\cdot S^2$, so $L\mid\dot LQ$. But $T\nmid S$, since no polynomial $H$ satisfies $S=TH$ by total degree and monomial support. Also $\gcd(T,TS)=T$, not $1$. Thus the coprimality hypothesis fails, and the conclusion need not hold.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The example verifies the premise, failure, and missing hypothesis.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Every divisibility assertion has a concrete witness or obstruction.

activities.title: Repeat the coefficient kernel at a new pair
activities.promptMarkdown:
For the same map $N$, work at $(A,B)=(T+S,T-S)$.

Verify directly that $(A,-B)$ is in the derivative kernel and explain why it spans the kernel.

Use the UFD divisibility argument for spanning; do not solve four coordinates by assertion.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Substitution gives $DN_{(A,B)}(A,-B)=AB-A B=0$, so $(A,-B)$ lies in the kernel. Since $A=T+S$ and $B=T-S$ are nonassociate linear forms, their gcd is $1$. If $\dot A B+A\dot B=0$, then $A\mid\dot A B$; coprimality gives $A\mid\dot A$. Both are linear, so $\dot A=\lambda A$. The equation becomes $A(\lambda B+\dot B)=0$. The polynomial ring is a domain and $A\ne0$, so $\dot B=-\lambda B$. Hence the kernel is $\mathbb C(A,-B)$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Membership and one-dimensional spanning are both proved.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof uses coprimality, equal degrees, and domain cancellation in order.

activities.title: Prove the exact kernel theorem
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $L\in V_1\setminus\{0\}$ and $Q\in V_2\setminus\{0\}$ satisfy $\gcd(L,Q)=1$, and let $DM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.

Prove $\ker DM_{(L,Q)}=\mathbb C(L,-Q)$.

Prove both inclusions and identify where coprimality, equal degree, and the domain property enter.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both kernel inclusions and all algebraic hypotheses are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof distinguishes membership, divisibility, scalar proportionality, and cancellation.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For every $\lambda\in\mathbb C$, $DM_{(L,Q)}(\lambda L,-\lambda Q)=\lambda LQ-\lambda LQ=0$, so $\mathbb C(L,-Q)$ is contained in the kernel. Conversely, let $(\dot L,\dot Q)$ lie in the kernel. Then $\dot LQ=-L\dot Q$, hence $L\mid\dot LQ$. Because $\gcd(L,Q)=1$ in the UFD $\mathbb C[T,S]$, Euclid's lemma gives $L\mid\dot L$. Both $L$ and $\dot L$ are linear, so $\dot L=\lambda L$ for some scalar $\lambda$. Substitution gives $L(\lambda Q+\dot Q)=0$. Since the ring is a domain and $L\ne0$, $\dot Q=-\lambda Q$. Thus $(\dot L,\dot Q)=\lambda(L,-Q)$, proving the reverse inclusion and the equality.

lessons.title: Non-domain boundaries and weekly synthesis
lessons.summary: Identify exactly which division, degree, cancellation, gcd, and factorization arguments need a domain, then integrate the week with scheduled retrieval.
objectives: Identify exactly which division, degree, cancellation, gcd, and factorization arguments need a domain, then integrate the week with scheduled retrieval.

content.markdown:
## Audit the proof before exporting it

A proof over a field can fail over a more general coefficient ring for several different reasons. Leading coefficients may not be invertible, nonzero products may vanish, degrees may drop, and cancellation may fail.

The correct conclusion is not that every polynomial theorem disappears. Division by a monic polynomial still works over any commutative ring. Today's task is to separate the surviving mechanism from the steps that genuinely require a domain or a field.

## Retrieve before synthesizing

The four labelled reviews below follow the frozen 16-, 8-, 3-, and 1-week schedule. Each uses an old object in a new setting and remains separate from the week's new non-domain boundary.

## Deliberate review: Week 7 — one counterexample defeats a universal claim

Use the zero polynomial to test a cancellation statement in an otherwise familiar domain. The ring may be a domain while cancellation still requires the factor being cancelled to be nonzero.

## Deliberate review: Week 20 — kernels record what a homomorphism forgets

## Deliberate review: Week 22 — quotient equality needs an ideal certificate

In a quotient, two representatives define the same class exactly when their difference belongs to the ideal.

Exact equality scope prevents quotient calculations from becoming informal substitutions.

Expand the proposed multiple and explicitly name the ambient ring and quotient ring.

content.markdown:
## What fails over a non-domain

In $R=\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$, the nonzero classes $[2]$ and $[3]$ multiply to zero. Consequently $(2t)(3t)=0$ in $R[t]$: nonzero products can vanish and product degrees need not add.

Cancellation also fails: $[2][1]=[2][4]$ although $[1]\ne[4]$. Proofs that infer a zero factor from a zero product, cancel a nonzero factor, or compare product degrees therefore require a domain.

Division by a polynomial whose leading coefficient is not a unit may fail because the leading term cannot be removed. These are separate defects, not one vague failure of algebra.

content.title: Trace three failed proof steps
content.introMarkdown: Use explicit examples to show failure of zero-product inference, degree additivity, and cancellation.

data.markdown:
Find the first example whose factors, degrees, or residues do not have the claimed properties.

Different failed steps require different repaired hypotheses.

Verify each residue calculation, then write the precise implication that the example makes false.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

In $(\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z)[t]$, divide $f=t^3+2t+1$ by the monic polynomial $g=t+1$.

Find quotient and remainder and explain why the leading-term procedure did not need a field.

### Strategy

The leading coefficient of $g$ is $1$, so each leading term can be removed without division by a nonunit.

### Hypotheses

$g$ is monic.

### Intermediate claims

$f=(t^2-t+3)(t+1)+4$ in $(\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z)[t]$.

### Justification

Expansion gives $(t^2-t+3)(t+1)=t^3+2t+3$ modulo $6$; adding $4$ gives $t^3+2t+1$. The remainder has degree zero, below the divisor's degree one.

### Conclusion

Monic division survives over this non-domain even though general cancellation and product-degree arguments do not.

content.title: Prove the surviving monic mechanism
content.introMarkdown: Explain why the leading-term cancellation step for dividing any $f\in R[t]$ by $g$ is always available.

data.markdown:
Locate any step that silently divides by the leading coefficient.

A precise boundary preserves the theorem that remains true instead of discarding too much.

Use the leading coefficient $1$ explicitly and restrict the conclusion to monic or unit-leading divisors.

content.markdown:
## Synthesize the theorem chain

Over a field, one-variable division gives a Euclidean algorithm and Bézout identities. Gauss's lemma then carries unique factorization into finitely many variables. In those multivariable rings, gcd one need not give a Bézout identity, but the UFD divisibility lemma remains valid.

Over a non-domain, identify the exact line that fails. Do not replace a theorem with a slogan such as “zero divisors are bad.”

content.title: Write the complete scope map
content.introMarkdown: Prove the valid theorem chain in the first two rings and give exact failure witnesses in the third.

data.markdown:
Find the earliest ring change, unsupported implication, or failure claim without a witness.

The capstone is the durable scope map needed for later algebra and geometry.

Organize the response by ring, state the theorem mechanism in each, and attach an explicit witness to every failure.

**Reading purpose:** Consolidate the exact hypotheses behind polynomial unique factorization and compare them with the non-domain boundary proved on the page.
Week 24 treats polynomial spaces as modules and introduces gradings, using the factorization discipline established here.

Week 23 is complete when you can derive a univariate Bézout identity, prove the multivariable divisibility theorem by unique factorization, compute the exact multiplication kernel, and explain precisely what changes over a non-domain.

activities.title: Refute cancellation by the zero polynomial
activities.promptMarkdown:
Consider the claim: for all $F,G,H\in\mathbb C[t]$, if $FG=FH$, then $G=H$.

Disprove the claim and state the corrected cancellation theorem.

Give explicit polynomials and identify the missing hypothesis.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown:
Take $F=0$, $G=0$, and $H=1$. Then $FG=0=FH$ but $G
e H$, so the universal claim is false. The corrected statement is: if $A$ is a domain, $F,G,H\in A$, $F
e0$, and $FG=FH$, then $G=H$. Indeed, $F(G-H)=0$ and the absence of zero divisors with $F
e0$ forces $G-H=0$.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The counterexample and corrected theorem are exact.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The missing nonzero hypothesis is located at the cancellation step.

activities.title: Recover the binary-form product
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.

Compute $LQ$ in the cubic monomial basis and explain why multiplication is bilinear.

Give all four coefficients and state linearity in each input separately.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $LQ=acT^3+(ad+bc)T^2S+(ae+bd)TS^2+beS^3$. For fixed $Q$, distributivity and scalar compatibility make $L\mapsto LQ$ linear in the coefficients $(a,b)$. For fixed $L$, the same laws make $Q\mapsto LQ$ linear in $(c,d,e)$. Hence multiplication is bilinear.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All product coefficients and the bilinearity claim are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Bilinearity is separated into the two required linearity statements.

activities.title: Analyze a polynomial sign homomorphism
activities.promptMarkdown:
Define $\sigma:(\mathbb Z[t],+)\to(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z,+)$ by $\sigma(f)=[f(1)]_2$.

Verify the homomorphism law and determine the kernel and image.

State injectivity and surjectivity from those calculations.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $\sigma(f+g)=[f(1)+g(1)]_2=\sigma(f)+\sigma(g)$, so $\sigma$ is a group homomorphism. Its kernel is the set of integer polynomials whose value at $1$ is even. Both residue classes occur, since $\sigma(0)=[0]$ and $\sigma(1)=[1]$, so the image is all of $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$. The map is surjective and not injective; for example, the nonzero polynomial $2$ lies in the kernel.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The operation law, kernel, image, and map properties are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Injectivity and surjectivity are derived from typed kernel and image evidence.

activities.title: Prove an equality in a new quotient
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $A=\mathbb Q[t]/(t^2-t-1)$.

Prove $[t^4]=[3t+2]$ and state why the ambient polynomials are not equal.

Give a multiple of the generator equal to their difference.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $t^4-(3t+2)=(t^2+t+2)(t^2-t-1)$, so the difference lies in $(t^2-t-1)$ and the two residue classes are equal in $A$. They are not equal in $\mathbb Q[t]$: their degrees and coefficients differ. The equality is a quotient-ring equality justified by the displayed ideal certificate.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The factor certificate proves the quotient equality.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Ambient equality and class equality remain distinct.

activities.title: Trace three failed proof steps
activities.promptMarkdown:
Work in $(\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z)[t]$.

Use explicit examples to show failure of zero-product inference, degree additivity, and cancellation.

Give a distinct equation for each failure and name the invalid inference.
activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: First, $[2][3]=[0]$ with both factors nonzero, so a zero product does not force a zero factor. Second, $(2t)(3t)=0$, so the product of two degree-one nonzero polynomials has no ordinary degree; thus $\deg(fg)=\deg f+\deg g$ fails. Third, $[2][1]=[2]=[2][4]$ while $[1]\ne[4]$, so cancelling the nonzero factor $[2]$ is invalid.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: All three examples are valid in the declared ring.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: Each equation is matched to the exact proof rule it refutes.

activities.title: Prove the surviving monic mechanism
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $g\in R[t]$ be monic and nonconstant.

Explain why the leading-term cancellation step for dividing any $f\in R[t]$ by $g$ is always available.

State only the existence mechanism; do not claim arbitrary nonmonic division.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The monic existence argument is valid over an arbitrary commutative ring.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof identifies exactly why no inverse of a nonunit is needed.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If the current remainder $r$ has degree $m\ge n=\deg g$ and leading coefficient $a$, then $a t^{m-n}g$ has leading term $a t^m$ because $g$ is monic. Subtracting it cancels the leading term of $r$ without dividing by any ring element. The degree strictly decreases, so finitely many repetitions produce $f=qg+s$ with $s=0$ or $\deg s<n$. This argument is specific to a monic divisor, or more generally a divisor with unit leading coefficient.

activities.title: Write the complete scope map
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $k$ be a field. Compare $k[t]$, $k[T,S,U]$, and $(\mathbb Z/8\mathbb Z)[t]$.

Prove the valid theorem chain in the first two rings and give exact failure witnesses in the third.

Include univariate Bézout, multivariable UFD divisibility, failure of multivariable Bézout, and one theorem that survives over the non-domain.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Every theorem and counterexample has the correct ambient ring and scope.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response connects each conclusion to its actual proof mechanism.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: In $k[t]$, division with remainder makes the ring Euclidean. The Euclidean algorithm computes a gcd and back-substitution writes it as $Af+Bg$; hence coprime pairs satisfy a Bézout identity. Gauss's theorem says a polynomial ring over a UFD is a UFD. Applying it three times from the field $k$ proves that $k[T,S,U]$ is a UFD. Therefore, if $\gcd(a,b)=1$ and $a\mid bc$ there, irreducible multiplicities force $a\mid c$. However, gcd one does not imply Bézout in several variables: $T,S$ share no nonunit factor, but $AT+BS=1$ is impossible after evaluation at $T=S=0$. In $(\mathbb Z/8\mathbb Z)[t]$, $(2t)(4t)=0$ shows failure of the domain and degree-product steps, and $[2][1]=[2][5]$ shows cancellation failure because both products equal $[2]$ while $[1]\ne[5]$. Nevertheless, division by a monic polynomial survives because its leading coefficient is $1$, so leading terms can be removed without inverting a nonunit.

lessons.title: Modules, submodules, and polynomial spaces
lessons.summary: Use the module axioms, distinguish submodules from subsets, and describe the relevant polynomial spaces as free modules over the correct coefficient ring.
objectives: Use the module axioms, distinguish submodules from subsets, and describe the relevant polynomial spaces as free modules over the correct coefficient ring.

content.markdown:
## Let a ring act on an additive space

A vector space allows scalars from a field to act on vectors. A module keeps the same additive structure but permits scalars from an arbitrary ring. This small change is decisive: bases need not exist, linear independence behaves less rigidly, and a finitely generated module need not be free.

The course needs modules for two different reasons. Polynomial spaces such as the binary forms are free modules over the coefficient field, while graded pieces and quotient constructions organize equations by weight. The coefficient ring must always be stated.

## Reactivate the exact inputs

Week 10 established vector spaces and bases. Week 21 established rings, units, and domains; Week 22 established ideals and quotients; Week 23 established polynomial rings. Week 19 supplied the rescaling action that later motivates weight. Today we generalize linear algebra without assuming that every module has a basis.

## The four module laws

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. An $R$-module $M$ is an abelian group under addition together with a scalar action $R\times M\to M$ satisfying $1m=m$, $(rs)m=r(sm)$, $(r+s)m=rm+sm$, and $r(m+n)=rm+rn$.

When $R=k$ is a field, this is exactly a vector space. When $R=\mathbb Z$, every abelian group becomes a $\mathbb Z$-module through repeated addition.

content.title: Audit a proposed module action
content.introMarkdown: Verify that the action is well-defined and satisfies the module laws.

data.markdown:
Find the first use of a residue class as though it had a unique integer representative.

An action on representatives does not define an action on a quotient until it is proved independent of representatives.

Compare two representatives differing by a multiple of six, then list the four laws separately.

content.markdown:
## Submodules must survive every scalar

A subset $N\subseteq M$ is an $R$-submodule when it contains $0$, is closed under addition and additive inverses, and satisfies $rn\in N$ for every $r\in R$ and $n\in N$.

The scalar ring matters. The polynomials of degree at most $n$ form a $k$-subspace of $k[t]$, but for $n>0$ they are not a $k[t]$-submodule under multiplication: multiplying $t^n$ by $t$ leaves the degree bound.

content.title: Distinguish two scalar rings
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $V_2$ is a $\mathbb Q$-submodule but not a $\mathbb Q[t]$-submodule of $\mathbb Q[t]$.

data.markdown:
Locate the first claim that omits the scalar ring or tests only addition.

The same additive set can be a module over one ring and fail to be a module over another.

Name the scalar ring in each sentence and test multiplication by the polynomial scalar $t$.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Let $V_2$ be the complex vector space of homogeneous binary quadratics $cT^2+dTS+eS^2$.

Prove that $V_2$ is a free $\mathbb C$-module of rank three.

### Strategy

Exhibit a generating family and then prove that its coefficient expression is unique.

### Hypotheses

Scalars are complex numbers, not arbitrary polynomials in $T$ and $S$.

### Intermediate claims

Every element is $cT^2+dTS+eS^2$, so $T^2,TS,S^2$ generate. If $cT^2+dTS+eS^2=0$, equality of polynomial coefficients gives $c=d=e=0$.

### Justification

Generation and uniqueness together say that the coordinate map $\mathbb C^3\to V_2$ is an isomorphism of $\mathbb C$-modules.

### Conclusion

$V_2\cong\mathbb C^3$ is free with basis $(T^2,TS,S^2)$.

content.title: Audit the basis proof
content.introMarkdown: Identify the two statements needed to prove a proposed monomial basis.

data.markdown:
Find the first missing generation or uniqueness argument.

Over a general ring, generators need not be a basis; freeness requires unique coordinates.

Write the general homogeneous cubic, then set it equal to zero and compare coefficients.

content.markdown:
## Free is stronger than finitely generated

A module is free when it has a basis: every element has one and only one finite linear combination of basis elements. It is finitely generated when a finite family spans, even if relations make the expression nonunique.

The $\mathbb Z$-module $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[1]$ but is not free: the nonzero scalar $2$ annihilates $[1]$. In a nonzero free $\mathbb Z$-module, no nonzero vector is annihilated by $2$.

content.title: Prove that a cyclic module is not free
content.introMarkdown: Prove that $M$ is finitely generated but not free.

data.markdown:
Locate the first jump from a relation to nonfreeness without explaining why free modules forbid it.

A relation among generators is evidence only after it is connected to uniqueness of basis coordinates.

Assume a basis, expand the torsion element in it, and compare the integer coordinates after multiplying by four.

content.markdown:
## Independent module classification

A complete module description always names the scalar ring, the additive object, and the action. A claim of freeness must then supply a basis and prove unique coordinates.

Do not call a bounded-degree polynomial space a module over the full polynomial ring unless the action has been changed or truncated. The natural structure used here is over the coefficient field.

content.introMarkdown: Prove that $W_n$ is free of rank $n+1$ over $k$, and prove that it is not a $k[T,S]$-submodule of the regular module $k[T,S]$.

data.markdown:
Find the first unstated scalar ring, missing uniqueness step, or invalid closure claim.

Later graded pieces are modules over the degree-zero part, not automatically over the whole graded ring.

Write the unique monomial expansion over $k$, then multiply one basis monomial by $T$ to test the larger action.

Day 1 is complete when every module claim names its scalar ring and every freeness claim includes unique coordinates.

activities.title: Audit a proposed module action
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $M=\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$ and let $\mathbb Z$ act by $n\cdot[m]=[nm]$.

Verify that the action is well-defined and satisfies the module laws.

Begin by checking independence of the representative of $[m]$, then address the four laws.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Well-definedness and all four module laws are checked.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The quotient representative issue is handled before the axioms.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $m'=m+6q$, then $nm'=nm+6nq$, so $[nm']=[nm]$; the action is well-defined. The identities $1m=m$, $(rs)m=r(sm)$, $(r+s)m=rm+sm$, and $r(m+n)=rm+rn$ follow from the corresponding integer identities and remain true modulo $6$. Hence $M$ is a $\mathbb Z$-module.

activities.title: Distinguish two scalar rings
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $V_2=\{a+bt+ct^2:a,b,c\in\mathbb Q\}\subset\mathbb Q[t]$.

Prove that $V_2$ is a $\mathbb Q$-submodule but not a $\mathbb Q[t]$-submodule of $\mathbb Q[t]$.

Verify closure for the first claim and give one scalar-action counterexample for the second.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Both module structures are classified correctly.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The proof changes only the scalar ring and isolates the failed closure law.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Coefficientwise addition, negatives, and multiplication by a rational scalar preserve degree at most two, so $V_2$ is a $\mathbb Q$-submodule. But $t^2\in V_2$ while the scalar $t\in\mathbb Q[t]$ gives $t\cdot t^2=t^3\notin V_2$. Thus $V_2$ is not stable under the $\mathbb Q[t]$-action.

activities.title: Audit the basis proof
activities.promptMarkdown:
Replace $V_2$ by the binary cubics $V_3$.

Identify the two statements needed to prove a proposed monomial basis.

State the four monomials and prove generation and uniqueness.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The correct basis and both halves of the basis proof are present.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response does not confuse a spanning set with a basis.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The proposed basis is $(T^3,T^2S,TS^2,S^3)$. Every homogeneous cubic has a unique expression $aT^3+bT^2S+cTS^2+dS^3$, so the monomials generate. If that expression is the zero polynomial, coefficient equality gives $a=b=c=d=0$, proving independence and uniqueness. Hence $V_3$ is free of rank four over $\mathbb C$.

activities.title: Prove that a cyclic module is not free
activities.promptMarkdown:
View $M=\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$ as a $\mathbb Z$-module.

Prove that $M$ is finitely generated but not free.

Give a generator, then use torsion and the structure of a nonzero free $\mathbb Z$-module.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: Finite generation and the torsion obstruction are both proved.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The nonfreeness argument identifies the exact property of free modules that fails.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The class $[1]$ generates $M$, since every class is $n[1]$, so $M$ is finitely generated. If $M$ were a nonzero free $\mathbb Z$-module with basis $(e_i)$, then $4x=0$ would force every coordinate of $x$ to be zero because $\mathbb Z$ has no zero divisors. But $[1]\ne0$ and $4[1]=0$. This contradiction proves that $M$ is not free.

activities.title: Classify polynomial spaces over two rings
activities.promptMarkdown:
Let $W_n\subset k[T,S]$ be the homogeneous binary forms of ordinary degree $n$, where $n\ge1$.

Prove that $W_n$ is free of rank $n+1$ over $k$, and prove that it is not a $k[T,S]$-submodule of the regular module $k[T,S]$.

Give the basis and both proofs, with the scalar ring named at every stage.

rubric.label: Mathematical result
rubric.description: The basis, rank, and failed larger-ring action are correct.

rubric.label: Reasoning and scope
rubric.description: The response separates the two scalar rings and proves both claims.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Every element of $W_n$ has a unique expression $\sum_{i=0}^n c_iT^{n-i}S^i$. Therefore $(T^n,T^{n-1}S,\ldots,S^n)$ is a $k$-basis, and $W_n$ is a free $k$-module of rank $n+1$. But $T^n\in W_n$ while multiplication by the scalar $T\in k[T,S]$ gives $T^{n+1}$, which has degree $n+1$ and is not in $W_n$. Thus $W_n$ is not a $k[T,S]$-submodule under ordinary multiplication.

lessons.title: Integer gradings and weighted polynomial rings
lessons.summary: Define a Z-grading, compute weighted degrees, decompose polynomials into homogeneous components, and prove that multiplication adds weights.
objectives: Define a Z-grading, compute weighted degrees, decompose polynomials into homogeneous components, and prove that multiplication adds weights.

content.markdown:
## Record how rescaling changes each monomial

Ordinary degree counts how many variables occur in a monomial. A weighted grading assigns an integer to each variable and extends additively to products. Negative weights are allowed; the index set is then $\mathbb Z$, not merely the nonnegative integers.

For the equations used later in the course, set $\operatorname{wt}(a)=1$, $\operatorname{wt}(b)=\operatorname{wt}(c)=0$, $\operatorname{wt}(d)=-1$, and $\operatorname{wt}(e)=-2$. The zero weights of $b$ and $c$ are part of the definition and must not be omitted.

## Reactivate direct sums and monomials

Week 10 used direct sums of vector spaces, Week 15 used homogeneous polynomial pieces, and Day 1 treated polynomial spaces as modules over the coefficient field. Today a ring becomes a direct sum of additive subgroups indexed by weight.

## A grading is a compatible direct-sum decomposition

A $\mathbb Z$-graded ring is a ring $A$ with additive subgroups $A_m$ such that $A=\bigoplus_{m\in\mathbb Z}A_m$ and $A_mA_n\subseteq A_{m+n}$. Every element has a unique finite decomposition into components from distinct weights.

An element of $A_m$ is homogeneous of weight $m$. A homogeneous element may be a sum of many monomials; the requirement is equal weight, not one term.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Let $f=a^2e+a^2d+b+ae+d^2$ in the weighted ring above.

Write the unique homogeneous-component decomposition of $f$.

### Strategy

Compute each monomial weight, group equal weights, and keep distinct groups separate.

### Hypotheses

The variable weights are $1,0,0,-1,-2$ for $a,b,c,d,e$.

### Intermediate claims

$a^2d$ has weight $1$; $a^2e$ and $b$ have weight $0$; $ae$ has weight $-1$; $d^2$ has weight $-2$.

### Justification

Monomials form a basis of the polynomial ring over $\mathbb C$, so groups supported on different monomials cannot cancel across weights.

### Conclusion

$f=f_1+f_0+f_{-1}+f_{-2}$ with $f_1=a^2d$, $f_0=a^2e+b$, $f_{-1}=ae$, and $f_{-2}=d^2$.

content.markdown:
## Why products add weights

For a monomial $a^ib^jc^kd^\ell e^m$, define its weight as $i-\ell-2m$. Multiplying monomials adds exponents, so it adds weights.

By distributivity, a product of a weight-$r$ polynomial and a weight-$s$ polynomial is a sum of monomials of weight $r+s$. This proves $A_rA_s\subseteq A_{r+s}$.

content.markdown:
## Weight spaces can be large

Because $b$ and $c$ have weight zero, each weight space contains arbitrary powers of $b$ and $c$. For example, $A_0$ contains every polynomial in $b$ and $c$, as well as balanced terms such as $ad$ and $a^2e$.

Thus $A_0$ is an infinite-dimensional $\mathbb C$-vector space. A grading decomposes the ring; it does not promise finite-dimensional pieces.

content.markdown:
## Independent construction of the grading

To define the grading completely, specify every component $A_m$: it is the span of monomials whose weight is $m$. Then prove directness, coverage, and compatibility with multiplication.

Saying only that three variables have assigned degrees is not yet a proof that the whole polynomial ring is graded.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Every monomial $u$ occurring in $p$ has weight $r$, and every monomial $v$ occurring in $q$ has weight $s$. activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For $m\in\mathbb Z$, let $A_m$ be the complex span of monomials $a^ib^jc^kd^\ell e^q$ satisfying $i-\ell-2q=m$. Every polynomial is a finite sum of monomials, so grouping its finitely many monomials by weight writes it as a finite sum of elements of the $A_m$. The expression is unique because distinct monomials form a $\mathbb C$-basis and each monomial has one weight; hence the sum is direct. If $u$ has weight $r$ and $v$ has weight $s$, exponent addition gives $\operatorname{wt}(uv)=r+s$. Expanding products therefore yields $A_rA_s\subseteq A_{r+s}$. This defines the required $\mathbb Z$-grading.

lessons.summary: Verify that the two supplied defining relations have weight zero, distinguish weighted from ordinary homogeneity, and prove that their quotient inherits a grading.
objectives: Verify that the two supplied defining relations have weight zero, distinguish weighted from ordinary homogeneity, and prove that their quotient inherits a grading.

content.markdown:
## Check the equations term by term

Let $A=\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,e]$ with the Week 24 weights, and set $F=a^2e-abd+cb^2-1$ and $G=ad+bc-1$. These are the two supplied equations labelled as defining $X$ in the syllabus.

At this stage, $X$ is only a label for the common-zero locus supplied by the course. Affine varieties and coordinate rings are taught later. Today's exact claim is algebraic: $F$ and $G$ are homogeneous of weight zero, and the ideal they generate respects the grading.

## Reactivate ideals and quotients

Week 22 defined $(F,G)$ as all combinations $PF+QG$ and defined the quotient $A/(F,G)$. Day 2 established the weight decomposition of $A$. We now combine those two constructions without importing the later algebra–geometry dictionary.

## Homogeneous means one weight

A polynomial is homogeneous of weight $m$ when every monomial with nonzero coefficient has weight $m$. Constants have weight zero because the empty product has weight zero.

Therefore the term $-1$ does not obstruct weight-zero homogeneity. It does obstruct ordinary positive-degree homogeneity when other terms have positive ordinary degree.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Let $H=a^3de-ab^2d+c^2-1$ and $K=a^2e+ad-bc$.

Determine whether each relation is homogeneous of weight zero.

### Strategy

Compute each monomial weight independently; do not infer the second relation from the first.

### Hypotheses

The weights of $a,b,c,d,e$ are $1,0,0,-1,-2$.

### Intermediate claims

For $H$, the weights are $3-1-2=0$, $1-1=0$, $0$, and $0$. For $K$, the weights are $2-2=0$, $1-1=0$, and $0$.

### Justification

Every term of each polynomial has the same weight, and that common weight is zero.

### Conclusion

Both $H$ and $K$ are homogeneous of weight zero.

content.markdown:
## A homogeneous ideal is generated degree by degree

An ideal is homogeneous when it is generated by homogeneous elements. If $F$ and $G$ have weight zero, then $(F,G)$ is homogeneous: decompose arbitrary coefficients $P$ and $Q$ into weight components, and each $P_mF+Q_mG$ remains in weight $m$.

This argument is stronger than observing that $F$ and $G$ lie in $A_0$. It explains why every homogeneous component of an element of the ideal again belongs to the ideal.

content.markdown:
## The quotient inherits the weights

If $I$ is homogeneous, define $(A/I)_m$ as the image of $A_m$ under the quotient map. Multiplication is well-defined and sends $(A/I)_r(A/I)_s$ into $(A/I)_{r+s}$.

The directness uses homogeneity of $I$: if a finite sum of distinct-weight representatives lies in $I$, then each of its components lies in $I$, so every corresponding quotient component is zero.

content.markdown:
## Verify the syllabus relations exactly

For $F=a^2e-abd+cb^2-1$, the four term weights are $2-2$, $1-1$, $0$, and $0$. For $G=ad+bc-1$, the three term weights are $1-1$, $0$, and $0$.

Thus both relations are weight-zero homogeneous and $I=(F,G)$ is a homogeneous ideal. They are not homogeneous for ordinary polynomial degree because their nonconstant and constant terms have different ordinary degrees.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The weights in $F$ are $2(1)+(-2)=0$, $1+0+(-1)=0$, $0+2(0)=0$, and $0$ for the constant. The weights in $G$ are $1+(-1)=0$, $0+0=0$, and $0$. Hence both are homogeneous of weight zero. If $P=\sum P_m$ and $Q=\sum Q_m$, then the weight-$m$ component of $PF+QG$ is $P_mF+Q_mG$, which remains in $(F,G)$; thus the ideal is homogeneous. Therefore the images of the $A_m$ form a direct-sum grading of $A/(F,G)$ and products add weights. Ordinary homogeneity fails because $F$ mixes ordinary degrees three and zero, while $G$ mixes degrees two and zero.

lessons.title: Ordinary degree, weight, and rescaling
lessons.summary: Distinguish ordinary polynomial degree from the Week 24 weight, prove the associated rescaling formula, and explain why weight-zero relations are invariant.
objectives: Distinguish ordinary polynomial degree from the Week 24 weight, prove the associated rescaling formula, and explain why weight-zero relations are invariant.

content.markdown:
## Two degrees answer different questions

Ordinary total degree assigns weight one to every variable and records polynomial growth. The Week 24 grading records how a monomial changes under the relative rescaling $a\mapsto\lambda a$, $d\mapsto\lambda^{-1}d$, $e\mapsto\lambda^{-2}e$, with $b$ and $c$ fixed.

This rescaling is a concrete action of $\mathbb C^\times$. The general language of torus weights and its use for resultants is only previewed here; today's assessed content is the explicit substitution and the integer grading already proved.

## Reactivate group actions carefully

Week 19 defined a group action and Week 20 distinguished an orbit from a chosen representative. For each $\lambda\ne0$, substitute the scaled coordinates. Composition holds because exponents add: applying $\mu$ and then $\lambda$ multiplies the factors to $(\lambda\mu)^w$.

## Ordinary degree counts factors; weight counts scaling

The ordinary total degree of $a^ib^jc^kd^\ell e^m$ is $i+j+k+\ell+m$. Its Week 24 weight is $i-\ell-2m$.

Neither number determines the other. The monomials $a^2e$ and $ad$ both have weight zero but ordinary degrees three and two; $e^2$ has ordinary degree two but weight minus four.
