## Complete worked model

$L=2T-S$ and $Q=3T^2+4TS+5S^2$.

Compute the resultant from both the determinant and the coefficient formula.

### Strategy

Construct the numerical matrix, expand its sparse first row, then substitute the five coefficients into the derived polynomial.

### Hypotheses

$(a,b,c,d,e)=(2,-1,3,4,5)$ and $M=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&0&3\\-1&2&4\\0&-1&5\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.

### Intermediate claims

The determinant is $2(10+4)+3(1)=31$. The formula gives $2^2\cdot5-2(-1)4+3(-1)^2=20+8+3=31$.

### Justification

Both calculations use the same ordered-basis convention and agree term for term.

### Conclusion

$\operatorname{Res}(2T-S,3T^2+4TS+5S^2)=31$.

lessons.title: Why the resultant detects a common projective root
lessons.summary: Prove for a nonzero binary linear form and binary quadratic over $\mathbb C$ that the resultant vanishes exactly when they share a projective root, including the root at infinity.
objectives: Prove for a nonzero binary linear form and binary quadratic over $\mathbb C$ that the resultant vanishes exactly when they share a projective root, including the root at infinity.

content.markdown:
## Evaluate the quadratic at the linear root

Week 26 proved that a nonzero $L=aT+bS$ has the unique projective root $p_L=[-b:a]$. Substituting that representative into $Q$ gives

$$Q(-b,a)=cb^2-dab+ea^2=a^2e-abd+cb^2.$$

Thus the resultant is not an unrelated coefficient trick: it is the quadratic evaluated at the canonical root vector $(-b,a)$.

## State the hypotheses before the equivalence

Work over $\mathbb C$. Let $L$ be nonzero, so $[-b:a]$ is defined and is its unique projective root. Let $Q$ be homogeneous of degree two. Homogeneity makes the statement $Q(p_L)=0$ independent of the nonzero representative chosen for $p_L$.

## The evaluation identity

Direct substitution yields

$$Q(-b,a)=c(-b)^2+d(-b)a+ea^2=cb^2-abd+a^2e.$$

After reordering terms, this is exactly $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)$. No division by $a$ or $b$ occurs.

content.markdown:
## The forward and reverse implications

Because $p_L=[-b:a]$ is the only projective root of $L$, the forms share a projective root exactly when $Q(-b,a)=0$.

Combining this statement with the evaluation identity gives

$$\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=0\iff L\text{ and }Q\text{ have a common projective root}.$$

## The root at infinity is not exceptional to the formula

If $a=0$, nonzeroness of $L$ forces $b\ne0$. Then $L=bS$ has root $[1:0]$, while

$$\operatorname{Res}(bS,Q)=cb^2=b^2Q(1,0).$$

Therefore the resultant vanishes exactly when $c=0$, which is exactly the condition $Q(1,0)=0$. The same formula detects the common root at infinity without a limiting argument.

## Complete worked model

$L=2T+S$, $Q_0=(2T+S)(T-3S)$, and $Q_1=T^2-3TS+2S^2$.

Use the projective root and resultant formula to distinguish the two pairs.

### Strategy

Find $p_L=[-1:2]$, evaluate each quadratic at $(-1,2)$, and compare with its coefficient resultant.

### Hypotheses

$L$ is nonzero. The first quadratic visibly contains $L$ as a factor; the second need not.

### Intermediate claims

$Q_0(-1,2)=0$, so $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q_0)=0$. For $Q_1$, $Q_1(-1,2)=1+6+8=15$, and the formula gives $2^2\cdot2-2\cdot1\cdot(-3)+1\cdot1^2=15$.

### Justification

The evaluation identity equates each value with the corresponding resultant. Uniqueness of the linear root converts vanishing into the common-root statement.

### Conclusion

$L,Q_0$ share $[-1:2]$, while $L,Q_1$ have no common projective root.

lessons.title: Bidegree and the scaling law
lessons.summary: Derive $\operatorname{Res}(\lambda L,\mu Q)=\lambda^2\mu\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)$ from both the coefficient formula and the Sylvester determinant, then state its geometric scope.
objectives: Derive $\operatorname{Res}(\lambda L,\mu Q)=\lambda^2\mu\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)$ from both the coefficient formula and the Sylvester determinant, then state its geometric scope.

content.markdown:
## The exponents count coefficient columns

The scaling identity is

$$\operatorname{Res}(\lambda L,\mu Q)=\lambda^2\mu\operatorname{Res}(L,Q).$$

The exponent two belongs to $L$ because two Sylvester columns are built from $TL$ and $SL$. The exponent one belongs to $Q$ because it contributes one column.

## Distinguish an algebraic identity from projective rescaling

The polynomial identity holds for all scalars $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb C$. To say that $\lambda L$ and $L$ define the same projective zero set, however, requires $\lambda\ne0$; similarly for $Q$. Zero scalars preserve the algebraic formula but destroy the declared nonzero form.

## Derive scaling from the coefficient formula

The coefficients of $\lambda L$ are $(\lambda a,\lambda b)$ and those of $\mu Q$ are $(\mu c,\mu d,\mu e)$. Substitution gives

$$(\lambda a)^2(\mu e)-(\lambda a)(\lambda b)(\mu d)+(\mu c)(\lambda b)^2$$

$$=\lambda^2\mu(a^2e-abd+cb^2).$$

content.markdown:
## Derive scaling from determinant columns

In $M(L,Q)$, the first two columns are the coefficient columns of $TL$ and $SL$; scaling $L$ multiplies each by $\lambda$. The third column is the coefficient column of $Q$; scaling $Q$ multiplies it by $\mu$.

Multilinearity of the determinant therefore extracts $\lambda\cdot\lambda\cdot\mu=\lambda^2\mu$.

## Complete worked model

$L=2T-S$, $Q=3T^2+4TS+5S^2$, $\lambda=-2$, and $\mu=3$.

Verify the scaling law numerically from the original and scaled coefficients.

### Strategy

Use the previously computed resultant $31$, predict the scaled value, then calculate it directly.

### Hypotheses

$\lambda^2\mu=4\cdot3=12$. The scaled coefficient tuple is $(-4,2,9,12,15)$.

### Intermediate claims

The law predicts $12\cdot31=372$. Direct substitution gives $(-4)^2(15)-(-4)(2)(12)+9(2)^2=240+96+36=372$.

### Justification

The direct calculation uses the same coefficient order and confirms both the even exponent of the negative scalar and the linear exponent of $\mu$.

### Conclusion

$\operatorname{Res}(-2L,3Q)=372=12\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)$.

content.markdown:
## Zero scalars and geometric meaning

If $\lambda=0$ or $\mu=0$, both sides of the polynomial identity are zero. This is algebraically correct.

But $0\cdot L$ is the zero polynomial, not another representative of the same nonzero projective form. Therefore the geometric statement that rescaling preserves roots uses $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb C^\times$.

## Independent bidegree proof

Bidegree $(2,1)$ means degree two in the coefficient group $(a,b)$ and degree one in the group $(c,d,e)$. It is not a statement that the full polynomial has ordinary degree two; its ordinary total degree is three.

A complete proof should show both the formula substitution and the determinant-column explanation, because they check different possible errors.

content.markdown:
## One coefficient polynomial, three meanings

The expression $a^2e-abd+cb^2$ is simultaneously a determinant, the value $Q(-b,a)$, and a bidegree-$(2,1)$ polynomial in two coefficient groups.

A strong proof moves between those meanings deliberately. The determinant constructs the invariant, evaluation proves the common-root criterion in this low-degree case, and column scaling explains the exponents.

## Keep the logical order visible

First define the Sylvester map and matrix. Second derive the formula. Third prove that it equals evaluation at the unique projective root of $L$. Fourth derive scaling. The common-root criterion must not be used as the definition while it is still being proved.

## State the theorem chain precisely

The coefficient formula and scaling law are

$$\operatorname{Res}(aT+bS,cT^2+dTS+eS^2)=a^2e-abd+cb^2,$$

$$\operatorname{Res}(\lambda L,\mu Q)=\lambda^2\mu\operatorname{Res}(L,Q).$$

Together with the common-root criterion, these identities form one theorem chain. State every equality, hypothesis, and quantifier explicitly so that the chain can be read without surrounding commentary.

Construct the Sylvester matrix, expand its determinant, evaluate $Q$ at $[-2:1]$, then count the scaled columns.

$L$ is nonzero, the ordered bases are fixed, and the coefficients are $(1,2,2,1,5)$.

$M=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0&2\\2&1&1\\0&2&5\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ has determinant $11$. Also $Q(-2,1)=8-2+5=11$. Under $(L,Q)\mapsto(\lambda L,\mu Q)$, two columns scale by $\lambda$ and one by $\mu$.

The determinant formula gives $5-2+8=11$. The evaluation identity proves that nonvanishing means the unique root of $L$ is not a root of $Q$. Determinant multilinearity gives the scaling factor.

### Conclusion

The pair has no common projective root, and every rescaled resultant is $11\lambda^2\mu$.

Hence zero resultant makes $p_L$ common, and any common root must equal the unique root $p_L$, proving the converse. If $a=0$, then $b\ne0$, $p_L=[1:0]$, and the identity becomes $\operatorname{Res}(bS,Q)=b^2Q(1,0)=b^2c$, so infinity is included. Finally, substituting the scaled coefficients—or extracting $\lambda$ from each of the first two matrix columns and $\mu$ from the third—gives $\operatorname{Res}(\lambda L,\mu Q)=\lambda^2\mu\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)$. This polynomial identity holds for all scalars; treating scaling as preservation of the same nonzero projective forms requires $\lambda,\mu\ne0$.

lessons.title: Root differences and the quadratic discriminant
lessons.summary: Define the standard discriminant from squared root differences, prove that it is symmetric, and derive $\operatorname{Disc}(ax^2+bx+c)=b^2-4ac$.
objectives: Define the standard discriminant from squared root differences, prove that it is symmetric, and derive $\operatorname{Disc}(ax^2+bx+c)=b^2-4ac$.

content.markdown:
## One coefficient detects a collision of roots

For a degree-$n$ polynomial $C(x)=a\prod_{i=1}^n(x-\alpha_i)$ with $a\ne0$, define the standard discriminant by

$$\operatorname{Disc}(C)=a^{2n-2}\prod_{i<j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2.$$

Every factor measures a separation between two roots. The product vanishes exactly when at least one pair collides.

## Reactivate roots, multiplicity, and symmetric expressions

Week 3 established complex roots and repeated roots. A change in the order of the roots must not change a polynomial invariant, because the coefficients do not remember an ordering.

Week 27 established resultants. Today begins with the root formula; Day 2 will connect it to $\operatorname{Res}(C,C')$ with the exact sign and leading-coefficient factor.

## Why the squared product is symmetric

A transposition of two roots changes the sign of their difference. Squaring removes that sign. The transposition also permutes all other squared difference factors, so the entire product is unchanged.

Because transpositions generate every permutation, the product is symmetric in the roots. The specialized theorem we need says that every symmetric polynomial in $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n$ is a polynomial in the elementary symmetric functions $e_1,\ldots,e_n$.

Viète's formulas identify $e_k=(-1)^k a_{n-k}/a$ for $C(x)=ax^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0$. The conventional factor $a^{2n-2}$ clears the denominators in the squared-difference product, so the discriminant is a polynomial in the coefficients and does not depend on an ordering of the roots.

## Derive the quadratic formula from Viète

Let $C(x)=a(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)=ax^2+bx+c$ with $a\ne0$. Viète gives $\alpha+\beta=-b/a$ and $\alpha\beta=c/a$.

For degree two, the root definition becomes $a^2(\alpha-\beta)^2$. Use

$$(\alpha-\beta)^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-4\alpha\beta$$

to eliminate the roots.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$C(x)=2x^2-5x+2$.

Compute the discriminant, factor the polynomial, and make the two calculations agree.

### Strategy

First use the coefficient formula. Then factor and evaluate the root-difference definition.

### Hypotheses

The leading coefficient is $a=2\ne0$, so this is a degree-two polynomial.

### Intermediate claims

$\operatorname{Disc}(C)=(-5)^2-4(2)(2)=9$. Also $C=(2x-1)(x-2)=2(x-1/2)(x-2)$.

### Justification

The two roots are $1/2$ and $2$. Therefore $a^2(1/2-2)^2=4(9/4)=9$.

### Conclusion

The nonzero value records two distinct roots and agrees in coefficient and root coordinates.

## The fixed-degree boundary

The formula $b^2-4ac$ is a polynomial in $(a,b,c)$, but its root interpretation as a quadratic assumes $a\ne0$.

If $a=0$, the coefficient triple lies on the boundary of quadratic coefficient space. A zero value there does not by itself describe a repeated root of a degree-two polynomial, because the degree has dropped.

content.markdown:
## A repeated root is shared with the derivative

If $C(x)=(x-r)^mH(x)$ with $H(r)\ne0$, differentiation gives

$$C'(x)=m(x-r)^{m-1}H(x)+(x-r)^mH'(x).$$

Thus $C(r)=C'(r)=0$ exactly when $m\ge2$. The derivative converts multiplicity into a common-root problem.

## Reactivate the Week 27 common-root detector

Week 27 proved that a resultant vanishes exactly when its two polynomial inputs share a root. Apply that theorem to $C$ and $C'$.

The symbol $\sim$ in the study goal hides a convention-dependent nonzero factor. Today makes that factor exact for the standard discriminant.

## Prove the derivative multiplicity lemma

Factor $C$ at a root $r$ as $(x-r)^mH(x)$ with $H(r)\ne0$. The displayed derivative has a factor $(x-r)^{m-1}$.

When $m=1$, evaluation gives $C'(r)=H(r)\ne0$. When $m\ge2$, both terms vanish at $r$.

## Make the resultant relation exact

Let $C(x)=a\prod_{i=1}^n(x-\alpha_i)$ with $a\ne0$. The product formula for the resultant gives

$$\operatorname{Res}(C,C')=a^{n-1}\prod_i C'(\alpha_i).$$

Now $C'(\alpha_i)=a\prod_{j\ne i}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)$. Pairing the ordered differences introduces $(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}$, so

$$\operatorname{Res}(C,C')=(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}a\operatorname{Disc}(C).$$

$C(x)=(x-1)^2(x+2)=x^3-3x+2$.

### Strategy

Use the factorization for multiplicity, differentiate the expanded polynomial, then apply the degree-three sign.

### Hypotheses

The polynomial is monic of degree three over $\mathbb C$.

### Intermediate claims

$C'=3x^2-3=3(x-1)(x+1)$, so $x-1$ is common. For $x^3+px+q$ with $(p,q)=(-3,2)$, the standard discriminant is $-4p^3-27q^2=0$.

### Justification

For $n=3$ and $a=1$, $(-1)^{3}=-1$, so $\operatorname{Res}(C,C')=-\operatorname{Disc}(C)=0$.

### Conclusion

The double root, common derivative root, zero resultant, and zero discriminant are four descriptions of the same event.

content.markdown:
## Separate characteristic behavior from fixed-degree normalization

This course works over $\mathbb C$, but the derivative criterion itself does not require characteristic zero. Over any field, pass to an algebraic closure and write $C=(x-r)^mH$ with $H(r)\ne0$. Then $C'=(x-r)^{m-1}[mH+(x-r)H']$, so $C'(r)=0$ exactly when $m\ge2$.

In characteristic $p$, the derivative of $x^p-t$ is zero. Over an algebraic closure, however, $x^p-t=(x-r)^p$, so the zero derivative records repeated roots rather than breaking the criterion. The separate fixed-degree condition $a\ne0$ is essential because the resultant and standard discriminant formulas must use the polynomial's actual degree and leading coefficient.

content.markdown:
## Remove the quadratic term before computing

A general cubic $C(x)=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$ with $a\ne0$ becomes a depressed monic cubic after dividing by $a$ and translating $x=y-b/(3a)$.

The depressed form $y^3+py+q$ exposes a two-parameter discriminant. Translation does not change root differences, while multiplying a cubic by $a$ multiplies its discriminant by $a^4$.

## Keep three transformations separate

Translation shifts every root by the same amount, so each difference is unchanged. Making the polynomial monic changes the leading coefficient normalization. The derivative resultant then supplies the exact depressed-cubic formula.

## Compute the depressed coefficients

Substitute $x=y-b/(3a)$ into $C/a$. The coefficient of $y^2$ cancels. The remaining coefficients are

$$p=\frac{3ac-b^2}{3a^2},\qquad q=\frac{27a^2d-9abc+2b^3}{27a^3}.$$

This change is invertible because $a\ne0$.

content.markdown:
## Compute the depressed resultant without a five-by-five expansion

Let $F(x)=x^3+px+q$ and $F'(x)=3x^2+p$. If $\beta$ is a root of $F'$, then $\beta^2=-p/3$ and

$$F(\beta)=\beta^3+p\beta+q=\frac{2p}{3}\beta+q.$$

The two derivative roots are $\beta$ and $-\beta$. The resultant product formula gives

$$\operatorname{Res}(F',F)=3^3F(\beta)F(-\beta)=27q^2+4p^3.$$

Because $2\cdot3$ is even, $\operatorname{Res}(F,F')=\operatorname{Res}(F',F)$. For a monic cubic, $\operatorname{Disc}(F)=-\operatorname{Res}(F,F')$.

## Complete worked model

$C(x)=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$ with $a\ne0$.

Use the depressed coefficients to derive the standard coefficient formula.

### Strategy

Translate and divide by $a$, apply the depressed formula, then restore the factor $a^4$ and simplify.

### Hypotheses

The field is $\mathbb C$, so $3a$ is invertible.

### Intermediate claims

With $p=(3ac-b^2)/(3a^2)$ and $q=(27a^2d-9abc+2b^3)/(27a^3)$, translation preserves root differences and $\operatorname{Disc}(C)=a^4(-4p^3-27q^2)$.

Substituting and collecting the common denominator gives $b^2c^2-4ac^3-4b^3d-27a^2d^2+18abcd$.

$$\operatorname{Disc}(ax^3+bx^2+cx+d)=b^2c^2-4ac^3-4b^3d-27a^2d^2+18abcd.$$

content.markdown:
## Coefficient space records how roots collide

A monic cubic $x^3+bx^2+cx+d$ is a point $(b,c,d)\in\mathbb C^3$. The equation $\Delta(b,c,d)=0$ cuts out the discriminant surface.

This week uses only explicit zero sets and gradients in coefficient space. The general theory of affine varieties begins in Week 31.

## Reduce the surface to one cusp slice

The translation $x=y-b/3$ changes $(b,c,d)$ invertibly to $(b,p,q)$. In these coordinates, the discriminant equation is $4p^3+27q^2=0$ and does not depend on $b$.

The depressed plane therefore displays the essential collision geometry; the extra $b$ coordinate records a common translation of all three roots.

## Match the three root types to three loci

A cubic over $\mathbb C$ has one of three multiplicity partitions: $1+1+1$, $2+1$, or $3$.

The first type has $\Delta\ne0$ and lies off the discriminant surface. The other two have $\Delta=0$. To separate them, inspect the local geometry of the zero set.

## Parametrize the double-root cusp

A depressed monic cubic with a double root $t$ must have third root $-2t$, because the sum of the roots is zero. Therefore

$$(x-t)^2(x+2t)=x^3-3t^2x+2t^3.$$

The discriminant curve is parametrized by $(p,q)=(-3t^2,2t^3)$. For $t\ne0$ the multiplicity is $2+1$; for $t=0$ it becomes a triple root.

## Complete worked model

$G(p,q)=4p^3+27q^2$.

Find the singular points of the plane discriminant curve and relate them to root multiplicity.

### Strategy

Solve $G=0$ together with both first partial derivatives.

### Hypotheses

The computation is over $\mathbb C$, where $12$ and $54$ are nonzero.

### Intermediate claims

$\nabla G=(12p^2,54q)$. It vanishes only at $(p,q)=(0,0)$, which lies on $G=0$.

### Justification

The parametrization identifies $(0,0)$ with $x^3$, the triple-root cubic. Every $t\ne0$ point has nonzero gradient and type $2+1$.

### Conclusion

Double-plus-simple collisions are smooth points of the discriminant curve; the triple collision is its cusp singularity.

content.markdown:
## Lift the cusp back to the full surface

In coordinates $(b,p,q)$, the monic discriminant surface is $4p^3+27q^2=0$ with $b$ free. Its singular locus is therefore $p=q=0$.

Translating back, $p=q=0$ means the cubic is $(x-r)^3$ for some $r$. In coefficient coordinates this locus is

$$(b,c,d)=(-3r,3r^2,-r^3).$$

content.markdown:
## One invariant, four coordinate systems

The discriminant can be read from roots, coefficients, a derivative resultant, or coefficient-space geometry.

A strong solution chooses the coordinate system that makes the current claim transparent and states every normalization when moving between them.

## Keep the theorem chain ordered

Define the standard root product first. Derive the exact resultant relation second. Use it to prove the repeated-root criterion. Then derive the low-degree formulas and interpret the cubic zero set.

## State the complete theorem with its normalization

For $C(x)=a\prod_{i=1}^n(x-\alpha_i)$ of fixed degree $n\ge2$ over $\mathbb C$, the chosen convention is

$$\operatorname{Disc}(C)=a^{2n-2}\prod_{i<j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2.$$ This normalization keeps the root-difference expression polynomial in the coefficients.

$$\operatorname{Res}(C,C')=(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}a\operatorname{Disc}(C).$$

The nonzero factor makes zero discriminant, zero derivative resultant, and repeated root equivalent.

## Complete worked model

$C(x)=x^3-3x+2=(x-1)^2(x+2)$.

Connect the root product, coefficient formula, derivative resultant, and discriminant geometry.

### Strategy

Start with the factorization, then compute in depressed coefficients, then use the derivative and cusp parametrization.

### Hypotheses

The cubic is monic and depressed over $\mathbb C$.

### Intermediate claims

The roots have type $2+1$, so the root product is zero. With $(p,q)=(-3,2)$, $-4p^3-27q^2=0$. Also $C'=3(x-1)(x+1)$ shares $x-1$ with $C$.

### Justification

For $n=3$, $\operatorname{Res}(C,C')=-\operatorname{Disc}(C)=0$. The coefficient point equals $(-3t^2,2t^3)$ with $t=1$ and has nonzero cusp gradient.

### Conclusion

All four descriptions agree: this is a smooth $2+1$ point of the discriminant locus.

content.markdown:
## Multiplication should respect a change of coordinates

A binary form is a polynomial in two variables, but its coefficients depend on a chosen basis. The correct question is therefore not whether a formula looks unchanged term by term, but whether it transforms compatibly when the variables change.

This day fixes one left-action convention and proves equivariance directly from evaluation. The convention matters: an omitted inverse reverses the order of multiplication in the action law.

## Reactivate actions and symmetric powers

Week 19 defined a left group action, and Week 20 used equivariant maps. Week 15 identified $V_d$ with the degree-$d$ homogeneous binary forms, a model of $\operatorname{Sym}^d((\mathbb C^2)^*)$.

Write vectors as columns $v=(T,S)^\mathsf T$. Every substitution below must specify whether it uses $g$ or $g^{-1}$.

## Fix the representation convention

The general linear group is $GL_2(\mathbb C)=\{g\in M_2(\mathbb C):\det g\ne0\}$. Its special linear subgroup is

$$SL_2(\mathbb C)=\{g\in GL_2(\mathbb C):\det g=1\}.$$

Every matrix in $SL_2(\mathbb C)$ is invertible because its determinant is one. Let $V_d$ be the vector space of homogeneous degree-$d$ polynomials in $T,S$, identified naturally with $\operatorname{Sym}^d((\mathbb C^2)^*)$.

Some texts abbreviate this as $\operatorname{Sym}^d(\mathbb C^2)$. For $SL_2$, the determinant pairing $(v,w)\mapsto\det(v,w)$ identifies $\mathbb C^2$ equivariantly with its dual, so the two conventions describe isomorphic representations. Here we keep the dual explicit and define the contragredient change-of-variables action by

$$(g\cdot F)(v)=F(g^{-1}v),\qquad g\in SL_2(\mathbb C),\ F\in V_d.$$

The identity acts trivially. Moreover $((gh)\cdot F)(v)=F(h^{-1}g^{-1}v)=(g\cdot(h\cdot F))(v)$, so this is a left action. Since substitution is linear in $F$, each $V_d$ is an $SL_2$-representation.

Prove $M(g\cdot L,g\cdot Q)=g\cdot M(L,Q)$ for every $g\in SL_2$.

### Strategy

Evaluate both sides at an arbitrary vector $v$; do not expand coefficients.

### Hypotheses

$g$ is invertible, so $g^{-1}v$ is defined, and all three actions use the same convention.

### Intermediate claims

$M(g\cdot L,g\cdot Q)(v)=L(g^{-1}v)Q(g^{-1}v)$, while $(g\cdot M(L,Q))(v)=(LQ)(g^{-1}v)$.

### Justification

Polynomial multiplication is pointwise multiplication after evaluation, so the two displayed values coincide for every $v$.

### Conclusion

The multiplication map is $SL_2$-equivariant.

objectives: Prove that the linear–quadratic resultant is separately homogeneous of degree two in the linear coefficients and degree one in the quadratic coefficients.

content.markdown:
## Two factor spaces require two degrees

Ordinary total degree records that $a^2e-abd+b^2c$ has degree three. It does not record which factor supplied those three coefficient occurrences.

Bidegree keeps the two coefficient blocks separate and is exactly the information needed to analyze relative scaling.

## Retrieve the exact resultant formula

For $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$, Week 27 proved

$$R(L,Q)=\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+b^2c.$$

Keep $(a,b)$ and $(c,d,e)$ as separate blocks throughout the calculation.

## Define separate homogeneity

A polynomial $P(x,y)$ has bidegree $(r,s)$ when scaling the first coefficient block by $\lambda$ and the second by $\mu$ gives

$$P(\lambda x,\mu y)=\lambda^r\mu^sP(x,y).$$

For a nonzero polynomial, the pair $(r,s)$ is unique. Here the first block is the coefficient vector of $L$ and the second is the coefficient vector of $Q$.

## Derive the scaling identity

Replacing $L$ by $\lambda L$ sends $(a,b)$ to $(\lambda a,\lambda b)$. Replacing $Q$ by $\mu Q$ sends $(c,d,e)$ to $(\mu c,\mu d,\mu e)$.

Substitution in each monomial gives the common factor $\lambda^2\mu$:

$$R(\lambda L,\mu Q)=\lambda^2\mu R(L,Q).$$

## Complete worked model

$L=T+2S$, $Q=3T^2-TS+4S^2$, $\lambda=-2$, and $\mu=3$.

Compute the original and scaled resultants and compare them with the predicted factor.

### Strategy

First compute $R(L,Q)$. Then use bidegree before checking the scaled coefficients directly.

### Hypotheses

The coefficient order is $(a,b;c,d,e)=(1,2;3,-1,4)$.

### Intermediate claims

$R(L,Q)=4+2+12=18$, and $\lambda^2\mu=12$, so the predicted scaled value is $216$.

### Justification

Direct substitution of $(-2,-4;9,-3,12)$ gives $(-2)^2(12)-(-2)(-4)(-3)+(-4)^2(9)=48+24+144=216$.

### Conclusion

The numerical check agrees with the symbolic bidegree identity.

## Recover the general degree count from the Sylvester determinant

For forms of degrees $m$ and $n$, the Sylvester matrix has $n$ shifted coefficient columns from the degree-$m$ form and $m$ shifted coefficient columns from the degree-$n$ form.

Scaling the first form by $\lambda$ scales $n$ determinant columns; scaling the second by $\mu$ scales $m$ columns. Multilinearity of determinant gives bidegree $(n,m)$.

## Separate a polynomial identity from a group action

The scaling formula is a polynomial identity and remains true when $\lambda=0$ or $\mu=0$.

The acting group $\mathbb G_m^2=(\mathbb C^\times)^2$ contains only nonzero scalars. Zero scaling destroys invertibility and is not a group element.

lessons.title: The relative-scaling subgroup
lessons.summary: Identify the one-parameter subgroup of $\mathbb G_m^2$ killed by multiplication and distinguish its orbit from the complete multiplication fiber.
objectives: Identify the one-parameter subgroup of $\mathbb G_m^2$ killed by multiplication and distinguish its orbit from the complete multiplication fiber.

content.markdown:
## Multiplication forgets how scale was divided

The product records the total scalar $\lambda\mu$, not the two scalars separately. When $\lambda\mu=1$, the product is unchanged.

This is a precise group-theoretic loss of information. It does not imply that every two factorizations of the same cubic differ only by relative scaling.

## Reactivate the product character

The group $\mathbb G_m^2=(\mathbb C^\times)^2$ acts by $(\lambda,\mu)\cdot(L,Q)=(\lambda L,\mu Q)$.

Multiplication transforms by $M(\lambda L,\mu Q)=\lambda\mu M(L,Q)$. The scalar $\lambda\mu$ is the character seen by the target.

## Compute the kernel of the product character

Define $\pi:\mathbb G_m^2\to\mathbb G_m$ by $\pi(\lambda,\mu)=\lambda\mu$.

Its kernel is

$$H=\{(t,t^{-1}):t\in\mathbb C^\times\}.$$

Every element of $H$ fixes the product: $(tL)(t^{-1}Q)=LQ$. This is the relative-scaling subgroup.

## Describe one relative-scaling orbit

For a fixed nonzero pair $(L,Q)$, its $H$-orbit is

$$H\cdot(L,Q)=\{(tL,t^{-1}Q):t\in\mathbb C^\times\}.$$

If both factors are nonzero, the parameter is faithful: $(tL,t^{-1}Q)=(L,Q)$ forces $t=1$.

### Conclusion

lessons.title: How the resultant detects relative scaling

content.markdown:
## A second output can remember what the product forgets

Along $(L,Q)\mapsto(tL,t^{-1}Q)$, multiplication remains fixed. The resultant does not: bidegree $(2,1)$ leaves one uncancelled power of $t$.

This detects relative scale only on the nonzero-resultant locus. At a common root, every point on the orbit has resultant zero.

## Combine the two transformation laws

From Day 2, $R(\lambda L,\mu Q)=\lambda^2\mu R(L,Q)$. From Day 3, relative scaling uses $(\lambda,\mu)=(t,t^{-1})$.

Substitute before interpreting: the restricted character is $t^2t^{-1}=t$.

## Restrict the bidegree character

On the relative-scaling subgroup $H$ one has

$$R(tL,t^{-1}Q)=t^2t^{-1}R(L,Q)=tR(L,Q).$$

Thus multiplication has restricted weight zero, while the resultant has restricted weight one. Full torus-weight language remains a preview until Week 53.

## Recover the parameter on a nonzero-resultant orbit

Fix $(L,Q)$ with $R(L,Q)\ne0$. If $(L',Q')=(tL,t^{-1}Q)$ lies on its relative-scaling orbit, then

$$t=\frac{R(L',Q')}{R(L,Q)}.$$

The denominator is the exact hypothesis. This formula compares two already known points in the same orbit; it does not decide that arbitrary equal-product factorizations belong to one orbit.

## Complete worked model

$L=T+2S$, $Q=3T^2-TS+4S^2$, and $(L',Q')=(5L,\frac15Q)$.

Verify equal products, compute both resultants, and recover the parameter.

### Strategy

Reuse the Day 2 value $R(L,Q)=18$, then apply the two transformation laws.

### Hypotheses

The original resultant is nonzero and the two pairs are declared to lie in the same relative-scaling orbit.

### Intermediate claims

$L'Q'=LQ$ and $R(L',Q')=5R(L,Q)=90$.

### Justification

The product scalars cancel, while bidegree contributes $5^2(1/5)=5$.

### Conclusion

The ratio $90/18=5$ recovers the scale erased by multiplication.

content.markdown:
## State the zero-locus boundary

If $R(L,Q)=0$, then $R(tL,t^{-1}Q)=t\cdot0=0$ for every $t$. The resultant is constant along that orbit and cannot recover the parameter.

The vanishing has geometric meaning—$L$ and $Q$ share a projective root—but it removes the numerical detector of relative scale.

## Preview the infinitesimal formulation

Over $\mathbb C$, differentiating the curve $s\mapsto(e^sL,e^{-s}Q)$ at $s=0$ gives the vector $(L,-Q)$.

The product derivative sends it to $LQ-LQ=0$, while the derivative of the resultant is $R(L,Q)$. This is the tangent-space version of the same character calculation, previewed here before affine tangent spaces are taught in Week 34.

content.markdown:
## One diagram, two characters, one exact boundary

The week has two compatible actions. $SL_2$ changes variables and multiplication is equivariant. $\mathbb G_m^2$ rescales factors; multiplication sees character $(1,1)$ and the resultant sees $(2,1)$.

Restricting to $(t,t^{-1})$ cancels the product character but leaves one power of $t$ in the resultant.

## Keep the proof chain ordered

Define $V_d$ and the inverse-substitution action. Prove multiplication equivariance. Prove resultant bidegree. Compute the relative subgroup. Only then explain detection and its zero-resultant failure.

## State the transformation table

For $g\in SL_2$, $M(g\cdot L,g\cdot Q)=g\cdot M(L,Q)$. For $(\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb G_m^2$,

$$M(\lambda L,\mu Q)=\lambda\mu M(L,Q),\qquad R(\lambda L,\mu Q)=\lambda^2\mu R(L,Q).$$

On $H=(t,t^{-1})$, these become $M\mapsto M$ and $R\mapsto tR$.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Let $(g\cdot F)(v)=F(g^{-1}v)$ on each $V_d$. Then $M(g\cdot L,g\cdot Q)(v)=L(g^{-1}v)Q(g^{-1}v)=(g\cdot(LQ))(v)$, so multiplication is $SL_2$-equivariant. For two declared points $(L',Q')=(tL,t^{-1}Q)$ with $R(L,Q)\ne0$, the ratio $R(L',Q')/R(L,Q)$ recovers $t$. If $R=0$, all orbit values remain zero. content.markdown:
## The capstone compresses the term into two equations

Write $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$. The five coefficients describe a factorization of a binary cubic.

The space $X$ imposes two different normalizations. Understanding which quantity each equation controls is more important than merely memorizing the displayed set.

## Bring forward the two transformation laws

Week 27 established $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+cb^2$. Week 29 showed that relative scaling fixes $LQ$ but multiplies the resultant by the orbit parameter.

Polynomial multiplication also gives $LQ=acT^3+(ad+bc)T^2S+(ae+bd)TS^2+beS^3$.

## Define the space without hiding either equation

Set

$$X=\{(a,b,c,d,e)\in\mathbb C^5:a^2e-abd+cb^2=1,\ ad+bc=1\}.$$

The first left-hand side is $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)$. The second is the coefficient of $T^2S$ in the product cubic $LQ$.

## Explain why the normalizations are different

Under $(L,Q)\mapsto(tL,t^{-1}Q)$, the product cubic and every one of its coefficients remain fixed, while the resultant becomes $t\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)$.

Thus $\operatorname{Res}=1$ chooses one relative scale whenever the resultant is nonzero. The equation $ad+bc=1$ instead restricts the product cubic to an affine coefficient slice.

content.markdown:
## On $a\ne0$, two equations solve two coordinates

The open part $X_a$ means the locus where $a$ is invertible. This is exactly the hypothesis needed to solve first for $d$ and then for $e$.

## Reactivate principal localization

Week 25 introduced localization by adjoining $a^{-1}$. At the level of complex points, this restricts attention to $a\ne0$.

No formula containing $1/a$ or $1/a^2$ may be used on the fiber $a=0$.

## Solve the coefficient equation first

## Complete worked model

$Y=\{(u,v,w,r,s):ur+vw=2,\ u^2s-uvr+wv^2=3\}$ on the principal open $u\ne0$.

### Strategy

Solve the first equation for $r$, substitute into the second to solve for $s$, and then verify projection and insertion in both directions.

### Hypotheses

$u\in\mathbb C^\times$ and $v,w\in\mathbb C$.

### Intermediate claims

$r=(2-vw)/u$ and $s=(3+2v-2v^2w)/u^2$.

The first formula gives $ur+vw=2$. It also gives $uvr=v(2-vw)=2v-v^2w$, so the second left-hand side becomes $(3+2v-2v^2w)-(2v-v^2w)+wv^2=3$.

objectives: Define affine space and the common zero set $V(S)$, replace a family of equations by its generated ideal, and distinguish a complex algebraic set from its real trace.

content.markdown:
# From equations to geometry

The capstone space from Week 30 was written as the simultaneous solution set of two polynomial equations. This week turns that notation into a general language.

Throughout the week, $k=\mathbb C$ unless another field is named. The affine space $\mathbb A_k^n$ is the set $k^n$ equipped with polynomial coordinates. Its Zariski topology will be built from polynomial zero sets rather than Euclidean distance.

## What you need from polynomial rings and ideals

Let $R=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$. If $S\subseteq R$, the generated ideal $(S)$ consists of finite sums $\sum_i a_i s_i$ with $a_i\in R$ and $s_i\in S$.

At a point where every $s\in S$ vanishes, every such finite sum also vanishes. This evaluation fact is the bridge from a list of equations to an ideal.

## Define the common zero set

For any family $S\subseteq k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, define

$$V(S)=\{p\in\mathbb A_k^n:f(p)=0\text{ for every }f\in S\}.$$

The quantifier “for every” matters. A point belongs to $V(S)$ only when it satisfies all equations in the family.

## Replace equations by the ideal they generate

The common zeros of $S$ and of $(S)$ are identical:

$$V(S)=V((S)).$$

One inclusion uses $S\subseteq(S)$. The other uses the fact that every element of $(S)$ is a polynomial combination of finitely many members of $S$.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$S_0=\{z-x^2,\ y-z\}\subseteq\mathbb C[x,y,z]$.

Describe $V(S_0)$ by a parameter and verify that the parameterization gives exactly the common zeros.

### Strategy

Use the equations in an order that eliminates dependent coordinates. Then prove both directions: every common zero has the proposed form, and every proposed point satisfies both equations.

### Hypotheses

The ambient set is $\mathbb A^3_{\mathbb C}$, and the equations are interpreted over $\mathbb C$.

### Intermediate claims

From $z=x^2$ and $y=z$, every common zero is $(t,t^2,t^2)$ for a unique $t\in\mathbb C$. Conversely, substituting $(t,t^2,t^2)$ makes both polynomials zero.

### Justification

The first coordinate can be chosen freely as $t=x$. The first equation then fixes $z=t^2$, and the second fixes $y=t^2$. Direct substitution proves sufficiency.

### Conclusion

$$V(S_0)=\{(t,t^2,t^2):t\in\mathbb C\}.$$ A real sketch shows only the points obtained when $t\in\mathbb R$; it does not display the full complex curve.

## Use real pictures without confusing the field

A real drawing of a complex algebraic set records only its real trace $V_{\mathbb C}(S)\cap\mathbb R^n$. That trace can miss most of the complex points and can even suggest the wrong decomposition.

For example, $x^2+y^2=(x+iy)(x-iy)$. Thus $V_{\mathbb C}(x^2+y^2)$ is the union of two complex lines, while its real trace is only the origin.

content.markdown:
# From points back to equations

The operator $V$ sends equations to points. The operator $I$ travels in the other direction by recording every polynomial relation satisfied by a set.

This direction is essential because different lists of equations can define the same point set. The vanishing ideal keeps all polynomial consequences visible.

## Reactivate the ideal axioms

A subset $J$ of a polynomial ring is an ideal when it contains $0$, is closed under addition and additive inverses, and absorbs multiplication by arbitrary polynomials.

To prove that a naturally defined collection is an ideal, verify those operations directly. Do not infer ideal structure from a geometric picture.

## Define the vanishing ideal

For any subset $X\subseteq\mathbb A_k^n$, define

$$I(X)=\{f\in k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]:f(p)=0\text{ for every }p\in X\}.$$

The same universal quantifier appears again, but now it ranges over points rather than equations.

content.markdown:
## Compute the ideal of one point

For $p=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$, evaluation at $p$ is a ring homomorphism

$$\operatorname{ev}_p:k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\to k.$$

Its kernel is $I(\{p\})=(x_1-a_1,\ldots,x_n-a_n)$. In two variables, repeated division by $x-a$ and $y-b$ makes this formula explicit.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$P=\{(0,0)\}\subseteq L=V(y)\subseteq\mathbb A^2_{\mathbb C}$.

Prove $I(L)\subseteq I(P)$ and identify both ideals.

### Strategy

First use the set inclusion pointwise. Then compute the two ideals to make the reversed containment concrete.

### Hypotheses

The field is infinite, and $L$ is the entire $x$-axis, not a finite sample from it.

### Intermediate claims

Any polynomial vanishing at every point of $L$ vanishes at $P$, so $I(L)\subseteq I(P)$. Moreover, $I(L)=(y)$ and $I(P)=(x,y)$.

### Justification

If $f$ vanishes on $L$, then the one-variable polynomial $f(x,0)$ vanishes for every $x\in\mathbb C$, hence is zero. Therefore every term of $f$ contains $y$, so $f\in(y)$. The point-ideal computation gives $I(P)=(x,y)$, and $(y)\subseteq(x,y)$.

### Conclusion

A larger point set imposes more evaluations and therefore admits fewer vanishing polynomials. The inclusion direction reverses.

## Prove the elementary closure containments

Every family of equations belongs to the ideal of its own zero set:

$$S\subseteq I(V(S)).$$

Every point set belongs to the zero set of its vanishing ideal:

$$X\subseteq V(I(X)).$$

These statements follow from the definitions. The stronger description $I(V(J))=\sqrt J$ is the Nullstellensatz and belongs to Week 32.

## Recover an algebraic set from all its equations

If $X$ is already algebraic, then $X=V(S)$ for some $S$. The elementary containments are enough to prove

$$V(I(X))=X.$$

This equality concerns point sets. It does not identify $I(V(J))$ with the original ideal $J$.

lessons.title: Build the Zariski topology from products and sums
lessons.summary: Compute $V(fg)$, prove the finite-union and arbitrary-intersection identities for ideals, and verify that algebraic sets are the closed sets of a topology.
objectives: Compute $V(fg)$, prove the finite-union and arbitrary-intersection identities for ideals, and verify that algebraic sets are the closed sets of a topology.

content.markdown:
# Why products create unions

A topology is determined by its closed sets. To use algebraic sets as the closed sets, we must prove that the whole space and empty set are algebraic, arbitrary intersections are algebraic, and finite unions are algebraic.

The field axiom has a decisive geometric consequence: a product of two scalars is zero exactly when at least one factor is zero.

## Keep three ideal operations distinct

For ideals $I,J\subseteq R$, the sum $I+J$ contains all $f+g$ with $f\in I$ and $g\in J$. The product $IJ$ is generated by all products $fg$. Their set-theoretic intersection $I\cap J$ is a third operation.

Zero sets reverse inclusions, so an algebraically smaller ideal generally has a geometrically larger zero set.

## Compute a concrete product zero set

In $\mathbb A^2$, the equation $xy=0$ holds exactly on the two coordinate axes:

$$V(xy)=V(x)\cup V(y).$$

The intersection point belongs to both components, but no additional points appear.

## Prove the product identity for two polynomials

For any $f,g\in k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$,

$$V(fg)=V(f)\cup V(g).$$

The statement depends on evaluating in a field. In a ring with zero divisors, a product can vanish even when neither factor vanishes.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$I=(x,z)\subseteq\mathbb C[x,y,z]$ and $J=(y-1,z)\subseteq\mathbb C[x,y,z]$.

Prove $V(IJ)=V(I)\cup V(J)$ for this pair.

### Strategy

Use the easy inclusion from products first. For the reverse inclusion, argue by contraposition: outside each zero set, choose one ideal element that does not vanish and multiply them.

### Hypotheses

Evaluation occurs in $\mathbb C$, so a product of two nonzero evaluated scalars remains nonzero.

### Intermediate claims

Every point in $V(I)$ or $V(J)$ annihilates every product $fg$ with $f\in I$, $g\in J$. If $p$ lies outside both sets, some $f\in I$ and $g\in J$ satisfy $f(p)\ne0$ and $g(p)\ne0$, so $(fg)(p)\ne0$.

### Justification

The product ideal is generated by finite sums of such products. Vanishing of one entire factor ideal kills every generator. Conversely, one nonvanishing product witnesses failure to lie in $V(IJ)$.

### Conclusion

$V(IJ)=V(I)\cup V(J)$. Explicitly, $V(I)=\{(0,t,0):t\in\mathbb C\}$ is the $y$-axis and $V(J)=\{(t,1,0):t\in\mathbb C\}$ is the line $y=1,z=0$.

content.markdown:
## Turn arbitrary intersections into sums of ideals

For any family $(I_\lambda)_{\lambda\in\Lambda}$,

$$\bigcap_{\lambda\in\Lambda}V(I_\lambda)=V\!\left(\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}I_\lambda\right).$$

An element of the sum uses only finitely many summands. A point annihilates the sum exactly when it annihilates every ideal in the family.

content.markdown:
## Verify the topology axioms

The whole affine space is $V((0))$, and the empty set is $V((1))$. The product-ideal formula gives finite unions, and the sum-ideal formula gives arbitrary intersections.

Therefore algebraic subsets are precisely the closed sets of a topology on $\mathbb A_k^n$. This is the Zariski topology.

content.markdown:
# More equations mean fewer points

The identity $V(I+J)=V(I)\cap V(J)$ is the algebraic form of simultaneous constraint. Adding the two ideals creates one ideal containing every equation from both systems.

The proof is short only after the quantifiers are controlled. Each direction uses a different feature of the sum.

## Reopen the definition of an ideal sum

The sum ideal is

$$I+J=\{f+g:f\in I,\ g\in J\}.$$

It contains both $I$ and $J$ because $f=f+0$ and $g=0+g$. Conversely, each of its elements is built from one element of each ideal.

## Compute a sum ideal before its zero set

For $I=(x)$ and $J=(y)$ in $\mathbb C[x,y]$,

$$I+J=(x,y).$$

Its zero set is the origin, which is exactly the intersection of the two coordinate axes.

## Prove the first inclusion from ideal containment

Because $I\subseteq I+J$ and $J\subseteq I+J$, zero sets reverse these containments:

$$V(I+J)\subseteq V(I)\quad\text{and}\quad V(I+J)\subseteq V(J).$$

Therefore $V(I+J)\subseteq V(I)\cap V(J)$.

## Complete worked model

$I_1,I_2,I_3\subseteq k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and $p\in V(I_1)\cap V(I_2)\cap V(I_3)$.

Prove that $p\in V(I_1+I_2+I_3)$ by evaluating an arbitrary element of the sum.

### Strategy

Do not reason from a picture. Choose a general element of the sum and use the three vanishing hypotheses term by term.

### Hypotheses

The point $p$ annihilates every element of each of the three ideals.

### Intermediate claims

Every $h\in I_1+I_2+I_3$ can be written $h=f_1+f_2+f_3$ with $f_i\in I_i$, and each $f_i(p)=0$.

### Justification

Evaluation is additive, so $h(p)=f_1(p)+f_2(p)+f_3(p)=0$. Since $h$ was arbitrary, $p$ annihilates the whole sum ideal.

### Conclusion

$V(I_1)\cap V(I_2)\cap V(I_3)\subseteq V(I_1+I_2+I_3)$. Together with order reversal, this yields equality for three ideals.

content.markdown:
# A new geometric language

Affine algebraic geometry begins with a controlled reversal: equations determine point sets through $V$, and point sets determine equations through $I$.

The Zariski topology remembers polynomial constraints. It is intentionally coarser than the usual topology on $\mathbb C^n$, so visual intuition must be checked against equations.

## The week’s four structural formulas

Keep these statements distinct:

$$V(S)=V((S)),\qquad V(fg)=V(f)\cup V(g),$$

$$V(I+J)=V(I)\cap V(J),\qquad V(I(X))=X\text{ for algebraic }X.$$

None of them identifies $I(V(J))$ with $J$ for every ideal. Radical ideals and the Nullstellensatz begin in Week 32.

## Audit a real picture against the complex equations

The equation $x^2+y^2=1$ draws a real circle, but its complex zero set contains every complex pair satisfying the equation. For example, $(i,\sqrt2)$ lies on the complex curve because $i^2+(\sqrt2)^2=-1+2=1$.

A drawing can suggest components or singularities, but the algebra decides the complex set.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$\mathbb A^1_{\mathbb C}$.

Prove that every Zariski-closed subset is finite or the whole line, and that every finite subset is closed.

### Strategy

Start from a defining family $S\subseteq\mathbb C[t]$. Split into the case where every polynomial in $S$ is zero and the case where $S$ contains a nonzero polynomial.

### Hypotheses

A nonzero one-variable polynomial over a field has only finitely many roots.

### Intermediate claims

If $S$ contains no nonzero polynomial, then $V(S)=\mathbb C$. Otherwise, for nonzero $f\in S$, $V(S)\subseteq V(f)$ is finite. Conversely, $\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}=V(\prod_i(t-a_i))$.

### Justification

Common zeros must in particular be zeros of the selected nonzero polynomial. The displayed product vanishes exactly at the listed scalars.

### Conclusion

The proper closed subsets of $\mathbb A^1_{\mathbb C}$ are exactly the finite sets. Thus Zariski-open sets are complements of finite sets, unlike ordinary disks or intervals.

content.markdown:
# Why equations forget multiplicity

Week 31 sent an ideal $J$ to its common zero set $V(J)$ and proved $V(I(X))=X$ for an algebraic set $X$. The reverse expression $I(V(J))$ needs a correction: a set of points cannot remember how many times an equation was repeated.

Throughout this week the base field is $\mathbb C$. This algebraic-closure hypothesis is essential for the Nullstellensatz and will be named whenever the theorem is used.

## Reactivate powers and ideal membership

If $J\subseteq R=\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ is an ideal and $f^m\in J$, then every common zero of $J$ also annihilates $f^m$. Because $\mathbb C$ is a field, $f(p)^m=0$ implies $f(p)=0$.

This one-line implication explains why the geometry sees $f$ as soon as it sees a positive power of $f$.

## Define the radical of an ideal

The radical of $J$ is

$$\sqrt J=\{f\in R: f^m\in J\text{ for some integer }m\ge1\}.$$

An ideal is radical when $J=\sqrt J$. Equivalently, the quotient $R/J$ has no nonzero nilpotent elements: if $\overline f^{\,m}=0$, then already $\overline f=0$.

Check the two containments separately. The likely first gap is the claim that a polynomial outside $(x,y)$ cannot have a power in $(x^2,y^3)$: identify its nonzero constant term and follow that term through every positive power.

A radical computation needs both containments. Showing only that $x$ and $y$ enter the radical does not exclude additional polynomials.

Repair the first missing containment with the constant-term argument, then state the equality of ideals. Next, use this power argument at a point to prove that radicalization preserves a zero set.

content.markdown:
## Prove that radicalization preserves the zero set

For every ideal $J\subseteq\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ one has

$$V(J)=V(\sqrt J).$$

The inclusion $J\subseteq\sqrt J$ reverses under $V$. For the other inclusion, take $p\in V(J)$ and $f\in\sqrt J$; a power $f^m$ lies in $J$, so $f(p)^m=0$ and therefore $f(p)=0$.

Check the direction forced by $J\subseteq\sqrt J$, then check that the reverse direction evaluates a witnessing relation $f^m\in J$ at an arbitrary point of $V(J)$.

The equality holds over any field, so invoking the Nullstellensatz would hide the elementary reason and add an unnecessary hypothesis.

Repair the first incorrect containment or missing power evaluation and name explicitly that fields have no nonzero nilpotents. Next, diagnose why the doubled equation $(x^2)$ and the reduced equation $(x)$ determine the same line.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$J_0=(x^2)\subseteq\mathbb C[x,y]$.

Compute $V(J_0)$ and $I(V(J_0))$, then explain why $I(V(J_0))=J_0$ is false.

### Strategy

First solve the point equation. Then compute every polynomial vanishing on the resulting line by division with remainder in the variable $x$.

### Hypotheses

The field is $\mathbb C$, the ambient space is $\mathbb A^2$, and $I(V(J_0))$ means all polynomials that vanish on every point of the zero set.

### Intermediate claims

$V(x^2)=V(x)=\{(0,b):b\in\mathbb C\}$. A polynomial $f(x,y)$ vanishes on this line exactly when its remainder $f(0,y)$ after division by $x$ is the zero polynomial.

### Justification

Write $f=xq+r(y)$. If $f(0,b)=0$ for every $b\in\mathbb C$, then the one-variable polynomial $r$ has infinitely many roots, so $r=0$ and $x$ divides $f$. Conversely, every multiple of $x$ vanishes on the line.

### Conclusion

$$I(V(x^2))=(x)=\sqrt{(x^2)}\ne(x^2).$$ The point set records the line but not the doubled equation.

Separate the three objects in the argument: the point set $V(J_1)$, its vanishing ideal $I(V(J_1))$, and the original nonradical ideal $J_1$.

A point set forgets the powers in the original equations. Confusing these ideals erases exactly the multiplicity that radicals are designed to remove.

## State exactly what the strong Nullstellensatz adds

The easy inclusion is always $\sqrt J\subseteq I(V(J))$: every polynomial whose power lies in $J$ vanishes on $V(J)$. The difficult reverse inclusion is Hilbert's strong Nullstellensatz.

Over the algebraically closed field $\mathbb C$,

$$I(V(J))=\sqrt J.$$

Consequently, $I$ and $V$ give inverse, order-reversing correspondences between affine algebraic sets and radical ideals. We use the theorem this week; proving it would require more commutative algebra than this syllabus allocates here.

Missing a branch changes the zero set and therefore changes the intersection of point and component ideals to which the Nullstellensatz applies.

## Use the corrected correspondence independently

The reliable chain is now

$$J\subseteq\sqrt J=I(V(J)),\qquad V(J)=V(\sqrt J).$$

Equality $I(V(J))=J$ is justified only after proving that $J$ is radical. That condition is part of the conclusion, not a detail to suppress.

content.markdown:
# Replace ambient formulas by functions on the variety

Two polynomials can differ in the ambient ring and still define the same function on $X$. The coordinate ring identifies exactly those formulas whose difference vanishes everywhere on $X$.

The quotient is not a decorative label. Its elements are the global polynomial, or regular, functions on the affine algebraic set.

## Reactivate quotient equality

In a quotient ring $R/I$, the classes $[f]$ and $[g]$ are equal exactly when $f-g\in I$. If $I=I(X)$, this condition says exactly that $f(p)=g(p)$ for every $p\in X$.

A proposed map out of a quotient must first annihilate the ideal. That well-definedness check is the first line of every coordinate-ring computation.

## Define the coordinate ring

For an affine algebraic set $X\subseteq\mathbb A^n_{\mathbb C}$, define

$$\mathbb C[X]=\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I(X).$$

The class $[f]$ acts on $X$ by $p\mapsto f(p)$. The action is well defined because changing $f$ by an element of $I(X)$ does not change any value on $X$.

## Prove that quotient classes are functions

The map

$$[f]\longmapsto (p\mapsto f(p))$$

is an injective $\mathbb C$-algebra homomorphism from $\mathbb C[X]$ to the algebra of all functions $X\to\mathbb C$. Its image is, by definition here, the regular functions on the affine algebraic set $X$.

Injectivity is built into the choice of $I(X)$: a class defines the zero function exactly when its representative lies in $I(X)$.

## Complete worked model

$J_0=(y-2x-1)\subseteq\mathbb C[x,y]$ and $L=V(J_0)\subseteq\mathbb A^2_{\mathbb C}$.

Prove $J_0=I(L)$ and construct an explicit $\mathbb C$-algebra isomorphism $\mathbb C[L]\cong\mathbb C[t]$.

### Strategy

First study the presentation algebra $A_0=\mathbb C[x,y]/J_0$. Build inverse maps between $A_0$ and $\mathbb C[t]$, use the resulting domain property to prove that $J_0$ is radical, and only then identify $J_0$ with $I(L)$ by the strong Nullstellensatz.

### Hypotheses

The base field is $\mathbb C$, $L=V(J_0)$, and $A_0=\mathbb C[x,y]/J_0$. At this stage $J_0=I(L)$ is a claim to prove, not an assumption.

### Intermediate claims

Define $\Phi:A_0\to\mathbb C[t]$ by $\Phi([f(x,y)])=f(t,2t+1)$ and $\Psi:\mathbb C[t]\to A_0$ by $\Psi(t)=[x]$. These maps are inverse, so $A_0$ is a domain. Hence $J_0$ is prime and therefore radical.

### Justification

The relation maps to zero, so $\Phi$ is well defined. Also $\Phi\Psi(t)=t$, while $\Psi\Phi([x])=[x]$ and $\Psi\Phi([y])=2[x]+1=[y]$. Thus both composites are identities. Since $J_0$ is radical, the strong Nullstellensatz gives $I(L)=I(V(J_0))=\sqrt{J_0}=J_0$.

### Conclusion

$$\mathbb C[L]=\mathbb C[x,y]/I(L)=A_0\cong\mathbb C[t].$$ The proof establishes the presentation ideal before calling the quotient a coordinate ring.

content.markdown:
## Let the ring expose a reducible crossing

For the union of the coordinate axes $X=V(xy)$,

$$\mathbb C[X]=\mathbb C[x,y]/(xy).$$

Here $(xy)=(x)\cap(y)$: a polynomial divisible by both $x$ and $y$ is divisible by $xy$. Because $(x)$ and $(y)$ are prime, they are radical, and their intersection is radical. The strong Nullstellensatz therefore gives $I(X)=(xy)$.

The nonzero classes $[x]$ and $[y]$ multiply to zero. The ring therefore remembers that two components meet even though the underlying set is easy to draw.

content.markdown:
# The arrow reverses because functions compose

Suppose $\varphi:X\to Y$ is given by polynomial coordinate functions. A regular function $g$ on $Y$ produces the regular function $g\circ\varphi$ on $X$. Thus geometry moves points forward while algebra pulls functions backward.

This reversal is the central structural fact of the affine algebra–geometry dictionary.

## Reactivate composition and generators

A $\mathbb C$-algebra homomorphism out of $\mathbb C[y_1,\ldots,y_m]/I(Y)$ is determined by the images of the coordinate classes $[y_i]$, provided those images satisfy every relation in $I(Y)$.

To prove that two such homomorphisms agree, it is therefore enough to compare them on the coordinate generators.

## Define pullback on regular functions

For a morphism $\varphi:X\to Y$, define

$$\varphi^*:\mathbb C[Y]\longrightarrow\mathbb C[X],\qquad [g]\longmapsto[g\circ\varphi].$$

Well-definedness means that if $g$ vanishes on $Y$, then $g\circ\varphi$ vanishes on $X$. The map preserves sums, products, scalars, and $1$ because composition does.

## Track composition in the reversed order

If $X\xrightarrow{\varphi}Y\xrightarrow{\psi}Z$, then

$$(\psi\circ\varphi)^*=\varphi^*\circ\psi^*.$$

Indeed, both sides send a function $h$ on $Z$ to $h\circ\psi\circ\varphi$ on $X$. The order reversal is forced by the domains of the functions.

Determine $\alpha([v])$, construct the corresponding morphism $\varphi:X\to Y$, and prove $\varphi^*=\alpha$.

### Strategy

Apply the relation in the source algebra, then use the images of the coordinate generators as the coordinate functions of the geometric map.

### Hypotheses

$\alpha$ is a $\mathbb C$-algebra homomorphism and $[v]=[u]^2$ in $\mathbb C[Y]$.

### Intermediate claims

$\alpha([v])=(t+1)^2$. The candidate morphism is $\varphi(t)=(t+1,(t+1)^2)$, which lands in $Y$.

### Justification

The relation $v-u^2$ vanishes after substitution, so the coordinate functions define a map to $Y$. Its pullback sends $[u]$ and $[v]$ to the same elements as $\alpha$. Equality on the generators proves equality of homomorphisms.

### Conclusion

$$\varphi(t)=(t+1,(t+1)^2),\qquad \varphi^*=\alpha.$$ This is the general construction: images of coordinate classes become coordinate functions of the reversed geometric map.

## Turn inverse algebra maps into inverse geometric maps

For affine varieties $X$ and $Y$, pullback gives a bijection

$$\operatorname{Mor}(X,Y)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C\text{-alg}}(\mathbb C[Y],\mathbb C[X]).$$

Consequently, $X\cong Y$ if and only if $\mathbb C[X]\cong\mathbb C[Y]$ as $\mathbb C$-algebras. If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are inverse algebra maps, their corresponding geometric maps are inverse because the pullback of each composite is the identity.

content.markdown:
# One geometric piece means no algebraic zero divisors

A Zariski closed set is irreducible when it cannot be written as the union of two proper closed subsets. The coordinate ring detects this property through multiplication.

If two nonzero functions multiply to zero, then every point lies in the zero set of one factor or the other. That is exactly the shape of a decomposition.

## Reactivate prime ideals and domains

An ideal $\mathfrak p\subset R$ is prime when $fg\in\mathfrak p$ implies $f\in\mathfrak p$ or $g\in\mathfrak p$. The quotient $R/\mathfrak p$ is an integral domain exactly when $\mathfrak p$ is prime.

For $X$, the relevant ideal is $I(X)$, not an arbitrary presentation ideal that happens to have the same zero set.

## Define irreducibility topologically

A nonempty algebraic set $X$ is irreducible if every equality $X=Y\cup Z$ with $Y$ and $Z$ closed in $X$ forces $Y=X$ or $Z=X$.

Equivalently, any two nonempty open subsets of $X$ intersect. Irreducible is stronger than connected: the coordinate cross is connected at the origin but reducible into two lines.

content.title: Exhibit a genuine reducible decomposition
content.introMarkdown: Prove from the definition that $X$ is reducible.

data.markdown:
Exhibit the two closed lines and give a different point proving that each line is a proper subset of the coordinate cross.

A union proves reducibility only when both closed pieces are proper; merely factoring $xy$ does not complete the topological definition.

Repair the first missing equality, closedness statement, or properness witness. Next, prove the general equivalence between geometric irreducibility and a prime vanishing ideal.

content.markdown:
## Prove the prime-ideal criterion

For an affine algebraic set $X$,

$$X\text{ is irreducible}\iff I(X)\text{ is prime}.$$

If $fg$ vanishes on $X$, then $X=(X\cap V(f))\cup(X\cap V(g))$. Irreducibility forces one factor to vanish everywhere. Conversely, a decomposition into closed subsets can be written using ideals, and primeness prevents both pieces from being proper.

data.markdown:
In the forward direction, turn $fg\in I(X)$ into a union of two closed subsets of $X$. In the reverse direction, explain why $JK\subseteq I(X)$ forces one entire ideal into the prime ideal.

Both directions are needed to translate a geometric decomposition into a ring-theoretic test and back again.

Repair the first incomplete union or ideal-product argument, then state which closed subset must equal $X$. Next, apply the criterion to a curve whose coordinate ring is already known to be a polynomial domain.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$P=V(y-x^2)\subseteq\mathbb A^2_{\mathbb C}$.

Prove that $P$ is irreducible by proving that $\mathbb C[P]$ is a domain.

### Strategy

Reuse the explicit coordinate-ring isomorphism from Day 2 and transport the absence of zero divisors.

### Hypotheses

$\mathbb C[P]\cong\mathbb C[t]$ by $[x]\mapsto t$ and $[y]\mapsto t^2$.

### Intermediate claims

$\mathbb C[t]$ is an integral domain, so the isomorphic ring $\mathbb C[P]$ is an integral domain. Therefore $I(P)$ is prime.

### Justification

A product of nonzero polynomials over the field $\mathbb C$ is nonzero. Ring isomorphisms preserve zero products and nonzero elements. The quotient-domain criterion then makes $I(P)$ prime, and the prime-ideal criterion makes $P$ irreducible.

### Conclusion

$P$ is irreducible. The argument proves more than a drawing suggests: it rules out every decomposition into proper Zariski closed subsets.

content.markdown:
## Identify global regular functions and the Week 33 boundary

On an affine algebraic set $X$, every global regular function in this variety-first setting is represented by an element of $\mathbb C[X]$. Thus the coordinate ring is simultaneously a geometric invariant and an algebra of functions.

A quotient $g/h$ with a denominator that does not vanish on a chosen open subset leads to localization. That local theory begins in Week 33. Today we use only globally defined coordinate-ring classes.

data.markdown:
Use $[x][y]=1$ in $\mathbb C[H]$ and distinguish that global identity from a fraction defined only on a smaller open set.

The relation proves that $1/x$ already has the global representative $[y]$; general localization belongs to the next week.

Repair the first missing coordinate-ring identity or scope distinction. Next, compare an irreducible parabola with a reducible pair of lines using both geometry and zero divisors.

content.markdown:
## Classify a new hypersurface from its algebra

For a hypersurface $V(f)$, factorization can suggest components, but a full argument must connect the polynomial, the ideal, the quotient ring, and the geometric definition. Over $\mathbb C[x,y]$, a principal ideal generated by an irreducible polynomial is prime.

data.markdown:
For the parabola, use the domain isomorphism. For $V(y^2-x^2)$, first prove that the square-free presentation ideal is radical, then prove both line components are proper and show that the two factor classes are nonzero before multiplying them to zero.

The comparison must first identify the actual vanishing ideal and then align the geometric decomposition with the exact algebraic obstruction in the coordinate ring.

Repair the first missing radical, domain, proper-component, or nonzero-zero-divisor step. Day 5 begins with scheduled retrieval before assembling the full dictionary in one affine proof.

# Use the dictionary as a chain of justified translations

The week has not produced six unrelated definitions. It has produced a system: points determine radical vanishing ideals; quotients by those ideals are function algebras; geometric maps pull functions backward; and ring-theoretic properties return geometric information.

Today's work begins with spaced retrieval, then builds one complete affine argument. Each review is labelled and changes context so repetition strengthens recall rather than replacing new teaching.

## Keep the hypotheses visible

The strong Nullstellensatz is being used over $\mathbb C$. Coordinate rings here belong to affine algebraic sets. The equivalence between morphisms and reversed algebra maps is an affine statement.

When a conclusion depends on one of these scopes, name it in the line where it is used.

## Deliberate review: repair the reverse $I$–$V$ direction

Week 31 proved that larger point sets have smaller vanishing ideals. Reuse that reversal now, but do not claim that an arbitrary ideal is recovered without taking its radical.

Recognize the source as $\mathbb C[\mathbb A^2]$, reverse both $\alpha$ and $\alpha^{-1}$ into geometric maps, then verify inverse composites through pullback.

### Hypotheses

$Y$ is affine, so the morphism–coordinate-ring correspondence applies. The isomorphism is one of $\mathbb C$-algebras, not merely vector spaces or rings without specified scalar structure.

### Intermediate claims

$\alpha$ corresponds to $f:Y\to\mathbb A^2$ and $\alpha^{-1}$ corresponds to $g:\mathbb A^2\to Y$.

### Justification

$(g\circ f)^*=f^*\circ g^*=\alpha\circ\alpha^{-1}=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C[Y]}$, while $(f\circ g)^*=\alpha^{-1}\circ\alpha=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C[u,v]}$. Faithfulness of the affine correspondence identifies both composites with identity morphisms.

### Conclusion

$Y\cong\mathbb A^2$. The proof isolates the three essential hypotheses: affineness, a $\mathbb C$-algebra isomorphism, and the contravariant correspondence.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: If $p\in V(K)$, then every element of $K$ vanishes at $p$; since $J\subseteq K$, every element of $J$ also vanishes, so $p\in V(J)$. activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The monomial $y^2$ has weight $2\cdot3=6$, while $x^3$ has weight $3\cdot2=6$, so $h=y^2-x^3$ is homogeneous of weight $6$. If $P=\sum_rP_r$ is the decomposition into homogeneous components, then the weight-$m$ component of $Ph$ is $P_{m-6}h$, which still lies in $(h)$. Thus $(h)$ is homogeneous. Let $A_m$ be the image of $R_m$ in $A$. If $\sum_m\bar f_m=0$ with $f_m\in R_m$, then $\sum_m f_m\in(h)$. Homogeneity of the ideal forces every $f_m\in(h)$, so every $\bar f_m=0$ and the sum is direct. Finally, products of representatives of weights $r$ and $s$ have weight $r+s$, hence $A_rA_s\subseteq A_{r+s}$. Therefore $A=\bigoplus_mA_m$ is a graded quotient.

lessons.title: Turn polynomial maps into reversed algebra maps
lessons.summary: Define an affine morphism by polynomial coordinate functions, prove that it induces a coordinate-ring homomorphism in the reverse direction, and reconstruct a morphism from compatible generator images.
objectives: Define an affine morphism by polynomial coordinate functions, prove that it induces a coordinate-ring homomorphism in the reverse direction, and reconstruct a morphism from compatible generator images.

content.markdown:
# A map can be studied through the functions it pulls back

Suppose $F:X\to Y$ sends points of one affine variety to another. Every regular function $h$ on $Y$ can now be measured on $X$ by first applying $F$: the new function is $h\circ F$.

This operation is called pullback. It reverses arrows:

$$F:X\longrightarrow Y \qquad\leadsto\qquad F^*:\mathbb C[Y]\longrightarrow\mathbb C[X],\quad h\longmapsto h\circ F.$$

The reversal is the central organizing fact of the day. We will derive it from formulas, not memorize it as a convention.

## Reactivate coordinate rings and quotient descent

Week 32 defined $\mathbb C[X]$ as polynomial functions on $X$. If $Y=V(J)\subseteq\mathbb A^m$ and a proposed map has coordinate functions $F_1,\ldots,F_m\in\mathbb C[X]$, then it lands in $Y$ exactly when every relation in $J$ vanishes after the substitution $y_i\mapsto F_i$.

The same relation check says that the substitution homomorphism from $\mathbb C[y_1,\ldots,y_m]$ descends through the quotient $\mathbb C[Y]$.

## Compute pullback on coordinate generators

Let $X\subseteq\mathbb A^n$ and $Y\subseteq\mathbb A^m$. A polynomial map

$$F(p)=\bigl(F_1(p),\ldots,F_m(p)\bigr)$$

that lands in $Y$ is a morphism of affine varieties. If $y_i$ is the $i$th coordinate function on $Y$, then

$$F^*([y_i])=[F_i]\in\mathbb C[X].$$

Because the coordinate classes generate $\mathbb C[Y]$, these images determine the entire pullback.

## Prove that the polynomial formula lands in the target

If the target is cut out by equations, landing is a mathematical obligation. For $Y=V(q_1,\ldots,q_r)$, one must prove

$$q_j(F_1,\ldots,F_m)=0\quad\text{in }\mathbb C[X]$$

for every $j$. These identities both prove $F(X)\subseteq Y$ and show that substitution annihilates $I(Y)$.

Skipping this check turns a proposed morphism into an unverified ambient formula.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$Q=V(xz-y^2)\subseteq\mathbb A^3_{x,y,z}$ and $\alpha:\mathbb C[Q]\to\mathbb C[r,s]$ sends $[x]\mapsto r^2$, $[y]\mapsto rs$, and $[z]\mapsto s^2$.

Construct the corresponding morphism $f:\mathbb A^2\to Q$, prove that it lands in $Q$, and verify that $f^*=\alpha$.

### Strategy

Check the target relation on the proposed generator images, use those images as coordinate functions, then compare pullbacks on the full generating set.

### Hypotheses

$\mathbb C[Q]=\mathbb C[x,y,z]/(xz-y^2)$, so a substitution descends exactly when the three images satisfy $xz-y^2=0$.

### Intermediate claims

The relation maps to $r^2s^2-(rs)^2=0$, and the only possible point formula is $f(r,s)=(r^2,rs,s^2)$.

### Justification

The relation calculation proves both quotient descent and landing in $Q$. Pullback sends $[x],[y],[z]$ to $r^2,rs,s^2$, respectively. Since these coordinate classes generate $\mathbb C[Q]$, equality on them proves $f^*=\alpha$.

### Conclusion

Compatible images of the target coordinate classes determine a unique affine morphism in the opposite direction.

An arbitrary tuple of source functions need not define a point of the target variety. The quotient relation supplies both descent and the landing proof.

Repair the first missing relation, landing, or generator comparison and keep the algebra and geometry arrows opposite. Next, use composition to check the order of two successive pullbacks.

content.markdown:
## Let the map types determine composition order

For morphisms $X\xrightarrow{F}Y\xrightarrow{G}Z$, a function $h\in\mathbb C[Z]$ is first pulled back along $G$ and then along $F$. Therefore

$$(G\circ F)^*=F^*\circ G^*:\mathbb C[Z]\longrightarrow\mathbb C[X].$$

At a point $x\in X$, both sides equal $h(G(F(x)))$. Writing the ring domains before composing makes the order unavoidable.

The order reversal follows from the domains of the maps and associativity of composition; it is not a mnemonic.

An affine-morphism proof now has a stable order: write the polynomial coordinates, verify the target relations, define the reversed substitution map, and prove any converse reconstruction on coordinate generators.

The final task changes both the curve and the parameter. It is not a repetition of the worked parabola.

lessons.title: Make fractions regular on distinguished opens
lessons.summary: Identify $D_X(f)$ as an affine open with coordinate ring $\mathbb C[X]_f$, compute regular fractions there, and prove when an apparent denominator is removable in the coordinate ring.
objectives: Identify $D_X(f)$ as an affine open with coordinate ring $\mathbb C[X]_f$, compute regular fractions there, and prove when an apparent denominator is removable in the coordinate ring.

content.markdown:
# A denominator carries a domain

The fraction $g/f^n$ is not automatically a function everywhere on $X$. It is regular where $f$ does not vanish:

$$D_X(f)=\{p\in X:f(p)\ne0\}.$$

Week 25 constructed localization algebraically. Today we connect that construction with geometry: the regular functions on a distinguished open are exactly the elements of $\mathbb C[X]_f$.

## Reactivate principal localization

For a ring $A$ and $f\in A$, the localization $A_f$ contains fractions $a/f^n$ and makes $f$ a unit. A map $A\to B$ factors uniquely through $A_f$ precisely when the image of $f$ is invertible in $B$.

In this chapter $A=\mathbb C[X]$. The geometric restriction to $D_X(f)$ and the algebraic operation of adjoining $f^{-1}$ describe the same passage.

## Read a localized fraction as a regular function

For an affine variety $X$ and $f\in\mathbb C[X]$, Milne's theorem identifies

$$\Gamma(D_X(f),\mathcal O_X)\cong\mathbb C[X]_f.$$

The fraction $g/f^n$ evaluates at $p\in D_X(f)$ as $g(p)/f(p)^n$. Its denominator is nonzero by the definition of the open set.

Two fractions represent the same regular function when they are equal in the localization. The coordinate-ring relations of $X$ may make that equality less obvious than ordinary cancellation.

## Complete worked model

$U=D_{\mathbb A^2}(x)\subseteq\mathbb A^2_{x,y}$ and $H=V(xu-1)\subseteq\mathbb A^3_{x,y,u}$.

Prove $U\cong H$ and identify $u$ with the regular function $x^{-1}$.

### Strategy

Adjoin a coordinate for the reciprocal, construct maps in both directions, and verify the equation and both composites.

### Hypotheses

Every point of $U$ has $x\ne0$, while every point of $H$ satisfies $xu=1$ and therefore also has $x\ne0$.

### Intermediate claims

Define $\Phi:U\to H$ by $\Phi(x,y)=(x,y,1/x)$ and $\Psi:H\to U$ by $\Psi(x,y,u)=(x,y)$.

### Justification

$x(1/x)-1=0$, so $\Phi$ lands in $H$. The map $\Psi$ lands in $U$ because $xu=1$ forbids $x=0$. Clearly $\Psi\Phi=\operatorname{id}_U$, and on $H$ the equation forces $u=1/x$, so $\Phi\Psi=\operatorname{id}_H$.

### Conclusion

$D(x)$ is affine, with coordinate ring $\mathbb C[x,y,u]/(xu-1)\cong\mathbb C[x,x^{-1},y]$.

## Prove equality of localized fractions from a relation

On a variety, a defining relation can turn a quotient into a simpler regular function. For the hyperbola $H=V(xy-1)$, the coordinate-ring equality $[x][y]=1$ says that $[x]$ is already a global unit with inverse $[y]$.

Consequently, the localized expression $1/x$ on $D_H(x)$ equals the global regular function $y$. Here $D_H(x)=H$ because $x$ never vanishes on the hyperbola.

content.markdown:
## Remove an apparent pole with the equations of $X$

Return to the normalized-factorization variety

$$X=V(F,G)\subseteq\mathbb A^5_{a,b,c,d,e},$$

$$F=a^2e-abd+cb^2-1,\qquad G=ad+bc-1.$$

In $\mathbb C[X]$ the two relations imply

$$b-1=a(2bd-ae).$$

Indeed, substituting $a^2e=1+abd-cb^2$ from $F=0$ gives

$$b-1-2abd+a^2e=b-abd-cb^2=b(1-ad-bc)=0$$

by $G=0$. Therefore $(b-1)/a$ on $D_X(a)$ is not merely regular there: it equals the global coordinate-ring class $2bd-ae$.

content.markdown:
## Test whether a denominator is removable

A written denominator is evidence of a restricted formula, not proof of a genuine pole. To decide whether $g/f$ extends globally, one seeks $h\in\mathbb C[X]$ such that $g=fh$ in the coordinate ring.

Conversely, to prove that no extension exists, one must rule out every global coordinate-ring representative. On affine line this becomes a degree or divisibility argument in $\mathbb C[t]$.

A formula can have a removable denominator, while a genuinely nonextendable regular function remains confined to its principal open.

lessons.title: Detect dense image through the pullback
lessons.summary: Define a dominant morphism, use injectivity of pullback to detect dominance between irreducible affine varieties, and distinguish dense image from surjectivity and isomorphism.
objectives: Define a dominant morphism, use injectivity of pullback to detect dominance between irreducible affine varieties, and distinguish dense image from surjectivity and isomorphism.

content.markdown:
# A dense image is large enough to determine functions

A morphism $F:X\to Y$ is dominant when the Zariski closure of $F(X)$ is all of $Y$. Dominance does not require every point of $Y$ to be hit.

For irreducible affine varieties, dominance has an exact algebraic signature:

$$F\text{ is dominant}\iff F^*:\mathbb C[Y]\to\mathbb C[X]\text{ is injective}.$$

Intuitively, a regular function that vanishes after pullback vanishes on the image. If the image is dense, that function must vanish everywhere.

## Reactivate density and kernels

The closure of a subset is the common zero set of all regular functions that vanish on it. Thus the kernel of $F^*$ records the equations satisfied by every image point.

The irreducibility hypotheses ensure that the coordinate rings are domains and place the criterion in the standard affine-variety setting. We will state them every time the equivalence is used.

## Apply the dominance criterion to a projection

The projection $\pi:\mathbb A^2_{s,t}\to\mathbb A^1_u$, $(s,t)\mapsto s$, has pullback

$$\pi^*:\mathbb C[u]\longrightarrow\mathbb C[s,t],\qquad u\longmapsto s.$$

This map is injective: a nonzero polynomial in $u$ remains a nonzero polynomial after replacing $u$ by the algebraically independent variable $s$. Therefore $\pi$ is dominant. In fact it is surjective, but surjectivity is stronger than the criterion needs.

content.markdown:
## Separate dominance from isomorphism on the cusp

Set $J=(y^2-x^3)$. Division by the monic polynomial $y^2-x^3$ in the variable $y$ gives every class in $\mathbb C[x,y]/J$ a unique normal form $A(x)+yB(x)$.

Under $x\mapsto t^2$ and $y\mapsto t^3$, this normal form becomes $A(t^2)+t^3B(t^2)$. The first summand contains only even powers of $t$; the second contains only odd powers at least three. If their sum is zero, both vanish, so $A=B=0$. The substitution is therefore injective. Its domain quotient is a domain, so $J$ is prime and radical; the strong Nullstellensatz gives $I(V(J))=J$.

Consequently, for $C=V(y^2-x^3)$ and $\nu:\mathbb A^1_t\to C$, $\nu(t)=(t^2,t^3)$, the pullback identifies

$$\mathbb C[C]\cong\mathbb C[t^2,t^3]\hookrightarrow\mathbb C[t].$$

It is injective, so $\nu$ is dominant. It is even bijective on complex points. But it is not an isomorphism: the function $t$ does not belong to the image subring $\mathbb C[t^2,t^3]$.

This example blocks a common overstatement. Dominant, surjective, bijective, and isomorphic are four different claims.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$F:\mathbb A^2_{s,t}\to\mathbb A^2_{u,v}$ is $F(s,t)=(s,st)$.

Prove that $F$ is dominant but not surjective, using both pullback and an explicit description of the image.

### Strategy

Prove injectivity of substitution by expanding in $v$, then solve the image equations separately for $u\ne0$ and $u=0$.

### Hypotheses

Both affine spaces are irreducible. The pullback is $F^*(u)=s$ and $F^*(v)=st$.

### Intermediate claims

If $P(u,v)=\sum_j a_j(u)v^j$, then $P(s,st)=\sum_j a_j(s)s^jt^j$. Vanishing forces every $a_j(s)s^j$ to be zero, hence every $a_j$ to be zero. Thus $F^*$ is injective.

### Justification

If $u\ne0$, the point $(u,v)$ is $F(u,v/u)$. If $u=0$, every image point has $v=0$. Hence $F(\mathbb A^2)=D(u)\cup\{(0,0)\}$, which contains the dense open $D(u)$ but misses every $(0,v)$ with $v\ne0$.

### Conclusion

$F$ is dominant because its pullback is injective, but it is not surjective. Dense image need not mean all points.

Every nonconstant monomial in this image has exponent in the semigroup generated by $2$ and $3$, namely $2,3,4,\ldots$; no image has a nonzero term of degree $1$, so $t$ is absent and the pullback is not surjective. Injectivity proves that $\nu$ is dominant, while nonsurjectivity proves that it is not an isomorphism. It is separately bijective on complex points: for a nonzero cusp point $t=y/x$, and the origin comes from $t=0$.
