content.markdown:
# A rational map may exist before it is defined everywhere

If $X$ is irreducible, its coordinate ring $\mathbb C[X]$ is a domain. Its fraction field

$$\mathbb C(X)=\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb C[X])$$

is the field of rational functions on $X$. A fraction in this field is regular wherever it has a representative whose denominator does not vanish.

A rational map records compatible regular formulas on dense open subsets. A morphism is stronger: it is regular at every point.

## Reactivate fractions in a domain

In a domain, $a/b=c/d$ in the fraction field exactly when $ad=bc$. The same rational function can therefore have several written expressions with different apparent denominators.

Regularity at a point is not decided by one expression alone. It asks whether some representative $g/h$ has $h$ nonzero at that point.

## Construct a rational function and its regular locus

Let $X$ be irreducible and affine. A rational function is an element of $\mathbb C(X)$. If $r=g/h$ with $g,h\in\mathbb C[X]$ and $h\ne0$, this representative defines a regular function on the dense principal open $D_X(h)$.

The rational function may be regular on a larger set if another representative removes part of the denominator. Its domain of regularity is the union of all opens on which it has a regular representative.

content.markdown:
## Define a rational map by dense-open representatives

For irreducible varieties $X$ and $Y$, a rational map $X\dashrightarrow Y$ is an equivalence class of morphisms $f:U\to Y$ defined on nonempty open subsets $U\subseteq X$.

Two representatives $f:U\to Y$ and $g:V\to Y$ are equivalent when they agree on a nonempty open subset of $U\cap V$. Because $X$ is irreducible, nonempty opens are dense and their intersections remain nonempty.

The largest open on which the class has a regular representative is its defined locus.

content.markdown:
## Find the rational inverse of the cusp parameterization

The dominant map $\nu:\mathbb A^1_t\to C$, $t\mapsto(t^2,t^3)$, has a rational inverse on the dense open $D_C(x)$:

$$\rho:C\dashrightarrow\mathbb A^1,\qquad \rho(x,y)=\frac yx.$$

Indeed, $\rho(\nu(t))=t^3/t^2=t$ when $t\ne0$, and a nonzero cusp point satisfies $\nu(y/x)=(x,y)$.

The inverse does not extend regularly across the origin. Such an extension would pull back to a global function $t$ in the subring $\mathbb C[t^2,t^3]$, but Day 3 proved that no such element exists.

The same formula gives a rational inverse on a dense open but fails to produce an isomorphism of affine varieties.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

On $X=\mathbb A^1_t$, compare $r=(t^3-t)/(t^2-1)$ and $q=1/(t^2-1)$.

Determine the rational functions and their full regularity loci.

### Strategy

Factor in the function field, search for polynomial representatives, and prove nonextension by clearing the remaining denominator.

### Hypotheses

$\mathbb C[t]$ is a unique factorization domain and the global regular functions on affine line are exactly its polynomials.

### Intermediate claims

$r=t(t^2-1)/(t^2-1)=t$, so it extends to all of $X$. The rational function $q$ is regular on $D(t^2-1)=X\setminus\{-1,1\}$.

### Justification

If $q$ were regular at $1$, it would have a local representative $p/h$ with $h(1)\ne0$. Equality in the fraction field would give $(t^2-1)p=h$, impossible after evaluating at $t=1$. The same argument at $-1$ rules out regularity there.

### Conclusion

The full regularity locus of $r$ is $X$, while that of $q$ is $X\setminus\{-1,1\}$. Cancellation changes the underlying rational function's domain only when it produces a regular representative.

content.markdown:
# Build one hierarchy instead of four disconnected definitions

A regular morphism has polynomial or localized coordinate formulas on its stated domain. A dominant morphism has dense image. A rational map needs only a compatible regular representative on a dense open. An isomorphism requires an everywhere-regular inverse.

These properties interact, but none can be substituted for another. Today's spaced reviews restore the underlying proofs before the final synthesis asks you to classify a new map.

## Keep the proof obligations in a fixed order

For a proposed affine map, verify landing and compute pullback. For dominance, test the pullback kernel. For a rational inverse, state the dense open on which its denominators are units. For a global inverse, prove that those formulas extend regularly everywhere and verify both compositions.

This order prevents a generic point calculation from being promoted silently to a global isomorphism.

## Deliberate review: Week 32 radicals on a principal open

Week 32 proved that an ideal and its radical have the same zero set. Retrieve that correction for a power of one coordinate, then connect it with localization.

The four reviews now meet in one calculation. The equations of $X$ define its coordinate ring, pullback carries their classes to any source, localization permits division by $a$ on $X_a$, and the identity $b-1=a(2bd-ae)$ proves that one such quotient extends globally.

## Complete worked model

Compare $p:\mathbb A^1_t\to\mathbb A^1_u$, $p(t)=t^2$, with $\nu:\mathbb A^1_t\to V(y^2-x^3)$, $\nu(t)=(t^2,t^3)$.

Prove that $p$ is dominant but not birational, while $\nu$ is birational but not an isomorphism.

### Strategy

Use coordinate-ring injections for dominance, function-field maps for birationality, and coordinate-ring surjectivity for isomorphism.

### Hypotheses

All varieties are irreducible over $\mathbb C$. Birationality requires an isomorphism of function fields, whereas an affine isomorphism requires an isomorphism of coordinate rings.

### Intermediate claims

For $p$, $\mathbb C[u]\hookrightarrow\mathbb C[t]$ sends $u$ to $t^2$, so $p$ is dominant. Its field image is $\mathbb C(t^2)$, a proper subfield of $\mathbb C(t)$ because the involution $t\mapsto-t$ fixes $t^2$ but not $t$.

### Justification

For $\nu$, Day 3's normal-form and parity proof identifies the coordinate ring with $\mathbb C[t^2,t^3]$, so the pullback is injective but not surjective. Its fraction field is nevertheless $\mathbb C(t)$ because $t=t^3/t^2$ in the fraction field. Thus $\nu$ has a rational inverse but no global regular inverse.

### Conclusion

Dominant does not imply birational, and birational does not imply isomorphic. Each stronger property requires a stronger algebra map.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The image $\varphi(x)=s^2$ is a unit with inverse $s^{-2}$. Therefore the localization universal property gives a unique homomorphism $\widetilde\varphi:A_x\to B$. It is $\widetilde\varphi(p/x^n)=\varphi(p)s^{-2n}$. If two fractions are equal, some power of $x$ kills their cross-difference; applying $\varphi$ and multiplying by the inverse power of $s^2$ proves that the displayed values agree. Uniqueness follows because an extension must send $x^{-1}$ to the unique inverse $s^{-2}$.

activities.title: Connect pullback, localization, and extension on $X$
activities.promptMarkdown:
$X=V(F,G)$ with $F=a^2e-abd+cb^2-1$ and $G=ad+bc-1$, and $j:X_a\hookrightarrow X$ is the open inclusion.

Describe $j^*$, prove that $(b-1)/a$ equals the restriction of $2bd-ae$, and state exactly which global conclusion follows.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: The inclusion has pullback $j^*:\mathbb C[X]\to\mathbb C[X]_a$, the canonical localization map. In $\mathbb C[X]$, $F=0$ gives $a^2e=1+abd-cb^2$, so $b-1-a(2bd-ae)=b-1-2abd+a^2e=b-abd-cb^2=b(1-ad-bc)=0$ by $G=0$. Hence $b-1=a(2bd-ae)$ globally. Since $a$ is a unit in $\mathbb C[X]_a$, $(b-1)/a=j^*(2bd-ae)$. Thus this rational-looking function extends globally on $X$; the argument does not construct three global coordinates or prove $X\cong\mathbb A^3$.

Prove that $\mu$ is dominant and birational but not an isomorphism, and write its rational inverse on a dense open.

Use the normal form $A(x)+yB(x)$ and parity to prove the substitution kernel is zero, justify the actual coordinate ring by the strong Nullstellensatz, prove nonsurjectivity, compute the function field using $t=y/x^2$, and state the inverse's domain.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Let $J=(y^2-x^5)$. Division by the monic polynomial in $y$ gives every class modulo $J$ a unique form $A(x)+yB(x)$. Substitution sends it to $A(t^2)+t^5B(t^2)$; the first summand has only even exponents and the second only odd exponents at least five. If their sum is zero, both vanish, so $A=B=0$ and the quotient map is injective. Therefore $J$ is prime and radical; over $\mathbb C$, the strong Nullstellensatz gives $I(C_5)=J$. The pullback thus identifies $\mathbb C[C_5]$ with $\mathbb C[t^2,t^5]$, proving dominance. The element $t$ is absent because degree one is not in the semigroup generated by $2$ and $5$, so the pullback is not surjective and $\mu$ is not an isomorphism. Its fraction-field image contains $t=t^5/(t^2)^2$ and is contained in $\mathbb C(t)$, so it equals $\mathbb C(t)$. Hence $\mu$ is birational, with rational inverse $(x,y)\mapsto y/x^2$ on $D_{C_5}(x)$.

activities.promptMarkdown:

Prove that $H$ is a dominant birational morphism but not an isomorphism, and determine its exact image and rational inverse domain.

rubric.description: independent-week33-map-synthesis. The response must complete this exact task: Compute and prove injectivity of $H^*$, solve the image equations, construct the rational inverse on $D(u)$, verify both compositions there, and prove that $(v-u)/u^2$ is not regular at the origin.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: $H$ is polynomial, with pullback $H^*(u)=s$ and $H^*(v)=s+s^2t$. Write $P(u,v)=\sum_j a_j(u)(v-u)^j$. Then $H^*(P)=\sum_j a_j(s)s^{2j}t^j$; comparison of powers of $t$ in the domain $\mathbb C[s,t]$ forces every $a_j=0$, so $H^*$ is injective and $H$ is dominant. If $u\ne0$, the unique preimage of $(u,v)$ is $(u,(v-u)/u^2)$. If $u=0$, every image point has $v=0$. Thus the image is $D(u)\cup\{(0,0)\}$ and is not all of $\mathbb A^2$. The formula $K(u,v)=(u,(v-u)/u^2)$ is regular on $D(u)$ and direct substitution gives $KH=\operatorname{id}$ on $D(s)$ and $HK=\operatorname{id}$ on $D(u)$, so $H$ is birational. If $(v-u)/u^2$ were regular at $(0,0)$, it would equal $p/q$ near that point with $q(0,0)\ne0$. Cross-multiplication would give $q(v-u)=pu^2$. Setting $u=0$ yields $q(0,v)v=0$ as a polynomial in $v$, hence $q(0,v)=0$ and in particular $q(0,0)=0$, a contradiction. Therefore the inverse is not regular at the origin and $H$ is not an isomorphism.

lessons.title: Read a tangent space from first-order terms
lessons.summary: Linearize a polynomial equation at a point, compute the resulting affine tangent line or plane, and explain why a vanishing linear term signals a singularity rather than a uniquely determined tangent line.
objectives: Linearize a polynomial equation at a point, compute the resulting affine tangent line or plane, and explain why a vanishing linear term signals a singularity rather than a uniquely determined tangent line.

content.markdown:
# Replace a nonlinear equation by the part visible at first order

An affine variety can curve, cross itself, or form a cusp. Near a chosen point, its first-order behavior is governed by the linear part of each defining equation after the point has been translated to the origin.

Today we define and compute the Zariski tangent space from the full vanishing ideal. On Day 3 we will deepen that definition by proving its equivalent intrinsic descriptions.

## Reactivate differentials and affine equations

For a polynomial $f$ and a point $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)$, Week 16 defined

$$df_p(u_1,\ldots,u_n)=\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}(p)u_j.$$

For an affine algebraic set $X\subseteq\mathbb A^n$, the Zariski tangent space is

$$T_pX=\{u\in\mathbb C^n:df_p(u)=0\text{ for every }f\in I(X)\}.$$

If the radical vanishing ideal is principal, $I(X)=(f)$, this becomes one kernel equation $df_p(u)=0$. We write tangent vectors with origin at zero; the corresponding affine tangent plane through $p$ consists of the points $p+u$.

## Differentiate after checking the base point

Let $X\subseteq\mathbb A^n$ have vanishing ideal $I(X)=(f)$ and let $p\in X$. The linearized equation is

$$df_p(u)=0.$$

The condition $f(p)=0$ must be checked first. Without it, the calculation concerns an ambient level set through a different value, not the tangent space to $X$ at $p$.

content.title: Compute a first tangent line
content.introMarkdown: Verify that $p\in C$, calculate $df_p$, and write both the vector equation and affine equation of the tangent line.

data.markdown:
Check first that the point satisfies the defining equation, then keep tangent-vector coordinates separate from ambient point coordinates.

The kernel equation is based at zero, whereas the affine tangent line must pass through the chosen point.

Repair the first substitution, derivative, or translation error. Next, linearize a surface equation in three variables.

content.markdown:
## The gradient is the coefficient row of the tangent equation

For one equation in three variables, the gradient $\nabla f(p)$ is a row vector. The tangent-vector space is its kernel:

$$T_pX=\ker\bigl(\nabla f(p):\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C\bigr).$$

A nonzero gradient gives one independent linear equation and therefore a two-dimensional tangent plane.

content.title: Linearize a quadric surface
content.introMarkdown: Compute the gradient row, the tangent-vector equation, and the affine tangent plane.

data.markdown:
Evaluate each partial derivative at the same base point before writing the kernel.

One unevaluated coordinate changes the linear map and can turn a tangent plane into a nonlinear expression.

Repair the first partial derivative or evaluation. Next, follow a complete model that derives a tangent plane from an exact first-order expansion.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$P=V(z-x^2-y^2)\subseteq\mathbb A^3$ at $p=(1,-1,2)$.

Derive the tangent plane by translating $p$ to the origin and isolating the terms of degree one.

### Strategy

Substitute $(x,y,z)=(1+u,-1+v,2+w)$, expand, and separate the linear part from terms of degree at least two.

### Hypotheses

The point lies on $P$ because $2-1^2-(-1)^2=0$. A tangent calculation retains the degree-one terms in the displacement variables.

### Intermediate claims

The translated equation is $w-2u+2v-u^2-v^2=0$. Its linear part is $-2u+2v+w$.

### Justification

The constant term cancels because $p\in P$. The quadratic terms vanish to second order, so the first-order condition is $-2u+2v+w=0$. This agrees with the gradient $(-2,2,1)$ at $p$.

### Conclusion

The tangent-vector space is the kernel of $(-2,2,1)$, and the affine tangent plane is $-2(X-1)+2(Y+1)+(Z-2)=0$.

content.title: Adapt the translated-expansion method
content.introMarkdown: Derive the tangent-vector equation both from a translated expansion and from the gradient.

data.markdown:
In the translated expansion, keep every term of total degree one and discard only products of two displacement variables.

The agreement between expansion and gradient is the reason the Jacobian records first-order geometry.

Repair the first missing linear term, then compare the resulting coefficient row with the four evaluated partial derivatives. Next, examine what happens when every linear term vanishes.

content.markdown:
## A zero gradient is information, not permission to choose a tangent

For the cusp $C=V(y^2-x^3)$ at the origin, every first partial derivative vanishes. The polynomial is square-free, so it generates the radical vanishing ideal. The first-order equation is therefore $0=0$, and the Zariski tangent space is all of $\mathbb A^2$.

The visible cusp may suggest the $x$-axis, but that line belongs to the tangent cone, which uses the first nonzero homogeneous part. The Zariski tangent space uses only degree one. Confusing these objects hides the singularity.

A different warning concerns nonradical presentations. The equations $x^2=0$ and $x=0$ have the same reduced zero set $X=\{0\}\subseteq\mathbb A^1$, but $d(x^2)_0=0$. The vanishing ideal is $I(X)=(x)$, so the correct tangent equation is $dx_0(u)=u=0$ and $T_0X=0$. Never replace $I(X)$ by arbitrary equations with the same zero set.

content.title: Contrast a smooth and singular point on the cusp
content.introMarkdown: Compute both tangent spaces and explain why the origin does not have a uniquely determined Zariski tangent line.

data.markdown:
If the origin was assigned a line, return to the linear part: both partial derivatives vanish there.

The excess tangent dimension is precisely the first-order warning that the cusp is singular.

Repair the first gradient or dimension claim and name the tangent cone only as a separate higher-order object. Next, solve an independent surface problem.

content.markdown:
## Independent tangent-plane calculation

A complete tangent calculation has four parts: membership of the point, evaluated differential, kernel description, and affine translation. Dimension follows from rank-nullity when the coefficient row is nonzero.

content.title: Determine a tangent plane independently
content.introMarkdown: Prove that the tangent-vector space has dimension two and write the affine tangent plane.

data.markdown:
Audit the argument in order: point membership, evaluated differential, kernel, basis, and translation.

Each step certifies a different claim; the plane equation alone does not establish the tangent-space dimension.

Repair the earliest failed step and restate the vector and affine forms separately. Day 2 replaces one gradient row by a Jacobian matrix for several equations.

content.markdown:
## Course reference

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-34, source lines 883 to 891.

**Resource version:** J. S. Milne Algebraic Geometry course notes, Course R registry snapshot 2026-07-28.

**Exact locator:** Chapter 4 §a, Definition 4.1 and Examples 4.2–4.6, pp. 81–83: tangent spaces to plane curves, smooth points, the cusp, and first-order equations in J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry, version 6.10.

**Reading purpose:** Compare the translated linear-part calculation with Milne's definition and smooth-versus-singular curve examples.
Day 2 stacks the differentials of several defining equations into one Jacobian matrix and computes its common kernel.
Day 1 is complete when you can move without ambiguity between a translated first-order expansion, a gradient kernel, and the affine tangent plane through the base point.

lessons.title: Use a Jacobian matrix for several equations
lessons.summary: Build the Jacobian matrix of a generated ideal, compute the common tangent kernel by row reduction, and use rank-nullity without confusing the number of written equations with their independent first-order constraints.
objectives: Build the Jacobian matrix of a generated ideal, compute the common tangent kernel by row reduction, and use rank-nullity without confusing the number of written equations with their independent first-order constraints.

content.markdown:
# Several equations impose simultaneous first-order constraints

If the vanishing ideal is generated by $I(X)=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$, a tangent vector must annihilate every differential $df_i|_p$. Writing those linear forms as rows produces the Jacobian matrix

$$J(p)=\left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}(p)\right),\qquad T_pX=\ker J(p).$$

The rank, not the number of displayed equations, counts the independent constraints.

## Reactivate kernels and rank-nullity

A matrix $A:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^r$ has $\dim\ker A=n-\operatorname{rank}A$. Row operations preserve the kernel equations. Today the rows come from polynomial differentials evaluated at one fixed point.

We will call this kernel $T_pX$ only when the displayed polynomials generate $I(X)$, or after a full-rank argument proves that they cut out the reduced variety $X$ locally. Arbitrary equations with the same zero set do not automatically compute the Zariski tangent space.

## Stack the differential rows

Each defining polynomial contributes one row. After evaluating at $p$, solve all rows simultaneously. A row that becomes zero imposes no first-order condition at that point.

content.title: Compute a two-row tangent kernel
content.introMarkdown: Compute $J(p)$, its rank, and a basis of $\ker J(p)$.

data.markdown:
Check that both rows are evaluated at $p$ before row reduction, then solve their common kernel rather than either row separately.

The tangent space to an intersection is governed by simultaneous constraints.

Repair the first row or kernel equation. Next, prove why replacing generators of the same ideal does not change the tangent space.

content.markdown:
## The generated ideal, not a favorite list of equations, owns the tangent space

Suppose $I(X)=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ and $g=\sum h_if_i$. At $p\in X$, the product rule gives

$$dg_p=\sum_i h_i(p)\,df_i|_p,$$

because every $f_i(p)$ is zero. Thus every differential from the ideal lies in the span of the generator rows. The common kernel is independent of the chosen generating set.

content.title: Verify a generator change at first order
content.introMarkdown: Show directly at $p=(1,-1,0)$ that $(f,g)$ and $(f,h)$ produce the same Jacobian row span and tangent kernel.

data.markdown:
Use $f(p)=0$ when differentiating $(x-y)f$; otherwise an extra term is incorrectly retained.

Generator independence is what makes the calculation a property of the variety rather than of its presentation.

Repair the product-rule evaluation and express the new row as an explicit linear combination of the old rows. Next, compare a Jacobian kernel with a parameter derivative.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$C=V(y-x^2,z-x^3)\subseteq\mathbb A^3$ at $p=(1,1,1)$, with parameterization $\gamma(t)=(t,t^2,t^3)$.

Compute the tangent kernel and prove that it is spanned by the derivative of the parameterization.

### Strategy

Differentiate the two defining equations, solve the kernel, and independently differentiate $\gamma$ at the parameter value that maps to $p$.

### Hypotheses

The point $p$ corresponds to $t=1$. The Jacobian rows are the differentials of $y-x^2$ and $z-x^3$.

### Intermediate claims

$J(p)=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1&0\\-3&0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so its kernel consists of $(u,2u,3u)$. Also $\gamma'(1)=(1,2,3)$.

### Justification

The two rows are independent, so the kernel is one-dimensional. Its nonzero vector $(1,2,3)$ is exactly the velocity obtained by differentiating the curve parameter.

### Conclusion

$T_pC=\mathbb C(1,2,3)=\mathbb C\gamma'(1)$; the equation-based and curve-based first-order descriptions agree.

data.markdown:
Use the parameter value $t=1$ and compare an entire one-dimensional subspace, not merely one coordinate.

The agreement connects the algebraic kernel computation with the geometric velocity of a curve.

Repair the first derivative or kernel relation, then state equality of the two spans. Next, see how rank distinguishes a smooth surface from a singular cone.

content.markdown:
## Excess kernel dimension detects loss of a first-order constraint

For a hypersurface in $\mathbb A^3$, a nonzero gradient has rank one and a two-dimensional kernel. If the gradient vanishes, the kernel jumps to dimension three.

The jump is local: the same equation may be smooth at most points and singular at a special point.

content.introMarkdown: Compute both tangent spaces and identify which equation loses its first-order constraint.

content.markdown:
# A tangent vector should belong to the variety, not to one chosen presentation

The Jacobian kernel is easy to calculate when its rows generate the vanishing ideal, but it begins with an embedding $X\subseteq\mathbb A^n$. An intrinsic tangent vector must survive a change of coordinates, generators, or affine embedding.

We obtain that invariant object by asking how a point can move through an infinitesimal parameter $\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon^2=0$.

## Reactivate quotient rings and first-order expansion

Let $A=\mathbb C[X]$ and let $p\in X$ correspond to the maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_p$. The dual-number ring is $\mathbb C[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$. Because every term containing $\varepsilon^2$ vanishes, substitution of $p+\varepsilon v$ records exactly first-order information.

## A dual-number point is a first-order motion

Let $R=\mathbb C[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$. A tangent vector at $p$ is a $\mathbb C$-algebra homomorphism $\alpha:A\to R$ whose reduction modulo $\varepsilon$ is evaluation at $p$. There is therefore a unique map $D:A\to\mathbb C$ such that

$$\alpha(f)=f(p)+\varepsilon D(f).$$

Comparing $\alpha(fg)$ with $\alpha(f)\alpha(g)$ proves that $\alpha$ is an algebra homomorphism exactly when $D$ is $\mathbb C$-linear and

$$D(fg)=f(p)D(g)+g(p)D(f).$$

Conversely, any $D$ with these properties defines an algebra homomorphism by the displayed formula. Thus dual-number points and pointwise derivations are mutually inverse descriptions.

In affine coordinates, $\alpha$ has the form $p+\varepsilon v$. For every $f\in I(X)$, Taylor expansion modulo $\varepsilon^2$ gives

$$f(p+\varepsilon v)=f(p)+\varepsilon\,df_p(v).$$

Since $f(p)=0$, this dual-number point lies on $X$ exactly when $df_p(v)=0$ for every defining equation.

content.markdown:
## Derivations are tangent vectors acting on functions

Let $\mathfrak m_p=\{f\in A:f(p)=0\}$. A pointwise derivation $D$ vanishes on $\mathfrak m_p^2$: if $a,b\in\mathfrak m_p$, then $D(ab)=a(p)D(b)+b(p)D(a)=0$. It therefore defines

$$\ell_D:\mathfrak m_p/\mathfrak m_p^2\to\mathbb C,\qquad \ell_D([g])=D(g).$$

Conversely, given a linear functional $\ell$ on $\mathfrak m_p/\mathfrak m_p^2$, define

$$D_\ell(f)=\ell\bigl([f-f(p)]\bigr).$$

The product $(f-f(p))(g-g(p))$ lies in $\mathfrak m_p^2$. Expanding it modulo $\mathfrak m_p^2$ proves the pointwise Leibniz rule for $D_\ell$. The two constructions are inverse because a derivation kills constants and $\mathfrak m_p^2$. Consequently

$$T_pX\cong\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb C}(A,\mathbb C)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(\mathfrak m_p/\mathfrak m_p^2,\mathbb C).$$

## Complete worked model

$C=V(y-x^3)$ at $p=(1,1)$ with $A=\mathbb C[x,y]/(y-x^3)$.

Identify the same tangent line as a Jacobian kernel, dual-number motion, derivation space, and dual cotangent space.

### Strategy

Compute one linear relation in each language and show that all four relations are $v=3u$.

### Hypotheses

The differential of $y-x^3$ at $p$ is $dy-3dx$. In $\mathfrak m_p/\mathfrak m_p^2$, the translated relation has the same linear part.

### Intermediate claims

The Jacobian row is $(-3,1)$. Substitution of $(1+\varepsilon u,1+\varepsilon v)$ gives $\varepsilon(v-3u)$. A derivation satisfies $D(y)=D(x^3)=3D(x)$. The cotangent relation is $d y=3d x$.

### Justification

Each description is determined by one free scalar $u=D(x)$. The corresponding values are $(u,v)=(u,3u)$, so every construction yields a one-dimensional space with basis $(1,3)$.

### Conclusion

The common tangent space is $\mathbb C(1,3)$, and the equivalence does not depend on treating the curve as a picture in the plane.

content.markdown:
## Differentials transport tangent vectors

A morphism $F:X\to Y$ induces a linear map $dF_p:T_pX\to T_{F(p)}Y$. For polynomial coordinates, its matrix is the ordinary Jacobian of the coordinate functions, restricted to the tangent kernel of $X$.

The chain rule gives $d(G\circ F)_p=dG_{F(p)}\circ dF_p$. If $F$ is an isomorphism, the differentials of $F$ and $F^{-1}$ are inverse linear maps.

The strongest way to verify an intrinsic tangent calculation is to compute the kernel and then exhibit an isomorphism whose differential identifies that kernel with a familiar vector space.

content.markdown:
# The capstone equations have no hidden singular point

Let $X\subseteq\mathbb A^5_{a,b,c,d,e}$ be defined by

$$F=a^2e-abd+cb^2-1,\qquad G=ad+bc-1.$$

The goal is global: prove by direct calculation that the two Jacobian rows are independent at every point of $X$. This establishes the smoothness input needed for the étale and covering arguments later in the course.

## Reactivate the full-rank criterion

Before rank is known, the two displayed rows define the common first-order kernel of $F$ and $G$. Once rank two is proved, the Jacobian criterion and complex implicit function theorem show that these equations cut out a reduced smooth complete intersection locally. The common kernel is then the Zariski tangent space and has dimension three.

The rank proof must use the equations defining $X$. Independence as symbolic rows in the polynomial ring is neither necessary nor sufficient at every evaluated point, and arbitrary equations for the same reduced zero set cannot replace generators of its vanishing ideal.

## Differentiate the first capstone equation carefully

Order the columns as $(a,b,c,d,e)$. Product-rule signs matter:

$$\nabla F=(2ae-bd,\ -ad+2bc,\ b^2,\ -ab,\ a^2).$$

A reliable check is to differentiate one term at a time and keep the constant $-1$ out of every partial derivative.

## Complete the matrix and test one point

The second equation has gradient

$$\nabla G=(d,c,b,a,0).$$

Thus

$$J_X=\begin{pmatrix}2ae-bd&-ad+2bc&b^2&-ab&a^2\\d&c&b&a&0\end{pmatrix}.$$

Evaluating at a point is essential: rank is a property of the numerical matrix $J_X(p)$.

## Complete worked model

$Y=V(xz-1,\ y+xw)\subseteq\mathbb A^4_{x,y,z,w}$.

Prove that the two Jacobian rows are independent at every point of $Y$.

### Strategy

Use the first equation to find a nonzero entry in the first row, then find a coordinate where the second row is nonzero and the first row is zero.

### Hypotheses

On $Y$, $xz=1$, so both $x$ and $z$ are nonzero. The Jacobian rows are $r_1=(z,0,x,0)$ and $r_2=(w,1,0,x)$.

### Intermediate claims

The row $r_1$ is nonzero because $x,z\ne0$. The $y$-entry of $r_1$ is zero, while the $y$-entry of $r_2$ is one.

### Justification

If $r_2=\lambda r_1$, comparison of the $y$-entries would give $1=0$. Therefore the rows are never proportional. Since the first row is nonzero, the rank is two everywhere.

### Conclusion

Every tangent kernel has dimension $4-2=2$, and the full-rank complete-intersection criterion makes $Y$ smooth.

content.markdown:
## The capstone rank proof

Let $r_F$ and $r_G$ be the two rows of $J_X(p)$. The relation $G=0$ implies $(a,b,c,d)\ne(0,0,0,0)$, so $r_G=(d,c,b,a,0)$ is nonzero.

Assume for contradiction that $r_F=\lambda r_G$. The last coordinate gives $a^2=0$, hence $a=0$. Now $G=0$ becomes $bc=1$, while $F=0$ becomes $cb^2=1$. Dividing the latter by the former gives $b=1$, and then $c=1$.

At $a=0,b=c=1$, the rows are $r_F=(-d,2,1,0,0)$ and $r_G=(d,1,1,0,0)$. Their $c$-entries force $\lambda=1$, but their $b$-entries would then require $2=1$. This contradiction proves rank two everywhere.

Each deduction removes a possible dependent-row case; skipping one leaves an unproved exceptional locus.

content.markdown:
## What the implicit function theorem adds—and what it does not

At each $p\in X$, some $2\times2$ minor of $J_X(p)$ is nonzero. The complex implicit function theorem solves locally for the corresponding two coordinates as analytic functions of the remaining three. Thus $X$ is locally a complex analytic manifold of dimension three, and its analytic tangent space is the same kernel $\ker J_X(p)$.

The algebraic calculation is global and presentation-aware: it proves the rank condition at every algebraic point. The implicit function theorem is local in the classical topology. It does not identify $X$ globally with $\mathbb A^3$, nor does it replace the later algebraic dimension theory.

content.markdown:
# One kernel connects algebraic equations with local geometry

This week began with linear terms and ended with a global rank proof. Friday now reconnects that kernel with four earlier structures: pullback along a morphism, affine zero sets, homogeneous projective equations, and holomorphic local solvability.

The reviews are deliberate and source-labelled. Each uses an earlier idea in a new tangent-space role before the final independent synthesis.

## Retrieval order

The four review checkpoints return to Weeks 33, 31, 26, and 18 at intervals of one, three, eight, and sixteen weeks. After those reviews, the final three checkpoints move from the capstone tangent kernel through a complete model to an independent proof.

## Deliberate review: differentiate a pullback

Week 33 reversed a morphism to obtain its pullback on functions. First-order information obeys the same typing: for $F:X\to Y$ and $h\in\mathbb C[Y]$, $d(h\circ F)_p=dh_{F(p)}\circ dF_p$.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$Y=V(x+y+z,\ xy-1)\subseteq\mathbb A^3$.

Prove smoothness everywhere, compute a tangent line at one point, and state the local complex analytic conclusion.

### Strategy

Use $xy=1$ to rule out a zero or dependent Jacobian row, then specialize to a point and solve the kernel.

### Hypotheses

The rows are $r_1=(1,1,1)$ and $r_2=(y,x,0)$. On $Y$, $x$ and $y$ are nonzero.

### Intermediate claims

If $r_2=\lambda r_1$, the third coordinate gives $\lambda=0$, which would force $x=y=0$, contradicting $xy=1$. Thus rank two holds everywhere. At $p=(1,1,-2)$, the kernel equations are $u+v+w=0$ and $u+v=0$, hence $w=0$ and the kernel is $\mathbb C(1,-1,0)$.

### Justification

Rank two in three variables leaves a one-dimensional tangent kernel. A nonzero $2\times2$ minor at each point lets the complex implicit function theorem solve locally for two coordinates as holomorphic functions of the third.

### Conclusion

$Y$ is a smooth affine curve, locally a complex analytic one-manifold, with tangent line $\mathbb C(1,-1,0)$ at the displayed point.

objectives: Define Krull dimension and codimension, compute them from an explicit quotient presentation, and explain why two independent equations in affine five-space are expected to define a threefold.

content.markdown:
# Dimension counts surviving parameters, not written equations

The slogan “two equations in five variables leave three dimensions” is useful only after independence has been justified. This week replaces that slogan with three compatible tools: prime chains or transcendence degree, quotient-ring computations, and regular sequences.

Today begins with quotient rings whose surviving parameters are visible. Later days explain what can go wrong and how the Jacobian criterion recovers the expected local dimension.

## Reactivate quotient rings and affine coordinates

If $A=\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I$, an explicit isomorphism $A\cong\mathbb C[t_1,\ldots,t_d]$ proves that the quotient has $d$ algebraically independent parameters. Recall also that an inclusion of ideals reverses the inclusion of their zero sets.

Vector-space dimension and Krull dimension are different notions. A polynomial ring is infinite-dimensional as a vector space, while its Krull dimension records the maximum length of a strict chain of prime ideals.

## Krull dimension records prime chains

For a commutative ring $A$, its Krull dimension is

$$\dim A=\sup\{r:\mathfrak p_0\subsetneq\mathfrak p_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak p_r\text{ are prime ideals of }A\}.$$

For an irreducible affine variety $X$ over $\mathbb C$, this equals the transcendence degree of the fraction field of $\mathbb C[X]$. Thus $\mathbb A^d$ has dimension $d$: the chain $(0)\subsetneq(t_1)\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq(t_1,\ldots,t_d)$ has length $d$, and no longer chain exists.

For a reducible affine algebraic set, its dimension is the maximum dimension of its irreducible components.

Naming two apparent free variables is evidence, but the two-sided quotient-ring isomorphism is what proves that no hidden relation remains.

content.markdown:
## Codimension measures the dimension lost

If $X\subseteq\mathbb A^n$ is equidimensional, its codimension is $n-\dim X$. A closed set of dimension $3$ inside $\mathbb A^5$ has codimension $2$.

Independent linear equations make the expected count exact. If $\ell_1,\ell_2$ are linearly independent, extend them to a basis of the five-dimensional space of linear forms. The resulting linear change of coordinates identifies

$$\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_5]/(\ell_1,\ell_2)\cong\mathbb C[t_1,t_2,t_3].$$

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Let $B=\mathbb C[x,y,z]/(x-y^2,z-y^3)$.

Prove that $B$ has dimension $1$ and that its affine zero set has codimension $2$ in $\mathbb A^3$.

### Strategy

Treat the equations as graph equations. Eliminate $x$ and $z$, then prove that the surviving coordinate $y$ satisfies no further relation.

### Hypotheses

Work over $\mathbb C$. The quotient is taken by the ideal generated by the two displayed polynomials.

### Intermediate claims

Define $\phi:\mathbb C[t]\to B$ by $t\mapsto[y]$. Define $\psi:B\to\mathbb C[t]$ by $[x]\mapsto t^2$, $[y]\mapsto t$, and $[z]\mapsto t^3$. Both defining relations lie in the kernel of the ambient substitution, so $\psi$ is well defined.

### Justification

The composite $\psi\phi$ fixes $t$. The other composite fixes $[y]$ and sends $[x]$ and $[z]$ to $[y]^2=[x]$ and $[y]^3=[z]$. Hence $B\cong\mathbb C[t]$.

### Conclusion

The quotient has Krull dimension $1$. Its zero set is therefore a curve of codimension $3-1=2$, even though the equations are nonlinear.

content.markdown:
# A Gröbner basis makes hidden parameters computable

A quotient is easy to understand when its relations solve directly for variables. A Gröbner basis extends that idea: its leading terms identify standard monomials, and their asymptotic growth determines dimension.

Two related arguments appear today. A direct quotient isomorphism works with any suitable elimination order. The general leading-ideal dimension theorem uses a graded order; the page keeps those hypotheses separate.

## Learn the Gröbner operations before using them

A monomial order is a well-order on monomials that is compatible with multiplication. Once an order is fixed, the leading term $\operatorname{LT}(f)$ is the coefficient and greatest monomial of a nonzero polynomial $f$. A reduction step cancels a term divisible by $\operatorname{LT}(g)$ by subtracting the appropriate monomial multiple of $g$.

For nonzero polynomials $f$ and $g$, their $S$-polynomial cancels their leading terms:

$$S(f,g)=\frac{\operatorname{lcm}(\operatorname{LM}(f),\operatorname{LM}(g))}{\operatorname{LT}(f)}f-\frac{\operatorname{lcm}(\operatorname{LM}(f),\operatorname{LM}(g))}{\operatorname{LT}(g)}g.$$

Buchberger's criterion says that a finite generating set $G$ is a Gröbner basis exactly when every $S$-polynomial of a pair in $G$ reduces to zero by $G$. For a Gröbner basis, the leading terms generate $\langle\operatorname{LT}(I)\rangle$, and monomials outside that leading ideal form a $\mathbb C$-basis of the quotient.

For a graded order over an algebraically closed field, the degree of the affine Hilbert polynomial of the quotient equals the dimension of the variety. With a non-graded elimination order, use the resulting quotient isomorphism directly unless the needed Hilbert-function hypothesis has been proved separately.

## Read free coordinates from an elimination basis

Suppose $G=\{u-v^2,w-v^3\}\subset\mathbb C[u,v,w]$ and use lexicographic order $u>w>v$. The leading terms are $u$ and $w$. Their $S$-polynomial reduces to zero, so $G$ is a Gröbner basis.

Here the least common multiple is $uw$, and the complete reduction is

$$S(u-v^2,w-v^3)=w(u-v^2)-u(w-v^3)=uv^3-wv^2\longrightarrow v^5-wv^2\longrightarrow v^5-v^5=0.$$

The first arrow replaces $u$ by $v^2$ using $u-v^2$; the second replaces $w$ by $v^3$ using $w-v^3$. Buchberger's criterion now applies because this is the only pair.

Every polynomial has a unique remainder in $\mathbb C[v]$. Equivalently, the quotient maps $u$ to $v^2$ and $w$ to $v^3$, giving an isomorphism with $\mathbb C[v]$ and dimension $1$.

## Complete worked model

Let $I=(y-x^2,z-xy)\subset\mathbb C[x,y,z]$ with lexicographic order $z>y>x$.

Prove that the quotient has dimension $1$ and the affine zero set has codimension $2$.

### Strategy

The second relation depends on the first rather than directly on the free coordinate. Verify the Gröbner basis, reduce the chain to powers of $x$, and then construct the quotient isomorphism.

### Hypotheses

The leading terms are $y$ and $z$, so their least common multiple is $yz$.

### Intermediate claims

The decisive calculation is $S(y-x^2,z-xy)=z(y-x^2)-y(z-xy)=xy^2-x^2z$. Reducing $z$ to $xy$ gives $xy^2-x^3y$, and reducing $y$ to $x^2$ gives $x^5-x^5=0$. Hence the pair is a Gröbner basis and its standard monomials are $1,x,x^2,\ldots$.

### Justification

Define $\mathbb C[t]\to R/I$ by $t\mapsto[x]$ and define the inverse by $[x]\mapsto t$, $[y]\mapsto t^2$, and $[z]\mapsto t^3$. Both defining relations vanish under the substitution, and both composites fix all generators. Thus $R/I\cong\mathbb C[t]$.

### Conclusion

The chained relation $z=xy$ becomes $z=x^3$ only after $y=x^2$ is imposed. The quotient nevertheless has Krull dimension $1$, and its zero set has codimension $2$ in $\mathbb A^3$.

content.markdown:
## A graded leading ideal preserves dimension

Let $I\subseteq R=\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and use a graded monomial order. The affine Hilbert function counts the dimension of the classes represented by polynomials of degree at most $s$.

For all large $s$ it agrees with a polynomial. The degree of that polynomial is $\dim R/I$, and the same function is obtained from the graded leading ideal. Therefore

$$\dim V(I)=\dim V(\langle\operatorname{LT}(I)\rangle).$$

For the monomial ideal $(x,y)\subset\mathbb C[x,y,z,w]$, the surviving monomials are $z^iw^j$. Those of total degree at most $s$ number $\binom{s+2}{2}$, a polynomial of degree $2$.

The degree of the affine Hilbert polynomial, rather than its value at one degree, is the dimension invariant.

content.markdown:
## A generating set can hide a new leading relation

Consider $I=(x^2+y,x^2-y)\subset\mathbb C[x,y]$ with lexicographic order $x>y$. The two written leading terms are both $x^2$, but subtracting the generators gives $2y\in I$.

Over $\mathbb C$, this adds the leading relation $y$. A Gröbner basis is $\{x^2,y\}$, whose standard monomials are $1,x$. The quotient is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb C$ and therefore has Krull dimension $0$.

A defensible Gröbner-basis dimension calculation records five links: the monomial order, the Gröbner check, the leading ideal, the standard monomials or their growth, and the final dimension statement.

When a direct quotient isomorphism is also visible, give it. Agreement between the computational and structural arguments is a useful error check.

content.markdown:
# Independence is tested after imposing the earlier equations

Linear independence is not the right condition for nonlinear equations. A regular sequence asks instead whether each new equation remains a non-zero-divisor after all previous equations have been imposed.

This test explains why some dependent-looking or reducible examples still have the expected codimension, while other two-equation lists collapse to one condition.

## Reactivate zero divisors and quotient rings

An element $f\in A$ is a non-zero-divisor when $fg=0$ implies $g=0$. In an integral domain every nonzero element is a non-zero-divisor. After quotienting, new zero divisors may appear.

A sequence $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ in a ring $R$ is regular when $(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\ne R$ and, for each $i$, the class of $f_i$ is a non-zero-divisor in $R/(f_1,\ldots,f_{i-1})$. The order is part of the test.

## Test one equation at a time

In $R=\mathbb C[x,y,z]$, the sequence $x,y$ is regular. The first element $x$ is nonzero in the domain $R$. After quotienting by $x$, the ring becomes $\mathbb C[y,z]$, where the class of $y$ is again a non-zero-divisor.

The quotient $R/(x,y)\cong\mathbb C[z]$ has dimension $1$, so the two equations cut codimension $2$. In a polynomial ring, a regular sequence of length $r$ produces the expected codimension $r$.

## A second equation can become a zero divisor

The sequence $x^2,xy$ in $\mathbb C[x,y,z]$ is not regular. The first element is a non-zero-divisor, but in $R/(x^2)$ the nonzero class of $x$ annihilates the class of $xy$:

$$[x]\,[xy]=[x^2y]=0.$$

Moreover $\sqrt{(x^2,xy)}=(x)$, so the underlying zero set is the plane $V(x)$ of dimension $2$ and codimension $1$. The second equation does not produce the expected second dimension drop.

## Complete worked model

Let $R=\mathbb C[u,v,w]$ and $I=(u,vw)$.

Prove that $u,vw$ is a regular sequence and that $V(I)$ is a codimension-two complete intersection, although it is reducible and singular at the origin.

### Strategy

Test regularity in successive quotient rings, then identify the irreducible components of the zero set and compute their dimensions.

### Hypotheses

The ambient polynomial ring is a domain. After imposing $u=0$, the quotient $\mathbb C[v,w]$ remains a domain.

### Intermediate claims

The nonzero element $u$ is a non-zero-divisor. The class of $vw$ is nonzero in $R/(u)\cong\mathbb C[v,w]$ and is therefore a non-zero-divisor. Also

### Justification

$$V(u,vw)=V(u,v)\cup V(u,w).$$ Each component is an affine line. Hence the union has dimension $1$ and codimension $2$ in $\mathbb A^3$.

### Conclusion

The two equations form a regular sequence and define a complete intersection. Reducibility and singularity do not contradict the complete-intersection property.

## Complete intersection does not mean smooth

Return to $V(u,vw)$. Its Jacobian matrix is

$$\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&w&v\end{pmatrix}.$$

Away from the origin on either line, the rank is $2$. At the origin it is $1$, so the Zariski tangent space has dimension $2$ while the variety has dimension $1$.

Thus a regular sequence gives the expected codimension, but the Jacobian must still be checked to decide smoothness.

content.markdown:
# “Two equations” can fail in more than one way

A pair may generate only one condition, define components of different dimensions, preserve a nilpotent thickening, or cut the expected codimension but remain singular.

These outcomes require different remedies. Today builds a diagnostic table from exact quotient, radical, regular-sequence, and Jacobian calculations.

## Reactivate radicals, components, and tangent rank

The radical $\sqrt I$ determines the underlying reduced zero set. Nilpotent classes in $R/I$ record nonreduced structure that the set $V(I)$ cannot see.

For a finite union of irreducible components, dimension is the maximum component dimension. At a point where ideal generators compute the Zariski tangent space, the Jacobian rank gives the tangent dimension.

## Dependence can be literal ideal redundancy

For $I=(x,2x)\subset\mathbb C[x,y,z,w]$, one has $I=(x)$. The quotient is $\mathbb C[y,z,w]$, so the zero set has dimension $3$ and codimension $1$.

The Jacobian rows $(1,0,0,0)$ and $(2,0,0,0)$ have rank $1$, recording the same failure at first order.

content.introMarkdown: Prove that $Y$ has dimension $4$ and show that its two Jacobian rows have rank one.

Ideal redundancy and rank dependence are compatible diagnoses, but neither is obtained merely by counting two rows.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Compare $I=(x,y)$ and $J=(x,xy)$ in $R=\mathbb C[x,y,z,w]$.

Compute dimensions, codimensions, and regular-sequence status for both pairs.

### Strategy

Simplify each ideal first. Then identify its quotient and finally test the second element in the quotient by the first.

### Hypotheses

The ambient ring is a four-variable polynomial domain.

### Intermediate claims

For $I$, the quotient is $\mathbb C[z,w]$, so the dimension is $2$ and the codimension is $2$; $x,y$ is regular. For $J$, the ideal equals $(x)$ because $xy\in(x)$.

### Justification

The quotient by $J$ is $\mathbb C[y,z,w]$, of dimension $3$ and codimension $1$. Modulo $x$, the second element $xy$ becomes zero, so the written sequence is not regular.

### Conclusion

The independent pair cuts codimension two. The absorbed second generator changes neither the ideal nor the dimension.

content.markdown:
## A common factor can create a high-dimensional component

Let $K=(xy,xz)=x(y,z)$ in $\mathbb C[x,y,z]$. A point annihilates both generators exactly when $x=0$, or when $y=z=0$. Therefore

$$V(K)=V(x)\cup V(y,z).$$

The plane has dimension $2$ and the line has dimension $1$, so the union has dimension $2$ and codimension $1$. The two equations have not produced pure codimension two.

A lower-dimensional component does not lower the dimension of a reducible union.

Repair the first missed component or dimension rule. Next, separate the reduced zero set from nilpotent quotient structure.

content.markdown:
## The radical forgets nilpotent thickness

For $L=(x^2,xy)\subset\mathbb C[x,y,z]$, the radical is $(x)$, so the underlying reduced zero set is the plane $V(x)$ of dimension $2$.

The quotient is not reduced: the class $[x]$ is nonzero but satisfies $[x]^2=0$. This scheme-theoretic information does not create a second geometric dimension drop.

data.markdown:
Check both radical inclusions and justify that the proposed nilpotent class is not already zero.

The underlying set and the quotient algebra carry different information; dimension alone does not detect reducedness.

Repair the first radical or nonzero-class claim. Next, synthesize dependence, regularity, and smoothness in one comparison.

content.markdown:
## Use the smallest correct diagnosis

For a pair of equations, ask in order: what ideal do they generate, what is its radical and component decomposition, what is the quotient dimension, is the sequence regular, and what does the Jacobian say at the chosen point?

No single one of these questions replaces all the others. Together they distinguish redundant equations from singular but valid complete intersections.

content.markdown:
# The capstone count now has a proof

The variety

$$X=V\!\left(a^2e-abd+cb^2-1,\ ad+bc-1\right)\subset\mathbb A^5$$

is presented by two equations. Week 34 proved that their Jacobian has rank $2$ at every point of $X$. This week can now turn that rank statement into the exact conclusion: every point has a three-dimensional smooth neighborhood, so $X$ is a smooth threefold.

## Retrieve before opening the proof

Close the earlier pages. For each scheduled item below, write the claim, its decisive justification, and one condition whose failure would invalidate it.

The review intervals are exact: Week 34 is one week back, Week 32 is three weeks back, Week 27 is eight weeks back, and Week 19 is sixteen weeks back.

## Deliberate review: one-week tangent-space transfer

For $Y=V(x,yz)\subset\mathbb A^3$, retrieve the Jacobian calculation at the origin and compare the one-dimensional variety with its two-dimensional tangent space.

The capstone argument will use full rank to make these dimensions agree; the singular boundary shows why that hypothesis matters.

## Deliberate review: three-week coordinate-ring reconstruction

For the graph curve $C=V(u-v^2,w-v^3)$, retrieve the two inverse coordinate-ring maps and the associated affine parametrization.

content.markdown:
## Full Jacobian rank gives the local threefold

Set

$$f_1=a^2e-abd+cb^2-1,\qquad f_2=ad+bc-1.$$

Week 34 proved that the two rows of $J(f_1,f_2)$ are independent at every point of $X=V(f_1,f_2)$. Therefore the Jacobian has rank $2$ everywhere.

The algebraic Jacobian criterion says that the two local equations form a regular sequence and that every point is smooth of dimension $5-2=3$. The complex implicit function theorem gives the matching analytic statement: near each point, two suitable coordinates can be solved as holomorphic functions of the remaining three.

The exact scope separates the proved smooth-threefold statement from the later global-coordinate theorem.

Repair the first incorrect dimension subtraction or global overclaim. Next, inspect a complete model that promotes the pointwise statement to all of $X$.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Let $X=V(f_1,f_2)\subset\mathbb A^5$ with $f_1,f_2$ as above, and assume the verified global rank-two calculation.

Prove that $X$ is a nonempty smooth affine threefold and state exactly what remains unproved.

### Strategy

First exhibit a point. Then apply the same local dimension theorem at an arbitrary point. Finally quantify over all points and retain the local scope.

### Hypotheses

At $(a,b,c,d,e)=(0,1,1,0,0)$, both equations vanish. At every point of $X$, the Jacobian has rank $2$.

### Intermediate claims

For arbitrary $p\in X$, the tangent kernel has dimension $3$. Full row rank makes the two equations a regular system of local parameters transverse to $X$, so the local ring has dimension $3$ and is regular.

### Justification

The algebraic Jacobian criterion proves smoothness and local dimension $3$ at $p$. Since $p$ was arbitrary and $X$ is nonempty, every irreducible component is smooth of dimension $3$.

### Conclusion

$X$ is a smooth affine threefold. This argument does not yet construct a global polynomial isomorphism $X\cong\mathbb A^3$; that stronger theorem requires the later explicit chart and inverse.

content.markdown:
## Close the week at the exact theorem boundary

The week has established three complementary claims. Quotient and Gröbner computations expose surviving parameters. Regular sequences certify expected codimension in explicit examples. Full Jacobian rank upgrades the capstone presentation to a smooth local complete intersection.

The conclusion available now is $\dim X=3$ and smoothness everywhere. A global isomorphism $X\cong\mathbb A^3$ is not inferred from local dimension; it will require explicit polynomial inverse maps later in the course.

lessons.title: Write a fiber from the equations of a map
lessons.summary: Define the fiber of a morphism over a point, translate the definition into explicit polynomial equations, and prove its point-pullback universal property.
objectives: Define the fiber of a morphism over a point, translate the definition into explicit polynomial equations, and prove its point-pullback universal property.

content.markdown:
# A fiber is the part of the source above one target point

A morphism groups source points according to their image. Fixing one target point and solving for every source point that maps to it produces a fiber.

This week begins with equations, not scheme terminology. The same construction will then be recognized as a fiber product and applied to the normalized factorization space.

## Reactivate inverse images and polynomial maps

For a map $f:X\to Y$ and $y\in Y$, the set-theoretic inverse image is $f^{-1}(y)=\{x\in X:f(x)=y\}$. When $f$ has polynomial coordinate functions, equality with $y$ becomes a list of polynomial equations.

Week 33 established that a polynomial map between affine varieties is a morphism. Today uses that concrete map language throughout.

## Define the fiber and derive its equations

Let $X\subseteq\mathbb A^n$, $Y\subseteq\mathbb A^m$, and let $f=(f_1,\ldots,f_m):X\to Y$ be a morphism. For $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\in Y$, the fiber over $y$ is

$$X_y=f^{-1}(y)=\{x\in X:f_i(x)-y_i=0\text{ for }1\le i\le m\}.$$

Thus the fiber inherits every equation of $X$ and gains the coordinate equations $f_i-y_i=0$. These equations are not optional notation: they are the concrete test for membership in the fiber.

content.markdown:
## One target point can impose several equations

Consider $f:\mathbb A^2\to\mathbb A^2$ given by $f(x,y)=(x+y,xy)$. The fiber over $(s,p)$ is

$$f^{-1}(s,p)=V(x+y-s,\ xy-p).$$

The two equations say that $x$ and $y$ are the roots, in either order, of $T^2-sT+p$. The fiber can therefore have two points, one point, or no points over a non-algebraically closed ground field.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Let $f:X\to Y$, let $y\in Y$, and let $i_y:\{y\}\hookrightarrow Y$ be the inclusion.

Prove that $X_y$ with its two projections is the pullback $X\times_Y\{y\}$.

### Strategy

Translate compatibility into the statement that a map lands in the fiber, then prove existence and uniqueness of the factorization.

### Hypotheses

The square uses the inclusion $j:X_y\hookrightarrow X$ and the unique map $q:X_y\to\{y\}$. By definition, $f\circ j=i_y\circ q$.

### Intermediate claims

Suppose maps $a:Z\to X$ and $b:Z\to\{y\}$ satisfy $f\circ a=i_y\circ b$. Since $b$ is the constant map to $y$, every $a(z)$ satisfies $f(a(z))=y$ and therefore lies in $X_y$.

### Justification

Define $u:Z\to X_y$ by $u(z)=a(z)$. Then $j\circ u=a$ and $q\circ u=b$. Any second factorization has the same composite with the inclusion $j$, so it has the same value $a(z)$ at every point.

### Conclusion

There is exactly one compatible map $Z\to X_y$. This existence-and-uniqueness statement is the universal property of the point fiber.

content.markdown:
## Distinguish empty, finite, and positive-dimensional fibers

The equations determine the size and shape of a fiber; the source and target dimensions alone do not settle every special case.

For $h:\mathbb A^2\to\mathbb A^1$, $h(x,y)=xy$, the fiber over $1$ is the hyperbola $xy=1$, while the fiber over $0$ is the union of the two coordinate axes. Both are one-dimensional, but their geometry differs.

content.markdown:
## Reconstruct the fiber definition independently

A complete fiber computation has four parts: state the target point, retain the source equations, add one equation for each target coordinate, and solve or analyze the resulting algebraic set.

The pullback description adds a fifth part when required: every compatible pair of maps must factor uniquely through that set.

Write the three equations, solve them in order, then quantify over an arbitrary compatible pair of maps. Next, generalize from a point to two maps with a common target.

content.markdown:
## Category boundary: this week uses reduced classical variety fibers

Days 1–3 construct fiber products in the category of classical algebraic varieties. In this category, a closed subvariety carries the reduced structure: equations with the same zero set define the same reduced variety. Scheme-theoretic fiber products can retain nilpotent information, but that language is an optional forward bridge and is not assessed this week.

The exit example above makes the distinction visible. After eliminating $y$ and $z$, the fiber over $(2,1)$ has equation $(x-1)^2=0$. As a classical variety it is the single reduced point with coordinate ring $\mathbb C$. The corresponding scheme fiber would have coordinate ring $\mathbb C[x]/((x-1)^2)$, where the class of $x-1$ is a nonzero nilpotent.

Day 4 contains the same boundary in a family: the classical special fiber written $V(z^2)$ is the reduced line $V(z)$ with coordinate ring $\mathbb C[x]$, whereas the scheme fiber is $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[x,z]/(z^2)$. Keep these two categories distinct whenever multiplicity matters.

**Syllabus source:** course-r.week-36, source lines 900 to 908.

**Reading purpose:** Match the set of solutions to the point-base-change square, keeping the concrete equations visible.
Day 2 replaces the point inclusion by an arbitrary second map and constructs the resulting fiber product explicitly.
Day 1 is complete when you can derive a fiber's equations, solve representative examples, recognize special-fiber changes, and prove the point-pullback property.

content.markdown:
# Compatibility cuts an ordinary product down to a fiber product

Suppose $f:X\to S$ and $g:Y\to S$. An arbitrary pair $(x,y)\in X\times Y$ need not have matching images in $S$. The fiber product keeps exactly the pairs for which $f(x)=g(y)$.

This definition turns a commuting square into equations and gives a precise test for every proposed construction.

## Start from the ordinary Cartesian product

The ordinary product $X\times Y$ carries projections to $X$ and $Y$. A fiber product is a subvariety of that product, selected by an equality in a shared target.

Day 1 treated the special case $Y=\{s\}$. Today allows both legs to vary.

## Define compatible pairs and the Cartesian square

For morphisms $f:X\to S$ and $g:Y\to S$, define

$$X\times_S Y=\{(x,y)\in X\times Y:f(x)=g(y)\}.$$

The restricted projections $p_X$ and $p_Y$ satisfy $f\circ p_X=g\circ p_Y$. The square is called Cartesian when this object has the universal property proved below.

content.markdown:
## Derive equations coordinate by coordinate

If $S\subseteq\mathbb A^r$ and $f=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$, $g=(g_1,\ldots,g_r)$, then $X\times_S Y$ is cut out inside $X\times Y$ by

$$f_1(x)-g_1(y)=\cdots=f_r(x)-g_r(y)=0.$$

The equations of $X$ and $Y$ remain present. Compatibility adds equations; it does not replace the source conditions.

## Complete worked model

$P=V(u^2-v^3)$ is the fiber product of $u\mapsto u^2$ and $v\mapsto v^3$ over $\mathbb A^1$.

Given compatible maps $\alpha:Z\to\mathbb A^1_u$ and $\beta:Z\to\mathbb A^1_v$, construct the unique map $Z\to P$.

### Strategy

Pair the two component maps, use compatibility to prove the pair lands in $P$, and use the projections to prove uniqueness.

### Hypotheses

Compatibility means $\alpha(z)^2=\beta(z)^3$ for every $z\in Z$.

### Intermediate claims

The formula $h(z)=(\alpha(z),\beta(z))$ defines a morphism to $\mathbb A^2$. The compatibility equation makes $u^2-v^3$ vanish on its image, so $h$ lands in $P$.

### Justification

The coordinate projections satisfy $p_u h=\alpha$ and $p_v h=\beta$. If $k$ has the same two composites, then both coordinates of $k(z)$ equal those of $h(z)$ for every $z$.

### Conclusion

The mediating map exists and is unique. Therefore the displayed commuting square is Cartesian.

content.markdown:
## Know when the fiber product is an ordinary product

If the common target is a one-point variety, every pair is automatically compatible, so $X\times_{\{*\}}Y=X\times Y$.

For a nontrivial target, the ordinary product is usually too large. The equality $f(x)=g(y)$ must be automatic before the two products coincide.

content.markdown:
## Construct and prove, not merely name

A complete explicit fiber-product argument proceeds in four stages: choose coordinates on the ordinary product, write every compatibility equation, specify the two projections, and prove unique factorization for arbitrary compatible maps.

content.markdown:
# The two capstone equations are compatibility equations

Write a binary linear form $L=aT+bS$ and a binary quadratic form $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$. Their product is a binary cubic. The normalized factorization space fixes one cubic coefficient and the resultant.

A fiber product expresses those two conditions as one equality of maps, revealing why the construction is stable under later base change.

## Reactivate the multiplication and resultant formulas

Direct multiplication gives

$$LQ=acT^3+(ad+bc)T^2S+(ae+bd)TS^2+beS^3.$$

For this linear–quadratic pair, the chosen resultant convention is $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=a^2e-abd+b^2c$. Week 30 established the formula; Week 34 differentiated the same two normalized equations.

## Name every space and map

Let $V_1\cong\mathbb A^2$ be the space of binary linear forms, $V_2\cong\mathbb A^3$ the space of binary quadratics, and $V_3\cong\mathbb A^4$ the space of binary cubics.

Define

$$\Phi:V_1\times V_2\longrightarrow V_3\times\mathbb A^1,\qquad (L,Q)\longmapsto(LQ,\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)).$$

Let $H\subseteq V_3$ be the affine hyperplane of cubics whose $T^2S$ coefficient is $1$. The map $j:H\times\{1\}\hookrightarrow V_3\times\mathbb A^1$ is the natural inclusion.

content.markdown:
## Expand compatibility into the two defining equations

The coefficient of $T^2S$ in $LQ$ is $ad+bc$. Therefore $LQ\in H$ is the equation $ad+bc=1$.

The second target coordinate gives $a^2e-abd+b^2c=1$. Hence the compatible-pair locus inside $V_1\times V_2\cong\mathbb A^5$ is

$$X=V(a^2e-abd+b^2c-1,\ ad+bc-1).$$

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$X=V(a^2e-abd+b^2c-1,ad+bc-1)\subseteq V_1\times V_2$.

Prove that $X$ represents $(V_1\times V_2)\times_{V_3\times\mathbb A^1}(H\times\{1\})$.

### Strategy

Start with arbitrary compatible maps to the two upper corners, use equality in both base coordinates to prove landing in $X$, and use the projections to prove uniqueness.

### Hypotheses

Let $\alpha:Z\to V_1\times V_2$ and $\beta:Z\to H\times\{1\}$ satisfy $\Phi\alpha=j\beta$.

### Intermediate claims

For every $z$, equality of the $V_3$ coordinates says that the product cubic of $\alpha(z)$ equals the cubic in $\beta(z)$ and therefore has $T^2S$ coefficient $1$. Equality of the $\mathbb A^1$ coordinates says its resultant is $1$. Thus $\alpha(z)$ satisfies both equations of $X$.

### Justification

Define $u:Z\to X$ by the same five coordinate functions as $\alpha$. The first projection recovers $\alpha$. The second projection sends those factors to $(LQ,1)$, which equals $\beta$ by compatibility. Any other factorization has the same five coordinates through the inclusion into $V_1\times V_2$.

### Conclusion

The compatible pair factors through $X$ exactly once, so the displayed square is Cartesian and the two descriptions of $X$ coincide.

## Keep ambient and pullback coordinates distinct

A point of the fiber product can be recorded as a pair $((L,Q),(C,1))$ with $C=LQ$, but the second component is determined by the first. This is why $X$ is conveniently realized inside the five-dimensional space $V_1\times V_2$.

The realization does not discard the projection to $H\times\{1\}$; that projection is $(L,Q)\mapsto(LQ,1)$.

The outcome is an exact equality of constructions. It is not yet a proof that the projection $X\to H$ is étale; Day 4 states the additional theorem needed for that conclusion.

content.markdown:
# Base change asks the same family over a new parameter space

Given $f:X\to S$ and a map $g:T\to S$, the pullback $X_T=X\times_S T$ comes with a projection $f_T:X_T\to T$. This is the family obtained after replacing the base $S$ by $T$.

The capstone square does exactly this: it restricts the multiplication–resultant family to normalized cubics and resultant value $1$.

## Reactivate yesterday's Cartesian square

Day 3 proved, rather than merely asserted, that $X=(V_1\times V_2)\times_{V_3\times\mathbb A^1}(H\times\{1\})$.

Today uses the same diagram in the opposite reading direction: the map $X\to H\times\{1\}$ is the base change of $\Phi$ along the inclusion $H\times\{1\}\hookrightarrow V_3\times\mathbb A^1$.

## Define the changed family

For $f:X\to S$ and $g:T\to S$, form $X_T=X\times_S T$. Its points are pairs $(x,t)$ satisfying $f(x)=g(t)$, and the changed map is $f_T(x,t)=t$.

The square with projections to $X$ and $T$ is Cartesian. Saying that $f_T$ is obtained from $f$ by base change records this precise construction.

## Fibers commute with the change of base

A point $t\in T$ maps to $g(t)\in S$. The fiber of $X_T\to T$ over $t$ consists of pairs $(x,t)$ satisfying $f(x)=g(t)$, so it is naturally the same as the original fiber $X_{g(t)}$.

This equality is concrete: fix the new parameter, substitute its image into the original family equations, and compare the resulting systems.

Prove that $p:X\to H\times\{1\}$ is the base change of $\Phi$ along $j$ and describe its fiber over $(C,1)$.

### Strategy

Use the defining Cartesian square for the first claim, then fix the lower-right point and translate compatibility into factorization equations.

### Hypotheses

Day 3 supplied the Cartesian square with upper map $X\to V_1\times V_2$ and lower map $j:H\times\{1\}\to V_3\times\mathbb A^1$.

### Intermediate claims

By definition, the other projection $p:X\to H\times\{1\}$ is the map obtained by base-changing $\Phi$. Its fiber at $(C,1)$ consists of pairs $(L,Q)$ satisfying $LQ=C$ and $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=1$.

### Justification

Because $C\in H$, the coefficient normalization is already built into the target point. Equality under $\Phi$ supplies both the cubic equation and the resultant equation.

### Conclusion

The capstone projection organizes normalized linear–quadratic factorizations of each cubic $C\in H$ as the fibers of one changed-base family.

content.markdown:
## Preview the étale base-change theorem without assessing it

A morphism between smooth varieties is étale at a point when its differential is an isomorphism there. Milne's definition is local and algebraic; an étale map need not be a Zariski-local isomorphism.

The theorem used later is: a base change of an étale morphism is étale. Therefore, once a later proof establishes that $\Phi$ is étale on the resultant-nonzero locus, this Cartesian square implies that $X\to H\times\{1\}$ is étale.

This week does not ask you to prove the étale criterion or the invertibility of $d\Phi$. It establishes the pullback to which that later theorem will apply.

## Keep the conditional theorem boundary explicit

The logical form is important: if $\Phi$ is étale on a locus containing the image of $X$, then its base change $p$ is étale. The Cartesian square alone does not prove the hypothesis.

Conversely, proving the two equations of the pullback does not require étale language. Construction and regularity are separate layers.

The capstone pullback is short to write and easy to under-justify. Today's sequence retrieves four earlier tools, then uses them in a proof that can be read without consulting the rest of the week.

## Complete worked model

$\Phi:V_1\times V_2\to V_3\times\mathbb A^1$ and $j:H\times\{1\}\hookrightarrow V_3\times\mathbb A^1$.

Give one self-contained proof that their pullback is the normalized two-equation variety $X$.

### Strategy

Type the diagram, compute the compatible-pair locus, define both projections, and prove the universal property.

### Hypotheses

$L=aT+bS$, $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$, $H$ fixes the $T^2S$ coefficient to $1$, and the resultant convention is $a^2e-abd+b^2c$.

### Intermediate claims

Compatibility gives $ad+bc=1$ and $a^2e-abd+b^2c=1$. The projections from this locus are $(L,Q)$ and $(LQ,1)$, and their composites into the base agree.

### Justification

For arbitrary compatible maps $\alpha$ and $\beta$ from $Z$, equality in $V_3$ and $\mathbb A^1$ proves that $\alpha$ lands in the equation locus. The first projection fixes all five coordinates, so the induced factorization is unique.

$X=(V_1\times V_2)\times_{V_3\times\mathbb A^1}(H\times\{1\})$ as an explicit affine variety with its universal mapping property.

objectives: Define finite and quasi-finite morphisms, translate an affine morphism into its coordinate-ring map, and prove the distinction between a finite module and finite point fibers.

content.markdown:
# Three similar words measure different kinds of control

A map may have only finitely many points over each target point and still fail the algebraic condition called finite. It may also fail to carry limits correctly, which is the phenomenon properness detects.

This week keeps those conditions separate. Today begins with the two notions governed directly by coordinate rings and fibers.

## Reactivate contravariance and fibers

For an affine morphism $f:X\to Y$, pullback of regular functions reverses the arrow: $f^*:\mathcal O(Y)\to\mathcal O(X)$. Week 36 defined the fiber $X_y=f^{-1}(y)$ by fixing every target coordinate.

The direction of $f^*$ matters. Finiteness asks how the source coordinate ring is generated as a module over the target coordinate ring acting through this pullback.

## Read a finite morphism on coordinate rings

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a morphism of affine varieties, put $A=\mathcal O(Y)$ and $B=\mathcal O(X)$, and let $A$ act on $B$ through $f^*$. The morphism is **finite** when $B$ is a finitely generated $A$-module.

This is stronger than saying that $B$ is a finitely generated $A$-algebra. An algebra may require only one algebra generator while still containing infinitely many independent powers as an $A$-module.

A finite list $b_1,\ldots,b_r$ proves module-finiteness only when every element of $B$ has the form $a_1b_1+\cdots+a_rb_r$ with $a_i\in A$.

content.markdown:
## Use a monic equation to control all powers

An element $b\in B$ is integral over $A$ when it satisfies a monic relation

$$b^n+a_{n-1}b^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0=0,\qquad a_i\in A.$$

The relation rewrites every power $b^m$ with $m\ge n$ as an $A$-linear combination of $1,b,\ldots,b^{n-1}$. If a finitely generated $A$-algebra is generated by integral elements, then it is finite as an $A$-module.

## Define quasi-finite by actual fibers

A morphism of algebraic varieties is **quasi-finite** when every fiber has finitely many points. This is a statement about all target points, not only a generic one.

For a polynomial map, solve the complete fiber equations. If one exceptional target leaves a free source coordinate, the map is not quasi-finite even when most fibers consist of one point.

## Complete worked model

$p:\mathbb A^1_t\to\mathbb A^1_u$, $u=t^3$.

Prove that $p$ is finite, then prove directly that each fiber has at most three points.

### Strategy

First use the coordinate-ring module criterion. Only afterward fix a target point and solve its fiber equation.

### Hypotheses

The pullback $p^*:\mathbb C[u]\to\mathbb C[t]$ sends $u$ to $t^3$, so $t$ satisfies the monic relation $T^3-u=0$ over $\mathbb C[u]$.

### Intermediate claims

Every polynomial in $t$ is uniquely $a(t^3)+t b(t^3)+t^2c(t^3)$. Therefore $1,t,t^2$ generate $\mathbb C[t]$ over $\mathbb C[u]$.

### Justification

For a fixed $u_0\in\mathbb C$, the fiber is $V(t^3-u_0)$. A nonzero cubic has at most three distinct roots, although roots may coincide when multiplicity is counted.

### Conclusion

The module calculation proves that $p$ is finite; the separate fiber calculation proves it is quasi-finite. The second fact illustrates the theorem proved on Day 3 but does not replace the first.

## Classify maps by definitions, not by appearance

The map $\mathbb G_m\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1$ has fibers of size at most one, so it is quasi-finite. Its coordinate ring is $\mathbb C[t,t^{-1}]$, which is not finite over $\mathbb C[t]$; this is the first warning that quasi-finite need not mean finite.

By contrast, the projection $\mathbb A^2\to\mathbb A^1$ is not quasi-finite because every nonempty fiber is a copy of $\mathbb A^1$.

content.markdown:
# A monic equation turns a nonlinear map into finite algebra

The map $F(x,y)=(x,y^2+xy)$ is not linear and its fibers change from two distinct points to one repeated point. Nevertheless, one monic equation controls the entire source ring over the target.

Today derives that equation from the map rather than assuming it, then keeps module rank, fiber cardinality, and multiplicity distinct.

## Reactivate the Day 1 criterion

If $B=A[y]$ and $y$ satisfies a monic polynomial of degree $n$ over $A$, then $1,y,\ldots,y^{n-1}$ span $B$ as an $A$-module.

To apply this fact to a morphism, first rename the target coordinates and write their pullbacks in the source ring.

## Derive the coordinate-ring presentation

Let $F:\mathbb A^2_{x,y}\to\mathbb A^2_{u,v}$ be $F(x,y)=(x,y^2+xy)$. The pullback is

$$F^*:\mathbb C[u,v]\longrightarrow\mathbb C[x,y],\qquad u\longmapsto x,\quad v\longmapsto y^2+xy.$$

After using $x=u$, the second identity becomes $y^2+uy-v=0$. Thus the source ring is presented over the target as $\mathbb C[u,v][y]/(y^2+uy-v)$.

## Reduce every source polynomial to two module generators

The relation gives $y^2=v-uy$. Therefore every power $y^m$ with $m\ge2$ reduces to $A+By$ with $A,B\in\mathbb C[u,v]$.

Because $x=u$, a general polynomial in $x,y$ also reduces to $A(u,v)+B(u,v)y$. Hence $1,y$ generate the source ring as a module over the target ring.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$K:\mathbb A^2_{r,s}\to\mathbb A^2_{a,b}$, $K(r,s)=(r,s^3+rs)$.

Prove that $K$ is finite and that every fiber has at most three points.

### Strategy

Write the target-to-source ring map, isolate a monic equation for the remaining source coordinate, then analyze a fixed fiber separately.

### Hypotheses

$K^*(a)=r$ and $K^*(b)=s^3+rs$, so $s$ satisfies $s^3+as-b=0$ over $A=\mathbb C[a,b]$.

### Intermediate claims

The monic cubic relation reduces every power of $s$ to an $A$-linear combination of $1,s,s^2$. Since $r=a$, these three elements span $\mathbb C[r,s]$ over $A$.

### Justification

Over $(a_0,b_0)$, the fiber equation is $r=a_0$ together with $s^3+a_0s-b_0=0$. The remaining nonzero polynomial has degree three, so there are at most three distinct solutions.

### Conclusion

$K$ is finite by the module criterion and quasi-finite by the independent fiber calculation. A repeated root may lower the number of distinct points without changing the module proof.

## Read the discriminant without changing the finiteness claim

Over $(a,b)$, the fiber of $F$ is governed by $y^2+ay-b=0$, whose discriminant is $\Delta=a^2+4b$.

When $\Delta\ne0$, the fiber has two distinct points. When $\Delta=0$, it has one point with multiplicity two in the equation. The map remains finite in both cases because the monic module relation did not depend on $\Delta$.

content.markdown:
# The theorem connects the conditions in one direction

The examples suggest that finite morphisms have finite fibers. The proof must explain why finite module generation survives after a target point is fixed.

A second theorem says finite morphisms are proper. Its proof uses two structural facts—base changes of finite maps remain finite, and finite maps are closed—rather than a point-counting argument.

## Reactivate fibers as base changes

Week 36 identified the fiber over $y\in Y$ with $X\times_Y\{y\}$. Algebraically, fixing $y$ replaces the target ring $A$ by its residue field $\kappa(y)$.

Day 1 established that finite module generation is the definition of a finite affine morphism. Today follows that generating set through the base change.

## Define properness by universal closedness

A morphism $f:X\to Y$ is **proper** when every base change $f_{Y'}:X\times_Y Y'\to Y'$ is a closed map. This property is called universal closedness.

The word “every” is essential. Being closed only before base change is not the definition, although failure to be closed for the identity base change is enough to prove that a map is not proper.

For complex algebraic varieties, compactness intuition is useful, but this course uses universal closedness as the algebraic definition.

content.markdown:
## Base-change the finite module to a point

Suppose $A\to B$ makes $B$ a finite $A$-module, generated by $b_1,\ldots,b_r$. Over a point $y$ with residue field $\kappa(y)$, the fiber algebra is

$$C_y=B\otimes_A\kappa(y).$$

This is the scheme-theoretic fiber algebra and it may contain nilpotents. In the classical-variety category used here, the reduced coordinate ring is $(C_y)_{\mathrm{red}}=C_y/\sqrt{(0)}$. Reduction does not change maximal ideals, and a quotient of a finite-dimensional vector space remains finite-dimensional.

The tensors $b_1\otimes1,\ldots,b_r\otimes1$ span $C_y$ over $\kappa(y)$. Hence both $C_y$ and its reduction are finite-dimensional.

content.markdown:
## Turn finite-dimensional algebra into finitely many points

Over $\mathbb C$, the points of the classical affine fiber correspond to maximal ideals of $(C_y)_{\mathrm{red}}$. These are the same maximal ideals as those of the scheme-theoretic algebra $C_y$, because every nilpotent lies in every prime ideal.

A finite-dimensional $\mathbb C$-algebra has only finitely many maximal ideals.

Indeed, if it had $n$ distinct maximal ideals, the Chinese remainder theorem would surject the algebra onto $\mathbb C^n$, forcing its vector-space dimension to be at least $n$. Since $n$ cannot grow without bound, only finitely many maximal ideals exist.
