## Complete worked model

A finite morphism $f:X\to Y$ of affine complex varieties, with $A=\mathcal O(Y)$ and $B=\mathcal O(X)$.

Prove that every fiber of $f$ has finitely many points.

### Strategy

Fix an arbitrary target point, base-change the finite module to its residue field, and use maximal ideals to count fiber points.

### Hypotheses

Because $f$ is finite, $B$ has a finite $A$-module generating set. For $y\in Y$, the scheme-theoretic fiber algebra is $C_y=B\otimes_A\kappa(y)$; the classical fiber has reduced coordinate ring $(C_y)_{\mathrm{red}}$.

### Intermediate claims

The images of the module generators span $C_y$, so it is finite-dimensional over $\kappa(y)=\mathbb C$. Its reduced quotient is also finite-dimensional and has the same maximal ideals.

### Justification

A finite-dimensional commutative $\mathbb C$-algebra has finitely many maximal ideals by the Chinese remainder dimension argument. Those maximal ideals are exactly the points of the affine fiber.

### Conclusion

The chosen fiber is finite. Since $y$ was arbitrary, $f$ is quasi-finite. The proof uses finite-module generation; it does not prove the converse.

content.markdown:
## Derive properness from finite base-change stability

Two theorems complete the argument: finite morphisms are closed, and every base change of a finite morphism is finite.

Let $f$ be finite and let $Y'\to Y$ be arbitrary. The changed map $f_{Y'}$ is finite, hence closed. Since this holds for every $Y'$, $f$ is proper.

This proof is independent of fiber cardinality. Finite fibers alone do not imply either finite-module generation or universal closedness.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Write $A=\mathcal O(Y)$ and $B=\mathcal O(X)$. content.markdown:
# Counterexamples show exactly which implication fails

A useful counterexample does more than attach a label to a map. It computes every fiber, identifies the missing algebraic or closedness condition, and points to the first invalid inference.

Today studies an open immersion and a polynomial quasi-finite map that is not finite, then models nonproperness on one polynomial map before an independent diagnosis of a different map.

## Keep yesterday's one-way theorem visible

Day 3 proved $\text{finite}\Rightarrow\text{quasi-finite}$ and $\text{finite}\Rightarrow\text{proper}$. It did not prove either converse.

To refute a converse, one example must satisfy the proposed hypothesis and fail the proposed conclusion. A map that already fails the hypothesis proves nothing about that converse.

## Use the punctured line as the cleanest converse failure

The open immersion $j:\mathbb G_m=\mathbb A^1\setminus\{0\}\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1$ has fibers of size zero or one, so it is quasi-finite.

Its coordinate-ring map is $\mathbb C[t]\to\mathbb C[t,t^{-1}]$. No finite set of Laurent polynomials can span all negative powers over $\mathbb C[t]$: multiplying by polynomials only moves exponents upward from a finite lower bound. Thus $j$ is not finite.

Its image $\mathbb A^1\setminus\{0\}$ is not closed, so $j$ is also not proper.

## Analyze a polynomial map with finite fibers but nonmonic algebra

Consider $H:\mathbb A^2_{x,y}\to\mathbb A^2_{u,v}$ defined by $H(x,y)=(x,xy^2+y+1)$. Over $(a,b)$, the remaining equation is $ay^2+y+1-b=0$.

If $a\ne0$, this is quadratic; if $a=0$, it is linear. Every fiber therefore has at most two points, so $H$ is quasi-finite.

Over the fraction field $\mathbb C(u,v)$, the minimal equation for $y$ is $uT^2+T+1-v$. It is not monic over $\mathbb C[u,v]$; Milne's Example 8.36 proves that $y$ is not integral over the target ring. Hence $H$ is not finite.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$J:\mathbb A^2_{x,y}\to\mathbb A^2_{u,v}$, $J(x,y)=(x,x^2y)$.

Prove that $J$ is not proper and explain what the sequence $(1/n,n^2)$ reveals.

### Strategy

First compute the image exactly and prove it is not closed. Then use the sequence as geometric intuition for the missing limit.

### Hypotheses

If $u\ne0$, every $(u,v)$ has preimage $(u,v/u^2)$. If $u=0$, the equation $x^2y=v$ permits only $v=0$.

### Intermediate claims

Therefore $J(\mathbb A^2)=D(u)\cup\{(0,0)\}$. The point $(0,1)$ lies in the Zariski closure because every polynomial vanishing on the dense open set $D(u)$ vanishes everywhere, but $(0,1)$ is not in the image.

### Justification

Thus the image of the closed source $\mathbb A^2$ is not closed. Proper maps are closed already for the identity base change, so $J$ cannot be proper.

### Conclusion

The sequence $(1/n,n^2)$ escapes every bounded subset of $\mathbb C^2$ while $J(1/n,n^2)=(1/n,1)\to(0,1)$, the missing image point. This visualizes the same obstruction; the nonclosed-image argument is the algebraic proof.

content.markdown:
## Do not use the wrong counterexample for a converse

The map $J(x,y)=(x,x^2y)$ is nonproper, but it does not refute “quasi-finite implies proper,” because $J^{-1}(0,0)$ is an affine line and $J$ is not quasi-finite.

The open immersion $\mathbb G_m\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1$ does refute that implication: it is quasi-finite and not proper. The same map also refutes “quasi-finite implies finite.”

content.markdown:
## Preview why a finite étale cover of affine space is restrictive

Week 38 will define étaleness algebraically. For this bridge, quote Milne's Riemann Existence Theorem: for a nonsingular complex variety $X$, analytification is an equivalence between finite étale covers of $X$ and finite topological covering spaces of $X(\mathbb C)$.

The analytic space $\mathbb A^n(\mathbb C)=\mathbb C^n$ is contractible, hence simply connected. Hatcher, Chapter 1 §1.3, Propositions 1.31–1.32, identifies the number of sheets of a connected covering with a subgroup index. Since the base fundamental group is trivial, a connected cover has one sheet.

Under Milne's equivalence, that one-sheet topological cover corresponds to the trivial algebraic cover, so a connected finite étale cover of complex affine space is an isomorphism. A finite cover with several components is only a disjoint union of trivial copies. This is the promised restriction. It does not say that every étale map is finite, and it does not replace Week 38's algebraic flatness and differential criteria.

## Complete worked model

$p(t)=t^3$, the open immersion $D(t-1)\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1$, and $K(x,y)=(x,x^2y)$.

Classify each map as finite, quasi-finite, and proper, with separate evidence for every label.

### Strategy

Use module generation for finiteness, every-fiber calculations for quasi-finiteness, and the finite-implies-proper theorem or a nonclosed image for properness.

### Hypotheses

For $p$, $\mathbb C[t]$ is generated by $1,t,t^2$ over $\mathbb C[u]$ with $u=t^3$. The open immersion has coordinate ring $\mathbb C[t,(t-1)^{-1}]$. The fibers and image of $K$ are found by separating the cases $u=0$ and $u\ne0$.

### Intermediate claims

The power map is finite, hence quasi-finite and proper. The open immersion is quasi-finite but not finite because negative powers of $t-1$ have no finite module span, and it is not proper because its image $D(t-1)$ is not closed.

### Justification

For $K$, the fiber over $(0,0)$ is the line $x=0$, so it is not quasi-finite and therefore not finite. Its image is $D(u)\cup\{(0,0)\}$, which is not closed, so it is not proper.

### Conclusion

These examples support only the arrows finite implies quasi-finite and finite implies proper. Each failed converse is witnessed by a map that satisfies its premise.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Milne's Riemann Existence Theorem says that analytification is an equivalence from finite étale covers of the nonsingular variety $\mathbb A^n_{\mathbb C}$ to finite topological covers of $\mathbb C^n$. For $G$, the fibers are one point when $a\ne0$, empty when $a=0\ne b$, and an affine line over $(0,0)$, so $G$ is not quasi-finite and therefore not finite. Its image is $D(u)\cup\{(0,0)\}$, which is not closed, so $G$ is not proper. lessons.title: Build Kähler differentials from derivations
lessons.summary: Define the universal module of Kähler differentials and derive the one-equation presentation for $A[t]/(f)$.
objectives: Define the universal module of Kähler differentials and derive the one-equation presentation for $A[t]/(f)$.

content.markdown:
# A derivative can be encoded without limits

Ordinary derivatives measure first-order variation. Kähler differentials keep that first-order information inside algebra: they record every derivation that obeys additivity, the Leibniz rule, and the requirement that base-ring elements remain constant.

The construction is abstract only long enough to become reusable. Every checkpoint returns to a quotient $A[t]/(f)$ and computes the single relation imposed on $dt$.

## Reactivate quotient rings

If $B=A[t]/(f)$, an identity in $B$ is an identity in $A[t]$ modulo the ideal $(f)$. A derivation over $A$ annihilates every coefficient from $A$.

The calculation $d(f(t))=f'(t)dt$ will therefore turn the defining equation $f(t)=0$ into a relation among differentials.

## Define an $A$-derivation

Let $A\to B$ be a ring map and let $M$ be a $B$-module. An **$A$-derivation** is an additive map $D:B\to M$ satisfying $D(a)=0$ for $a\in A$ and

$$D(bb')=bD(b')+b'D(b).$$

The condition $D(a)=0$ says that the base is held fixed. The Leibniz rule then determines $D(t^m)=mt^{m-1}D(t)$ for every positive integer $m$.

content.markdown:
## State the universal property of $\Omega_{B/A}$

The module of Kähler differentials $\Omega_{B/A}$ comes with a distinguished $A$-derivation $d:B\to\Omega_{B/A}$.

It is **universal**: for every $B$-module $M$ and every $A$-derivation $D:B\to M$, there is a unique $B$-linear map $\varphi:\Omega_{B/A}\to M$ such that $D=\varphi\circ d$.

For the polynomial ring $A[t]$, the module is free on $dt$. Choosing an $A$-derivation out of $A[t]$ is therefore the same as choosing the image of $dt$.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$A=\mathbb C[s]$ and $B=A[t]/(t^2-s)$.

Compute $\Omega_{B/A}$ and justify every quotient.

### Strategy

Start with the free module for $A[t]$, then impose the differential of the defining relation.

### Hypotheses

$\Omega_{A[t]/A}=A[t]dt$. For the quotient by $I=(t^2-s)$, the conormal sequence maps $I/I^2$ to $Bdt$ by $f\mapsto df$.

### Intermediate claims

Because $s\in A$, $d(t^2-s)=2t\,dt$. Hence the image of $I/I^2$ is the submodule generated by $2t\,dt$.

### Justification

Exactness says that $\Omega_{B/A}$ is the cokernel of this map. Therefore

### Conclusion

$$\Omega_{B/A}\cong B\,dt/(2t\,dt).$$ The module can vanish after localization, but $2t$ has not yet been declared invertible globally.

content.markdown:
## Read the general one-equation formula

For any $B=A[t]/(f)$, the same argument gives

$$\Omega_{B/A}\cong B\,dt/(f'(t)dt).$$

If $f'(t)$ is a unit in $B$, then $dt=f'(t)^{-1}f'(t)dt=0$, so the whole module vanishes. The converse also holds in this rank-one presentation: if the quotient is zero, the ideal generated by $f'$ is all of $B$.

content.markdown:
# A simple root has no first-order thickening in its fiber

Day 1 turned a defining polynomial into the relation $f'(t)dt=0$. Today asks where that relation actually kills $dt$.

At a point $t=\alpha$, the coefficient becomes the scalar $f'(\alpha)$. A nonzero scalar is invertible over a field, so simple roots and unramified points become the same local calculation.

## Reactivate the quotient formula

For $B=A[t]/(f)$, $\Omega_{B/A}=Bdt/(f'dt)$. After localizing at a prime $\mathfrak q$, the coefficient $f'$ is a unit exactly when it lies outside $\mathfrak q$.

In the finite-type setting used this week, a ring map is unramified when its module of relative differentials vanishes. At a point, this condition is checked after localization.

## Separate simple and repeated roots

A root $\alpha$ of $f\in k[t]$ is **simple** when $f'(\alpha)\ne0$ and **repeated** when $f'(\alpha)=0$.

Equivalently, $t-\alpha$ divides both $f$ and $f'$ exactly in the repeated case. This criterion is algebraic and remains meaningful over fields where a graph is unavailable.

## Translate the root test into differentials

Let $B=k[t]/(f)$ and let $\mathfrak m_\alpha=(t-\alpha)$ correspond to a root. Tensoring the quotient formula with the residue field gives

$$\Omega_{B/k}\otimes_B k(\alpha)\cong k(\alpha)dt/(f'(\alpha)dt).$$

This vector space is zero when $f'(\alpha)\ne0$ and one-dimensional when $f'(\alpha)=0$. Thus the simple-root condition detects unramifiedness at the point.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$A=\mathbb C[s]\to B=\mathbb C[t]$ with $s\mapsto t^2$.

Compute $\Omega_{B/A}$ and determine the exact unramified locus.

### Strategy

Present $B$ as $A[t]/(t^2-s)$, then localize the differential relation.

### Hypotheses

Day 1 gives $\Omega_{B/A}\cong Bdt/(2t\,dt)$. Over $\mathbb C$, the scalar $2$ is invertible.

### Intermediate claims

At a prime not containing $t$, the element $2t$ is a unit and the localized module vanishes. At the prime $(t)$, the relation becomes zero in the residue field, leaving a nonzero class of $dt$.

### Justification

The finite-type differential criterion says vanishing is equivalent to unramifiedness at the point.

### Conclusion

The square map is unramified on $D(t)=\mathbb G_m$ and ramified at $t=0$. Analytically, the same boundary is where the derivative $2t$ ceases to be invertible.

## Keep characteristic in the hypotheses

Derivative tests change in positive characteristic. Over a field of characteristic $p$, the map $s\mapsto t^p$ has derivative $pt^{p-1}=0$ everywhere.

Its geometric fibers may have only one underlying point, but the fiber equation $t^p-a=(t-\alpha)^p$ is nonreduced. The map is therefore nowhere unramified.

This is another reason finite point sets do not imply étaleness: nilpotent first-order structure is invisible to a point count and visible to differentials.

objectives: Define étaleness as finite presentation, flatness, and unramifiedness, then prove a standard one-variable algebra is étale.

content.markdown:
# Vanishing differentials is necessary but not sufficient

Day 2 isolated unramifiedness. Étaleness adds a second local demand: the family must vary flatly over the base, without a fiber appearing or disappearing through torsion.

For a monic one-variable equation, the proof is unusually concrete. The monic relation gives a finite free module, hence flatness; the invertible derivative kills differentials; and the displayed quotient gives finite presentation.

## Keep the three hypotheses separate

A finitely presented map is **étale** when it is flat and unramified. In this course's affine examples, unramifiedness is proved from $\Omega_{B/A}=0$.

Analytically, an étale map of smooth complex varieties behaves as a local biholomorphism. This is a local statement. It does not imply global injectivity, finiteness, or properness.

## Recognize flatness in a free module

An $A$-module $M$ is **flat** when tensoring with $M$ preserves injections, equivalently finite exact relations do not acquire new kernels after tensoring.

Every free module is flat. Therefore, when a monic polynomial $f$ of degree $n$ gives $B=A[t]/(f)$ with basis $1,t,\ldots,t^{n-1}$, the $A$-algebra $B$ is flat as an $A$-module.

The basis must be proved from the monic division algorithm. Merely having at most $n$ points in each fiber is not a flatness proof.

content.markdown:
## See why unramified need not mean étale

Consider the quotient $A=\mathbb C[x]\to B=A/(x)\cong\mathbb C$. Because the map is surjective, every $A$-derivation out of $B$ is zero, so $\Omega_{B/A}=0$.

The map is not flat. Multiplication by $x$ is injective on $A$, but after tensoring with $B$ it becomes the zero map $B\to B$.

Thus finite presentation plus vanishing differentials still does not imply étaleness. Flatness rules out this collapsed-fiber behavior.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$A=\mathbb C[s,s^{-1}]$ and $B=A[t]/(t^2-s)$.

Prove that $A\to B$ is étale and reconcile the proof with the analytic square map on $\mathbb C^*$.

### Strategy

Verify finite presentation, flatness, and unramifiedness separately before interpreting the result analytically.

### Hypotheses

The polynomial $t^2-s$ is monic, so $B$ is free over $A$ with basis $1,t$. It is presented by one generator and one relation.

### Intermediate claims

In $B$, $t^2=s$ and $s$ is a unit, so $t$ is a unit with inverse $t/s$. Hence $2t$ is a unit and $\Omega_{B/A}=Bdt/(2t\,dt)=0$.

### Justification

Finite presentation is explicit, freeness implies flatness, and vanishing differentials gives unramifiedness.

### Conclusion

Therefore $A\to B$ is étale. On complex points this is $t\mapsto t^2$ on $\mathbb C^*$; its derivative never vanishes, so it is locally biholomorphic, although globally it has two points in each fiber.

content.markdown:
## Match the algebraic and analytic local pictures

For maps between smooth complex varieties of equal dimension, the differential is the induced linear map between tangent spaces. When it is invertible, the complex inverse function theorem gives a local biholomorphism.

The algebraic definition packages the corresponding behavior over arbitrary base rings: local finite presentation controls size, flatness controls variation in families, and unramifiedness removes infinitesimal vertical directions.

Neither formulation is global injectivity. The square map on $\mathbb C^*$ is étale and locally invertible, yet every target has two preimages.

## Execute the complete standard-étale argument

A **standard étale** algebra has the form $A[t]_g/(f)$ with $f$ monic and $f'$ invertible in the localization.

The monic quotient is finite free over $A$, localization preserves flatness and finite presentation, and the invertible derivative kills $dt$. This supplies a reusable proof template rather than a definition by slogan.

lessons.title: Prove étaleness survives base change
lessons.summary: Compute base-changed polynomial algebras explicitly and prove that étaleness is stable under arbitrary base change.
objectives: Compute base-changed polynomial algebras explicitly and prove that étaleness is stable under arbitrary base change.

content.markdown:
# Base change substitutes new coefficients without changing the local type

A base change $A\to A'$ replaces an $A$-algebra $B$ by $B'=B\otimes_A A'$. In a polynomial presentation, this simply transports the coefficients of the defining equation to $A'$.

For a standard étale algebra, monicity survives, units remain units, and the derivative relation transports exactly. The general stability theorem is visible in the computation.

## Reactivate tensor-product fibers

Week 36 identified pullbacks with tensor products on coordinate rings. If $B=A[t]/(f)$, then

$$B\otimes_A A'\cong A'[t]/(f'),$$

where $f'$ is obtained by applying $A\to A'$ to every coefficient. This prime on $f'$ means transported polynomial, not derivative; the derivative will be written $\partial f/\partial t$.

## Transport a standard presentation

Suppose $B=A[t]_g/(f)$ is standard étale. After a base change $A\to A'$,

$$B'=B\otimes_AA'\cong A'[t]_{g'}/(f').$$

The transported polynomial $f'$ remains monic. If $\partial f/\partial t$ had inverse $h$ in $B$, their transported classes still multiply to $1$ in $B'$. Thus the derivative remains invertible and the new algebra is again standard étale.

content.markdown:
## Base-change the differential module

Differentials satisfy their own base-change formula:

$$\Omega_{B'/A'}\cong\Omega_{B/A}\otimes_AA'.$$

If $A\to B$ is unramified, the right side is zero. Flatness and local finite presentation are also stable under base change, so every clause in the étale definition survives.

This proves the general implication: if $A\to B$ is étale, then $A'\to B\otimes_AA'$ is étale for every $A\to A'$.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$A=\mathbb C[s,s^{-1}]$, $B=A[t]/(t^2-s)$, and $A'=\mathbb C[u,u^{-1}]$ with $s=u^2$.

Prove $B\otimes_AA'\cong A'\times A'$ and explain why the two factors are comaximal.

### Strategy

Factor the transported polynomial and apply the Chinese remainder theorem only after proving comaximality.

### Hypotheses

The base-changed algebra is $B'=A'[t]/(t^2-u^2)=A'[t]/((t-u)(t+u))$.

### Intermediate claims

The ideals $(t-u)$ and $(t+u)$ are comaximal because their difference contains $2u$, a unit in $A'$.

### Justification

The Chinese remainder theorem therefore identifies the quotient by their product with the product of the two linear quotients.

### Conclusion

$$B'\cong A'[t]/(t-u)\times A'[t]/(t+u)\cong A'\times A'.$$ The base change has trivialized the two-sheeted cover into two disjoint copies of the new base.

content.markdown:
## Do not expect base change to repair ramification automatically

Stability says an étale map stays étale after base change. It does not say that the base change of a nonétale map becomes étale.

For $\mathbb C[s]\to\mathbb C[t]$, $s=t^2$, base-changing by $s=u^2$ gives $\mathbb C[u,t]/(t^2-u^2)$. At $(u,t)=(0,0)$ the derivative $2t$ vanishes and the two components meet.

Removing $u=0$ produces the split étale cover from the model. Keeping $u=0$ preserves a ramified intersection.

content.markdown:
## Prove a cubic cover splits after base change

Let $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/3}$. Over a ring containing $\zeta$ and a unit $u$,

$$t^3-u^3=(t-u)(t-\zeta u)(t-\zeta^2u).$$

The pairwise differences are nonzero complex scalars times the unit $u$, so the three linear ideals are pairwise comaximal. The Chinese remainder theorem then splits the algebra into three copies of the base.

content.markdown:
# The full proof has four layers

Today retrieves the quotient, localization, regular-sequence, and finite-module tools that the étale proof silently depends on. Each retrieval is labelled and uses its source result in a new context.

The final synthesis must then keep four layers visible: the polynomial presentation, the flatness proof, the differential or simple-root proof, and the local analytic or base-change interpretation.

## Retrieve before reopening the week

Close Days 1–4. Reconstruct each scheduled result from its source week, then use feedback to repair only the earliest failed step.

The reviews occur at one, three, eight, and sixteen weeks. Repetition is deliberate; the mathematical object or required independence changes each time.

## Deliberate review · one-week monic-module retrieval

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$A=\mathbb C[q]$ and $B=(A[w]/(w^2+w-q))_{2w+1}$.

Prove $A\to B$ is étale, describe the analytic local behavior, and state what arbitrary base change preserves.

### Strategy

Use the monic basis before localization, invert the derivative, then invoke the three-clause definition and its stability.

### Hypotheses

$f=w^2+w-q$ is monic, so $A[w]/(f)$ is free over $A$ with basis $1,w$. Localization preserves flatness and finite presentation.

### Intermediate claims

The derivative is $2w+1$, which is a unit by construction. Therefore $\Omega_{B/A}=0$.

### Justification

The map is finitely presented, flat, and unramified, hence étale. At a complex point where $2w+1\ne0$, the implicit or inverse function theorem solves locally for $w$ as a holomorphic function of $q$.

### Conclusion

For every $A\to A'$, $B\otimes_AA'$ remains étale over $A'$. This local statement does not claim that the original map is globally injective or proper.

## Reject a two-clause proof

A proposed proof says: “The fibers are finite and $\Omega_{B/A}=0$, so the map is étale.” Neither statement proves flatness.

The final response begins with the universal differential formula, then proves flatness from a monic basis, proves unramifiedness from an invertible derivative, and ends with analytic and base-change consequences.

It must also state the boundaries: local does not mean global, finite fibers do not mean flat, and base change preserves étaleness only after étaleness has been established.

lessons.summary: Define monomial orders, leading terms, and Gröbner bases, then enter the capstone ideal in an exact Sage polynomial ring.
objectives: Define monomial orders, leading terms, and Gröbner bases, then enter the capstone ideal in an exact Sage polynomial ring.

content.markdown:
# Several variables need a disciplined notion of “first term”

In one variable, polynomial division has an obvious direction: remove the highest power first. In several variables, monomials such as $x^4y$ and $x^2y^7$ are not naturally comparable until we choose a monomial order.

A Gröbner basis converts that chosen order into a reliable division system. It will let Sage verify identities in the capstone coordinate ring and eliminate variables, but every output will still need a mathematical interpretation.

## Reactivate ideals and quotient equality

Week 22 established that $p$ and $q$ represent the same class in $R/I$ exactly when $p-q\in I$. Week 23 supplied division with remainder in one variable. This week extends that mechanism to multivariate ideals.

The capstone variety is $X=V(f,g)\subseteq\mathbb A^5$, where $f=a^2e-abd+b^2c-1$ and $g=ad+bc-1$. Its coordinate ring is $\mathbb C[a,b,c,d,e]/(f,g)$.

## Define a monomial order

A **monomial order** is a total order $\prec$ on monomials that is a well-order and is compatible with multiplication: if $x^\alpha\prec x^\beta$, then $x^{\alpha+\gamma}\prec x^{\beta+\gamma}$.

For lexicographic order with $x\succ y\succ z$, compare the exponent of $x$ first, then $y$, then $z$. Thus $x^2z\succ xy^{100}$ because the first exponent differs: $2>1$.

The well-order condition prevents an infinite descent during division. Multiplicative compatibility ensures that cancelling a leading term behaves consistently after multiplication.

content.markdown:
## Extract leading data

For a nonzero polynomial $p$, the **leading monomial** $\operatorname{LM}(p)$ is its largest monomial, the **leading coefficient** $\operatorname{LC}(p)$ is that monomial's coefficient, and the **leading term** is $\operatorname{LT}(p)=\operatorname{LC}(p)\operatorname{LM}(p)$.

The leading-term ideal of $I$ is $\operatorname{LT}(I)=\langle\operatorname{LT}(h):0\ne h\in I\rangle$. It contains leading terms of every polynomial in $I$, not only those of a convenient generating set.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Let $J=(x-y^2,y^3-1)\subseteq\mathbb Q[x,y]$ with lexicographic order $x\succ y$.

Show that $G=(x-y^2,y^3-1)$ is a Gröbner basis and reduce $x^2y$.

### Strategy

Check the only $S$-polynomial, then cancel leading monomials in order.

### Hypotheses

The leading monomials are $x$ and $y^3$. Their least common multiple is $xy^3$, so the only $S$-polynomial is $y^3(x-y^2)-x(y^3-1)=x-y^5$.

### Intermediate claims

Reduce $x-y^5$ by $x-y^2$ to $y^2-y^5$, then by $y^3-1$ to zero. Buchberger's criterion therefore proves that $G$ is a Gröbner basis.

### Justification

For the target polynomial, $x^2y\equiv y^5\pmod{x-y^2}$ and $y^5\equiv y^2\pmod{y^3-1}$. No leading monomial in $G$ divides $y^2$.

### Conclusion

The normal form is $\operatorname{NF}_G(x^2y)=y^2$. The conclusion depends on both the basis and its order.

Check whether a relation was used as an informal substitution without reducing to a remainder irreducible by both leading monomials.

A normal form is not merely an equivalent expression; it must satisfy the division stopping condition.

content.markdown:
## Define a Gröbner basis precisely

A finite set $G=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)\subseteq I$ is a **Gröbner basis** of $I$ when

$$\langle\operatorname{LT}(g_1),\ldots,\operatorname{LT}(g_s)\rangle=\operatorname{LT}(I).$$

This is stronger than generating $I$. For a Gröbner basis, division has the decisive membership property: $h\in I$ exactly when its remainder is zero. With a reduced Gröbner basis, the normal form is unique.

content.markdown:
## Enter the capstone ideal over an exact field

Use rational coefficients for exact arithmetic. Every defining polynomial has rational coefficients, and an identity proved in the rational polynomial ring remains valid after extending scalars to $\mathbb C$.

The variable order is part of the calculation. In Sage, the first variable is greatest for `order='lex'`:

```sage
R.<b,c,d,e,a> = PolynomialRing(QQ, order='lex')
f = a^2*e - a*b*d + c*b^2 - 1
g = a*d + b*c - 1
I = R.ideal(f, g)
```

This code enters $I=(f,g)$ exactly. It does not yet prove that an output describes the geometry one intends to study.

content.markdown:
# A normal form is a canonical representative, not a numerical approximation

Day 1 made the term order explicit. Sage can now compute a reduced Gröbner basis for the capstone ideal and reduce any polynomial to the unique remainder determined by that basis.

A zero normal form is an exact certificate of ideal membership. A nonzero normal form names the residue class that remains in the quotient ring.

## Reactivate the ring and the membership theorem

Continue with `R.<b,c,d,e,a> = PolynomialRing(QQ, order='lex')` and $I=(a^2e-abd+b^2c-1,ad+bc-1)$.

For the reduced Gröbner basis $G$ of $I$, $\operatorname{NF}_G(h)=0$ exactly when $h\in I$. Consequently, $p=q$ in $R/I$ exactly when `I.reduce(p-q)` returns zero.

## Ask for the reduced basis and record the context

In Sage, `G = I.groebner_basis()` computes the reduced Gröbner basis for the polynomial ring's declared order. With the present lexicographic order, one monic presentation is

$$ad+bc-1,$$

$$abd-\tfrac12a^2e-\tfrac12b+\tfrac12,$$

$$a^2ce+2a^2d^2-3ad-c+1.$$

Software may print terms in a different visual order, but the ring, variable priority, and monic polynomials determine the same reduced basis.

Check whether zero reduction of one generator was inflated into a claim that the quotient ring is zero.

Normal-form evidence is polynomial-specific; overgeneralizing it destroys the meaning of the quotient.

content.markdown:
## Use `I.reduce` as the exact membership interface

Sage's `I.reduce(h)` reduces $h$ by the ideal's reduced Gröbner basis. The result is exact because the coefficient field is $\mathbb Q$.

For the capstone ideal:

```sage
I.reduce(a*d - (1-b*c))
# 0
I.reduce(a)
# a
```

The first result certifies $ad=1-bc$ in $R/I$. The second says $a\notin I$ and that the class of $a$ is not zero.

data.markdown:
Find whether nonmembership was confused with invertibility or with being a non-zero-divisor.

A nonzero residue class can still be a zero-divisor and need not have an inverse.

Restrict the output to the one fact it certifies: zero or nonzero class modulo $I$.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

In $R/I$, Week 30 predicted $d=(1-bc)/a$ and $e=(1+b-2b^2c)/a^2$ on the open set $D(a)$.

Verify the corresponding denominator-free identities without pretending that $a$ is globally invertible.

### Strategy

Clear denominators first and reduce each polynomial difference modulo $I$.

### Hypotheses

The denominator-free candidates are $ad-(1-bc)$ and $a^2e-(1+b-2b^2c)$.

### Intermediate claims

Sage returns zero for both `I.reduce(a*d-(1-b*c))` and `I.reduce(a^2*e-(1+b-2*b^2*c))`.

### Justification

Zero normal form places both differences in $I$, so the equalities hold in $R/I$. Only after localizing at $a$ may one divide by $a$ or $a^2$.

### Conclusion

The computation verifies the polynomial identities globally and the rational formulas on $D(a)$. It does not make $a$ a unit on all of $X$.

data.markdown:
Check whether the response divided by $a$ even though the requested identity is already polynomial.

Clearing denominators preserves a global identity and keeps the open-chart hypothesis visible.

Reduce the polynomial difference directly and, if helpful, factor it through the already verified relation $ad-(1-bc)$.

content.markdown:
## Separate exact arithmetic from complex geometry

The ring `QQ` avoids floating-point tolerances: zero means algebraic zero, not “numerically small.”

Because $I$ and every candidate identity have rational coefficients, membership in $I\subseteq\mathbb Q[a,b,c,d,e]$ implies the same identity after extending coefficients to $\mathbb C$.

The converse question—whether a polynomial vanishes on all complex points and therefore belongs to an ideal—can require radical ideals and the Nullstellensatz. Normal-form reduction avoids that detour by proving direct ideal membership.

content.introMarkdown: Explain why $h=0$ in the complex coordinate ring and identify the direction not proved.

data.markdown:
Locate whether the argument moved in the wrong direction from complex pointwise vanishing to rational ideal membership.

Scalar extension is elementary, whereas recovering ideal membership from points is a different theorem with additional hypotheses.

Exhibit the rational ideal combination and carry that exact equation into the complex polynomial ring.

content.markdown:
## Audit a normal-form claim independently

A reproducible claim records the ring, order, ideal, candidate polynomial, exact command, exact output, and the mathematical conclusion.

It also records what was not established. A zero remainder proves equality in the quotient; it does not discover the formula, prove that a rational map is globally defined, or explain why the formula matters geometrically.

content.introMarkdown: Verify $pr=q^5$ and $p^3=r^2$ in $\mathbb Q[p,r,q]/J$ and give the strongest justified conclusion.

data.markdown:
Find the first missing item among the Gröbner-basis justification, either tested difference, either zero reduction, the quotient translations, and the parametrization boundary.

The two identities are certified only after the declared basis makes zero normal form an exact membership test, and they do not by themselves prove a complete parametrization theorem.

Check the relatively prime leading monomials, reduce both polynomial differences to zero, state both quotient equalities, and stop before any unproved claim about the image, kernel, or inverse.

content.markdown:
# A computation can certify an identity without explaining it

Normal-form reduction is logically strong: zero proves exact equality in the quotient. Yet it answers a narrow question. It does not tell us how a candidate was discovered, whether denominators are defined, or whether a displayed coordinate change is globally invertible.

Today makes that boundary explicit. You will learn to write a complete computational certificate and then attach the conceptual argument needed for the intended geometric conclusion.

## Reactivate the quotient criterion

For a Gröbner basis $G$ of $I$, $[p]=[q]$ in $R/I$ exactly when $\operatorname{NF}_G(p-q)=0$.

A proof report must therefore specify $p-q$, the ring and order, the ideal, and the zero result. If the desired theorem mentions a map, chart, or inverse, it must also check the domain and the relevant compositions.

## Write a computational certificate in four lines

A complete certificate has four parts: **claim**, **difference**, **exact reduction**, and **scope**.

For example: claim $[p]=[q]$ in $R/I$; difference $h=p-q$; exact result `I.reduce(h) == 0`; conclusion $h\in I$. The scope sentence states that this proves only the residue-class equality.

This format makes the computation auditable without dumping an unexplained screen of software output.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Let $S=\mathbb Q[u,w,v]$ with lexicographic order $u\succ w\succ v$, and let $J=(u-v^2,w-v^3)$.

Prove $uw=v^5$ in $S/J$ and separate the normal-form certificate from the conceptual explanation.

### Strategy

First verify that the displayed generators form a Gröbner basis; then reduce the difference; finally explain the parametrization.

### Hypotheses

The leading monomials $u$ and $w$ are relatively prime, so their only $S$-polynomial reduces to zero. Hence $G=(u-v^2,w-v^3)$ is a Gröbner basis.

### Intermediate claims

The difference is $uw-v^5$. Reduction by $u-v^2$ gives $v^2w-v^5$, and reduction by $w-v^3$ gives zero.

### Justification

Thus $uw-v^5\in J$, so $[uw]=[v^5]$ in $S/J$. Conceptually, the quotient records the parametrized curve $(u,w)=(v^2,v^3)$, where the identity becomes $v^2v^3=v^5$.

### Conclusion

The normal form certifies the identity; the parametrization explains why that identity is natural. Neither part alone should be mislabeled as the other.

Return to $I=(f,g)$. The equality $ad=1-bc$ is immediate from the generator $g$, but reducing it is still useful: it tests that the software ring and ideal were entered correctly.

A successful check of a relation already known from the definition is a **sanity check**. It should not be advertised as a new theorem.

## Preview one useful coordinate identity without claiming an inverse

Define $y=2bd-ae$. Exact reduction gives

```sage
I.reduce(b - 1 - a*(2*b*d-a*e))
# 0
```

Therefore $b=1+ay$ in $R/I$. This identity will be useful in a later coordinate analysis.

For now, it is only a verified relation involving a named polynomial $y$. It does not prove that $y$ belongs to a full global coordinate system, and it does not produce an isomorphism $X\cong\mathbb A^3$.

content.markdown:
## Separate verification, discovery, and proof

**Verification** checks a specified identity against exact definitions. **Discovery** proposes a useful identity or coordinate system. **Conceptual proof** explains why the statement holds and establishes every domain, hypothesis, and composition required by the theorem.

A Gröbner calculation may contribute to all three stages, but the report must say which role it is playing. In particular, checking candidate inverse formulas modulo $I$ proves a quotient equality; a global inverse additionally requires both maps to be defined everywhere and both composites to be identities.

content.markdown:
# Forgetting coordinates leaves algebraic consequences

Suppose a variety is described in variables $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ and we retain only some of those coordinates. Every polynomial consequence involving only the retained variables must vanish on the projected points.

An elimination ideal collects exactly those consequences. Lexicographic Gröbner bases make them visible, but the geometric output is generally the Zariski closure of a projection, not automatically the set-theoretic image itself.

## Reactivate ideals of equations

For $I\subseteq k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, eliminating $x_1,\ldots,x_\ell$ means taking the intersection $I\cap k[x_{\ell+1},\ldots,x_n]$.

Week 31 related ideals to zero sets and reversed inclusions. Here the retained equations are algebraic consequences of the original ideal, so every projected point satisfies them.

## Define the elimination ideal

The $\ell$th **elimination ideal** is

$$I_\ell=I\cap k[x_{\ell+1},\ldots,x_n].$$

It contains precisely the members of $I$ that no longer involve the first $\ell$ variables. To eliminate chosen variables in Sage, place them first in a lexicographic ring and call `I.elimination_ideal([...])`.

## Complete worked model

$J=(u-v^2,w-v^3)\subseteq\mathbb Q[u,w,v]$ with lexicographic order $u\succ w\succ v$.

Eliminate $u$ alone, then eliminate both $u$ and $w$, and interpret the results.

### Strategy

Use the Gröbner basis with leading monomials $u,w$ and select the basis elements involving only retained variables.

### Hypotheses

The basis is $u-v^2,w-v^3$. Eliminating $u$ retains $w,v$; eliminating $u,w$ retains only $v$.

### Intermediate claims

The first intersection is $(w-v^3)\subseteq\mathbb Q[w,v]$. The second is the zero ideal in $\mathbb Q[v]$ because no nonzero basis relation involves only $v$.

### Justification

Geometrically, the projection to $(w,v)$ is the graph $w=v^3$. The projection to $v$ is all of $\mathbb A^1$: every $v$ has the point $(v^2,v^3,v)$ above it.

### Conclusion

The algebra and geometry agree: one retained pair obeys an equation, whereas the free parameter alone obeys none.

## Eliminate four capstone variables

To retain only $a$, keep the lexicographic order $b\succ c\succ d\succ e\succ a$ and run

```sage
I.elimination_ideal([b,c,d,e])
# Ideal (0) of Multivariate Polynomial Ring in b, c, d, e, a over Rational Field
```

To eliminate $e$, create a lexicographic ring with $e$ first, rebuild the ideal, and request `I.elimination_ideal([e])`.

content.markdown:
# Replace a five-by-five determinant with the geometry of factorization

Let $V_n$ be the vector space of homogeneous binary forms of degree $n$. The multiplication map

$$M:V_1\times V_2\longrightarrow V_3,\qquad (L,Q)\longmapsto LQ$$

has a five-dimensional source and a four-dimensional target. One tangent direction must therefore disappear. The important question is whether coprimality makes that lost direction the only one.

## Reactivate the ingredients before differentiating

A tangent vector to the vector space $V_1\times V_2$ is simply a pair $(\ell,q)\in V_1\times V_2$. Week 34 taught that the differential is the coefficient of $t$ after substituting a first-order path. Week 23 supplied divisibility in polynomial rings, and Week 27 established that $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)\ne0$ is equivalent to $\gcd(L,Q)=1$.

All forms in this lesson are homogeneous in $T,S$ over $\mathbb C$. Degree bounds are part of the proof: $L$ and $\ell$ both have degree one, while $Q$ and $q$ both have degree two.

## Differentiate multiplication from a first-order path

Insert $(L+t\ell,Q+tq)$ and expand:

$$(L+t\ell)(Q+tq)=LQ+t(\ell Q+Lq)+t^2\ell q.$$

Therefore

$$dM_{(L,Q)}(\ell,q)=\ell Q+Lq.$$

This product rule is the entire differential; no coordinate matrix is needed.

## Turn a zero differential into a divisibility statement

Suppose $\gcd(L,Q)=1$ and $dM_{(L,Q)}(\ell,q)=0$. Then

$$\ell Q=-Lq.$$

The right side is divisible by $L$, so $L\mid\ell Q$. Because $L$ is linear, it is irreducible and hence prime in the unique factorization domain $\mathbb C[T,S]$. Coprimality says $L\nmid Q$, so Euclid's lemma forces $L\mid\ell$.

Since $L$ and $\ell$ have the same degree, $\ell=\lambda L$ for one scalar $\lambda$.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

Let $A\in V_2$ and $B\in V_1$ be coprime, and let $N(A,B)=AB\in V_3$.

Prove $\ker dN_{(A,B)}=\mathbb C(A,-B)$.

### Strategy

Differentiate first, then use the factor of degree two rather than guessing from dimensions.

### Hypotheses

A tangent vector $(a,b)$ satisfies $aB+Ab=0$. Thus $A\mid aB$. Since $\gcd(A,B)=1$, every irreducible factor of $A$ is absent from $B$.

### Intermediate claims

Unique factorization forces $A\mid a$. The equal degree condition gives $a=\lambda A$, and substitution yields $A(\lambda B+b)=0$.

### Justification

The polynomial ring is a domain, so $b=-\lambda B$. Conversely, $(A,-B)$ maps to $AB-AB=0$.

### Conclusion

Every kernel vector is $\lambda(A,-B)$, and every such vector is killed. Hence the kernel is exactly one-dimensional.

# Add one scalar that sees the missing direction

Multiplication forgets relative scaling: to first order, $(L,Q)$ and $((1+t)L,(1-t)Q)$ have the same product. The resultant is deliberately added as a fifth output coordinate because its scaling weight is unbalanced.

Today derives that imbalance from homogeneity. The conclusion will be a directional derivative, not a slogan about determinants.

## Reactivate the kernel and the resultant's two degrees

Day 1 proved that coprimality gives $\ker dM_{(L,Q)}=\mathbb C(L,-Q)$. Week 27 established that the resultant of a degree-$m$ form and a degree-$n$ form obeys

$$\operatorname{Res}(\alpha A,\beta B)=\alpha^n\beta^m\operatorname{Res}(A,B).$$

For a linear $L$ and quadratic $Q$, the exponents are two and one respectively.

## Read the bidegree in the correct order

The exponent attached to the first form is the degree of the second form. Thus

$$\operatorname{Res}(\alpha L,\beta Q)=\alpha^2\beta\operatorname{Res}(L,Q).$$

This asymmetry is the key. If both weights were equal, opposite scaling would have zero first derivative.

content.markdown:
# Solve the linear-algebra problem before touching coordinates

Define

$$\Phi:V_1\times V_2\longrightarrow V_3\times\mathbb C,\qquad \Phi(L,Q)=\bigl(LQ,\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)\bigr).$$

Both source and target have dimension five. Rather than expand a five-by-five Jacobian determinant, we will prove directly that no nonzero tangent vector is killed.

## Bring the two previous conclusions together

Day 1 gave $\ker dM_{(L,Q)}=\mathbb C(L,-Q)$ on the coprime locus. Day 2 gave $D\operatorname{Res}_{(L,Q)}(L,-Q)=\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)\ne0$ there.

Rank–nullity also gives $\operatorname{rank}dM=5-1=4=\dim V_3$, so the multiplication differential is surjective. The proof of $d\Phi$ needs injectivity, equal dimensions, and no determinant expansion.

## Convert the one-dimensional kernel into surjectivity

The source of $dM$ is $V_1\times V_2$, of dimension $2+3=5$. Its kernel has dimension one. Rank–nullity therefore gives rank four.

Since $V_3$ also has dimension four, $dM_{(L,Q)}$ is surjective. This is useful context, although the shortest proof for the full map starts directly from a vector in $\ker d\Phi$.

## Use a functional that is nonzero on the kernel

A reusable linear-algebra lemma is hiding here. Let $T:U\to W$ be surjective with one-dimensional kernel $\mathbb Ce$, and let $\alpha:U\to\mathbb C$ satisfy $\alpha(e)\ne0$. Then

$$(T,\alpha):U\longrightarrow W\times\mathbb C$$

is injective: a vector killed by both lies in $\mathbb Ce$, and $\alpha$ kills no nonzero vector on that line.

If $\dim U=\dim W+1$, this injective map is automatically an isomorphism.

### Strategy

Find the kernel of $T$, test $\alpha$ on its generator, then use equal dimensions.

### Hypotheses

The equations $T(x)=0$ give $x_1=x_2$ and $x_3=x_4=0$. Hence $\ker T=\mathbb C(1,1,0,0)$.

### Intermediate claims

On the kernel generator, $\alpha(1,1,0,0)=2\ne0$. Therefore a vector killed by both $T$ and $\alpha$ must be zero.

### Justification

The combined map is injective. Its source and target both have dimension four.

### Conclusion

Finite-dimensional injectivity between equal-dimensional spaces proves that $(T,\alpha)$ is an isomorphism.

## Apply the lemma to the coefficient–resultant map

Suppose $d\Phi_{(L,Q)}(\ell,q)=0$. Its first component gives $dM(\ell,q)=0$, so Day 1 yields $(\ell,q)=\lambda(L,-Q)$.

The second component is then

$$0=D\operatorname{Res}(\ell,q)=\lambda\operatorname{Res}(L,Q).$$

On the nonzero-resultant locus, $\lambda=0$. Thus $d\Phi$ is injective. Since both tangent spaces have dimension five, it is an isomorphism.

## Recognize the general degree condition

For degrees $m$ and $n$, the same construction maps $V_m\times V_n$ to $V_{m+n}\times\mathbb C$. The dimensions are equal because $(m+1)+(n+1)=(m+n+1)+1$.

When $A,B$ are coprime, multiplication again has kernel $\mathbb C(A,-B)$. The resultant derivative on its generator is $(n-m)\operatorname{Res}(A,B)$. Thus the same proof works whenever $m\ne n$ and the resultant is nonzero.

content.markdown:
# The five-dimensional calculation exists to control a threefold

Day 3 proved that $d\Phi$ is invertible wherever the resultant is nonzero. The target of the course, however, is the normalized factorization space $X$ and its map to the hyperplane $H$ of cubic forms whose $T^2S$ coefficient is one.

The bridge is a Cartesian square already constructed in Week 36. Étaleness is stable under base change, so the five-dimensional theorem descends without a second Jacobian calculation.

## Reactivate the exact square and the local criterion

Let $U=\{(L,Q):\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)\ne0\}\subseteq V_1\times V_2$. The map $\Phi|_U:U\to V_3\times\mathbb A^1$ has an invertible differential at every point.

Let $j:H\times\{1\}\hookrightarrow V_3\times\mathbb A^1$. Week 36 proved that

$$X=U\times_{V_3\times\mathbb A^1}(H\times\{1\}),$$

where $X$ is cut out by $ad+bc=1$ and $a^2e-abd+b^2c=1$. The second projection $p:X\to H\times\{1\}\cong H$ is the map to be proved étale.

## Convert invertible differentials into an étale morphism

The source $U$ and target $V_3\times\mathbb A^1$ are smooth complex varieties of dimension five. For a morphism between smooth varieties of equal dimension, the Jacobian criterion says that an invertible tangent map at a point is equivalent to being étale at that point.

Analytically, the complex inverse function theorem gives a local biholomorphism. Algebraically, étale means locally of finite presentation, flat, and unramified. In this smooth equal-dimensional setting, the nonsingular Jacobian criterion connects the two descriptions.

## Apply the criterion on the whole resultant-open locus

Day 3 applies at every point of $U$, not at one chosen factorization. Therefore $\Phi|_U$ is étale.

The locus $U$ is open because the resultant is a polynomial in the coefficients and $U=D(\operatorname{Res})$. Restricting the source before invoking the theorem keeps the nonzero hypothesis visible.

## Complete worked model

$f:\mathbb G_m\to\mathbb G_m$, $z\mapsto z^2$, is pulled back along $g:\mathbb G_m\to\mathbb G_m$, $u\mapsto u^3$.

Describe the pullback and prove its projection to the $u$-line is étale.

### Strategy

Write the compatibility equation, identify the projection as a base change, and invoke stability; then verify the derivative directly.

### Hypotheses

The pullback is $P=\{(z,u)\in\mathbb G_m^2:z^2=u^3\}$ with projection $p(z,u)=u$. The square with $f$ and $g$ is Cartesian by the equality $z^2=u^3$.

### Intermediate claims

The map $f$ is étale because its derivative $2z$ is invertible on $\mathbb G_m$. Étaleness is stable under base change, so $p$ is étale.

### Justification

Directly, $P$ is cut out by $F(z,u)=z^2-u^3$, and $\partial F/\partial z=2z$ is nonzero everywhere on $P$ because $z$ is invertible.

### Conclusion

The pullback projection is étale. The proof uses an established property of the original map, not the bare existence of a fiber product.

content.markdown:
## Keep local injectivity separate from global injectivity

Étale maps need not be globally injective. The map $z\mapsto z^3$ on $\mathbb C^\times$ has derivative $3z^2\ne0$ everywhere, but $1,\omega,\omega^2$ have the same cube.

The capstone conclusion is therefore local: near each normalized factorization, the coefficient–resultant data determine the factors uniquely. A global sheet count requires additional properness and covering arguments developed later.

content.markdown:
## Pull the theorem back to the normalized threefold

Every point of $X$ has resultant one, so $X$ lies over the étale locus $U$. The Cartesian square is

$$\begin{array}{ccc}X&\longrightarrow&U\\ \downarrow p&&\downarrow\Phi\\ H\times\{1\}&\xrightarrow{j}&V_3\times\mathbb A^1.\end{array}$$

Since $p$ is the base change of $\Phi|_U$ along $j$, stability under base change proves that $p:X\to H\times\{1\}\cong H$ is étale. Both $X$ and $H$ therefore have dimension three locally, and the map is locally injective in the complex analytic topology.

The final proof is short only after its ingredients are understood. Today begins with four scheduled retrievals, each chosen because it controls a possible gap: exact polynomial reasoning, global map boundaries, affine coordinate language, and graded scaling.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: Let $M(L,Q)=LQ$. Differentiating gives $dM_{(L,Q)}(\ell,q)=\ell Q+Lq$. If $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)\ne0$, then $L,Q$ are coprime. From $\ell Q=-Lq$, unique factorization gives $L\mid\ell$; equal degrees yield $\ell=\lambda L$, and substitution gives $q=-\lambda Q$. Conversely $(L,-Q)$ is killed, so $\ker dM=\mathbb C(L,-Q)$. Resultant bidegree $(2,1)$ gives $\operatorname{Res}((1+t)L,(1-t)Q)=(1+t)^2(1-t)\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)$, hence $D\operatorname{Res}(L,-Q)=\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)\ne0$. Therefore a vector killed by both components of $d\Phi$ must be zero. The source dimension is $2+3=5$ and the target dimension is $4+1=5$, so $d\Phi$ is an isomorphism. On the open set $D(\operatorname{Res})$, the smooth equal-dimensional Jacobian criterion makes $\Phi$ étale. Finally, the square with $X$ above $H\times\{1\}$ and $D(\operatorname{Res})$ above $V_3\times\mathbb A^1$ is Cartesian, because $X$ imposes $LQ\in H$ and resultant one. Thus $X\to H\times\{1\}\cong H$ is étale by stability under base change. Analytically it is locally biholomorphic and locally injective near each point; the argument does not prove global injectivity, properness, or a global number of sheets.

lessons.title: Build the projective line from two affine charts
lessons.summary: Define the projective line as one-dimensional directions, construct its two standard affine charts, and derive their transition formula.
objectives: Define the projective line as one-dimensional directions, construct its two standard affine charts, and derive their transition formula.

content.markdown:
# One extra point closes the affine line

The affine coordinate $t$ records every finite complex number, but it cannot describe a direction whose denominator is zero. The projective line keeps all nonzero directions in $\mathbb C^2$, including that missing direction.

It is not one coordinate chart with an informal symbol $\infty$. It is a space assembled from two honest affine charts whose coordinates agree by an explicit transition map.

## Reactivate quotients, functions, and homogeneous scaling

Week 26 introduced homogeneous coordinates. A point of $\mathbb P^1$ is an equivalence class

$$[T:S]=[\lambda T:\lambda S]\qquad(\lambda\in\mathbb C^\times),$$

of a nonzero pair $(T,S)$. The brackets record a line through the origin, not an ordered pair with fixed length.

The polynomial and group-action prerequisites matter immediately: homogeneous equations respect common scaling, and scalar matrices act trivially on projective points.

## Define the quotient precisely

Set

$$\mathbb P^1=(\mathbb C^2\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb C^\times.$$

Two representatives determine the same point exactly when one is a nonzero scalar multiple of the other. Thus $[2:4]=[1:2]$, while $[1:2]\ne[2:1]$.

The pair $(0,0)$ is excluded because it spans no one-dimensional subspace.

content.markdown:
## Construct the chart where $S\ne0$

On $U_S=\{[T:S]:S\ne0\}$, scale by $S^{-1}$ to obtain the unique representative $[t:1]$, where

$$t=T/S.$$

This identifies $U_S$ with $\mathbb A^1_t$. The missing point is $[1:0]$, because no representative of that class has nonzero second coordinate.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$P=[2:5]$ lies in both $U_S$ and $U_T$.

Compute $t=T/S$ and $s=S/T$, then verify the transition $s=1/t$.

### Strategy

Normalize once by $S$ and once by $T$, then compare the two affine coordinates.

### Hypotheses

Both homogeneous coordinates are nonzero. In $U_S$, $P=[2/5:1]$, so $t=2/5$.

### Intermediate claims

In $U_T$, $P=[1:5/2]$, so $s=5/2$.

### Justification

Their product is $ts=(2/5)(5/2)=1$. Hence $s=1/t$ on $U_S\cap U_T$.

### Conclusion

The transition is regular on the overlap where $t\ne0$ and $s\ne0$; neither formula is asserted at a missing denominator.

The transition map is what makes the two affine descriptions one geometric space.

Normalize the same representative twice and multiply the resulting ratios.

content.markdown:
## Keep chart domains visible

The formula $s=1/t$ holds only on the overlap. At $[0:1]$, one has $t=0$ but no $s$-coordinate; at $[1:0]$, one has $s=0$ but no $t$-coordinate.

Writing $1/0=\infty$ may be a useful mnemonic, but it is not the chart transition. The rigorous statement always names the open set on which division is legal.

Roots at infinity will be ordinary points in the second chart, so chart discipline is essential.

content.markdown:
## Translate a fresh projective point in both directions

A coordinate translation should be reversible. Starting from $t\in\mathbb C$, the chart map gives $[t:1]$. When $t\ne0$, the other coordinate is $s=1/t$. Starting from $s$, one obtains $[1:s]$ and, when $s\ne0$, $t=1/s$.

The two exceptional origins correspond to the two points omitted by the opposite chart.

Build $[1:s]$ first, check $s\ne0$, rationalize $1/s$, and verify the two representatives differ by one scalar.

lessons.title: Locate the root of a binary linear form
lessons.summary: Derive the projective root $[-b:a]$ of $aT+bS$ and interpret the case $a=0$ in the correct affine chart.
objectives: Derive the projective root $[-b:a]$ of $aT+bS$ and interpret the case $a=0$ in the correct affine chart.

content.markdown:
# A leading coefficient can vanish without making the root disappear

For an affine polynomial $at+b$, the formula $t=-b/a$ stops when $a=0$. Homogeneous coordinates reveal what happened: the root moved to the chart omitted by the affine coordinate $t=T/S$.

The projective formula is uniform and does not divide until a chart condition has been checked.

## Reactivate homogeneous vanishing

A nonzero linear binary form is $L(T,S)=aT+bS$ with $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$. Its projective zero set is well defined because

$$L(\lambda T,\lambda S)=\lambda L(T,S).$$

Thus vanishing is unchanged when a representative is rescaled. Day 1 supplied the two chart coordinates used below.

## Derive the root without dividing

The vector $(-b,a)$ is nonzero and satisfies

$$a(-b)+b(a)=0.$$

Every nonzero solution of $aT+bS=0$ is proportional to $(-b,a)$, because the kernel of the nonzero linear functional $(T,S)\mapsto aT+bS$ is one-dimensional.

Therefore the unique projective root is $[-b:a]$.

content.markdown:
## Recover the affine formula when $a\ne0$

If $a\ne0$, then the root $[-b:a]$ lies in $U_S$. Its affine coordinate is

$$t=T/S=-b/a.$$

This is the familiar affine root, now derived from a chart. The formula is legal precisely because the second homogeneous coordinate $a$ is nonzero.

## Complete worked model

$L(T,S)=4S$, so $a=0$ and $b=4$.

Locate the root in $\mathbb P^1$ and both charts.

### Strategy

Use the homogeneous equation first, then ask which chart contains the resulting point.

### Hypotheses

The equation $4S=0$ forces $S=0$. A nonzero representative must then have $T\ne0$.

### Intermediate claims

Every solution represents $[1:0]$. This point is not in $U_S$, so no finite $t$-coordinate exists.

### Justification

The point lies in $U_T$ and has $s=S/T=0$. The formula $[-b:a]=[-4:0]=[1:0]$ agrees.

### Conclusion

The root has not vanished; it is the ordinary point $s=0$ in the second affine chart.

content.markdown:
## Exclude the zero form from the unique-root statement

The formula $[-b:a]$ requires $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$. The zero form vanishes at every point of $\mathbb P^1$, not at one distinguished root.

The nonzero hypothesis is therefore part of the theorem, not a technical convenience.

## Recognize every form whose root is at infinity

A complete solution distinguishes the homogeneous theorem from its chart expressions: $[-b:a]$ always exists for a nonzero form, $t=-b/a$ only when $a\ne0$, and $s=-a/b$ only when $b\ne0$.

The reverse question is more demanding than substituting one more scalar multiple: which nonzero linear forms have their unique root at $[1:0]$? Answering it requires both directions of a classification.

content.markdown:
# A form remembers roots without choosing an order

A degree-$n$ binary form has exactly $n$ projective roots over $\mathbb C$ when multiplicity is counted. The natural record is not an ordered tuple but a formal sum of points.

This divisor language prepares Week 42, where unordered collections of projective points become symmetric powers.

## Reactivate factorization and projective roots

Let $F(T,S)$ be a nonzero homogeneous form of degree $n$. Over $\mathbb C$, it factors as

$$F=c\prod_{j=1}^r L_j^{m_j},\qquad c\ne0,\quad \sum_jm_j=n,$$

with pairwise nonproportional linear forms $L_j$. Day 2 associates one projective point $p_j$ to each $L_j$.

## Define the root divisor

The effective divisor of zeros is

$$\operatorname{div}_0(F)=\sum_{j=1}^r m_j[p_j].$$

It is unordered: permuting the factors does not change the sum. Multiplying $F$ by a nonzero scalar also does not change it.

The total degree of the divisor is $\sum_jm_j=n$.

content.markdown:
# Projective coordinates should respect changes of basis

An invertible linear map of $\mathbb C^2$ sends lines through the origin to lines through the origin. It therefore acts on $\mathbb P^1$.

Scalar matrices move each vector only along its own line, so they act trivially. The effective symmetry group is $PGL_2=GL_2/\mathbb C^\times I$.

## Fix one action convention

For

$$g=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\\gamma&\delta\end{pmatrix}\in GL_2,$$

let $g[T:S]=[\alpha T+\beta S:\gamma T+\delta S]$. On the $t$-chart, whenever the new second coordinate is nonzero,

$$t\longmapsto\frac{\alpha t+\beta}{\gamma t+\delta}.$$

The determinant condition ensures that $g$ has an inverse and the action is bijective.

## Prove the action is well defined

If $[T:S]=[\lambda T:\lambda S]$, linearity gives

$$g(\lambda T,\lambda S)=\lambda g(T,S),$$

so the image projective point does not depend on the representative. Invertibility prevents a nonzero vector from mapping to zero.

If $g$ is replaced by $cg$ with $c\ne0$, every image vector is rescaled by $c$, so the projective action is unchanged.

## Derive the fractional-linear formula and its pole

For a point $[t:1]$, the image is

$$[\alpha t+\beta:\gamma t+\delta].$$

If $\gamma t+\delta\ne0$, the new affine coordinate is $(\alpha t+\beta)/(\gamma t+\delta)$. If the denominator vanishes, the image is $[1:0]$, not an undefined projective point.

## Complete worked model

$g=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $F(T,S)=T(T-S)^2$.

Compute $g\operatorname{div}_0(F)$ and the divisor of $(g\cdot F)(v)=F(g^{-1}v)$.

### Strategy

Move the roots as projective points, then compute the transformed form with the inverse matrix.

### Hypotheses

The divisor of $F$ is $[0:1]+2[1:1]$. The action sends $[T:S]$ to $[T+S:S]$, so these points move to $[1:1]$ and $[2:1]$.

### Intermediate claims

The inverse sends $(T,S)$ to $(T-S,S)$. Thus $(g\cdot F)(T,S)=F(T-S,S)=(T-S)(T-2S)^2$.

### Justification

Its divisor is $[1:1]+2[2:1]$, exactly the moved divisor.

### Conclusion

$\operatorname{div}_0(g\cdot F)=g\operatorname{div}_0(F)$; using $g^{-1}$ in the action on functions produces the forward action on zeros.

This does not mean every two matrices represent the same projective transformation. They must differ by one nonzero scalar multiplying every entry.

content.markdown:
# Roots become coordinates

Week 41 attached an unordered divisor of roots to a nonzero binary form. This week reverses that viewpoint: start with the points, multiply their linear equations, and read the resulting coefficients as one projective point.

The construction is concrete. Its inputs are projective points with multiplicity; its output is a coefficient vector, defined up to one nonzero scalar.

## Separate two meanings of symmetric power

The notation $\operatorname{Sym}^n(\mathbb P^1)$ here means the **symmetric product**: unordered degree-$n$ effective divisors $p_1+\cdots+p_n$ on $\mathbb P^1$.

This is related to, but not the same object as, the symmetric tensor power $\operatorname{Sym}^n(V)$ of a vector space. Binary degree-$n$ forms constitute $\operatorname{Sym}^n((\mathbb C^2)^*)$, and their one-dimensional scalar classes form $\mathbb P^n$ after a basis is chosen.

## Write the linear factor of one projective point

For $p=[u:v]\in\mathbb P^1$, define

$$\ell_p(T,S)=vT-uS.$$

It vanishes at $p$ because $vu-uv=0$. Replacing $(u,v)$ by $(\lambda u,\lambda v)$ multiplies $\ell_p$ by $\lambda$, so the factor is determined up to nonzero scalar.

content.markdown:
## Multiply factors and read projective coefficients

For an unordered divisor $D=p_1+\cdots+p_n$, set

$$F_D=\prod_{j=1}^n\ell_{p_j}.$$

Writing $F_D=A_0T^n+A_1T^{n-1}S+\cdots+A_nS^n$ gives a nonzero coefficient vector $[A_0:\cdots:A_n]\in\mathbb P^n$.

The basis $T^n,T^{n-1}S,\ldots,S^n$ is fixed throughout; changing it would change coordinates, not the underlying projective coefficient space.

## Complete worked model

$D=[2:1]+[1:0]$.

Compute the coefficient class twice after reordering and rescaling the point representatives.

### Strategy

Build the original factors, then track how each allowed change affects their product.

### Hypotheses

The factors from $(2,1)$ and $(1,0)$ are $T-2S$ and $-S$. Thus $F_D=-ST+2S^2$.

### Intermediate claims

Use representatives $(6,3)$ and $(-2,0)$ in the opposite order. Their factors are $3T-6S$ and $2S$.

### Justification

The new product is $(2S)(3T-6S)=6ST-12S^2=-6F_D$. Commutativity removes the ordering, and the representative scalars contribute $3(-2)=-6$.

### Conclusion

Both choices give the coefficient point $[0:-1:2]=[0:6:-12]$ in $\mathbb P^2$.

content.markdown:
## Exclude the zero coefficient vector

A degree-$n$ divisor produces a product of $n$ nonzero linear forms, so $F_D$ is nonzero. Its coefficient vector can never be $(0,\ldots,0)$.

Conversely, the zero binary form has no finite unordered divisor of degree $n$: it vanishes at every projective point. This is why the target is projective space, whose zero vector is excluded.

data.markdown:

The excluded zero form is the boundary that makes factorization correspond to a fixed finite degree.

content.markdown:
## Prove the general construction is well defined

The preceding calculations reveal the general proof. Permuting the $p_i$ permutes commuting factors. Replacing $p_i$ by a representative scaled by $\lambda_i\ne0$ multiplies the product by $\prod_i\lambda_i\ne0$.

Therefore the output is an intrinsic point of projective coefficient space, even though no individual factor was canonically normalized.

content.markdown:
# Two unordered points need exactly three homogeneous coefficients

A binary quadratic has three coefficients, hence a point of $\mathbb P^2$ after common scaling. Its two projective roots, counted with multiplicity, recover an unordered pair.

The formulas below show both directions; the symbol $\cong$ is not justified by a dimension count alone.

## Expand the coefficient map before invoking factorization

For $p_i=[u_i:v_i]$, multiply

$$(v_1T-u_1S)(v_2T-u_2S)=AT^2+BTS+CS^2,$$

where $A=v_1v_2$, $B=-(u_1v_2+u_2v_1)$, and $C=u_1u_2$. These expressions are symmetric in the two points and bihomogeneous of degree one in each representative.

## Compute all three quadratic coordinates

The coefficient formulas make the map explicit:

$$\{[u_1:v_1],[u_2:v_2]\}\longmapsto[v_1v_2:-(u_1v_2+u_2v_1):u_1u_2].$$

Swapping the points changes nothing. Rescaling either representative rescales all three coordinates by the same factor.

## Recover an unordered pair by factorization

A point $[A:B:C]\in\mathbb P^2$ represents the nonzero quadratic $AT^2+BTS+CS^2$. Over $\mathbb C$, it factors into two linear forms, counted with multiplicity.

Each factor has one projective root. Changing the factorization by nonzero scalars or swapping factors does not change the resulting unordered divisor.

### Strategy

### Hypotheses

The two factors are $-S$ and $T-2S$. Their product is $-TS+2S^2$.

### Intermediate claims

The coefficient point is $[0:-1:2]=[0:1:-2]$. Its zero leading coefficient records a factor $S$.

### Justification

Factoring $S(T-2S)$ recovers $[1:0]$ from $S$ and $[2:1]$ from $T-2S$.

### Conclusion

The coefficient map and its inverse retain the point at infinity; the affine polynomial alone would hide it.

## Explain why the two constructions are inverse

Starting from a divisor, multiplying its factors and then factoring the product recovers the same factors up to scalars and permutation. Starting from a nonzero quadratic, factoring and multiplying the recovered factors returns the original form up to scalar.

The coefficient formulas are polynomial and symmetric in the two point coordinates. They therefore define the concrete morphism on the symmetric square, while factorization proves that every coefficient point has exactly one unordered preimage with multiplicity.

# Three roots become four homogeneous coordinates

A nonzero binary cubic has four coefficients, so its scalar class lies in $\mathbb P^3$. Over $\mathbb C$, its three projective roots, counted with multiplicity, recover an unordered triple.

The cubic case is the coefficient model used by the marked-root incidence map in Week 43.

## Keep the same factor convention

For $p_i=[u_i:v_i]$, the cubic associated with $p_1+p_2+p_3$ is

$$F_D=\prod_{i=1}^3(v_iT-u_iS)=AT^3+BT^2S+CTS^2+DS^3.$$

Its coefficient point is $[A:B:C:D]\in\mathbb P^3$. The construction is symmetric in the three points and multihomogeneous of degree one in each representative.

## Expand a cubic from three points

One can multiply the factors in any order. The four coefficient slots correspond to $T^3,T^2S,TS^2,S^3$.

A zero coefficient remains part of the projective point; omitting it changes the coordinate position.

content.markdown:
# Colliding points do not disappear

The symmetric product includes repeated points. Under the coefficient map, a repeated point produces a repeated linear factor.

This is the geometric meaning of root multiplicity: the divisor coefficient and the factor exponent are the same integer.

## Read multiplicity from a factor exponent

If $D=m_1p_1+\cdots+m_rp_r$, then

$$F_D=c\prod_{j=1}^r\ell_{p_j}^{m_j},\qquad \sum_jm_j=n.$$

The integer $m_j$ is simultaneously the coefficient of $p_j$ in the divisor and the multiplicity of the corresponding projective root.

## Translate a repeated point into a squared factor

For a cubic divisor $2p+q$, the coefficient form is $\ell_p^2\ell_q$. Reordering the three entries cannot separate the two copies of $p$ because the symmetric product records multiplicity, not labels.

The total exponent remains three.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$\Phi_2:\operatorname{Sym}^2(\mathbb P^1)\to\mathbb P^2$ is the quadratic coefficient map from Day 2.

Prove that the already-established quadratic bijection has regular local inverses and is therefore an algebraic isomorphism.

### Strategy

Work first on the open where both roots avoid infinity, use elementary symmetric coordinates on the unordered pair, then cover the remaining divisors by projective coordinate changes.

### Hypotheses

Write the finite roots as $[t_1:1]$ and $[t_2:1]$. Their product is $(T-t_1S)(T-t_2S)=T^2-e_1T S+e_2S^2$, where $e_1=t_1+t_2$ and $e_2=t_1t_2$.

### Intermediate claims

The monic coefficient chart is $[1:-e_1:e_2]$. The invariant-ring identity $\mathbb C[t_1,t_2]^{S_2}=\mathbb C[e_1,e_2]$ identifies the unordered-pair chart with $\mathbb A^2$; changing $e_1$ to $-e_1$ is a polynomial coordinate automorphism.

### Justification

Every degree-two divisor omits some projective point. A projective change of coordinates moves an omitted point to $[1:0]$, placing the divisor in a translated finite-root chart. These charts cover the source and target. Their local inverses agree on overlaps because each recovers the same intrinsic unordered root divisor.

### Conclusion

Thus $\Phi_2$ and its root-divisor inverse are regular locally on a covering and glue to inverse morphisms: $\operatorname{Sym}^2(\mathbb P^1)\cong\mathbb P^2$ as varieties.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: For general $n$, define $\Phi_n(p_1+\cdots+p_n)=[\prod_i(v_iT-u_iS)]$ in $\mathbb P(\operatorname{Sym}^n((\mathbb C^2)^*))\cong\mathbb P^n$. Permutations do not change the product, and rescaling representatives multiplies it by one nonzero scalar. The product is nonzero. Conversely, every nonzero complex binary form factors into linear forms uniquely up to scalars and permutation; their projective roots with exponents give a degree-$n$ divisor. These constructions are set-theoretic inverses. On the finite-root chart, $\prod_i(T-t_iS)=T^n-e_1T^{n-1}S+e_2T^{n-2}S^2-\cdots+(-1)^ne_nS^n$, so normalized coefficients are $(1,-e_1,e_2,\ldots,(-1)^ne_n)$. Every finite divisor omits a projective point; projective-coordinate translates of this chart therefore cover, and the intrinsic local inverses glue. For the given divisor, use factors $S$ for $[1:0]$ and $(T+S)^2$ for $2[-1:1]$. Thus $F_D=S(T+S)^2=T^2S+2TS^2+S^3$, so $\Phi_3(D)=[0:1:2:1]$. Factoring that form recovers $S(T+S)^2$, hence one point at infinity and the double point $[-1:1]$, exactly $D$. The zero form and non-algebraically-closed ground fields lie outside the stated inverse argument.

content.markdown:
# A cubic can remember one chosen root

Week 42 represented a binary cubic by its unordered divisor of three projective roots. Week 43 adds one piece of information: choose one occurrence of a root, keep the other two as an unordered degree-two divisor, and then forget that choice.

The resulting map is the geometric source of the later three-sheeted picture. Before counting sheets, we must define exactly what a point in the source records.

## Divisor notation keeps multiplicity visible

Write an effective cubic divisor as $D=p+q+r$, allowing equal points. The marked incidence source is

$$I=\mathbb P^1\times\operatorname{Sym}^2(\mathbb P^1).$$

A source point $(p,E)$ contains a distinguished point $p$ and an unordered quadratic divisor $E$. Its image is the sum $p+E$, not an ordered triple.

## Define addition of effective divisors

For $(p,q+r)\in I$, define

$$\pi(p,q+r)=p+q+r\in\operatorname{Sym}^3(\mathbb P^1).$$

The braces sometimes used around $\{q,r\}$ mean that $q+r=r+q$. They do not remove multiplicity: $q+q=2q$ is a valid quadratic divisor.

## Complete worked model

$(p,E)=([1:1],[0:1]+[1:0])$.

Compute the linear factor of the marked point, the quadratic factor of the complement, and their cubic product.

### Strategy

Use $\ell_{[u:v]}=vT-uS$ for each point and keep the marked factor separate until the last multiplication.

### Hypotheses

The marked point $[1:1]$ gives $L=T-S$. The complement points $[0:1]$ and $[1:0]$ give $T$ and $-S$, so one representative of its quadratic is $Q=-TS$.

### Intermediate claims

Multiplication gives $LQ=(T-S)(-TS)=-T^2S+TS^2$.

### Justification

Its projective roots are precisely $[1:1]$, $[0:1]$, and $[1:0]$. The first factor records which of these roots is marked; the product forgets that separation.

### Conclusion

In coefficient coordinates, the incidence map is projective multiplication $([L],[Q])\mapsto[LQ]$.

Choose coefficient representatives $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$. Then

content.markdown:
# A fiber records every permissible mark

Fix a cubic divisor $D$. A point in $\pi^{-1}(D)$ is a decomposition $D=p+E$ with $p$ a point and $E$ an effective divisor of degree two.

The decisive observation is simple: $p$ may be any distinct support point of $D$, and then $E=D-p$ is forced.

## Cardinality is not scheme-theoretic length

This lesson counts ordinary points in a set-theoretic fiber. Over a collision, two possible marks remain for type $2+1$, and one remains for type $3$.

Week 44 will study ramification and multiplicity. Do not replace the present $3,2,1$ count by a constant degree-three scheme-theoretic length.

## Identify a fiber with the support

For $D=\sum_xm_xx$, define $\operatorname{Supp}(D)=\{x:m_x>0\}$.

The map

$$\pi^{-1}(D)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Supp}(D),\qquad(p,E)\longmapsto p,$$

is bijective: the inverse sends $p$ to $(p,D-p)$. Effectivity of $D-p$ holds exactly because $p$ lies in the support.

## Derive the three fiber types

If $D=p+q+r$ with three distinct points, its support has size three. If $D=2p+q$ with $p\ne q$, its support has size two. If $D=3p$, its support has size one.

Therefore the ordinary set-theoretic fiber cardinalities are

$$1+1+1\mapsto3,\qquad2+1\mapsto2,\qquad3\mapsto1.$$

## Complete worked model

$D=2[1:1]+[-1:1]$.

Prove directly that the ordinary fiber has exactly two points.

### Strategy

Show first that a marked point must belong to the support, then construct the unique complement for each possible mark.

### Hypotheses

If $(x,E)$ maps to $D$, then $D=x+E$ with $E$ effective, so the coefficient of $x$ in $D$ is positive. Thus $x$ is either $[1:1]$ or $[-1:1]$.

### Intermediate claims

For $x=[1:1]$, subtraction gives $E=[1:1]+[-1:1]$. For $x=[-1:1]$, subtraction gives $E=2[1:1]$.

### Justification

Each complement is effective of degree two and is forced by the equality $E=D-x$. No third support point exists, and marking the repeated point twice does not produce a new point of the symmetric product.

### Conclusion

The fiber contains exactly $([1:1],[1:1]+[-1:1])$ and $([-1:1],2[1:1])$.

content.markdown:
# Marking a root separates one factor

A cubic divisor and a cubic binary form carry the same roots with multiplicity. Choosing one support point $p$ therefore selects the projective linear factor $[\ell_p]$.

After that choice, the remaining degree-two divisor determines a complementary projective quadratic. This equivalence is the bridge from incidence geometry to the later normalized pairs $(L,Q)$.

## Divisibility is projective

If $F$ is a nonzero binary cubic and $p=[u:v]$, then $p$ is a root exactly when $\ell_p=vT-uS$ divides $F$ over $\mathbb C$.

The factor is defined only up to nonzero scalar. Consequently the quotient quadratic is also projective data until representatives are normalized.

## Extract the factor of a marked root

Suppose $D=p+E$ and $F_D$ represents its cubic form. Then

$$F_D\sim\ell_pF_E.$$

The symbol $\sim$ means equality up to a nonzero scalar. It is the correct equality for projective coefficient points.

## Prove the complement is unique after the mark

Fix projective classes $[F]$ and $[L]$ with $L\mid F$. If $F=LQ=LQ'$ for nonzero representatives, cancellation in $\mathbb C[T,S]$ gives $Q=Q'$.

If the representatives of $F$ or $L$ change, the quotient changes by a nonzero scalar. Thus the projective class $[Q]$ is uniquely determined.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$D=[2:1]+2[-1:1]$, with $[2:1]$ marked.

Pass from the incidence divisor to a projective pair $([L],[Q])$ and recover the divisor from that pair.

### Strategy

Translate the marked point and the complementary divisor separately, multiply, and then factor the result back.

### Hypotheses

The marked factor is $L=T-2S$. The complement $2[-1:1]$ gives $Q=(T+S)^2=T^2+2TS+S^2$.

### Intermediate claims

Their product is $F=T^3-3TS^2-2S^3$.

### Justification

Factoring $F$ returns $(T-2S)(T+S)^2$. The distinguished linear factor recovers $[2:1]$, while the quadratic exponent two recovers the complementary divisor $2[-1:1]$.

### Conclusion

The pair $([T-2S],[(T+S)^2])$ represents exactly the incidence point $([2:1],2[-1:1])$.

content.markdown:
# One geometric point has many affine representatives

The incidence variety uses projective classes $([L],[Q])$. Multiplying either representative by a nonzero scalar leaves that source point unchanged.

If a particular cubic polynomial $F$ is fixed as an exact representative, the allowed rescaling is more specific: $(L,Q)\mapsto(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$ preserves the equality $LQ=F$.

## Keep two levels of equality separate

Projectively, $[LQ]=[(\lambda L)(\mu Q)]$ for any nonzero $\lambda,\mu$ because the product changes by $\lambda\mu$.

Affinely, the exact equation $LQ=F$ survives only when the two scalars multiply to one. Neither operation changes the zero of $L$, so neither operation changes the marked root.

## Rescale projective factor representatives

A point of $\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^2$ is a pair of classes. Thus $(L,Q)$, $(\lambda L,Q)$, and $(L,\mu Q)$ all represent the same source point.

Their products differ by overall scalars and therefore have the same image in $\mathbb P^3$.

Fix an actual cubic polynomial $F=LQ$. Then

$$(\lambda L)(\lambda^{-1}Q)=F$$
