## Complete worked model

$m:\operatorname{Sym}^r(V^*)\times\operatorname{Sym}^s(V^*)\to\operatorname{Sym}^{r+s}(V^*)$, $m(P,Q)=PQ$.

Prove $m(g\cdot P,g\cdot Q)=g\cdot m(P,Q)$ under the substitution action.

### Strategy

Evaluate both sides at an arbitrary vector $v$.

### Hypotheses

$(g\cdot P)(v)=P(g^{-1}v)$ and likewise for $Q$.

### Intermediate claims

$m(gP,gQ)(v)=P(g^{-1}v)Q(g^{-1}v)$.

### Justification

The product equals $(PQ)(g^{-1}v)=(g\cdot(PQ))(v)$.

### Conclusion

Since the two forms agree on every $v$, polynomial multiplication is equivariant.

## Separate equivariance from invariance

Equivariance is a property of a map between representations. Invariance is a property of a vector, subspace, or scalar-valued function.

The identity map is always equivariant, even when most vectors are not invariant.

## Transfer equivariance to differentiation

If $F$ is differentiable and equivariant, differentiating $F(gv)=gF(v)$ at $v$ shows $dF_{gv}\circ g=g\circ dF_v$.

At a fixed point, the differential is itself an equivariant linear map.

content.markdown:
# Some functions stay fixed; others change by one predictable scalar

An invariant function is constant along every orbit. A semi-invariant is allowed to scale by a character, recording controlled failure of invariance.

## Reactivate characters and $SL_2$

A character is a homomorphism $\chi:G\to\mathbb G_m$. Recall that $SL_2$ consists of matrices with determinant one and acts on binary forms by change of variables.

## Define invariant and semi-invariant functions

A polynomial function $f$ on a representation $V$ is invariant when $f(gv)=f(v)$.

It is semi-invariant of character $\chi$ when $f(gv)=\chi(g)f(v)$. The invariant case is the trivial character.

## Prove a semi-invariant zero set is invariant

If $f(gv)=\chi(g)f(v)$ and $\chi(g)\ne0$, then $f(v)=0$ exactly when $f(gv)=0$.

Thus a semi-invariant equation can define an invariant hypersurface even when the function itself is not invariant.

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$q(T,S)=aT^2+bTS+cS^2$ and $\Delta(q)=b^2-4ac$.

Verify invariance under both elementary-unipotent substitutions and apply their generation of $SL_2(\mathbb F)$.

### Strategy

For a field $\mathbb F$, the upper and lower elementary matrices $U(u)$ and $L(v)$ generate $SL_2(\mathbb F)$. It is therefore enough to check both corresponding substitutions.

### Hypotheses

For $(T,S)\mapsto(T+uS,S)$, the coefficients become $a$, $2au+b$, and $au^2+bu+c$. For $(T,S)\mapsto(T,S+vT)$, they become $a+bv+cv^2$, $b+2cv$, and $c$.

### Intermediate claims

The two transformed discriminants are $(2au+b)^2-4a(au^2+bu+c)$ and $(b+2cv)^2-4c(a+bv+cv^2)$.

### Justification

In each expression, the linear and quadratic parameter terms cancel, leaving $b^2-4ac$. Since $U(u)$ and $L(v)$ generate $SL_2(\mathbb F)$, invariance under both families proves invariance under every group element.

### Conclusion

The binary-quadratic discriminant is $SL_2(\mathbb F)$-invariant, with no unchecked generator left in the proof.

Equivariance explains why constructions respect symmetry. It does not by itself prove dimension, covering, incidence, or properness claims, so each retrieved theorem keeps its own hypotheses.

The product map is equivariant; the resultant-one source is a normalized locus; marked roots label generic sheets; and dimension controls whether an invertible differential is possible.

activities.referenceAnswerMarkdown: A representation is a homomorphism $G\to GL(V)$, and $F$ is equivariant when $F(gv)=gF(v)$. For binary forms, $(gP)(v)=P(g^{-1}v)$, so $(gP)(v)(gQ)(v)=P(g^{-1}v)Q(g^{-1}v)=(g(PQ))(v)$; multiplication is equivariant. These identities transport symmetry and stable loci, but they do not count roots, prove smoothness, or establish properness; those require the separate arguments retrieved above.

content.markdown:
# Binary forms carry a natural $SL_2$ symmetry

A determinant-one matrix changes the basis of a two-dimensional space. Vectors transform by the matrix; polynomial coordinate functions transform by the inverse matrix so that evaluation remains compatible.

## Fix the convention before calculating

Let $g=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\\gamma&\delta\end{pmatrix}\in SL_2$, so $\alpha\delta-\beta\gamma=1$ and $g^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\delta&-\beta\\-\gamma&\alpha\end{pmatrix}$.

## Define $SL_2$ and its standard representation

$SL_2(\mathbb F)$ is the group of $2\times2$ matrices of determinant one.

On column vectors, $g\cdot(x,y)^T=(\alpha x+\beta y,\gamma x+\delta y)^T$. Matrix multiplication proves the representation law.

## Complete worked model

The polynomial action is $(g\cdot P)(v)=P(g^{-1}v)$.

Prove $g\cdot(h\cdot P)=(gh)\cdot P$.

### Strategy

Evaluate both sides at an arbitrary vector $v$ and simplify inverse products.

### Hypotheses

$(h\cdot P)(w)=P(h^{-1}w)$ and $(gh)^{-1}=h^{-1}g^{-1}$.

### Intermediate claims

$(g\cdot(h\cdot P))(v)=(h\cdot P)(g^{-1}v)=P(h^{-1}g^{-1}v)$.

### Justification

The final expression is $P((gh)^{-1}v)=((gh)\cdot P)(v)$.

### Conclusion

Inverse substitution reverses the inverse matrices exactly once and therefore produces the desired left action.

content.markdown:
# Symmetric powers turn a two-variable substitution into coefficient formulas

A binary quadratic is a vector in $\operatorname{Sym}^2(V^*)$. Its coefficient action is obtained by one substitution and careful collection, not by guessing a matrix.

## Reactivate the inverse substitution

Set $U=\delta T-\beta S$ and $V=-\gamma T+\alpha S$. Then $g\cdot q=q(U,V)$.

## Expand a general quadratic in transformed variables

For $q=aT^2+bTS+cS^2$, write $g\cdot q=aU^2+bUV+cV^2$.

Keeping the three products separate prevents sign and factor-of-two errors.

## Derive the coefficient transformation

Collecting the previous expansions gives

$$a'=a\delta^2-b\delta\gamma+c\gamma^2,$$

$$b'=-2a\delta\beta+b(\delta\alpha+\beta\gamma)-2c\alpha\gamma,$$

$$c'=a\beta^2-b\alpha\beta+c\alpha^2.$$

content.markdown:
## Complete worked model

$h(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1})\in SL_2$ and $q=aT^2+bTS+cS^2$.

Compute the transformed coefficients and prove $b'^2-4a'c'=b^2-4ac$.

### Strategy

Use inverse substitution $(T,S)\mapsto(t^{-1}T,tS)$.

### Hypotheses

$a'=t^{-2}a$, $b'=b$, and $c'=t^2c$.

### Intermediate claims

$b'^2-4a'c'=b^2-4(t^{-2}a)(t^2c)$.

### Justification

The two powers cancel because the extreme coefficients scale oppositely.

### Conclusion

The quadratic discriminant is unchanged under every diagonal determinant-one matrix.

# The cubic formulas are long, but their structure is simple

Every coefficient comes from the same substitution $P(U,V)$. Organizing the four basis terms prevents the expansion from becoming a memory exercise.

## Keep the basis and substitution visible

Write $P=AT^3+BT^2S+CTS^2+DS^3$, $U=\delta T-\beta S$, and $V=-\gamma T+\alpha S$.

## Derive the extreme cubic coefficients

The $T^3$ coefficient is $A'=A\delta^3-B\delta^2\gamma+C\delta\gamma^2-D\gamma^3$.

The $S^3$ coefficient is $D'=-A\beta^3+B\alpha\beta^2-C\alpha^2\beta+D\alpha^3$.

## Complete worked model

$P=T^3+2T^2S-TS^2+4S^3$ and $g=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.

Compute all four transformed coefficients by direct expansion.

### Strategy

Substitute $T-S$ for $T$ and expand each basis term.

### Hypotheses

$(T-S)^3=T^3-3T^2S+3TS^2-S^3$ and $(T-S)^2S=T^2S-2TS^2+S^3$.

### Intermediate claims

Adding $(T-S)^3+2(T-S)^2S-(T-S)S^2+4S^3$ gives coefficients term by term.

### Justification

The coefficients are $A'=1$, $B'=-1$, $C'=-2$, and $D'=6$.

### Conclusion

$g\cdot P=T^3-T^2S-2TS^2+6S^3$.

content.markdown:
# Binary forms are symmetric tensors with a computational basis

The monomials $T^{n-k}S^k$ form the natural basis of $\operatorname{Sym}^n(V^*)$. This makes the induced action and its diagonal behavior visible.

## Reactivate symmetric powers

Recall that $\dim\operatorname{Sym}^n(V^*)=n+1$ when $\dim V=2$. The general theory of torus weights begins in Week 53; today we compute only the exponents for one diagonal subgroup.

## Complete worked model

Order monomials by the exponent in $h(t)\cdot m=t^r m$.

Identify the minimum- and maximum-exponent monomials in $\operatorname{Sym}^n(V^*)$.

Use the formula $r=-n+2k$ and its monotonicity in $k$.

$k$ ranges from $0$ to $n$.

The exponent increases by two whenever one $T$ is replaced by one $S$.

At $k=0$ the exponent is $-n$; at $k=n$ it is $n$.

# A one-parameter subgroup turns symmetry into integer bookkeeping

Restricting a representation to $\mathbb G_m$ replaces a matrix action by powers of one scalar. Characters record those powers and make compatible products easy to recognize.

## Activate group homomorphisms and diagonal actions

Write $\mathbb G_m=\mathbb F^\times$ under multiplication. A one-parameter subgroup is an algebraic group homomorphism $\lambda:\mathbb G_m\to G$; a character is an algebraic homomorphism $\chi:G\to\mathbb G_m$.

## Verify a diagonal one-parameter subgroup

For integers $r_1,\ldots,r_n$, the map $t\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(t^{r_1},\ldots,t^{r_n})$ is a one-parameter subgroup of $GL_n$.

The integer exponents may be negative because $t$ is nonzero.

## Complete worked model

$\chi(t)=ct^n$ is a nonzero Laurent monomial on $\mathbb G_m$.

Determine when it is a group character.

### Strategy

Impose $\chi(st)=\chi(s)\chi(t)$ and the identity value.

### Hypotheses

$\chi(1)=c$, while a homomorphism must satisfy $\chi(1)=1$.

### Intermediate claims

Thus $c=1$, and then $(st)^n=s^nt^n$ proves multiplicativity.

### Justification

No additional scalar coefficient is permitted in a character.

### Conclusion

Among nonzero Laurent monomials, the characters are exactly $t^n$ with $n\in\mathbb Z$.

objectives: Define weight spaces for a one-parameter subgroup, decompose explicit representations, and prove that tensor and polynomial products add weights.

content.markdown:
# Weight spaces diagonalize one chosen scaling symmetry

Once a one-parameter subgroup is fixed, vectors with the same exponent form a linear subspace. The representation becomes a direct sum of these subspaces when the action is diagonalizable.

## Fix the sign convention

A vector $v$ has weight $n$ when $\lambda(t)v=t^n v$ for every $t\in\mathbb G_m$. These weights refer to the declared action; dual actions negate them.

## Define and verify a weight space

$V_n=\{v\in V:\lambda(t)v=t^n v\text{ for all }t\}$ is a vector subspace.

Closure follows because the same scalar $t^n$ factors from linear combinations.

## Compute a direct weight-space decomposition

If $\lambda(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t^2,1,t^{-1})$ on basis $e_1,e_2,e_3$, then $V=V_2\oplus V_0\oplus V_{-1}$.

Distinct weights have zero intersection: a nonzero vector cannot scale simultaneously by two different powers for every $t$.

## Complete worked model

$v\in V_r$ and $w\in W_s$.

Prove $v\otimes w$ has weight $r+s$.

### Strategy

Apply the tensor-product action to the pure tensor.

### Hypotheses

$\lambda(t)v=t^rv$ and $\lambda(t)w=t^sw$.

### Intermediate claims

$\lambda(t)(v\otimes w)=(t^rv)\otimes(t^sw)$.

### Justification

Scalars multiply to $t^{r+s}$ in the tensor product.

### Conclusion

$v\otimes w\in(V\otimes W)_{r+s}$.

If $v_r\in V_r$ and $v_s\in V_s$ with $r\ne s$, then a nonzero sum $v_r+v_s$ is generally not an eigenvector for the one-parameter subgroup.

content.markdown:
# A torus action writes geometry as a grading

When coordinate functions have integer weights, multiplication adds those integers. The coordinate ring splits into homogeneous pieces, and invariant equations are precisely weight-zero equations.

## Transfer Day 2 into ring language

Weight spaces were defined for vector representations. A coordinate ring is also a representation, and its multiplication is equivariant, so products of homogeneous functions add weights.

## Define the torus-weight grading

For a $\mathbb G_m$ action on an algebra $A$, set $A_n=\{f:t\cdot f=t^n f\}$.

Then $A_rA_s\subseteq A_{r+s}$. When $A=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z}A_n$, this is a $\mathbb Z$-graded ring. Negative degrees are allowed.

## Complete worked model

$A=\mathbb F[x,y]$ with $\deg x=1$, $\deg y=-1$, and $I=(xy-1)$.

Prove $I$ is homogeneous and the quotient inherits a $\mathbb Z$-grading.

### Strategy

Check the generator has one weight, then define quotient components by images of $A_n$.

### Hypotheses

$xy$ and $1$ both have degree zero.

### Intermediate claims

Therefore $xy-1\in A_0$, and multiplying it by a homogeneous element of degree $n$ stays in degree $n$.

### Justification

The ideal is generated by a homogeneous element, so relations never identify different total degrees.

### Conclusion

$A/I$ inherits the grading $(A/I)_n=(A_n+I)/I$.

# The five weights explain why the equations fit together

The action $(a,b,c,d,e)\mapsto(ta,b,c,t^{-1}d,t^{-2}e)$ is designed so every monomial in the two constraints has total weight zero.

## Write the source before checking invariance

Let $F_1=a^2e-abd+cb^2-1$ and $F_2=ad+bc-1$. The variety is $X=V(F_1,F_2)\subseteq\mathbb A^5$.

## Verify the coordinatewise rule is a group action

Define $t\cdot(a,b,c,d,e)=(ta,b,c,t^{-1}d,t^{-2}e)$.

Applying $s$ after $t$ multiplies each coordinate by the corresponding product power, giving the same result as $st$.

## Read off the coordinate weights

The rule gives $\deg a=1$, $\deg b=0$, $\deg c=0$, $\deg d=-1$, and $\deg e=-2$.

These are torus weights, not ordinary polynomial degrees.

## Complete worked model

$x=(a,b,c,d,e)\in X$ and $t\in\mathbb G_m$.

Prove $t\cdot x\in X$ by direct substitution.

### Strategy

Evaluate $F_1$ and $F_2$ on the transformed coordinates.

### Hypotheses

$F_1(x)=F_2(x)=0$.

### Intermediate claims

$F_1(t\cdot x)=t^2a^2t^{-2}e-(ta)b(t^{-1}d)+cb^2-1=F_1(x)$.

### Justification

Likewise $F_2(t\cdot x)=(ta)(t^{-1}d)+bc-1=F_2(x)$.

### Conclusion

Both equations remain zero, so $X$ is invariant under the action.

$F_1$ and $F_2$ are invariant functions, while $a,d,e$ are only semi-invariant coordinate functions.

Their zero sets or level sets at invariant constants can be stable even though individual coordinates scale.

A homogeneous equation is stable under scaling. Fiber size, finiteness, twisted-cubic geometry, and étaleness still need their distinct arguments.

A proposed formula is compatible with the torus action only if every equality is homogeneous of the same weight.

This catches impossible terms but does not prove the equality itself.

## Complete worked model

$Y=V(xz-y^2)\subseteq\mathbb A^3$ with weights $(1,0,-1)$.

Prove the equation is invariant and identify the fixed locus of the torus action.

### Strategy

Check term weights, then solve for points fixed by every $t$.

### Hypotheses

$xz$ and $y^2$ both have weight zero.

### Intermediate claims

A fixed point must satisfy $tx=x$ and $t^{-1}z=z$ for all $t$, forcing $x=z=0$.

### Justification

The defining equation then imposes $y^2=0$, so $y=0$ over a field.

### Conclusion

The surface is invariant and its torus-fixed locus is the origin.

# The kernel direction is the velocity of a symmetry orbit

Multiplication forgets the relative scale of two factors. The one-parameter orbit $(tL,t^{-1}Q)$ makes that forgotten direction visible before any coordinate calculation.

## Activate differentiation and group actions

For a one-parameter action $t\cdot x$, its infinitesimal generator at $x$ is the derivative at the identity. Use the additive parameter $t=e^s$ when differentiating multiplicative scaling.

## Write the relative-scaling orbit

The action of $\mathbb G_m$ on factor pairs is $t\cdot(L,Q)=(tL,t^{-1}Q)$.

It preserves the product because $(tL)(t^{-1}Q)=LQ$.

content.markdown:
# Symmetry gives one kernel direction; coprimality rules out all others

Differentiating invariance proves inclusion in the kernel. To prove equality, one must use the factorization structure of the polynomial ring.

## Activate the product rule and Euclid's lemma

For $M(L,Q)=LQ$, the differential is $dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$. On the resultant-nonzero locus, $\gcd(L,Q)=1$.

## Derive the multiplication differential

Expand $(L+\varepsilon\dot L)(Q+\varepsilon\dot Q)$ modulo $\varepsilon^2$.

The coefficient of $\varepsilon$ is $\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.

Because $\gcd(L,Q)=1$, Euclid's lemma gives $L\mid\dot L$. Since both are linear, $\dot L=\mu L$.

# Multiplication forgets one scale; the resultant measures exactly that scale

The same relative-scaling orbit that leaves $LQ$ unchanged multiplies the resultant by $t$. Its derivative is therefore nonzero in the forgotten direction.

## Reactivate bidegree and tangent level sets

$\operatorname{Res}(\lambda L,\mu Q)=\lambda^2\mu\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)$ for a linear and a quadratic form. Tangent vectors to $R=1$ satisfy $dR=0$.

## Compute the resultant character

Under $(L,Q)\mapsto(tL,t^{-1}Q)$, bidegree $(2,1)$ gives

$$R(tL,t^{-1}Q)=t^2t^{-1}R(L,Q)=tR(L,Q).$$

Thus the product has weight zero and the resultant has weight one.

## Complete worked model

$M(x,y)=xy$ on $(\mathbb F^\times)^2$ and $R(x,y)=x$.

Show the orbit $(tx,t^{-1}y)$ is a product fiber and the slice $R=1$ meets each orbit once.

### Strategy

Compute product and solve the scalar normalization.

### Hypotheses

$M(tx,t^{-1}y)=xy$ and $R(tx,t^{-1}y)=tx$.

# The whole differential proof is one symmetry-and-slice argument

Coprimality says the only infinitesimal ambiguity is relative scaling. Resultant weight one says the normalization slice removes it. Equal dimensions turn injectivity into an isomorphism.

## Assemble the three prior conclusions

Use $\ker dM=\mathbb F(L,-Q)$ on the coprime locus, $dR(L,-Q)=1$ on $R=1$, and equality of the source and target tangent dimensions.

## State the coordinate-free étaleness theorem

At a normalized coprime pair, the differential of multiplication has only the orbit direction in its ambient kernel.

The resultant-one tangent condition excludes that direction, so the restricted differential is injective. Equal finite dimensions make it an isomorphism.

content.markdown:
# The boundary divisor has a simple exact core

Before expanding near $a=0$, first solve the equations exactly on it. The two constraints force the apparently free coordinates $b,c$ to equal one.

## Write the two equations and the boundary

Let $X=V(F_1,F_2)\subseteq\mathbb A^5$ with $F_1=a^2e-abd+cb^2-1$ and $F_2=ad+bc-1$. Define $E=X\cap V(a)$.

## Restrict both constraints to $a=0$

On $E$, the equations become $cb^2=1$ and $bc=1$.

Both equations are needed: the second says $b,c$ are nonzero; their combination fixes the scale.

# The boundary is not merely plane-shaped; it is an affine plane

The quotient ring records the full algebraic structure. Eliminating $a,b-1,c-1$ leaves the polynomial ring in $d,e$ with no hidden relation.

## Activate coordinate rings

$\mathbb F[E]=\mathbb F[a,b,c,d,e]/(F_1,F_2,a)$. Day 1 proved set-theoretically that the boundary forces $b=c=1$.

## Simplify the boundary ideal

After imposing $a=0$, the ideal becomes $(a,cb^2-1,bc-1)$.

Inside the quotient, $cb^2=b(bc)=b$, so the relations force $b-1$ and then $c-1$.

## Complete worked model

$Y=V(x,y-1,z-2)\subseteq\mathbb A^5_{x,y,z,u,v}$.

Prove $Y\simeq\mathbb A^2_{u,v}$ by coordinate rings and point maps.

### Strategy

Quotient by the three linear coordinate relations.

### Hypotheses

$\mathbb F[Y]=\mathbb F[x,y,z,u,v]/(x,y-1,z-2)$.

### Intermediate claims

The quotient sends $x,y,z$ to $0,1,2$ and leaves $u,v$ freely polynomial.

### Justification

Thus $\mathbb F[Y]\cong\mathbb F[u,v]$; geometrically $(u,v)\mapsto(0,1,2,u,v)$ is inverse to projection.

### Conclusion

$Y$ is an affine plane with coordinates $u,v$.

content.markdown:
# The coefficients $2$ and $-3$ are forced by a two-equation linear system

Near $E$, the variables $b,c$ begin at one. Their first normal changes are not guessed: they are determined by the first-order parts of both constraints.

## Fix one boundary point and one normal parameter

At a boundary point $(0,1,1,d_0,e_0)$, the Jacobian of $(F_1,F_2)$ with respect to $(b,c)$ is $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ and has determinant $1$. The implicit-function theorem therefore solves $b,c$ uniquely as local functions of $(a,d,e)$; equivalently, the unit determinant gives unique formal power-series expansions along $E$.

It is now justified to write $b=1+a\beta+O(a^2)$, $c=1+a\gamma+O(a^2)$, $d=d_0+O(a)$, and $e=e_0+O(a)$. The coordinate $a$ is a valid normal parameter, while only the constant boundary values of $d,e$ contribute to first order.

## Linearize the equation $ad+bc=1$

$ad=a d_0+O(a^2)$ and $bc=(1+a\beta)(1+a\gamma)+O(a^2)=1+a(\beta+\gamma)+O(a^2)$.

The coefficient of $a$ must vanish, giving $d_0+\beta+\gamma=0$.

## Complete worked model

$u+v=-r$ and $3u+v=3r$.

Substitution gives $2r-3r=-r$ and $6r-3r=3r$.

content.markdown:
# The fraction $-3/2$ is a ratio of two forced first-order coefficients

Day 3 found $b-1=2ad_0+O(a^2)$ and $c-1=-3ad_0+O(a^2)$. Comparing them gives the structural ratio; nothing is chosen to manufacture it.

## Keep proved facts and previews separate

Use only the first-order expansions already established. Preview only: Week 56 will package $2d_0$ into a regular function and study second normal order; no such higher-order claim is assessed today.

## Extract the first-order ratio

The normal coefficients are $\partial_a b|_E=2d$ and $\partial_a c|_E=-3d$ when $d,e$ are held at their boundary values.

Where $d\ne0$, their ratio is $(\partial_a c)/(\partial_a b)=-3/2$. The polynomial identity $2\partial_a c+3\partial_a b=0$ also holds where $d=0$ and avoids division.

# A normal coefficient becomes useful only after its extension is proved

Week 55 found $b=1+2ad+O(a^2)$. Today the defining equations turn that first-order pattern into the exact global identity $b=1+ay$.

## Keep both equations of $X$ visible

Work in the coordinate ring of $X=V(F_1,F_2)$, where $F_1=a^2e-abd+cb^2-1$ and $F_2=ad+bc-1$. The boundary is $E=V(a)$ with $b=c=1$.

## Eliminate $cb^2$ without dividing by $a$

From $F_2=0$, $bc=1-ad$, so $cb^2=b(bc)=b-abd$.

Substitution into $F_1=0$ gives $a^2e-2abd+b-1=0$, hence $b-1=a(2bd-ae)$.

# Correct the first-order part before reading the second

The raw function $c-1$ starts with $-3ad$. Since $y|_E=2d$, adding $\frac32ay$ cancels exactly that first normal term.

## Work modulo a declared power

The notation $f\equiv g\pmod{a^2}$ means $f-g$ has normal order at least two in the formal or local expansion along $E$. It does not by itself provide a global polynomial formula for $(f-g)/a^2$.

## Reduce the first normal coordinate modulo $a$

$y=2bd-ae$ and $b\equiv1\pmod a$ give $y\equiv2d\pmod a$.

# A jet records successive transverse coefficients

The first jet records the coefficient of $a$ after restricting to the boundary. A corrected second jet first removes the already-known first-order contribution and then reads the coefficient of $a^2$.

For $f=b-1$, the exact identity $b-1=ay$ gives first jet $y|_E=2d$.

# Weights predict which corrections can coexist

The residual action assigns weights $1,0,0,-1,-2$ to $a,b,c,d,e$. A useful normal coordinate must make every defining identity homogeneous.

## Restore the weight ledger

Products add weights and sums are homogeneous only when every nonzero summand has the same weight. Constants have weight zero.

## Compute the weight of $y$

$bd$ has weight $0+(-1)=-1$ and $ae$ has weight $1+(-2)=-1$.

Therefore $y=2bd-ae$ is homogeneous of weight $-1$, and $ay$ has weight zero like $b-1$.

# The construction uses four different kinds of evidence

An exact identity defines $y$ globally. A controlled expansion motivates $z$. Weights predict its character. A later coordinate-ring identity must still prove its global polynomial representative.

## Retrieve the dependency chain

Week 55 supplies the boundary and first-order system; Week 53 supplies weights; Week 48 separates local sheets from global claims; Week 40 supplies exact map-and-differential reasoning.

## Build the normal-jet evidence map

Exact algebra: $b-1=ay$. Formal order: $c-1+\frac32ay=O(a^2)$. Homogeneity: $\deg y=-1$, $\deg z=-2$. Deferred theorem: a global polynomial representative for $z$.

# Ideal membership is the intrinsic global proof

Direct substitution checks the formula in proposed coordinates. An ideal identity proves it on $X$ using only the equations that define $X$.

## Fix the difference polynomial

Let $y=2bd-ae$, $P=2d^2+ce+6bd^2+3bce-\frac92e$$, and $D=c-1+\frac32ay-a^2P$. The goal is $D\in(F_1,F_2)$.

## Expand the difference before reducing

$D=c-1+3abd+3a^2e-2a^2d^2-a^2ce-6a^2bd^2-3a^2bce$.

Keeping this exact polynomial visible prevents an accidental sign change in the coefficient $9/2$.

# Normal form provides a reproducible algebraic checksum

The ideal certificate is readable; a reduced remainder is systematic. Agreement between them is strong evidence, but their explanatory roles differ.

## Declare the ring and order

Work over a characteristic-zero field with lexicographic variable order $c>b>a>d>e$. Compute a Gröbner basis of $(F_1,F_2)$ before reducing $D$.

## Record the computed basis

One lexicographic Gröbner basis is

$$G_1=ad+bc-1,$$

$$G_2=a^2ce+2a^2d^2-3ad-c+1,$$

$$G_3=-a^2e+2abd-b+1.$$

$I=(u-xv-1,v-x-2)$ and $H=u-1-2x-x^2$.

On $D(a)$, division gives the original quotient, so the new definition is an extension rather than a replacement with unrelated values.

## Complete worked model

$R=\mathbb F[x,u,v]/(u-xv-1,v-x-2)$ and $H=u-1-2x-x^2$.

Verify $H=0$ by substitution, ideal certificate, and normal form.

Use $v=x+2$ and $u=1+xv$.

Substitution gives $u=1+x^2+2x$, hence $H=0$.

### Intermediate claims

$H=(u-xv-1)+x(v-x-2)$ is the ideal certificate.

### Justification

Reduction by the two generators has zero remainder.

### Conclusion

The three methods agree while retaining different proof roles.

# An inverse formula is irrelevant until the forward map lands in its claimed target

Weeks 56 and 57 found global coordinates on $X$. This capstone begins in the opposite direction: use $(a,y,z)$ to reconstruct all five ambient coordinates and verify that the reconstruction actually lies on $X$.

## Keep the source and target visible

Assume that $2$ is invertible and let $X=V(F_1,F_2)\subseteq\mathbb A^5_{a,b,c,d,e}$, where $F_1=a^2e-abd+cb^2-1$ and $F_2=ad+bc-1$. Define $\Phi(a,y,z)=(a,b,c,d,e)$ by the four formulas displayed in the syllabus.

## Write the complete forward packet

$$b=1+ay,\qquad c=1-\frac32ay+a^2z,$$

$$d=\frac12y-az+\frac32ay^2-a^2yz,$$

$$e=-2z+4y^2-4ayz+3ay^3-2a^2y^2z.$$

Every coordinate is polynomial in $(a,y,z)$, so these formulas define a morphism to $\mathbb A^5$. The remaining question is whether its image lies in $X$.

## Complete worked model

$S=V(v-u^2-w)\subseteq\mathbb A^3_{u,v,w}$ and $\alpha(s,t)=(s,s^2+t,t)$.

Prove that $\alpha$ is a polynomial map into $S$.

### Strategy

First establish polynomiality into ambient affine space, then substitute into the defining equation.

### Hypotheses

The source is $\mathbb A^2_{s,t}$ and the ambient codomain is $\mathbb A^3_{u,v,w}$.

### Intermediate claims

$(v-u^2-w)\circ\alpha=(s^2+t)-s^2-t=0$ identically.

### Justification

The vanishing identity makes the ambient map factor uniquely through the closed subvariety $S$.

### Conclusion

Thus $\alpha:\mathbb A^2\to S$ is a globally defined polynomial morphism.

# The easy composition is still a three-coordinate theorem

The coordinate $a$ is visibly unchanged, but the other two coordinates contain the real content. Both must be recovered as exact polynomials, not only to low order along the boundary.

The resulting polynomial simplifies to $y$; the cancellation is exact and does not use $a\ne0$.

# The difficult composition must be proved inside the coordinate ring of X

Substituting the forward formulas into the inverse proves only one direction. To recover an arbitrary point of $X$, start from its two defining equations and derive the forward expressions without assuming that the point already came from $\Phi$.

## Work modulo the defining ideal

Let $I=(F_1=a^2e-abd+cb^2-1,F_2=ad+bc-1)$ and work in $A=\mathbb F[a,b,c,d,e]/I$. Retain the global definitions $Y=2bd-ae$ and $Z=2d^2+ce+6bd^2+3bce-\frac92e$.

## Recover b without cancelling a

The second equation gives $cb^2=b(1-ad)=b-abd$.

Substitution in the first equation gives $a^2e-2abd+b-1=0$, hence

$$b-1=a(2bd-ae)=aY.$$

content.markdown:
# Exact reduction replaces an unsafe cancellation

The relation $a(d-D)=0$ follows quickly from $ad+bc=1$, but cancelling $a$ would fail exactly where the global theorem matters. A zero normal form proves the identity without deleting the boundary.

## Fix the recovered coordinate polynomials

Use $Y=2bd-ae$, $Z=2d^2+ce+6bd^2+3bce-\frac92e$, $D=\frac12Y-aZ+\frac32aY^2-a^2YZ$, and $E=-2Z+4Y^2-4aYZ+3aY^3-2a^2Y^2Z$. Work in the ideal $I=(F_1,F_2)$ over a field in which $2$ is invertible.

## Build a Gröbner basis with visible provenance

For graded lexicographic order $e>d>c>b>a$, use

$$G_3=ad+bc-1,$$

$$G_2=a^2e+2b^2c-b-1,$$

$$G_1=abce-ae-2b^2cd+bd+d,$$

$$G_0=b^2c^2e+2b^2cd^2-2bce-bd^2-d^2+e.$$

# The capstone is a theorem, not a collection of formulas

A polished proof must say why both maps exist on their full domains, why both compositions are identities, and what the coordinates reveal about the geometry of $X$.

## Organize the proof into four obligations

The obligations are: $\Phi$ is polynomial and lands in $X$; $\Psi$ is polynomial on $X$; $\Psi\Phi$ is the identity on $\mathbb A^3$; and $\Phi\Psi$ is the identity on $X$.

## State the theorem with its coefficient-field hypothesis

Over a field in which $2$ is invertible, the displayed maps

$$\Phi:\mathbb A^3_{a,y,z}\longrightarrow X,\qquad \Psi:X\longrightarrow\mathbb A^3_{a,y,z}$$

are inverse polynomial morphisms. Consequently $X\simeq\mathbb A^3$.

## Complete worked model

$S=V(v-u^2-w)\subseteq\mathbb A^3$ with $\alpha(s,t)=(s,s^2+t,t)$ and $\beta(u,v,w)=(u,w)$.

Prove $S\simeq\mathbb A^2$.

### Strategy

Verify the target equation, polynomiality, and both compositions.

### Hypotheses

$(v-u^2-w)\alpha=0$, and both maps use polynomial coordinates.

### Intermediate claims

$\beta\alpha(s,t)=(s,t)$. For $(u,v,w)\in S$, the relation gives $v=u^2+w$, so $\alpha\beta(u,v,w)=(u,u^2+w,w)=(u,v,w)$.

### Justification

The first identity holds on affine space; the second uses the defining equation of $S$.

### Conclusion

Thus $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are inverse polynomial morphisms.

# A derivation becomes auditable when every sentence declares its burden of proof

The same paragraph may define an object, calculate a formula, invoke a theorem, and suggest a geometric picture. Reading all four as if they were the same kind of claim is how plausible prose outruns its evidence.

## Use one four-column record

For each claim, record: **Claim | Definition used | Proof supplied | Your independent verification**. Add one of five labels: definition, exact calculation, standard theorem, geometric interpretation, or speculation/possible extension.

## Give each category a precise job

A definition fixes meaning. An exact calculation follows by symbolic manipulation. A standard theorem is reusable only after its hypotheses are matched. # A theorem name is the beginning of verification, not its end

The derivation's crucial local step is valid only after the source, target, locus, dimension, and differential hypotheses have all been checked.

## Separate the supplied proof from your verification

Coprimality implies that $\dot LQ+L\dot Q=0$ forces $(\dot L,\dot Q)=\lambda(L,-Q)$. Differentiating the resultant along this line gives a nonzero multiple of $\lambda\rho$.

content.markdown:
# Geometry explains the construction only when the correspondence is proved

The marked-root picture is valuable because it predicts three sheets. Its explanatory power does not remove the need to prove normalization, distinctness, and completeness of the fiber.

## Use the square-free locus

For a binary cubic with three simple roots, each marked root gives a linear factor $L$ and residual quadratic $Q$. Nonzero resultant permits a unique relative normalization in the chosen convention.

content.markdown:
# Reconstruct the map before invoking its geometry

The research derivation begins with a natural operation: multiply a binary linear form by a binary quadratic form. Every later tangent and fiber argument depends on getting this coordinate map exactly right.

## Fix bases and coefficient order

Let $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$. Write cubic forms in the ordered basis $(T^3,T^2S,TS^2,S^3)$.

## Expand without skipping cross terms

$$LQ=acT^3+(ad+bc)T^2S+(ae+bd)TS^2+beS^3.$$

The four coefficient functions are therefore $c_3=ac$, $c_2=ad+bc$, $c_1=ae+bd$, and $c_0=be$.

# The fifth coordinate must detect what multiplication forgets

Multiplication cannot distinguish $(L,Q)$ from $(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)$. The resultant changes along this relative-scaling orbit and therefore supplies the missing infinitesimal direction.

## Fix the resultant convention

For a linear form and quadratic form, use $\rho=\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=Q(-b,a)$. This convention gives a polynomial homogeneous of degree two in $(a,b)$ and degree one in $(c,d,e)$.

## Evaluate Q at the root of L

The vector $(-b,a)$ represents the projective root of $L=aT+bS$.

$$Q(-b,a)=cb^2-abd+a^2e,$$

so $\rho=a^2e-abd+cb^2$.

# The kernel is the infinitesimal symmetry that multiplication forgets

The relative rescaling orbit visibly lies in the multiplication fiber. The substantive step is proving that coprimality leaves no other tangent direction.

## Differentiate the bilinear map

For tangent variations $(\dot L,\dot Q)$, bilinearity gives $dM_{(L,Q)}(\dot L,\dot Q)=\dot LQ+L\dot Q$.

## Find the visible kernel line

The relative-scaling path $(e^tL,e^{-t}Q)$ has derivative $(L,-Q)$ at $t=0$.

$$dM(L,-Q)=LQ-LQ=0.$$

## Use coprimality to prove uniqueness

Suppose $\dot LQ+L\dot Q=0$. Then $L$ divides $\dot LQ$. On $\rho\ne0$, $\gcd(L,Q)=1$, so $L$ divides $\dot L$.

Because $L$ and $\dot L$ are linear, $\dot L=\lambda L$, and then $\dot Q=-\lambda Q$.

# The conceptual proof explains why the determinant factors

A determinant can certify invertibility, but it does not identify the lost symmetry or why the resultant repairs it. The tangent-kernel proof supplies that mechanism first.

## Combine the two differentials

For $H=(M,\rho)$, a vector lies in $\ker dH$ only if it lies in $\ker dM$ and is also killed by $d\rho$.

## Differentiate the resultant along scaling

Because $\rho(e^tL,e^{-t}Q)=e^t\rho(L,Q)$, differentiation at zero gives

$$d\rho_{(L,Q)}(L,-Q)=\rho(L,Q).$$

# The threefold is cut out by two output coordinates

Week 60 built a five-dimensional map $H=(c_3,c_2,c_1,c_0,\rho)$. Fixing the coefficient $c_2$ and the resultant leaves the three output coordinates that later form the counterexample map.

$c_2=ad+bc$ is the $T^2S$ coefficient of $LQ$, and $\rho=a^2e-abd+cb^2$ is the resultant.

Let $S=\{(c_3,c_2,c_1,c_0,\rho):c_2=1,\rho=1\}\simeq\mathbb A^3_{c_3,c_1,c_0}$.

Then

$$H^{-1}(S)=V(a^2e-abd+cb^2-1,ad+bc-1)=X.$$

# Base change transfers the mechanism established in Week 60

The clean proof does not recompute a mysterious determinant on $X$. It restricts an already étale map along the exact target slice.

## Draw the Cartesian square

$X=\mathbb A^5\times_{\mathbb A^5}S$, where the top map is $H|_X:X\to S$ and the bottom map is $H:\mathbb A^5\to\mathbb A^5$ restricted to $D(\rho)$.

## Apply stability of étale maps under base change

Week 60 proves $H$ étale on $D(\rho)$. Since $S\subseteq D(\rho)$, its base change

$$h=H|_X:X\longrightarrow S$$

is étale.

# The open stratum is solved by legitimate division

Once $a$ is invertible, the two equations determine $d$ and $e$ from $(a,b,c)$. The chart is useful precisely because its denominator is attached to the open set where it is legal.

## Work in the localization at a

On $X_a=D_X(a)$, the element $a$ is a unit. The coordinate ring may therefore use $a^{-1}$ and $a^{-2}$.

## Solve first for d

From $ad+bc=1$ one obtains

$$d=\frac{1-bc}{a}.$$

# A formula is not a coordinate chart until its identities are proved

Week 58 supplied the maps. Week 62 deliberately reconstructs their verification in four different ways, beginning with exact polynomial arithmetic.

## Fix the maps and domains

Let $X=V(F_1=a^2e-abd+cb^2-1,F_2=ad+bc-1)$. Define $\Phi:\mathbb A^3_{a,y,z}\to\mathbb A^5_{a,b,c,d,e}$ by $b=1+ay,\ c=1-\frac32ay+a^2z,\ d=\frac12y-az+\frac32ay^2-a^2yz,\ e=-2z+4y^2-4ayz+3ay^3-2a^2y^2z$ and $\Psi|_X=(a,Y,Z)$ with $Y=2bd-ae$ and $Z=2d^2+ce+6bd^2+3bce-\frac92e$.

## Separate the four global obligations

$\Phi$ must land in $X$; $\Psi$ must be regular on all of $X$; and both compositions must be identities on their stated domains. A single successful composition is not a two-sided inverse proof.

# The boundary is the decisive test

On $D_X(a)$ the equations can be solved by division. The polynomial chart matters because it extends through $a=0$, where its derivative must still have full rank.

## Restrict the chart

At $a=0$, the forward formulas give $(b,c,d,e)=(1,1,y/2,-2z+4y^2)$.

## Compute a boundary coordinate minor

For output coordinates $(a,d,e)$, differentiation at $a=0$ gives

$$\frac{\partial(a,d,e)}{\partial(a,y,z)}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\-z+\frac32y^2&\frac12&0\\-4yz+3y^3&8y&-2\end{pmatrix},$$

with determinant $-1$.

content.markdown:
# The counterexample map is transported geometry

Week 62 did more than simplify the equations of $X$. Its polynomial chart lets us carry the three unfixed cubic coefficients back to ordinary affine three-space, where they become one explicit polynomial self-map.

## Keep the chart and coefficient order attached

Let $\Phi(a,y,z)=(a,b,c,d,e)$, where $b=1+ay$, $c=1-\frac32ay+a^2z$, $d=\frac12y-az+\frac32ay^2-a^2yz$, and $e=-2z+4y^2-4ayz+3ay^3-2a^2y^2z$. On $X$, the coefficient $ad+bc$ and the resultant are fixed at one. The remaining ordered coefficient triple is $(ac,ae+bd,be)$.

## Identify the three free target coordinates

The five-dimensional coefficient-resultant map is

$$H_5(a,b,c,d,e)=(ac,ad+bc,ae+bd,be,a^2e-abd+cb^2).$$

On the normalized slice $X$, its second and fifth coordinates are both one. The information that still varies is therefore $(ac,ae+bd,be)$, in that order.

## Complete worked model

$\Theta(s,t)=(p,q,r)=(s,1+st,t^2-s)$ and $C_0(p,q,r)=(pq,q+r)$.

Compute $K=C_0\circ\Theta$ and verify that the intermediate coordinates have been used in their declared order.

### Strategy

Write the two arrows first, then substitute all three intermediate coordinates at once.

### Hypotheses

$\Theta:\mathbb A^2_{s,t}\to\mathbb A^3_{p,q,r}$ and $C_0:\mathbb A^3_{p,q,r}\to\mathbb A^2$ have matching intermediate space.

$pq=s(1+st)=s+s^2t$, while $q+r=1+st+t^2-s$.

### Justification

Each output is a polynomial in the original source variables.

### Conclusion

$K(s,t)=(s+s^2t,1+st+t^2-s)$.

$\Theta(u,v,w)=(x,p,q)=(u,1+uv,w-uv^2)$ and $C_0(x,p,q)=(xp,xq+p,pq)$.

Compute $K=C_0\circ\Theta$ by keeping each product visible before collecting.

### Strategy

Substitute the three chart coordinates, then collect by powers of $u$.

### Hypotheses

$K_1=xp$, $K_2=xq+p$, and $K_3=pq$.

### Intermediate claims

$K_1=u+u^2v$ and $K_2=uw-u^2v^2+1+uv$.

### Justification

$K_3=(1+uv)(w-uv^2)=w+uvw-uv^2-u^2v^3$.

### Conclusion

The complete composite is polynomial and every coefficient comes from a named product.

content.markdown:
# The direct calculation is an exact check

A Keller map is a polynomial self-map with constant nonzero Jacobian determinant. The all-variable determinant calculation verifies that $G$ has this property, but it does not yet explain why the cancellation had to occur.

## Differentiate in the declared order

Use coordinates $(a,y,z)$ and the exact rows $G_1=a-\frac32a^2y+a^3z$, $G_2=\frac12y-3az+6ay^2-6a^2yz+\frac92a^2y^3-3a^3y^2z$, and $G_3=-2z+4y^2-6ayz+7ay^3-6a^2y^2z+3a^2y^4-2a^3y^3z$. Write $DG=(\partial G_i/\partial x_j)$ with columns ordered as $(a,y,z)$.

## State the Keller condition before checking it

For this course, a Keller map is a polynomial endomorphism $F:\mathbb A^n_{\mathbb C}\to\mathbb A^n_{\mathbb C}$ whose Jacobian determinant is a nonzero constant.

The condition is local and differential. It does not assert that $F$ has a global polynomial inverse.

## Complete worked model

$P(u,v,w)=(u+v^2,\ v+w(u+v^2),\ w)$.

Prove directly that $\det DP=1$ even though the displayed map is not triangular in the source coordinates.

### Strategy

Differentiate the expanded formula, then use the last row to reduce the determinant to a two-by-two minor.

### Hypotheses

$P_2=v+uw+v^2w$.

### Intermediate claims

$$DP=\begin{pmatrix}1&2v&0\\w&1+2vw&u+v^2\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$

### Justification

Expansion along the last row gives $1(1+2vw)-2vw=1$.

### Conclusion

The cancellation is exact for all $(u,v,w)$, so $P$ is a Keller map with determinant one.

content.markdown:
## Organize the large determinant by powers of z

Write the first row as $(A,B,C)$, the second as $(D,E,F)$, and the third as $(H,I,K)$. Set $t=ay$ and use the Laplace terms

$$L_1=A(EK-FI),\qquad L_2=-B(DK-FH),\qquad L_3=C(DI-EH).$$

Exact collection in $z$ gives

$$\begin{array}{c|ccc|c}

&[z^2]L_1&[z^2]L_2&[z^2]L_3&[z^2]\det DG\\\hline

&-18a^4(t+1)^4&0&18a^4(t+1)^4&0

\end{array}$$

and

$$\begin{aligned}

[z]L_1&=3a^2(t+1)^2(15t^3+22t^2+t-3),\\

[z]L_2&=9a^2(t+1)^4,\\

[z]L_3&=-3a^2t(t+1)^2(15t^2+25t+7).

\end{aligned}$$

The three $z$ coefficients sum to zero. For the constant coefficient, the three Laplace terms expand in $t$ as

$$\begin{aligned}

[1]L_1&=-27t^6-81t^5-66t^4+5t^3+18t^2-1,\\

[1]L_2&=-\frac{27}{2}t^5-45t^4-\frac{99}{2}t^3-18t^2,\\

[1]L_3&=27t^6+\frac{189}{2}t^5+111t^4+\frac{89}{2}t^3.

\end{aligned}$$

These sum to $-1$. Hence the complete determinant is $-1$.

content.markdown:
# Geometry explains the cancellation

The direct determinant is a valid check, but its cancellations look accidental. The normalized factorization threefold explains them: $G$ is the coordinate expression of an étale map between two affine three-spaces.

## Recover the normalized target slice

Let $S=V(c_2-1,\rho-1)\subseteq\mathbb A^5_{c_3,c_2,c_1,c_0,\rho}$. Week 61 identifies $X=H_5^{-1}(S)$, and Week 62 supplies the isomorphism $\Phi:\mathbb A^3\to X$.

## Factor G through the target slice

Write $h=H_5|_X:X\to S$. The coordinate projection

$$\pi:S\longrightarrow\mathbb A^3,\qquad(c_3,1,c_1,c_0,1)\longmapsto(c_3,c_1,c_0)$$

is an affine isomorphism. With these names,

$$G=\pi\circ h\circ\Phi.$$

content.markdown:
## Apply the chain rule on tangent spaces

For $u=(a,y,z)$ and $p=\Phi(u)$, the chain rule is

$$DG_u=d\pi_{h(p)}\circ dh_p\circ d\Phi_u.$$

The chart is an isomorphism, so $d\Phi_u$ is invertible. The map $H_5$ is étale on $D(\rho)$; since $X\subseteq\{\rho=1\}$, base change makes $h$ étale and $dh_p$ invertible. Finally, $\pi$ is a linear coordinate isomorphism. Hence $DG_u$ is invertible for every $u$.

Establish that every factor is a polynomial automorphism, so the composite differential is invertible everywhere.

### Hypotheses

The chain rule makes $DK$ invertible at every point. Thus its polynomial determinant has no zero over $\mathbb C$ and is a unit, hence a nonzero constant.

At the origin, $D\Theta$ and $DE$ are identity matrices, while $DP$ swaps two coordinates and has determinant $-1$.

### Conclusion

Therefore $\det DK=-1$ everywhere; the isomorphism argument explains constancy and the base point fixes the sign.

## Turn everywhere nonvanishing into constancy

The chain rule proves $\det DG(u)\ne0$ for every $u\in\mathbb C^3$. Since $\det DG$ is a polynomial and $V(\det DG)=\varnothing$, the Nullstellensatz gives $(\det DG)=(1)$. Therefore $\det DG$ is a unit of $\mathbb C[a,y,z]$, hence a nonzero constant.

At $u_0=(0,0,0)$, the derivative matrix is triangular with diagonal $(1,\frac12,-2)$. Thus the constant is $-1$.

The direct computation protects the exact formula. The compositional proof reveals why a constant appears. Keeping these roles distinct makes the construction easier to audit and prepares the linear-equivalence calculation in Week 64.

## Complete worked model

$F:\mathbb A^n\to\mathbb A^n$ is a polynomial composite $B\circ E\circ A$, where $A,B$ are polynomial isomorphisms and $E$ is étale.

Design a proof that its determinant is a specified nonzero constant while keeping explanation and direct verification distinct.

### Strategy

Use the chain rule for the mechanism and a separate symbolic calculation for the exact formula.

### Hypotheses

The differentials $dA,dE,dB$ are invertible at every source point.

### Intermediate claims

Thus $dF=dB\,dE\,dA$ is invertible everywhere and $\det dF$ is a nowhere-zero polynomial, hence a constant over $\mathbb C$.

### Justification

One base-point evaluation determines the constant; an all-variable derivative expansion independently verifies the identity.

### Conclusion

The chain proof explains why the determinant is constant, while the expansion checks the authored coefficients.

# The displayed map has not appeared from nowhere

Week 63 produced a Keller map in the chart coordinates $(a,y,z)$. The published formula uses $(z_1,z_2,z_3)$ and a different order and scale in the target. Linear equivalence records those two changes exactly.

## Define linear equivalence with typed maps

Two polynomial self-maps $F,G:\mathbb A^3\to\mathbb A^3$ are linearly equivalent when there are invertible linear maps $A$ on the source and $B$ on the target such that $F=B\circ G\circ A$.

This relation changes the labels on both affine spaces. It is not the pointwise equality $F=G$.

## Complete worked model

$Q(u,v)=(u+2v,v)$, $A_0(x,y)=(x-y,y)$, and $B_0(r,s)=(s,r)$.

### Strategy

Apply the maps in source-to-target order.

### Hypotheses

$A_0,Q,$ and $B_0$ have determinants $1,1,$ and $-1$.

$Q(A_0(x,y))=(x+y,y)$ and $P(x,y)=(y,x+y)$.

The derivative matrix of $P$ is $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, whose determinant is $-1=(\det B_0)(\det DQ)(\det A_0)$.

### Conclusion

The displayed formulas and determinant product prove the claimed linear equivalence; neither fact is inferred from resemblance.

content.markdown:
# Start with the coordinates that expose every sign convention

The third output tests the substitution $z=-z_3/2$ once. The second output tests it in three different monomials. Together they reveal whether the source and target scalings have been applied in the correct order.

## Keep the comparison data on the page

Use $G_1=a-\frac32a^2y+a^3z$, $G_2=\frac12y-3az+6ay^2-6a^2yz+\frac92a^2y^3-3a^3y^2z$, and $G_3=-2z+4y^2-6ayz+7ay^3-6a^2y^2z+3a^2y^4-2a^3y^3z$. The displayed original map is $F_{\mathrm{orig}}=(F_1,F_2,F_3)$, where $F_1=z_3+4z_2^2+3z_1z_2z_3+7z_1z_2^3+3z_1^2z_2^2z_3+3z_1^2z_2^4+z_1^3z_2^3z_3$, $F_2=z_2+3z_1z_3+12z_1z_2^2+6z_1^2z_2z_3+9z_1^2z_2^3+3z_1^3z_2^2z_3$, and $F_3=2z_1-3z_1^2z_2-z_1^3z_3$.

Let $A(z_1,z_2,z_3)=(z_1,z_2,-z_3/2)$ and $B(u_1,u_2,u_3)=(u_3,2u_2,2u_1)$. The desired coordinate equations are $F_3=2G_1\circ A$ and $F_2=2G_2\circ A$.

## Verify the shortest coordinate term by term

Substituting $(a,y,z)=(z_1,z_2,-z_3/2)$ gives

$$2G_1\circ A=2z_1-3z_1^2z_2+2z_1^3\left(-\frac12z_3\right)=2z_1-3z_1^2z_2-z_1^3z_3=F_3.$$

## Track the three z-terms in the second coordinate

First double $G_2$:

$$2G_2=y-6az+12ay^2-12a^2yz+9a^2y^3-6a^3y^2z.$$

The substitution $z=-z_3/2$ sends the three $z$-terms to $3z_1z_3$, $6z_1^2z_2z_3$, and $3z_1^3z_2^2z_3$. The terms without $z$ are unchanged.

## Complete worked model

$G_1=a-\frac32a^2y+a^3z$, $A(z_1,z_2,z_3)=(z_1,z_2,-z_3/2)$, and $F_3=2z_1-3z_1^2z_2-z_1^3z_3$.

Prove $F_3=2G_1\circ A$ as a polynomial identity.

### Strategy

Substitute before comparing coefficients.

### Hypotheses

$A$ supplies $a=z_1$, $y=z_2$, and $z=-z_3/2$.

### Intermediate claims

$G_1\circ A=z_1-\frac32z_1^2z_2-\frac12z_1^3z_3$.

### Justification

Doubling gives $2z_1-3z_1^2z_2-z_1^3z_3$, exactly $F_3$.

### Conclusion

Therefore the third coordinate of $B\circ G\circ A$ agrees with the third coordinate of $F_{\mathrm{orig}}$.

content.markdown:
# The long coordinate is the decisive polynomial check

Every term of $G_3$ survives the substitution. A complete ledger is shorter and safer than an unlabelled expansion because it shows exactly where each $z_3$ term acquires its sign and factor.

## Bring forward the established coordinate matches

$F_2=2G_2\circ A$ and $F_3=2G_1\circ A$ are now proved. It remains to compare $G_3\circ A$ with $F_1$.

Use $G_1=a-\frac32a^2y+a^3z$, $G_2=\frac12y-3az+6ay^2-6a^2yz+\frac92a^2y^3-3a^3y^2z$, and $G_3=-2z+4y^2-6ayz+7ay^3-6a^2y^2z+3a^2y^4-2a^3y^3z$. The displayed original map is $F_{\mathrm{orig}}=(F_1,F_2,F_3)$, where $F_1=z_3+4z_2^2+3z_1z_2z_3+7z_1z_2^3+3z_1^2z_2^2z_3+3z_1^2z_2^4+z_1^3z_2^3z_3$, $F_2=z_2+3z_1z_3+12z_1z_2^2+6z_1^2z_2z_3+9z_1^2z_2^3+3z_1^3z_2^2z_3$, and $F_3=2z_1-3z_1^2z_2-z_1^3z_3$. Let $A(z_1,z_2,z_3)=(z_1,z_2,-z_3/2)$ and $B(u_1,u_2,u_3)=(u_3,2u_2,2u_1)$.

## Separate terms that contain z

In $G_3$, the four terms containing $z$ are $-2z$, $-6ayz$, $-6a^2y^2z$, and $-2a^3y^3z$. Under $z=-z_3/2$, their coefficients become $1,3,3,1$.

The remaining terms $4y^2$, $7ay^3$, and $3a^2y^4$ keep their coefficients.

## Complete worked model

$G_3=-2z+4y^2-6ayz+7ay^3-6a^2y^2z+3a^2y^4-2a^3y^3z$, $A(z_1,z_2,z_3)=(z_1,z_2,-z_3/2)$, and $F_1=z_3+4z_2^2+3z_1z_2z_3+7z_1z_2^3+3z_1^2z_2^2z_3+3z_1^2z_2^4+z_1^3z_2^3z_3$.

Prove $F_1=G_3\circ A$ without omitting any monomial.

### Strategy

Partition $G_3$ by whether a term contains $z$.

### Hypotheses

The $z$-free terms become $4z_2^2+7z_1z_2^3+3z_1^2z_2^4$.

### Intermediate claims

The $z$-linear terms become $z_3+3z_1z_2z_3+3z_1^2z_2^2z_3+z_1^3z_2^3z_3$.

### Justification

Their sum is the displayed polynomial $F_1$.

### Conclusion

Thus the first coordinate of $B\circ G\circ A$ equals the first coordinate of $F_{\mathrm{orig}}$.

# The determinant is transported, not recomputed from the long formula

Direct differentiation of the displayed map would verify the answer but hide its origin. The linear-equivalence factorization explains why the determinant stays constant and why its value changes from $-1$ to $-2$.

## Use the proved map identity

$F_{\mathrm{orig}}=B\circ G\circ A$, with $\det A=-1/2$, $\det DG=-1$, and $\det B=-4$.

Days 2 and 3 matched the three displayed coordinates exactly, so the determinant argument begins from a proved polynomial identity rather than from visual similarity between formulas.

## Differentiate the typed composition

Because $A$ and $B$ are linear, their derivatives are their constant matrices. The chain rule gives

$$DF_{\mathrm{orig}}(x)=B\,DG(Ax)\,A.$$

The evaluation point $Ax$ remains visible even though $\det DG$ is constant.

## Complete worked model

$F_{\mathrm{orig}}=B\circ G\circ A$, $\det A=-1/2$, $\det DG=-1$, and $\det B=-4$.

Recover the Jacobian determinant of the original map and state the scope of the conclusion.

### Strategy

Differentiate first and take determinants second.

### Hypotheses

$A,B$ are invertible linear maps and $G$ is the established polynomial Keller map.

### Intermediate claims

$DF_{\mathrm{orig}}(x)=B\,DG(Ax)\,A$.

### Justification

Multiplicativity gives $\det DF_{\mathrm{orig}}(x)=(-4)(-1)(-1/2)=-2$ for every $x$.

### Conclusion

Thus $F_{\mathrm{orig}}$ is also a Keller map. The calculation proves a constant nonzero Jacobian; it does not by itself prove global injectivity or a polynomial inverse.

## State the fiber correspondence without a pointwise claim

For a target value $t$,

$$A:F_{\mathrm{orig}}^{-1}(t)\longrightarrow G^{-1}(B^{-1}t)$$

is a bijection. Source points move under $A$ and target values move under $B^{-1}$. The two maps therefore have corresponding fiber structures, not identical fibers inside one fixed coordinate space.

# A fiber point begins with a marked root

The later collision is not found by solving three unrelated polynomial systems. It comes from remembering which root of one cubic was assigned to the linear factor.

## Fix the root convention

A nonzero linear form $L=aT+bS$ vanishes at $[-b:a]\in\mathbb P^1$. The factors $T$, $S$, and $T-S$ therefore include the affine points and the point at infinity without changing coordinates.

## Read the full projective support

The factorization $C=TS(T-S)=T^2S-TS^2$ gives the three roots

$$[0:1],\qquad[1:0],\qquad[1:1].$$

All three are simple because their linear factors occur once.

content.markdown:
# Resultant one removes the remaining scaling

Day 1 produced three inverse-scaling orbits. The equation $\rho=1$ must now select one point from each orbit without changing the product.

## Fix the coefficient formula

For $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$, set $\rho=a^2e-abd+b^2c$. It vanishes exactly when $L$ and $Q$ share a projective root.

## Derive the normalization rule

The resultant has degree two in $L$ and degree one in $Q$. Therefore

$$\operatorname{Res}(\lambda L,\lambda^{-1}Q)=\lambda\operatorname{Res}(L,Q).$$

If $r=\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)\ne0$, the unique choice $\lambda=r^{-1}$ makes the new resultant equal to one.

content.markdown:
# One exact collision decides injectivity

A constant nonzero Jacobian controls each point locally. Global injectivity fails as soon as two proved-distinct source points have the same proved image.

## Fix the source and map

Let $X$ consist of coefficient tuples $(a,b,c,d,e)$ satisfying $ad+bc=1$ and $\rho=1$. The normalized product map is

$$\mu:X\longrightarrow\mathbb A^3,\qquad(a,b,c,d,e)\longmapsto(ac,ae+bd,be),$$

because the omitted $T^2S$ coefficient is fixed at one.

## Place the three pairs in X

The normalized pairs give $P_0=(-1,0,0,-1,1),\quad P_\infty=(0,1,1,-1,0),\quad P_1=(1,-1,0,1,0)$.

Each point satisfies $ad+bc=1$ and $\rho=1$, so all three belong to $X$.

content.markdown:
# One table answers only the question named by its columns

The normalized source remembers simple marked roots. Root collisions change which marks remain admissible, but the resulting counts do not by themselves decide properness or describe an asymptotic set.

## Work in the normalized target slice

For a cubic $D$ whose $T^2S$ coefficient is one, a point of $\mu^{-1}(D)$ is a factorization $D=LQ$ with $\operatorname{Res}(L,Q)=1$. The root of $L$ must be simple in $D$.

## Identify the admissible marks

For type $1+1+1$, all three roots are simple. For type $2+1$, only the root of multiplicity one is simple. For type $3$, no root is simple.

Unique resultant normalization then converts the simple-mark counts directly into normalized fiber counts $3,1,0$.

## Prove the fiber–simple-root bijection

Given a simple root, divide by its linear factor and normalize the nonzero resultant uniquely. Conversely, resultant one makes $L$ coprime to $Q$, so the root of $L$ occurs only once in $LQ$.

## Assign one proof to each global claim

The generic degree is three because the squarefree target locus has three normalized preimages. An actual fiber cardinality is computed target by target and here follows the $3,1,0$ table.

The normalized map is étale at every point of its source, so its surviving points are unramified. The repeated marked branches of the larger incidence space lie on $\rho=0$ and are absent from this source.

The empty fiber over $E=\frac13(T+S)^3$ proves that this target is omitted. This table does not prove nonproperness; that requires an independent escaping-source, convergent-image argument. It also does not identify the complete omitted or asymptotic set.

## Complete worked model

A cubic $D$ in the fixed coefficient slice with three distinct projective roots.

Prove that $\mu^{-1}(D)$ has exactly three points.

### Strategy

Construct one point from each root, then prove that no other point exists.

### Hypotheses

Every root is simple, so its linear factor is coprime to the complementary quadratic and has a nonzero resultant.

### Intermediate claims

Each factor pair has a unique inverse scaling with resultant one.

### Justification

Conversely, every normalized pair has a linear factor whose root is simple in $D$, and different normalized points cannot carry the same root because normalization is unique.

### Conclusion

Thus the fiber is in bijection with the three roots and has exactly three points.

# The capstone joins a local theorem to a global counterexample

Étaleness explains the nonzero Jacobian. The marked-root fiber explains noninjectivity. They are compatible because local invertibility does not bound the total number of global sheets.

## The normalized product map

For $L=aT+bS$ and $Q=cT^2+dTS+eS^2$, use $H=(ac,ad+bc,ae+bd,be,\rho)$ with $\rho=a^2e-abd+cb^2$. Restrict to $X=\{ad+bc=1,\rho=1\}$ and retain $(ac,ae+bd,be)$.

## Derive the three-variable map

Compose the retained product coordinates with the affine chart. The result is $G=(G_1,G_2,G_3)$, where

$$G_1=a-\frac32a^2y+a^3z,$$

$$G_2=\frac12y-3az+6ay^2-6a^2yz+\frac92a^2y^3-3a^3y^2z,$$

$$G_3=-2z+4y^2-6ayz+7ay^3-6a^2y^2z+3a^2y^4-2a^3y^3z.$$

# Formulas become memorable when the geometry is visible

The geometric document must explain why the construction exists, why three sheets are expected generically, and where local versus global behavior enters.

## The objects

Binary forms of degrees $1,2,3$ are elements of $\operatorname{Sym}^1V^\vee$, $\operatorname{Sym}^2V^\vee$, and $\operatorname{Sym}^3V^\vee$. Multiplication sends $(L,Q)$ to $LQ$.

## Build the marked-root incidence picture

A factorization $C=LQ$ marks the projective root cut out by $L$. For a cubic with three simple roots, each root can be marked and leaves a complementary quadratic.
